500: Rays play important ecological roles in benthic ecosystems as mesopredators and bioturbators, yet the seasonal and reproductive dynamics of many species remain poorly understood, particularly in Southwestern Atlantic. We examined the seasonal habitat use of the endemic stingray Dasyatis hypostigma across three Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) of southeastern Brazil, by integrating two complementary approaches: citizen science and acoustic telemetry, between 2023 and 2025. We implemented a citizen science program with recreational scuba divers, to assess seasonal patterns of ray species abundance and occurrence in the Alcatrazes Archipelago MPA and two neighboring MPAs. Concurrently, we tagged 26 individuals (19 females and 5 males) with sensor acoustic transmitters to monitor their movements throughout the Alcatrazes Archipelago MPA. Using citizen science abundance data, Generalized Additive Models indicated that D. hypostigma abundance peaked in late May and early June, followed by a decline across all three MPAs. Simultaneously with the abundance peaks, citizen science videodocumented aggregations predominantly composed of pregnant females. Time-to-event analysis based on acoustic telemetry data revealed that 50% of tagged individuals departed by mid-June, coinciding with the end of the austral autumn. These results suggest that the MPAs along the coast of São Paulo function as seasonal gestation sites, where gravid females may exploit thermal conditions following seasonal thermocline breakdown to support embryonic development. Our findings highlight the value of integrating citizen science and acoustic telemetry for monitoring elasmobranchs in MPAs and underscore the importance of these protected areas for the reproductive ecology of an endemic stingray of the Southwestern Atlantic. Barry Chernoff
501: Chimaeras (Chondrichthyes: Chimaeriformes) are a diverse group of ~62 understudied species of cartilaginous fishes found in deep water environments worldwide. Increased exploration of deep water habitats has facilitated taxonomic advances, including description of Chimaera stellata Teramura, Senou & Hirase 2024 and redescription of Chimaera owstoni Tanaka 1905. These and seven other species of family Chimaeridae are native and/or endemic to Japanese waters: Chimaera jordani Tanaka 1905; C. phantasma Jordan & Snyder 190Hydrolagus barbouri Garman 1908; H. eidolon Jordan & Hubbs, 1925; H. mitsukurii Jordan & Snyder, 1904; H. ogilbyi Waite, 1898; and H. purpurescens Gilbert, 1905. Several species are poorly known. The goal of this study is to provide an overview of taxonomic and morphological information for the species of Chimaeridae in Japan. We identified and analyzed morphological characters for five species preserved in the Harvard University Museum of Comparative Zoology (MCZ) and Smithsonian Institution National Museum of Natural History (USMN) ichthyology collections. Additionally, we made in-situ observations on morphology and related behaviors of these species using remote-operated vehicle (ROV) footage from the JAMSTEC E-Library of Deep Sea Images BISMaL database. Lastly, we reviewed literature and available genetic information for each species to highlight areas of taxonomic uncertainty. Jacob M Daane
502: The order Rajiformes (skates) has the most species of any elasmobranch order and it is common for multiple skate species to have overlapping spatial ranges. Skates, however, are highly morphologically conserved and tend to all be benthic mesoconsumers. This poses the question “how do multiple overlapping skate species partition the environment in order to reduce competition?” We investigated niche partitioning by building species distribution models for three common, co-occurring skate species (Clearnose Skates: Rostroraja eglanteria, Little Skates: Leucoraja erinaceus, and Winter Skates: Leucoraja ocellata) found off the New Jersey coast using 30 years of trawl survey data collected by the state of New Jersey. Our results demonstrate clear interspecific variability in the spatial and temporal distribution of abundance for these species, with our models suggesting that bottom temperature is a strong driver of this variability. Clearnose Skates were most abundant in nearshore habitats during the summer, while Little and Winter skates were most abundant in cooler months (winter/spring). Notably, during the summer, Little Skates were more abundant than Clearnose Skates in cooler offshore waters. We also tested if there were variations in spatial grouping and the locations of hotspots between the three skate species. Overall, our results suggest that competition may influence the broad scale distribution of these species off the New Jersey coast, including potentially responding to seasonal cues that lead to differences in migratory phenology between the three skate species. Delana Gonzales
503: The California Current Large Marine Ecosystem (CCLME) is a highly productive upwelling zone of ecological and economic importance along the west coast of North America and is home to the broadnose sevengill shark (Notorynchus cepedianus), a large, high-order marine predator found in temperate coastal waters worldwide. Yet despite extensive research focused on the region’s fisheries, the ecological role of sevengill sharks remains poorly understood. We aim to address this knowledge gap by examining the movement and foraging ecology of sevengill sharks within the CCLME. Here we present results from passive acoustic monitoring (n = 80), stable isotope analysis (n = 329), and stomach content analysis using non-lethal lavage techniques (n = 59), conducted in two CCLME estuarine regions (Willapa Bay and Puget Sound, Washington, USA). We provide evidence of high seasonal residency along with broader connectivity within the CCLME, as well as preliminary diet patterns indicating feeding at high trophic levels. Stomach content data reveal frequent predation on marine mammals and elasmobranchs, complemented by benthic prey such as crustaceans and demersal fishes, suggesting a flexible and opportunistic foraging strategy. Together with stable isotope values, these early results point to broad niche width and the potential for sevengills to exert significant top-down influence across multiple habitat types. This work represents the first effort to characterize sevengill foraging ecology within the CCLME and has important implications for ecosystem-based understanding along the U.S. West Coast, particularly as managers consider how apex predator dynamics shape productivity and trophic interactions within the region. Sydney Schumacher
504: The onset of global climate change has increased the variability and frequency of extreme temperatures. These changes in temperature may be difficult for amphibians to cope with due to ectothermic constraints. Blanchard’s cricket frog (Acris blanchardi) has been in decline throughout the northern extent of their range since the late 1970s. Various studies have investigated the cause of this decline, but few have examined the effects of climate change. Little is known about the thermal capacity of A. blanchardi and whether plasticity exists in these traits. In this study, we collected data on the critical thermal maximum (CTmax) and minimum (CTmin) of A. blanchardi across seasons and across ontogeny to determine whether acclimation or life history plays a role in thermal tolerance. Our study was conducted from early spring to late fall of 2025 in southwest Ohio. We found that thermal tolerance changes throughout the year, with CTmin increasing throughout the season, and CTmax increasing from spring to summer, and then decreasing in the fall. Additionally, we found that tadpoles tolerate more extreme temperatures than juveniles and adults. This study serves as a basis for the thermal biology of A. blanchardi and presents implications for amphibians in the face of climate change. Abby Bednarski
505: Freshwater turtles face compounding threats from climate change, river fragmentation, and habitat degradation, yet species-specific projections integrating climatic and hydrological predictors remain scarce for South and Southeast Asian taxa. We used ensemble species distribution models to assess current and future habitat suitability for five extant softshell turtle species in the genus Nilssonia: N. gangetica (n = 122), N. leithii (n = 47), N. hurum (n = 32), N. nigricans (n = 25), and N. formosa (n = 23). We built models using four bioclimatic and two hydrological variables for each species (AUC 0.804-0.898, Boyce index 0.847-0.935). We projected future suitability under 12 climate scenarios (3 GCMs × 2 SSPs × 2 time periods) and found sharply divergent trajectories. N. gangetica gained 11-70% climatically suitable range, while N. hurum (9-30% loss), N. leithii (2-27% loss), N. nigricans (up to 41% loss), and N. formosa (up to 19% loss) all contracted. We quantified landscape fragmentation and found that habitat broke into more numerous, smaller patches across all species and scenarios, even where total area was maintained. We then overlaid the connectivity status index and degree of regulation onto suitable habitat and found that 4-6% is already heavily regulated by dams, and that N. gangetica's newly gained habitat disproportionately coincides with dammed river reaches, creating a climate-connectivity paradox. Our findings demonstrate that conservation planning for obligate freshwater species such as Nilssonia must jointly address climate-driven range shifts, habitat fragmentation, and river connectivity. Félicie Dhellemmes Félicie Dhellemmes; Joffrey Baeyaert; Raquel Braun; Liam Dickson; Jean-Sébastien Finger; Harry Gray; Samuel
506: Florida hosts diverse aquatic and marine ecosystems that support rich biodiversity, yet traditional survey methods are costly, labor-intensive, and often unable to capture the full extent of species diversity needed for biogeographic research and ecosystem management. Environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding — sequencing DNA shed by organisms into the water column — can overcome many of these limitations by providing higher-resolution species inventories with reduced effort and cost. Here, we use eDNA to survey biogeographic patterns in nearshore fish communities across Florida’s coastline and compare these patterns with commonly applied regional biogeographic schemes. Our statewide dataset improves understanding of how fish communities are structured across Florida and evaluates the effectiveness of eDNA metabarcoding for detecting biogeographic breaks in a species-rich, environmentally complex region. This work demonstrates the potential of eDNA to support large-scale biodiversity assessments and offers a framework for integrating eDNA into future biogeographic and management applications. Kayla M. Fast Kayla Fast; Matthew Niemiller; Zachariah Alley; Tyler Muller; H Post; Pamela Hart; Edward Burress; Bernie
507: The blue-spotted salamander (Ambystoma laterale) is a highly fossorial species outside of its annual breeding season, which has resulted in a lack of knowledge regarding its ecology, particularly in winter. While they cannot survive freezing, blue-spotted salamanders primarily inhabit regions with harsh winters. As climate change progresses and winter weather becomes more erratic, species like the blue-spotted salamander could suffer from higher mortality and lower fecundity rates. However, before the effects of climate change can be assessed, their winter-survival method must first be characterized. A novel method was developed in which blue-spotted salamanders were implanted with PIT tags and housed in temperature-monitored underground enclosures over winter. Throughout the winter (October-April), these salamanders were monitored using RFID telemetry to determine depth, habitat temperature, and whether burrows were used as a winter refuge. This study also sought to determine if there was a difference in activity levels and wintering depth between A. laterale (LL) and their triploid-unisexual hybrids (LLJ). It was determined that blue-spotted salamanders remain active throughout the winter and that diploid (LL) blue-spotted salamanders were more active throughout the winter than the triploid-unisexual hybrids (LLJ). In addition, triploid-unisexual (LLJ) salamanders overwinter significantly shallower than the diploid (LL) salamanders. Furthermore, this study showed that A. laterale does use soil depth to thermoregulate throughout the winter despite being unaffected by day-to-day temperature fluctuations. This offers valuable insight into the winter behavior of fossorial salamanders, which is crucial for conservation purposes. John Hlavin
508: Indirect effects of predators on primary producers are generally well-described, but interactions between some groups still need investigation. Previous work has documented larval amphibians affecting algal biomass, but effects of post-metamorphic amphibians on plants have received less attention. In previous work we observed slugs consuming plants and showed that frogs tended to increase violet survival and increased columbine survival in outdoor pens under warming chambers. We conducted two experiments in an attempt to identify the mechanisms behind these effects. First, we raised violets and columbines in growth chambers to assess whether herbivory by slugs varied with temperature. Slugs consumed more violets at cooler temperatures but did not consume columbines at either temperature. Second, we used outdoor pens with either zero or ten slugs crossed with either zero or four wood frogs to assess whether frogs affect plant survival through effects on slugs. More violets were consumed in pens with slugs, but no columbines were consumed. Frogs did not affect survival of violets or columbines. Mass of violets was greater in pens with slugs, but there were no effects on root:shoot mass ratio. Frogs were more likely to be recovered from pens with slugs. Few studies have investigated effects of post-metamorphic amphibians on plant herbivory. Amphibians in the tropics have been found to reduce herbivory, whereas temperate studies, including this one, did not see significant effects. The limited evidence raises the intriguing possibility that amphibian declines in the tropics may come with greater changes in herbivory than in temperate zones. Jeff Parmelee
509: Cichlids have repeatedly evolved specialization on attached benthic prey across both African and Neotropical radiations, yet the degree to which ecologically similar species are morphologically, functionally and behaviorally convergent deserves greater attention. We compared benthic- and suction-feeding performance in trophically diverse cichlids from the Neotropical Heroini to species from Lakes Malawi and Tanganyika to test for patterns of feeding performance in association with similar feeding ecology. Among Neotropical species we find a clear trade-off between performance in suction feeding on elusive prey and the ability to feed on attached, benthic food. Interestingly, some African benthic-feeding cichlids outperformed their ecological counterparts from the Neotropics, with Malawi mbuna exhibiting exceptional benthic-feeding proficiency while maintaining moderate suction performance, while one Tanganyikan benthic feeder performed poorly in both feeding trials. Using highspeed videography and morphological analyses, we quantified behavioral, kinematic, and morphological traits associated with feeding performance. Our results indicate that Malawi mbuna achieve high benthic-feeding performance through behavioral modifications that decouple morphology from performance, highlighting the importance of behavior in augmenting the mechanical design of the feeding apparatus to shape trophic diversity in cichlids. Savannah Ryburn Savannah Ryburn; Eldridge Wisely; Eduardo Espinoza; Daniel Armijos; Haley Capone; Diana Pazmiño; Alex
510: Prairie streams within the Southern Great Plains (SGP) exhibit spatial and temporal (i.e., seasonal) variability in hydrology and habitat conditions, supporting unique assemblages of freshwater fish with diverse lifehistory strategies. These strategies alongside intensifying climatic (e.g., drought severity) and anthropogenic (e.g., land-use) stressors play central roles in driving patterns of species distribution and occurrence. Using 50-years of survey data from the upper Red River basin (SGP, Texas), we identified key regional variables (e.g., land cover, climate) influencing the occurrence of three fish species of greatest conservation need (SGCN) including the Red River Pupfish (RRPF, Cyprinodon rubrofluviatilis), Red River Shiner (RRS, Notropis bairdi), and Prairie Chub (PC, Macrhybopsis australis), across historical (1980–2002) and contemporary (2003–2025) time periods. Random Forest Classification models revealed the probability of occurrence of RRPF increasing across habitats with high proportions of emergent shrubs and lower average annual rainfall, supporting the species’ tolerance of harsh environmental conditions. For pelagic-broadcast spawners (RRS and PC), rainfall was also a top predictor of these two species occurrences across both time periods. In addition, other climatic variables of drought severity and average summer temperature emerged as top variables likely describing preferences of these species for wetter environments with moderate thermal conditions. Future research will examine the hydrological variables at the stream-segment scale to understand how flow timing, frequency, duration, and magnitude; and stream fragmentation influence the occurrence of these SGCN species within the SGP. Meredith Barney
511: The behavioral and physiological flexibility to inhabit multiple environments is considered a property of generalist organisms; however, it is unclear how this paradigm fits when at least one of the environments is harsh and imposes strong selection for specialization. Facultative cave-dwelling organisms must persist in surface and subsurface habitats, contending with opposing selective forces when moving between habitats. Percopsiformes fishes occupy the full gradient of surface, surface-cave, and cave environments. Eyed, facultative cave-dwelling Spring Cavefishes (Forbesichthys) spend most of the year in subterranean habitats but move into surface waters during the spring. Spending time in both surface and subterranean environments, Forbesichthys have been hypothesized as intermediate in form and function between surface fishes and the obligate cavefishes. We measure 11 linear traits describing general dimensions of the body, head, and jaws of percopsiform fishes using microcomputed tomography of 11 species.  In 10 of 11 traits, Forbesichthys have a unique phenotype not observed in obligate cavefishes or surface species. Forbesichthys have an intermediate phenotype in only one trait, and a similar phenotype to obligate cavefishes and surface fishes in two and three traits, respectively. Facultative cavefishes do not balance selection imposed by surface and cave environments via an intermediate phenotype, nor do they adopt a cave-adapted phenotype in response to the harsh conditions imposed by cave environments or maintain the surface ancestral phenotype. Rather, facultative cavefishes have a novel phenotype in response to the combined selection pressures associated with occupying both surface and cave environments. Gabriela Bilbrey
512: Flatfishes (Carangaria: Pleuronectiformes) represent the most striking example of vertebrate asymmetric body-plan evolution, yet whether this defining trait evolved once or multiple times remains contentious, with roughly half of molecular studies favoring monophyly and the other half polyphyly. A recent whole-genome study proposed that flatfishes are polyphyletic, with Psettodes placed sister to non-flatfish carangarian taxa. However, this conclusion was subsequently shown to be driven by base-compositional nonstationarity artifacts and inadequate substitution modeling. Here we revisit the question using whole-genome phylogenomic and synteny data from 17 carangarian species spanning flatfishes, billfishes, jacks, barracudas, and their allies. We generated three new chromosome-level genome assemblies, including the key early-diverging flatfish Psettodes. Nucleotidebased phylogenomic analyses using coalescent approaches (e.g., ROADIES and CASTER) yield strong support for flatfish monophyly (FM), placing Psettodes sister to all other flatfishes. Microsynteny analyses based on conserved gene-order blocks corroborate this result: topology tests, cluster-profile counts, and rearrangementdistance trees all favor FM over two competing polyphyly hypotheses. Macrosynteny (chromosome-scale rearrangements), by contrast, yields a more mixed signal, with support for FM depending on the metric and taxonsampling scheme. We interpret this hierarchical concordance pattern in light of Carangaria's explosive postCretaceous radiation along the benthic-pelagic axis: short internodes during rapid diversification allow microsyntenic rearrangements to accumulate as phylogenetic synapomorphies, whereas macrosyntenic changes (rare, large-scale events) are too infrequent to resolve such rapid splits. Our multi-scale genomic evidence, combined with shared developmental mechanisms (thyroid hormone pathway, bmp4 signaling) and the fossil record, supports a single evolutionary origin of cranial asymmetry in flatfishes. Ashley Galloway
513: Morphology is an important tool used in evolutionary studies that provides key insights into evolutionary relationships and diversification dynamics. In fishes, morphological characteristics often align with habitat specialization that reflects ecological pressures. Darters (Percidae) are a highly diverse group of North American freshwater fishes that contain several genera and more than 200 species. Percina is the only darter genus possessing functional swim bladders of various sizes, with some species lacking one entirely. Furthermore, some species of Percina previously have been classified as exhibiting benthic or hyperbenthic behaviors, suggesting that there may be a relationship between swim bladder morphology and habitat. The aim of this study is to examine volume within Percina using micro-computed tomography (microCT scanning). Specimens from 50 species of Percina, and several outgroups were iodine stained in preparation for microCT scanning. We will provide a summary of presence/absence and volumetric data for all examined species. We incorporated multiple phylogenetic comparative methods, including tests of correlated trait evolution and models of discrete trait rate variation using corHMM and BiSSE, to assess the relationships between swim bladder morphology and habitat. The results indicate that swim bladder evolution is correlated with habitat, with benthic species more often lacking swim bladders while hyperbenthic species typically retain them. A strong phylogenetic signal was detected, indicating that closely related species tend to share similar swim bladder traits. Models allowing habitat-specific transition rates were strongly supported. Estimated transition rates indicate that swim bladder loss occurs more rapidly in benthic lineages than in hyperbenthic lineages. Jensyn Scott
514: Competition among entire clades is widely thought to shape macroevolutionary trajectories, yet direct tests have relied almost exclusively on paleontological evidence. Here, we present phylogenetic comparative interaction methods (PCIMs) for evaluating historical inter-clade competition. We apply this approach to North American cavefishes (Amblyopsidae), an iconic system characterized by repeated transitions into subterranean habitats. Integrating dated phylogenies with comparative reconstructions of diversification dynamics (testing whether diversification bursts in other clades align temporally with cave colonization) and body shape and size, geography, and trophic ecology, we quantify ecological overlap between amblyopsids and co-occurring freshwater fish clades, then synthesize these axes into an integrated ranking of putative competitors. Our results identify darters as the most consistent ecological competitors across dimensions, whereas other clades show high similarity along isolated axes. By demonstrating how inter-clade competitive signatures can be extracted from phylogenies of living taxa, this study provides a generalizable framework for testing macroevolutionary ecological interactions. Madeline Zickgraf
515: Climate change can influence host-parasite dynamics by altering the abundance and distribution of hosts and their parasites as well as the physiology of both parasite and host. While the physiological effects of hosting parasites have been extensively studied in aquatic and laboratory model systems, these dynamics have been much less studied in wild terrestrial vertebrates, such as ectotherms that live in tropical forests. These organisms are particularly vulnerable to climate change because they have limited scope for behavioral buffering of stressful temperatures while already living at body temperatures close to their heat tolerance limits. Thus, it is imperative to understand how parasitism and tolerance to stressful thermal conditions, both of which are changing under climate warming, might interact to shape survival of non-model organisms. We measured heat tolerance and assessed endoand ecto-parasites in slender anole lizards (Anolis apletophallus; a lowland tropical forest species from central Panama). We then treated lizards with the antiparasitic drugs Ivermectin and Praziquantel and measured changes in immune function and heat tolerance compared to an unmanipulated control group. Immune function was not altered by treatment; however, heat tolerance increased in treated lizards. Additionally, higher endo- and ectoparasite abundance was associated with lower heat tolerance in a separate set of wild-caught lizards. Our results suggest that increasing environmental temperatures may have especially severe effects on host survival when parasites are present and highlight the need to consider interactions between thermal physiology and host-parasite dynamics when forecasting the responses of tropical animals to climate change. Yasin Bakış

516: Deserts around the world are experiencing rising temperatures and reduced rainfall due to the climate crisis. While many desert animals have adaptations to withstand dehydration and avoid high temperatures, changing conditions could place them at risk. For lizards, evaporative water loss represents a major source of water loss, suggesting that lizards should possess adaptations for reducing water loss across their skin. We measured cutaneous evaporative water loss (CEWL) and plasma osmolality of nine species of lizards in the Mojave Desert in California, USA, shortly after capture and after acclimation to two days of humid conditions. We found that CEWL is remarkably low among most species of desert lizards, approximately half that of a comparably sized mesic lizard species. CEWL was impacted mainly by species, body mass, and the ambient temperature and vapor pressure deficit at the time of measurement. In addition, for most of the species, CEWL was very inflexible, demonstrating little change following acclimation. Only lizards with big fat bodies with water sacs show plasticity. Chuckwallas however, showed significant plasticity in their CEWL values. Meredith Barney
Stoye General Herpetology 2 / Physiology & Physiological Ecology
517: Head-starting programs are widely used in reptile conservation to improve early survival by promoting rapid growth. In gopher tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus), head-starting environments often bypass natural first-year cold dormancy, yet how this affects growth and metabolism remains poorly understood. We experimentally tested the effects of bypassing first-year cold dormancy on body size, growth rate, and metabolic markers. Sixty hatchlings from 14 clutches were assigned to two treatments: (1) constant-warmth (standard head-starting) or (2) colddormancy (simulated Alabama winter). We estimated body size from straight carapace length, calculated growth rate from body mass, and quantified plasma glucose, total triglycerides, and acetyl-CoA at four timepoints: BeforeDormancy (BD), End-Dormancy (ED), 3-Week Post-Dormancy (3wkPD), and 3-Month Post-Dormancy (3moPD). Body size was measured again 1.5 years later in the wild (1.5yrPD). Cold-dormancy animals were on average 11.4 mm smaller at 3moPD (p < 0.0001) due to lower growth rates at ED and 3wkPD (p < 0.001). Although growth rates between the treatments converged by 3moPD, cold-dormancy animals remained on average 13.7 mm smaller through 1.5yrPD (p < 0.0001), indicating no size catch-up. Additionally, plasma glucose was reduced in the colddormancy group at ED (p < 0.001), total triglycerides increased in both groups from 3wkPD to 3moPD (p = 0.02 and p = 0.04), and acetyl-CoA was lower in cold-dormancy animals at 3wkPD (p = 0.03). Our results indicate that dormancy temporarily suppresses metabolism without inducing a slow-living trajectory. These findings suggest that supporting natural physiological rhythms may be important for optimizing growth and metabolic health in reintroduced gopher tortoises. Brittany Finucci
Stoye General Herpetology 2 / Physiology & Physiological Ecology
518: Aquatic ecosystems have long been influenced by human-induced pollutants that impact freshwater environments worldwide. Of recent concern is a degradant compound, 6PPD-Q, derived from a vehicle tire additive, 6PPD, that is acutely toxic to migrating Coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) at low concentrations (0.79 μg/L). Research has primarily focused on the effects of 6PPD-Q on economically relevant game species; however, little is known about its effects on non-game species. Thus, this study examines lethal and sublethal effects of 6PPD-Q on larval amphibian species. Amphibian larvae (Gosner stages 27-30) were exposed to 0 μg/L, 0.01 μg/L, 0.10 μg/L, 1.0 μg/L, and 10.0 μg/L for 96-hour range finder experiments. Given that no mortality was observed, multiple 24-hour sublethal behavioral tests were conducted with treatments: 0 μg/L, 5 μg/L, and 10 μg/L. Moreover, a series of burst swim trials were completed for control vs treated hatchlings in a standardized arena to assess the sublethal effects of 6PPD-Q exposure on swim performance. There were no deaths recorded for any hatchlings exposed to varying concentrations of 6PPD-Q for both range finder and sublethal bioassays. These data suggest that amphibian larvae are not highly susceptible to 6PPD-Q toxicity even at relatively high concentrations. Future studies should assess cellular damage from 6PPD-Q exposure in amphibian larvae to confirm minimal sublethal effects. This study contributes to the growing body of research focused on the effects of 6PPD-Q on non-game species and contributes to research focused on amphibian conservation and preservation. Benjamin M. Fitzpatrick
Stoye General Herpetology 2 / Physiology & Physiological Ecology
519: Human-mediated species introductions are becoming increasingly common through global trade, exposing species to novel environmental conditions that are hard to predict. Species distribution models (SDMs) are commonly used to predict habitat suitability, but they typically rely on environmental variables alone, overlooking species-specific information. This has led to historic difficulty predicting SDMs for introduced species due to their limited time in these environments and being unable to reach an equilibrium with their environment. Here, we investigate how including trait data (e.g., physiological and morphological data) can improve SDM performance for the introduced Mediterranean House Gecko (Hemidactylus turcicus). We collected field data from 71 adult individuals across the western United States. We extrapolated these trait values across their range using either distance-based (IDW) or environmental-based (RF, GAM, GLM) methods to generate spatially explicit trait surfaces. These surfaces were then used to estimate trait values for pseudoabsence locations. Next, we compared three models: (1) trait-only, (2) environment-only, and (3) combined trait-environment models. Presence data was formed using our field surveys and online occurrence records from GBIF. All models were compared using AUC and TSS metrics, across four model algorithms: GAM, GLM, GBM, and RF, and 15 runs. We found that our combined models outperformed our other models, improving predictive accuracy and refining habitat suitability estimates. Our results indicate the value of incorporating known species information for SDM performance to help account for the difficulty in accurate modeling of introduced species. Casse Ka'apu-Lyons

520: River fragmentation poses challenges for the conservation and persistence of desert fishes. Connectivity in streams is impaired by anthropogenic changes, including road crossings, prompting the installation of engineered fish passage structures at low-water road crossings, raising questions about the dispersal of aquatic species past these structures. This project used close-kin mark-recapture (CKMR) to compare movement patterns in Loach Minnow Tiaroga cobitis between a restored stream (including a fish passage) and a stream without rehabilitation efforts. A 316-locus GT-seq panel was developed and optimized for relatedness analysis. Across three years (2023-2025), 385 individuals were sampled from the San Francisco (unrestored) and Tularosa (fish passage restoration) Rivers in the upper Gila River Basin. We identified parent-offspring pairs (POPs) and full-sibling pairs (FSPs) and mapped their collection locations to infer dispersal distances and directions in both rivers.  Spatial analysis indicates that Loach Minnow dispersed in both directions across road crossings in both rivers, including the fish passage in Tularosa. Average dispersal distances were 0.19/0.38 km (POPs/FSPs) in the Tularosa River and 0.59/0.09 km in the San Francisco River. However, a substantial proportion of dispersal events occurred over distances <0.5 km in both rivers (TR: 84.5%/60.6%; SF: 64.3%/99.3%). Loach Minnow tends to disperse small distances when suitable intervening habitat between localities is available. More generally, CKMR is a promising tool for evaluating movement patterns in small-bodied fish species where physical tagging is difficult or impossible to implement. Owen Bachhuber
521: Providing natural diets for larval amphibians in captivity is challenging because many tadpoles feed on algae, detritus, and other plant-based materials that are difficult to provide. In Creston, British Columbia, Canada, the historic range of the Rocky Mountain northern leopard frog (Lithobates pipiens) has been reduced to one location in the south-east corner of the province. Here, egg masses collected in the spring are commonly protected in predator-exclusion cages in situ, and tadpoles are reared on a diet of boiled lettuce. We compared the effects of this commonly used diet with a nutritionally-enriched functional diet (FD) recipe developed by the Phoenix Zoo. Tadpoles from naturally-occurring egg masses were transferred to 10 paired cages (20 cages total), with 25 animals per cage, and were then raised on a diet of either FD or boiled lettuce. We found the FD treatment caused greater increases in both tadpole length (5.50 ± 0.30 cm vs. 3.76 ± 0.22 cm; p < 0.001) and mass (2.29 ± 0.45 g vs. 1.27 ± 0.25 g; p < 0.001) over a four-week period compared to the lettuce diet (LD). However, survival did not differ significantly between treatments, suggesting that although the FD treatment influenced growth, basic energy requirements for survival were met under both feeding regimes, albeit in cages that were largely predator-free. Overall, our results suggest that the FD provides a more effective diet for larval growth under field-rearing conditions and may help improve conservation efforts for this population and possibly other at-risk amphibian species. Ellery Brownlee
522: Small dams are rapidly constructed across India, yet their socio-ecological consequences remain poorly understood. This interdisciplinary research focuses on Bavikarra Dam, a non-powered dam on the Chandragiri River, Kerala, that threatens the only-known breeding population of the Critically Endangered freshwater turtle Pelochelys cantorii (Cantor’s Giant Softshell Turtle) in India. The dam stores freshwater for nearby communities from January to May, but this period overlaps with the nesting season of P. cantorii and floods critical nesting grounds. Since 2019, we have sustained a community-led conservation program to protect nests from dam-induced inundation. However, long-term protection requires examining dam operations through interconnected ecological, social, and political lenses to identify pathways that balance human water needs with species conservation. We use ecological field surveys, including camera trapping and daily water-level monitoring, to recommend safe fluctuation limits at nesting locations. In 2025–2026, we located and monitored 15 nests, resulting in over 62 hatchlings, and continue to track additional nests this season. Additionally, Q-methodology and participatory workshops reveal how community members, and external actors perceive dam's benefits and costs, as well as viewpoints on different management options for future dams. These insights highlight the social and political dimensions that shape feasible conservation strategies. This research has already catalyzed institutional change, including the formation of the first intergovernmental communication committee and an agreement to conduct Environmental Impact Assessments for small dams. Together, these findings demonstrate how integrating ecological evidence with community perspectives can guide sustainable small-dam governance. David Janik
523: Invasive lionfish (Pterois spp.) in the Western Atlantic and Caribbean Sea have caused considerable disruption to coral reef communities. Effective management relies on understanding lionfish behavior and movement across all invaded habitats, because any single remaining stock may re-colonize previously culled areas. Most lionfish movement studies in their invasive range have been conducted on continental shelves with gradual slopes (e.g., Florida), though many Caribbean islands are characterized by insular shelves and steep wall reefs. In such systems, we expect depth to be a primary axis of movement, and that known crepuscular activity peaks would present as a diel vertical migration. We tagged 30 lionfish with internal acoustic transmitters with pressure sensors from May to July 2017. We deployed 16 receivers along the edge of Bloody Bay Wall on the north side of Little Cayman, which extends vertically from 20m to over 1000m. Lionfish depth measurements from the transmitters reveal a strong and consistent diel vertical migration across individuals with peaks at dawn and dusk, and troughs mid-day. Despite the common trend, vertical migration distance and activity space varied, explained in part by fish size. Lionfish ranged from the surface to 150m, and several lionfish had mean depths below diver access (~40m). Predicting when lionfish will be within diver access at sites with steep reef structure can inform management actions and more effectively control invasive populations. Additionally, interactions between lionfish and native species shape invasive dynamics, so we compared abnormal movements to typical local predator activity to investigate suspected predation events. Diana Methner
524: The multiscale nature of lotic ecosystems makes it challenging to study and guide conservation and management plans for fish species. We used a hierarchical sampling design to evaluate how environmental variables at nested local (mesohabitat, sub-reach, and site) and regional (sub-watershed, watershed) scales influence the occurrence of two species of greatest conservation need (SGCN) in Texas, the Sabine Shiner (Notropis sabinae) and the Spotted Sucker (Minytrema melanops). Fish and local habitat surveys were conducted in the fall and summer of 2025 across 11 streams and 9 river sites within the Neches and Sabine River basins in East Texas. Land cover variables were gathered for each regional scale. For both species, generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were performed at each spatial scale. Sabine Shiner occurrence was best predicted at the sub-reach scale by shallow waters, wider stream segments, and coarser substrates. At both regional scales, a decrease in forest cover best predicted species occurrence. For Spotted Sucker, several variables at the mesohabitat and sub-reach scales were important in predicting species occurrence, including longer and wider stream segments, with more lentic and deeper waters. At the sub-watershed scale, the best predictor for species occurrence was decreasing wetland cover, while at the watershed scale, less open water was the best predictor. Differences in species occurrence across spatial scales could be attributed to the complexity of these lotic systems. Thus, high similarity of instream variables within sites, life history traits of each species, and environmental interactions likely influenced such occurrence relationships. Caroline Muscat
525: Freshwater ecosystems are highly vulnerable to environmental change, and organisms that inhabit them are frequently exposed to a suite of co-occurring stressors. These stressors can interact in complex and unpredictable ways, obscuring our understanding of organismal responses to global change. Although multiplestressor research has expanded in recent decades, few quantitative syntheses have focused specifically on freshwater fish, despite their ecological and socio-economic importance. Moreover, the growing body of experimental work on multiple-stressor interactions in freshwater fish has not been comprehensively synthesized, limiting our ability to identify patterns in species responses. Our objectives were to synthesize experimental studies of stressor interactions in freshwater fish and to test how interaction types vary across biological and environmental contexts. We conducted a meta-analysis of 138 experiments from 57 publications evaluating the interactive effects of elevated temperature and other stressors (e.g., pollutants) on freshwater fish. Across studies, the overall mean interaction was antagonistic, indicating that combined thermal and pollutant stress may be less detrimental than would be predicted based on the sum of their single-stressor effects. However, interaction types varied across taxa, stressor combinations, and response variables, indicating substantial context dependence. These results suggest that some species may exhibit physiological co-tolerance that buffers against concurrent stressors as environmental conditions continue to change. We also highlight the limited representation of non-game species and the scarcity of studies incorporating climate-related stressors beyond temperature, and emphasize the need for more experiments on multiple-stressor effects that will allow for more realistic assessments of species vulnerability.
526: Species reintroduction efforts have historically relied on population demographics rather than genetic diversity to evaluate their success. Genetic evaluations of reintroduction efforts performed for fishes have mostly focused on large, mobile species while few exist for small, low dispersal species like the Citico Darter (Etheostoma sitikuense). Etheostoma sitikuense is federally endangered, native to Citico Creek and Abrams Creek in eastern Tennessee. In response to extirpation of the Abrams Creek population in 1957, US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and Conservation Fisheries Inc. used Citico Creek fish as a source to reintroduce E. sitikuense into Abrams Creek in 1993 and introduce to Tellico River in 2003, with population augmentation efforts that continue today. In 2012, USFWS conducted a genetic assessment of Citico Creek and Abrams Creek populations using microsatellite loci and found low levels of overall genetic diversity and conflicting results regarding population differentiation. We used the same microsatellite loci and ddRADseq to evaluate contemporary population structure and diversity within E. sitikuense. Our SNP data indicate more population structure (K=3) than expected given the management history of this species. The three genetic clusters identified correspond to upper, middle, and lower sections of Citico Creek that have been unevenly transferred into Abrams Creek and Tellico River. We also detected signatures of outbreeding at sites across the range of E. sitikuense. Given these findings, we suggest modifying translocation strategies to improve gene flow across structured populations. Sam Troast
527: Emergent infectious diseases (EIDs), particularly fungal pathogens, have caused significant declines in various vertebrate populations, including snakes. One such pathogen, Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola (Oo), affects snake populations across the United States, particularly rattlesnakes. Soil is suspected to play a key role in the persistence and transmission of Oo, but the mechanisms involved remain unclear. This study aims to explore the role of soil in the persistence of Oo. Microcosm experiments were conducted using autoclaved silty loam soil, mimicking the shallow layers of the Bennington series of soils, with shed skins and Oo conidia added to treatment groups. A control group without shed skins was used for comparison. After 30 days, fungal growth was analyzed using qPCR to quantify fungal DNA into conidia genomic equivalents. We found that growth was significantly higher in soils containing shed skin versus control groups, with no differences between shed groups. These results provide insights into how shed skins within den sites may allow the fungus to persist in the environment, potentially acting as reservoirs for Oo. Understanding the environmental factors that contribute to the longevity and transmission of this fungal pathogen is crucial for snake conservation, particularly for species like the timber rattlesnake. This research may help inform targeted interventions, such as treating den soils, to reduce the spread of Oo and prevent further declines in vulnerable snake populations. Jon Adamski
528: Temperature constrains the physiology, behavior, and ecology of ectotherms, influencing where species live, when they are active, and how they interact with their environments. Understanding how ectotherms persist across climatic gradients is therefore central to ecology, particularly in the context of insular systems and predicted climate change. The Northern Channel Islands are substantially cooler than adjacent Southern California, presenting a potential thermal challenge for endemic Island Fence Lizards (Sceloporus becki), the sister taxon to thermophilic Western Fence Lizards (S. occidentalis). Our study tests whether island populations have evolutionarily shifted their thermal biology or persist through behavioral and temporal adjustments. We compared thermal biology metrics (operative temperatures, field and preferred body temperatures, thermal tolerances, and temperature-dependent locomotor performance) among island and mainland populations. Field and preferred body temperatures and panting thresholds did not differ among island and mainland populations, suggesting conservation of core thermal traits despite cooler island climates. However, critical thermal minima varied seasonally, suggesting temporal plasticity in cold tolerances rather than population-level divergences. Our findings suggest island and mainland fence lizards differ less in thermal preferences than in the quantity and quality of thermally suitable conditions they experience on a daily and seasonal basis. Ongoing analyses of operative temperatures and thermoregulatory efficacy will quantify how cooler island climates shape activity windows and performance. By integrating physiological, behavioral, and environmental data, our study offers a synthetic understanding of how insular reptiles persist in cooler climates and provides critical information for the conservation of this island endemic under ongoing climate warming. Eli Greenbaum Everett Madsen; Werner Conradie; Hanlie Engelbrecht; Eugene Vaughan; Olivier Pauwels; Jean-François Trape; Marius Burger; Zena Timmons; Chifundera Kusamba; Eli Greenbaum
529: The Central Highlands forests of Madagascar (CHM) are critical but fragmented habitats where reptiles assemblage face local extirpation. How this habitat modification has impacted the forest’s native reptiles, such as the poorly studied yet prominent chameleon assemblage is largely unknown. To assess the impacts of this degradation, we examined the abundance and microhabitat selection of four sympatric chameleon taxa (Calumma crypticum, C. gastrotaenia, C. globifer, and the C. nasutum group) across three forest remnants. Our results show that population densities are influenced by seasonal variation and exhibit a female-biased structure and we also discuss our preliminary population genetic analyses for these chameleons. Surprisingly, despite being a threatened species, C. globifer remained abundant during the wet season with high densities in non-protected forest patches. While we identified niche overlap among the four species, their community structure is primarily driven by vertical stratification and specific roost site preferences rather than overall habitat type. Factors such as limited dispersal capacity, geographical isolation, and physical barriers likely drive this diversification and also lead to genetic structuring of populations. These charismatic chameleons serve as vital ecological indicators and tools for public engagement. Ultimately, understanding their habitat use and population genetic diversity is essential for identifying priority areas for management and conservation within Madagascar’s imperiled forest systems. Stella Raymond Stella Raymond; Deanni Armstrong; Christiann Dipietrantonio; May Jiang; Mercy Bourgeois; Nathan Forbes; Hazel Hayashi; Ethan Heck; Kyler Pinkowski; Brenden Saraf; Arman Khasru; Paul Christman; Steve Adolph; George Brusch; Kris Karsten; David Daversa; Monica McNamara; Javier Monzon; Marion Preest; Kinsey Brock; Emily
530: Veiled chameleons (Chamaeleo calyptratus) have been invasive in Florida for over 25 years and have spread throughout the southern peninsula, yet they remain understudied. We sought to better understand the spatial ecology and habitat use of C. calyptratus in Southwest Florida using radio telemetry, vegetation surveys, and dronebased LiDAR. We also conducted nocturnal visual encounter surveys and used occupancy and detection modeling to determine factors that could influence site occupancy and our ability to find C. calyptratus. We found that habitat use and movement varies by individual, but larger males seem to have very small home ranges compared to females and smaller males, which had the largest home ranges of the study. It also appears that the most important factor for site occupancy is the tree species evenness of the site, while the most important factors for nocturnal detection are the ambient light level of the site and the search light type (looking in darker areas with brighter lights). Understanding how these lizards use their new environment is essential to not only determine their impact on our ecosystems and know how to manage them, but to give us a better idea about their ecology in their native range. This project is one of the first to gather ecological data on wild veiled chameleons and can support further research on C. calyptratus and other similar species as well.
531: Environmental heterogeneity poses many challenges to individuals, which can decrease their fitness. As a result, natural selection favors strategies that help organisms overcome these challenges. One such strategy is behavior, which can reduce variation in environmental exposure and limit environmentally induced phenotypic differences. Parental behaviors, in particular, can shield offspring from harsh environments, providing favorable developmental conditions with long-term benefits. This is the basis of the silver spoon hypothesis (SSH): individuals who experience advantageous early-life environments tend to have higher fitness throughout their lives. The main goal of this project was to understand how early-life environments influence individuals' responses to environmental variation. We tested the hypothesis that maternal nesting behavior shields embryos from suboptimal environments and enhances offspring survival in the brown anole lizard (Anolis sagrei). Two complementary experiments were conducted. In a field experiment, eggs were incubated in nests chosen by mothers and in randomly selected nests. In a lab experiment, eggs were incubated under thermal conditions matching the maternally chosen and random nest sites. The hatchlings from the second experiment were then raised to sexual maturity to assess the long-term effects of maternal nest-site selection on offspring. Preliminary results indicate that individuals from maternal nests grew faster during later developmental stages, suggesting that early environmental conditions influence growth rate. These differences may have significant fitness implications, influencing survival, competitive ability, and resilience to environmental stressors. These findings support the silver spoon hypothesis by demonstrating that favorable early environments can produce lasting effects on developmental trajectories. Jacqueline Webb
532: In wetlands across the Southeastern Coastal Plain, two large aquatic salamanders, Amphiuma means and Siren lacertina, can be abundant. As aquatic mesopredators, these species likely influence wetland community structure and biogeochemistry, yet their ecology remains poorly understood. To address this, we conducted a radiotelemetry study to quantify home range size and seasonal movement patterns of A. means and S. lacertina. We surgically implanted radio transmitters in 10 individuals of each species and collected locations 2-3x weekly from March through June 2025. We generated minimum convex polygons for individuals with ≥5 unique locations. Mean home range size was 251.2 m2 for S. lacertina (n = 7) and 37.1 m2 for A. means (n=9). S. lacertina exhibited the largest home range (736.6 m2) with high intraspecific variation, whereas A. means exhibited the smallest home range (14.5 m2) with less variability. We modeled movement probability across time and environmental variables including dissolved oxygen, water temperature, and water depth using generalized linear mixed models. A. means had a slightly higher movement probability throughout the study period, however, both species exhibited similar seasonal patterns with movement peaking April-May and declining through June. Early-season movement differed significantly, with probabilities of 0.58 for A. means and 0.36 for S. lacertina. Water depth was the only environmental predictor of movement for both species with A. means showing a more peaked response to increasing water depth. These results provide insight into potential differences in temporal activity with implications for how these species affect the ecosystem across the hydroperiod. Christopher Zobek
533: Trophic polymorphism in the hexaploid African cyprinid genus Labeobarbus complicates species delimitation and obscures the relationship between morphological and genetic divergence. This study evaluates whether independently defined genetic lineages (candidate species) of Labeobarbus inhabiting the Komo and Ogooué river systems differ morphologically. We integrate mitochondrial (COI) data with multi-axis phenotyping of 66 voucher specimens, including traditional morphometrics, 3D geometric morphometrics of CT-derived cranial morphology, lip phenotype characterization, and meristic traits. Morphology-based identifications using extant keys fail to separate genetic lineages, highlighting limitations of existing taxonomic frameworks. Morphometric analyses of body and skull shape reveal structured but overlapping separation among candidate species, indicating that morphology captures evolutionary signal despite incomplete differentiation. Integration of categorical lip traits and meristics does not substantially improve lineage discrimination beyond morphometric analyses alone. These results show that morphology alone does not fully resolve species boundaries in Labeobarbus but retains meaningful signal when analyzed quantitatively. This work establishes a phenotypic framework that will support integrative species delimitation based on genome-wide analyses in this complex, polyploid genus. Baylie Fadool
534: Identifying the mechanisms that generate and maintain population level divergence is central to our understanding of adaptive responses to local conditions and environmental change, particularly in species with low vagility. The Gulf pipefish (Syngnathus scovelli) is widely distributed across the Atlantic and Gulf coasts and exhibits strong genetic breaks that separates Florida into at least three subpopulations. This species occupies shallow habitats spanning a broad salinity range, including both marine and freshwater environments. Previous studies identified populations of S. scovelli in isolated freshwater systems, yet genomic analyses using SNPs revealed limited evidence for genetic adaptation to freshwater conditions, with outlier loci not associated with candidate genes for osmoregulation or freshwater tolerance. This raises the possibility that non-genetic mechanisms, such as DNA methylation, may contribute to adaptation in this system. DNA methylation is tissue-specific and highly responsive to environmental conditions, allowing cells to regulate gene expression in response to environmental variation faster than genetic adaptation. To investigate whether DNA methylation is an underlying mechanism for salinity acclimation, we sampled S. scovelli across a salinity gradient (5 ppt vs. 28 ppt) in Charlotte Harbor, Florida. We then used enzymatic methylation sequencing (EM-seq) to quantify genome-wide methylation patterns across four tissue types (liver, gill, muscle, and gut). Based on these data, we found tissue specific responses to salinity that provide insight into the potential role of epigenetic variation in mediating environmental responses in natural populations and set the stage for future epigenetic studies. Harold Gridley
535: Evolutionary relationships are traditionally represented using a tree metaphor, in which lineages may only arise through the splitting of a single ancestor lineage. This model of evolution provides the fundamental context underlying the origin of traits and species themselves, however, it fails to account for hybridization between divergent lineages. Thus, hybridization can be a source of conflicting phylogenetic signal and confound the reconstruction of trait evolution that may appear across distantly related species. Among taxa that hybridize frequently in nature are the North American minnows of the family Leuciscidae. High contemporary hybridization rates and persistent phylogenetic instability across leuciscid studies suggests that ancient introgression may be a major, unaccounted-for source of conflict. Unfortunately, the inference of phylogenies with reticulate branches (i.e. phylogenetic networks) is limited to small sets of taxa (<30) due to greater computational complexity than tree inference. Thus, a divide-and-conquer approach is necessary to address this challenge in the species-rich Leuciscidae family. Three distinct subsetting schemes were tested on a previously published phylogenomic dataset including 1004 loci across 93 leuciscid taxa, with special focus on the pelagic shiners of the Pogonichthyinae subfamily. Additionally, we tested whether explicit reticulate networks provide a better explanation for the observed levels of gene tree discordance compared to strictly bifurcating histories. Subsetting schemes had large effects on the phylogenetic network topology recovered and inferred constraint networks differed significantly in their fit to the observed gene tree discordance. Audra Hicks
536: Mimicry in animals is a complex system that has evolved in many forms, such as morphological, chemical, or behavioral resemblance between organisms. Luring behavior is a type of aggressive mimicry where a predator mimics something desirable to their prey to entice the prey closer. In this study, I reviewed literature and documented examples of luring behavior in fishes and herpetofauna. I considered luring behavior broadly as number of independent evolutions, as well as the development of the lure at a species level. Placement of the lure on the body, the physical structure associated with the lure, the shape of the lure, and behavior related to luring were compared across organisms. I found that there is incredible variety in luring, but also interesting examples of convergence. For example, modification of the dorsal fin into a lure can be found in the Lophiiformes, as well as in other groups of fishes such as the flatfish genus Asterorhombus. Lures originating inside of the mouth can be found in fishes in the family Uranoscopidae (stargazers) and can also be found in the alligator snapping turtle Macrochelys temminckii. Caudal luring can be found in many snakes, best represented by the spider-tailed horned viper (Pseudocerastes urarachnoides) but has also been suggested in fishes such as the gulper eels (Saccopharynx spp.). Overall, luring behavior represents incredible morphological and phylogenetic diversity, but these examples demonstrate convergent evolution across disparate taxonomic groups. Leo MacLeod
537: Key innovations open ecological opportunities and can redirect evolutionary trajectories. In spinyfinned fishes, the pelvic suction cup—a fused adhesive structure formed from the pelvic fins and supported by a modified girdle—appears to be one such trait. Using a novel 960-species phylogeny spanning 940 exons and 67 newly sequenced snailfish genomes, we show that the suction cup evolved independently three times across lineages separated by over 100 million years. By enabling adhesion in high-energy habitats such as tide pools and waterfalls, the suction cup set the stage for body depression and accompanying shifts in scales, teeth, and clade-specific ecofunctional profiles. Comparative analyses reveal convergence in a distinctive region of morphospace and bodyshape evolution accelerated two- to fivefold. Diversification analyses uncover heterogeneous but elevated rates, with a clear burst in rock-climbing gobies associated with suction cup evolution. By opening novel habitats and fostering phenotypic novelty, the suction cup emerges as a key innovation that reshaped spiny-finned fish evolution. Patrick McGrath
538: The order Alepocephaliformes (slickheads and tubeshoulders) is a diverse group of mesopelagic and bathypelagic fishes characterized by scaleless heads and a variety of luminous organs. Although Alepocephaliformes is the sister group of Ostariophysi, the largest radiation of freshwater fishes, relationships within the order have remained poorly resolved because most species are rare, poorly sampled, and frequently described from juvenile specimens. Here, we present the most densely sampled phylogeny of the order to date, comprising 1,105 exonic markers and including 84 of 147 species across 31 of the 33 recognized genera. This degree of taxonomic coverage was achieved by generating whole-genome sequences from fresh tissues for 51 species, historical DNA sequencing from four species lacking any fresh tissue samples collected during the last three decades, and legacy markers for 29 species. Our tree resolves long-ambiguous nodes and identifies three of the largest genera as polyphyletic: Conocara, Alepocephalus, and Rouleina. We then quantified body and head shape variation across more than 300 specimens using linear measurements following those in the FishShapes dataset. Preliminary results contradict the hypothesis of a clear delineation between mesopelagic and bathypelagic lineages within either family (Alepocephalidae or Platytroctidae), with implications for body-plan evolution across deep-sea fish lineages more broadly. These analyses establish a phylogenomic and morphometric framework for Alepocephaliformes and link bathymetric gradients to body-plan evolution in rarely collected deep-sea fishes. Patrick O'Bryan
539: Blanding's Turtle (Emydoidea blandingii) populations in Illinois occupy small, highly fragmented sites due to the state losing more than 90% of its historic wetlands. Blanding’s Turtles are state endangered in Illinois and have low population densities, causing low capture rates in many areas. Additionally, fragmentation hinders surveys and detectability, making it difficult for managers to assess population demographics and identify the best conservation strategies. Robust detection probability estimates are essential because imperfect detection can bias vital demographic estimates. We estimated detection probability by pooling decades of capture data across five Illinois sites and found site was the strongest predictor among the 30 covariates we investigated (temporal, effort, and weather covariates). Next, we estimated the vital rates (survival, recruitment, and population size) of each site independently to compare demographic health across the five populations. By combining sitespecific detection probabilities with vital rate estimates, we assessed and compared the overall status of each population. Our objective is to provide managers with a clearer picture of population status across the five sites to support targeted conservation efforts for Blanding's Turtles in Illinois. Katelyn Arrizon
540: The past century has been marked by the growing effects of anthropogenic change, posing threats to global biodiversity, such as via reductions in many species’ population sizes and genetic health. As populations dwindle in size, lower genetic diversity, inbreeding depression, and a reduced ability to adapt to environmental changes greatly increase extinction risk. We analyzed the population genomics of two Caribbean boa species to explore how small population sizes and inbreeding affect endangered species. The first species is the Critically Endangered Conception Bank Silver Boa (Chilabothrus argentum), which is the most endangered boa on the planet and has an estimated census population of only 128 individuals. The second focal species is its close relative, the Turks and Caicos Island (TCI) Boa (Chilabothrus chrysogaster), which is listed as Near Threatened, and for which we have assembled and annotated the first de novo long-read reference genome. We performed high-depth wholegenome sequencing of 10 Silver Boas (only population) and 30 TCI Boas (three selected islands, census 20, 200, >2,000 snakes). Then, we calculated overall heterozygosity and run of homozygosity (ROH) estimates for each species. We found that the Silver Boa displays a critically low nucleotide diversity (?) of 1.86x10-4. ROH estimates of the TCI Boa show patterns consistent with higher inbreeding levels in smaller populations. Moving forward, we plan to use our Iso-Seq-based annotation of the TCI Boa reference genome to estimate genomic load and contextualize potential accumulation versus purging of deleterious mutations in both species, as well as to make conservation management recommendations. Cristhian Conde
541: A critical component of female life history is reproductive frequency, particularly for animals with relatively short lifespans. In ectotherms—such as snakes—changes in the thermal environment will be expected to have an impact on reproductive frequency. For northern species, climate changes thus may effect significant changes. Research from the 1980s indicated adult female Western Rattlesnakes (Crotalus oreganus) near their northern limit did not reproduce annually, rather, every second or third year (biennial or triennial). In this study, we use a morerecent 24 yr database of Western Rattlesnakes mark/recaptures to (1) provide a current assessment of reproductive frequency in the population, and (2) identify the relationship between reproductive output and environmental conditions such as temperature and precipitation. From a sample size of 50 female rattlesnakes (n=50), results suggest that despite a warming trend in the northern limits of this species, female rattlesnakes have remained largely biennial. We will discuss how other environmental and life-history constraints (i.e. length of season) may form reproductive constraints that cannot yet be overcome by these females. This study adds to our knowledge of reproductive constraints in northern reptile populations, including how they may respond to shifting climates. John Henry Fowler
542: Human attitudes towards animals have major conservation implications. One of the major challenges in conservation projects is to not only measure human attitudes towards the animal species involved, but to obtain public “buy in” to want to conserve animals in the first place. Reptiles are no stranger to eliciting strong human attitudes. Traditionally humans react to reptiles (especially snakes) with fear, disgust and at best ambivalence. Can we change this attitude, and if so, how? This presentation is a contribution towards ethnoherpetology. Examining many popular (and little known) movies, I argue that cultural depictions of reptiles in movies are changing how humans think about reptiles. Changing peoples’ perceptions of reptiles can at best stimulate motivation for conservation, and at the very least foster an appreciation of them. In the Age of the Anthropocene with human encroachment on natural habitats occurring at an accelerating pace, human-reptile encounters will be increasingly more common. Ethnoherpetological studies fill an important niche in herpetology and have the potential to form interdisciplinary collaborations with many academic areas in the humanities. Sara Loetzerich
543: The collection of wild amphibians for human consumption and the pet trade may directly reduce populations through overexploitation. Another factor is the human mediated movement of amphibians may facilitate the spread of wildlife diseases and invasive species. This causes market fluctuations in the amphibian trade and may directly impact conservation goals with potential global consequences. With that in mind, we examined changes in the market values of native species of amphibians in the United States by carrying out systematic surveys of U.S. based sellers of live amphibians. Our data was collected at three time points over 10 years from 2016 to 2026. Additionally, this data was also compared to a historical price data set from 1989. Nearly all species increased in price dramatically during the entire study period of 37 years. We found the market value is significantly higher for caudates with declining populations than other groups. We also found price increase to be positively correlated to range size from IUCN maps, indicating these maps may be insensitive to underlying range changes. Additionally, we discuss the prices of U.S. caudate species that were affected by a contentious 2016 emergency trade ban. The results provide valuable information on price trends of commonly traded North American amphibian species. We urge increased monitoring of amphibian market pressures and price dynamics to ensure the pet trade is sustainable. Katherine Polatchek Katherine Polatchek; Amber Ringle; Emily Yeager; Colin Foord; Christian Pankow; Julia Saltzman; Catherine
544: The Mississippi Alluvial Plain within northeastern Arkansas has experienced fragmentation and degradation of historic wetlands. The Agricultural Conservation Easement Program - Wetland Reserve Easement (WRE) program supports land conversion from agricultural into wetland habitat to support wildlife. Amphibians in Arkansas rely on wetlands for refugia, breeding, and juvenile development. Therefore, understanding how amphibians utilize restored wetlands compared to natural or disrupted habitats is crucial for conservation efforts as amphibian populations continue to decline globally. We employed a variety of survey techniques uniformly across 40 wetlands categorized into three types: (1) Reference - sites over 25 years of age within wildlife refuges that present ideal habitat conditions for amphibians; (2) Control - agricultural ditches that sustain a population of at least one amphibian species; and (3) Restored/WRE - parcels under 20 years of age enrolled in the WRE program. Our primary objective was to model the relationships between habitat variables and amphibian diversity to inform conservation efforts in these diverse wetland habitats. Amphibians were found to widely occupy WRE parcels, with a range of habitat variables supporting occupancy and persistence of amphibian communities. The age of a wetland was found to be more important than other habitat features in predicting higher levels of amphibian diversity. We discuss the means by which WRE parcels are suitable for amphibians that are ecological generalists, but might require continued management in order to support populations of imperiled species that are considered habitat specialists. Ben Thompsky
545: Evaluating introgression rates between sympatric species is crucial when one of the species is threatened with extinction. We measured interspecific admixture in endangered Houston toads (Bufo [=Anaxyrus] houstonensis) and sympatric Gulf Coast toads (Bufo [=Incilius] nebulifer) using multilocus genotypes and mitochondrial sequence data to evaluate the level and direction of admixture on a recovery site over a 2-year period (2020–2021). Prior assessments (2000–2008) detected higher genetic admixture in Houston toads than was indicated by phenotypic assessments, with asymmetric backcrossing in which F1 hybrids backcrossed more frequently with Houston toads during a period of critically low Houston toad abundance (n = 30 - 171 annually) relative to more abundant Gulf Coast toads (n > 100 annually). An increase in Houston toad abundance and larger breeding aggregations was hypothesized to alleviate hybridization by reducing hybridization opportunities under decreased rarity. Although we observed an increase in Houston toad breeding aggregate sizes (n = 114 - 422), potentially due to population supplementation efforts, we observed no corresponding change in levels of interspecific admixture in Houston toads. We confirmed a strong discrepancy between genotypic and phenotypic identification of hybrids based on distinguishing morphological characteristics of the focal species, indicating that phenotypic identification of hybrids is unreliable whereas genotypic identification is effective. Historically, the peaks in breeding of the rare and common taxa in this system were reported as non-overlapping, but under changing climatic conditions the prezygotic isolating mechanisms may now differ from those described previously, potentially enabling the maintenance of stable hybridization rates. Jordan Zulli
546: For invasive species, transient populations may lead to extirpation, establishment, or expansion. Transience refers to short-term population dynamics that arise when populations are displaced from equilibrium. Although all invading populations may experience transient dynamics, transient populations have been poorly studied in invasion biology, especially in lizards. Once introduced, habitat selection plays an important role in the establishment of invasive species, as areas with higher habitat quality may provide greater opportunities for establishment. Podarcis siculus is an ideal species for examining shifts in habitat selection in transient populations due to its widespread distribution, success as an invader, and long-documented history of a transient population. Here, we test whether habitat selection differs between a transient population and its mainland counterparts. We conducted habitat and visual encounter surveys along 70 transects on the transient population of P. siculus on Elba Island to estimate habitat use and availability and quantify habitat selection, and compared these to two native mainland populations (Calci and Livorno) in Tuscany, Italy. We found differences in perch selection (p = 0.01) and refuge range (p = 0.001) among populations. Selection coefficients suggested the strongest perch type selection in Elba (rock, wall, path) and Livorno (wall, path), with lower overall selection in Calci, where path and wall perches were most selected. Temperature and perch height did not differ between transient and mainland populations. Understanding habitat selection differences between established and transient populations may provide insight into how invasion processes manifest across stages and contribute to invasion success. Jeremy M. Higgs
547: The all-female, polyploid salamanders in the genus Ambystoma reproduce through a unique strategy called kleptogenesis. Female salamanders use sperm from males of other sympatric Ambystoma species, occasionally introducing these nuclear genomes into their clonal offspring. Because kleptogenesis exists in the middle ground between clonal and sexual reproduction, unisexual salamanders provide a unique study system to test how reproductive mode—and resulting genetic diversity—affects parasite resistance. In this study, I tested the hypothesis that sexual reproduction increases salamander parasite resistance, resulting in higher parasite loads within unisexual salamanders compared to small-mouthed salamanders (Ambystoma texanum) from the same sites. I collected 120 salamanders and quantified helminth abundance, intensity, and prevalence among individuals. I tested the effect of sexual reproduction using a generalized linear mixed-modeling approach. This study helps elucidate the relationship between sexual strategy and parasite resistance by examining a lineage that is not strictly asexual or sexual, while being the first to examine parasite communities within unisexual and small-mouthed salamanders. Zander Perelman
548: Illegal gold mining threatens a 78 ha tract of primary rainforest along Ecuador’s Chumbiyacu Stream, a biodiversity hotspot situated between the Pitalala and Jatun Sacha reserves. To secure this parcel and create a continuous protected corridor, the Khamai Foundation had three months to document an endangered species that would meet grant criteria for land acquisition. We executed a five-day BioBlitz employing diurnal and nocturnal visual-encounter surveys, acoustic monitoring, and macro-photography to inventory herpetofauna. More than 40 reptile and amphibian taxa were recorded, including dense assemblages of rocket-frog (Hyloxalus) tadpoles. On the final survey day we captured, imaged, and released an adult Hyloxalus maculosus—the Spotted Rocket Frog— confirming the first known population of this IUCN-Endangered species inside a potential protected area. This record provides the biological evidence required to unlock conservation financing for the land purchase, thereby safeguarding habitat for thousands of co-occurring species and linking two existing reserves.
