The BioBlitz also galvanized local engagement and produced high-resolution imagery now driving crowdfunding and ecotourism campaigns that offer sustainable economic alternatives to gold extraction.
549: To understand a species’ relationship to its environment requires that we first separate true habitat associations from artifacts of sampling bias, particularly for reptiles where detections are often road-based. Bogertophis subocularis has historically been described as either a lowland or montane species, but these classifications remain qualitative and inconsistently supported. This study quantitatively evaluates the ecological niche of B. subocularis while explicitly accounting for road detection sampling bias. Occurrence records (n = 928) were obtained from iNaturalist and paired with adjacent available habitat points (n = 2000) generated from buffered road networks to represent accessible sampling space. Environmental variables, including elevation and landcover, were extracted using GIS. Generalized linear mix models (GLMMs) were used to evaluate the effects of elevation (including a quadratic term) and habitat class on occurrence, with model selection conducted using Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC). Top supported model (AIC = 5930.4) included both elevation and habitat variables and outperformed elevation-only models. Occurrence probability exhibited a unimodal relationship with elevation, peaking at mid-elevations (~800–1100 m). This pattern persisted after accounting for roadside sampling bias, indicating that the observed distribution is not solely driven by detections along roads. Habitat class further structured occurrence, with marginal and mixed habitats increasing odds of occurrence, while rocky habitats were associated with reduced occurrence probability. These results demonstrate that B. subocularis is best characterized, a mid-elevation species whose distribution is shaped by both elevation and habitat. More broadly, this study highlights the value of citizen science datasets when sampling bias is addressed. Jake J Wood
550: As ectotherms, most reptiles rely on their environment to thermoregulate. Most existing research on reptile thermoregulatory behavior was done either ex-situ, usually using artificial thermal gradients, or in-situ, using telemetry. However, replicating natural thermal conditions and variations indoors is difficult. Telemetry equipment is expensive and often too large for many reptile species. Furthermore, telemetry is labor intensive (which limits data collection frequency) and potentially affects the animal’s behavior. Therefore, we decided on using Light-level Geolocators—tiny devices weighing less than one gram originally developed to track the relative latitudes of migratory birds—to record the thermoregulatory patterns of the Desert Spiny Lizard (Sceloporus magister) in their natural habitat, without requiring direct human observation. We used light level data to approximate the microhabitat type (i.e. underground, shade, or above ground) the lizards were present at any given time of day, and we analyzed microhabitat type against weather variables provided by our operative temperature models and weather station. Our data showed that S. magister exhibited surface activity active year-round, despite the harsh summer conditions that some other lizard species (i.e. Gambelia sila) coped by entering aestivation underground. Certain weather variables were also shown to impact the timing of lizard activities, and these patterns shifted as the seasons changed. Our study will be one of the first to record thermoregulatory shuttling behavior in a small reptile in the wild for extended periods of time, and this research will add to our growing knowledge in reptile biologging and device miniaturization. Erin Yang
551: Pacific newts (Taricha spp.) possess a deadly neurotoxin called tetrodotoxin (TTX) which is concentrated on the surface of their skin. TTX is considered a keystone molecule, meaning it has a relatively strong impact on community structures despite its low abundance. Studies in laboratory settings demonstrate that small quantities of TTX leach off the skin of adult newts into surrounding water. Taricha spp. gather in incredible densities in freshwater ponds and streams annually to breed; however, it is unknown whether newts meaningfully influence TTX levels in these aquatic habitats. This study takes advantage of seasonal patterns of newt abundance in a breeding pool to evaluate whether Taricha spp. may serve as a source of environmental TTX. We performed visual newt counts and measured TTX levels in water and sediment from a breeding pond that houses rough skinned and California newts (T. granulosa and T. torosa) and a nearby control pond that lacks newts. Sampling was performed every three weeks for a year, generating a longitudinal dataset that allows us to determine whether newt abundance is correlated with environmental TTX levels. Additionally, we collected data on the rate of TTX leaching from individual newt egg masses, larvae and adults at our site of interest. This is the first study of TTX levels in freshwater and sediment in North America and the first to use modern analytical techniques. Findings may provide insight into indirect ecological consequences of Taricha spp. chemical defenses and breeding behavior, and how TTX functions as a keystone molecule.
552: I will discuss my field-based research program on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, and our team’s application of phylogenomic and population genomic approaches to study species delimitation and historical biogeography on this remarkable island. Ever since Alfred Russel Wallace, Sulawesi has been noted for its extremely high degree of endemism. Here we reinforce this understanding using modern approaches. Our work furthermore shows that in situ species diversification on Sulawesi has been substantially underestimated, and that the diverse mechanisms driving speciation on Sulawesi are directly tied to the island’s extremely complex tectonic history and extensive history of mountain-building. Case studies involving lizards and frogs will illustrate this underestimated diversity, as well as the roles of both typical and atypical modes of speciation on the island. Mei Lin McLaughlin
553: Whereas consensus on the moral of Southey’s (1837) classic fable has yet to be reached, the “Goldilocks Principle” has been applied to various disciplines, including astronomy, economics, and biology. My interpretations of what is “just right” in the field of herpetology have been informed by examining the impacts of habitat structure on predatory performance. I review how predators should forage optimally by assessing both risks and rewards, including variability in the resources and niches available from the habitats in which they seek prey. An effective environment for quantifying foraging performance represents a middle ground between lab-based control and field-based realism. Such mesocosms are available in display enclosures at zoological parks, meaning that opportunities for continued experimentation can explore a range of ethological and ecological questions. Another interpretation of what is “just right” for professional herpetologists is uniting the scientific societies in North America that share this taxonomic focus. Given the speed at which advances in our field are being made in the 21 century, merging under a single administrative umbrella provides the best assurance for the future persistence and health of our community and its members. Steve Mullin
554: ASIH and other professional organizations across the spectrum of biodiversity research value human diversity — differences in culture, ethnicity, gender, age, ability, lived experience, and thought. However, ASIH, and other biodiversity research societies, have struggled with increasing the diversity of their memberships.  We are told that diversity is a fundamental driver of innovation, creativity, and resilience in both professional organizations and society at large. Why then is it so difficult for us to make our organizations more inclusive? In this presentation, I will discuss my experiences as an African American ASIH member, researcher and long-term advocate for Diversity, Equity and Inclusion in STEM. I will describe how my ethnicity brought new perspectives and innovations to the way I approached curation and improvement of a large fish collection I was responsible for at Tulane University, and how this led to my many accomplishments in research, grantsmanship and scholarly work. Henry L. Bart Jr.
556: Understanding the spatial ecology of gravid sharks is critical for identifying habitats that support gestation and parturition. Such knowledge informs site-based management strategies to safeguard vulnerable life stages. Given sharks’ K-selected traits - slow maturation and low fecundity - protection of reproductive habitats is fundamental to population persistence. In Mo’orea, French Polynesia, home to one of the world’s largest shark sanctuaries, adult blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus) are relatively well studied, but movements of gravid females remain poorly understood. To address this, free-ranging adult females were captured via handlines in October 2025 at two contrasting lagoon sites: Ha’apiti (relatively undisturbed) and Vai’are (more urbanized). Reproductive status was assessed with ultrasonography, and 10 late-stage gravid individuals (124.8-148.0 cm TL) were equipped with SPOT6 fin-mounted satellite tags. After filtering, data from 8 individuals were retained for state-space modeling. Tracks were regularized to 12-hour intervals, yielding 41-261 predicted locations per individual over 20-130 days. Movement analyses revealed strong site fidelity and clear spatial segregation between sites. Kernel density estimates indicated small home ranges, with mean 95 % utilization distributions of 17.2 km² (7.0-39.8 km²) and mean core (50 %) areas of 3.8 km² (1.2-8.5 km²). These patterns indicate site-specific habitat use and potential maternal strategies, including selection of stable or optimal conditions that may influence gestation. Together, these findings highlight the need to explicitly consider maternal habitat use when evaluating shark sanctuaries and designing management strategies that protect reproduction as well as species presence. Kirsty Ballard
557: The angelshark, Squatina squatina, is a Critically Endangered species with its last stronghold of abundance around the Canary islands. Although now protected, the long-term resilience of this species relies on its adaptability to future environmental changes. We used genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to assess the genetic status of Canary Island angelsharks. The SNPs revealed the islands of Gran Canaria, Tenerife, and Lanzarote each harbor a genetically distinct subpopulation. Genomic autosomal heterozygosity (0.000212) was the lowest of all Critically Endangered shark species and populations assessed to date, suggesting low future adaptive potential. However, inbreeding levels were also low across all subpopulations (mean F = 0.0104), implying inbreeding depression is not the cause of the low genetic diversity. Effective population size (Ne) estimates of the angelshark at Gran Canaria island included point estimates over 1,000 and lower Jackknife 95% confidence intervals above 500, suggesting resilience against genetic diversity loss in the foreseeable future. The Ne estimates for Lanzarote and Tenerife islands, although having limited precision, possessed lower confidence intervals with minimum Ne estimates of over 100, indicating resilience to genetic diversity loss over at least the next five generations in both populations. Overall, our results suggest that despite the notably low current genetic diversity of angelsharks, future genetic diversity loss in this species at the Canary Islands may be preventable with the continuation and enhancement of current conservation efforts. Hung-Chia Chang (Vincent)
558: Sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus) inhabit the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB) from early summer through mid-to-late fall when they migrate south. Though they are federally protected, the species is legally targeted for catch-and-release during portions of their migration. The plasticity of their movements on and offshore, coupled with logistical challenges associated with tracking highly migratory sharks, leaves the movement behavior of sandbar sharks unresolved throughout their southern migration. Here, we describe the three-dimensional habitat use of sandbar sharks off coastal New York and throughout their southerly migration. In the summer and fall of 2024 and 2025, thirty-six pop-off satellite archival tags (PSATs) were deployed on sandbar sharks (ranging from 109 – 205 cm total length) in the MAB and programmed to pop off after 6 or 9 months. We applied an integrated step- selection analysis to illuminate movement behavior and habitat selection throughout their migration. The tagged sharks were tracked for 4–249 days (mean = 135 days). Sandbar sharks displayed clear seasonal migrations from July 2024 through mid-April 2026, spending the summer and early fall months in the Mid-Atlantic Bight, migrating south in the fall and overwintering off the coast of North and South Carolina, then migrating north in the spring. Sandbar sharks recorded depths of 0.5 – 300 m (mean = 26.8 m) and temperatures between 7.6⁰C – 27.5 ⁰C (mean = 20.4 ⁰C). This work contributes to the growing body of literature on shark migratory patterns and builds our understanding of sandbar shark habitat use throughout understudied regions of their annual migration. Fernando Marquez
559: Citizen science - also known as community science - is a low-cost research tool capable of generating large amounts of data, and has increasingly been employed for chondrichthyan research globally. This meta-analysis of published research (n=128) identifies trends and gaps in how citizen science is used to address research questions in shark, ray, skate, and chimaera biology and conservation. Studies addressed a total of 352 species (213 batoids, 139 sharks, and 0 chimaeras). Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus; 26 studies), tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier; 21 studies), and oceanic manta rays (Mobula birostris; 20 studies) were most commonly studied using these tools. While a higher total number of batoid species were studied, more studies were focused on sharks. These trends were primarily driven by carcharhiniform and myliobatiform species. 93% of studies included at least one species of IUCN Red List conservation concern. Most studies collected data in the Temperate Northern Atlantic (47 studies) and Central Indo-Pacific (37 studies). Over 75% of studies were subsidized in some way by the ecotourism or fishing industries, and the majority of studies collected data via no- or low-engagement programs and featured visual media/basic sightings as the basis of citizen-contributed data. It is clear, however, that use of citizen science in the study of chondrichthyans was under-detected by the systematic literature search. Meta-analysis reveals reporting on study methods and participant training requires increased attention, and that how the term “citizen science” is defined and used varies widely within the field. Ashley Willis Mascarenas
560: The Tiger Shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) is a large, highly migratory predator that exhibits variable growth patterns across its circumglobal distribution. Current and reliable life history data are necessary for informed management of Tiger Sharks in the western North Atlantic (WNA), for which the stock status remains unknown. Age estimates were derived from vertebral band counts for 252 Tiger Sharks collected from the Gulf of America (GOA) and U.S. Atlantic coast between 2005 and 2025. Results from multiple growth functions fitted to length-atage data demonstrated little difference in Tiger Shark growth between sexes or regions within the WNA. Overall, these updated parameters suggest that WNA Tiger Sharks grow more quickly and reach smaller sizes (L∞=317 cm fork length; k=0.17 years-1) than previously reported. Similarly, population maturity parameters calculated for the GOA (n=166) suggest that Tiger Sharks mature earlier and at smaller sizes than previously estimated, with females exhibiting the greatest deviation from previous research (L50=254.1 cm, A50= 9.5 years). Findings from this study underscore the advantages of a multi-model approach to age and growth studies and highlight potential impacts of sampling design on elasmobranch life history parameter estimates. Lucille McCain
561: The Stingray Sandbar site in the North Sound of Grand Cayman hosts a year-round, largely resident aggregation of southern stingrays (Hypanus americanus), resulting from four decades of daily ecotourismprovisioning. Behavioral shifts in these stingrays from provisioning have been well documented, but potential genomic impacts remain unexamined. Since mating and parturition have been observed here, there is concern that this multi-decadal human-provisioning may be altering the aggregation’s evolutionary trajectory. We used restriction site-associated DNA sequencing to compare genome-wide variation in the Cayman aggregation stingrays and non-provisioned stingrays from three other Caribbean sites: Grand Cayman south side, Bimini-Bahamas, and Belize. Stingrays from Grand Cayman, Bimini, and Belize comprise distinct genetic populations, with no population differentiation found within Grand Cayman. Relatedness analysis of the Cayman aggregation individuals detected 97 first order and 188 second order relatives, which was notably higher than the number of relatives identified in the Bimini population. Pedigree reconstruction of the Cayman aggregation revealed three generations of stingrays captured during the 21-year sampling period and one prominent family group. Lack of substructure within Grand Cayman, coupled with minimal estimates of inbreeding and similar genetic diversity estimates in the aggregation compared to the non-provisioned Caribbean stingrays, suggests that ecotourism feeding is not adversely affecting the aggregation’s genetic health. However, given the genetic and geographic isolation of Grand Cayman stingrays from other Caribbean populations and high number of relatives in the aggregation, continued genetic monitoring is recommended to support the Caymanian ecotourism industry while promoting long-term sustainable management of the iconic aggregation. Kannon C Pearson
562: Shark populations are declining worldwide, making it critical to evaluate how environmental variability influences their occurrence within protected areas. Cabo Pulmo National Park (CPNP), a no-take marine protected area in the Gulf of California, provides a rare opportunity to assess shark responses under long-term protection. We analyzed six years of land-based visual surveys (2013–2019; 1,210 observation hours) using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) to examine relationships between shark catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) and oceanographic and astronomical variables. Sea surface temperature, the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), proximity to the continental slope, wave height, particulate organic carbon flux, and photoperiod emerged as significant predictors of overall shark abundance. Species-specific models revealed contrasting environmental drivers: bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) were most influenced by ONI and productivity pulses, blacktip sharks (C. limbatus) by temperature, lunar phase, and slope proximity, and lemon sharks (Negaprion brevirostris) by salinity and lunar phase. These results demonstrate that both large-scale climatic oscillations and local habitat features shape shark occurrence within CPNP, generating pronounced seasonal variability and periods of absence. Incorporating environmental variability into monitoring frameworks is essential for interpreting population trends and for developing adaptive conservation strategies that extend beyond static marine reserve boundaries. Ethan Personius
563: Understanding the spatiotemporal movements of marine organisms within marine protected areas are essential for evaluating the efficacy of management practices designed to protect and conserve species. However, establishing measures to encompass species with large spatial extents can impose significant challenges when baseline data are limited. Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary (FGBNMS) in the Gulf of Mexico is a unique MPA for evaluating these concerns, as its remote offshore location provide benthic habitat for tropical fishes and foraging opportunities for many highly migratory species such as tunas, billfishes, and sharks. The silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis) and sandbar shark (Carcharhinus plumbeus) are two species that frequent the sanctuary and surrounding habitats, yet their spatiotemporal movement patterns within this region remain poorly understood. Movement patterns for 24 silky and 24 sandbar sharks were investigated using acoustic telemetry from August 2022 to October 2025. Acoustic receivers were deployed along the continental shelf at 17 sanctuary banks, four nonsanctuary banks, and 13 artificial reefs. Silky sharks displayed variable connectivity preferring natural banks during the winter and spring, shifting to artificial reefs in the summer. Conversely, sandbar sharks showed consistent, yearround presence across both natural banks and artificial habitats, with 46% of tagged individuals detected beyond the FGBNMS acoustic network compared to only 9% of tagged silky sharks. These findings expand our understanding of species-habitat linkages and demonstrate that sanctuary banks, non-sanctuary banks, and artificial reefs collectively constitute dynamic habitat use that is integral for two highly migratory shark species in the Gulf of Mexico. Dominic Swift Dominic Swift; Eric Anderson; Christopher Hollenbeck; Kevin Feldheim; R. Grubbs; Gregg Poulakis; John Carlson;
564: Caves are naturally-formed passages which lack natural light and contain species adapted to darkness. Shallow undersea caves have a distinct community structure to the local ecosystem, including bioluminescent species and those which thrive in dim light and low current, although this has never been studied within the deep sea. We conducted visual surveys at the Daito Islands in Okinawa, which possess caves on land, in 2024 and 2025 utilizing remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and discovered two cave systems: one through-cave at Minamidaito Island (400 m) and one blind-end cave at Kitadaito Island (340 m). The interior of both cave systems was surveyed using a miniature ROV, and the exterior slope was surveyed from 250–500 m to compare with the community inside both caves. Overall fish richness and diversity were higher at Minamidaito, although Kitadaito was surveyed for less time and the cave system has not yet been fully explored. While species richness, diversity, and density of fishes were not significantly different inside both caves compared to the slope, some species were only observed within caves although none were endemic. Similar trends were observed with corals, yet echinoderms had higher density within the through-cave at Minamidaito which was driven by an abundance of brisingid sea stars. More precise mapping of the caves and deploying a stationary camera this year will allow us to examine the impacts of current flow on fishes and if the community changes based on time of day. Emily Bergman
565: The Florida Reef Track represents the only barrier reef system in continental North America, functioning within an interconnected mosaic of seagrass meadows, mangroves, and coral reefs. Seagrass beds are critical marine ecosystems providing essential fish habitat, nursery grounds, and feeding areas for numerous species. In the Florida Bay (FB), Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary (FKNMS), and the Dry Tortugas National Park (DT), these ecosystems are the predominant benthic community type, supporting both commercially and ecologically important, as well as cryptic fish species. We examined fish community structure across 62 permanent seagrass sites spanning FB, FKNMS, and DT by conducting underwater visual censuses using 200 m² belt transects during winter and summer seasons to characterize the complete fish community. Our surveys documented 144 fish species from 51 families. The most important families in terms of richness were Gobiidae, Labridae, Serranidae, Syngnathidae and Scaridae. Labridae, Haemulidae, Gobiidae, Lutjanidae, and Gerreidae were the most important families in terms of abundance. Diversity metrics showed no significant seasonal variation; however, they revealed significant spatial heterogeneity. Offshore seagrass beds exhibited higher species richness and Shannon diversity compared to Bay habitats, with community composition significantly structured by spatial location (PERMANOVA: R² = 0.18, p < 0.001). Multivariate analyses were conducted to assess which environmental variables drive the diversity patterns in fish communities in seagrass meadows across the surveyed area. Seagrass canopy, seagrass meadow type, depth, distance to other ecosystems (reefs, shore), and sediment type emerged as critical predictors of fish diversity. Christopher Cousins
566: Ectoparasitism is rare among vertebrates, yet these interactions may strongly influence food-web dynamics because ectoparasites feed at a high trophic position. The wimple piranha, Catoprion, feeds on the scales of other fishes; however, which species it targets and why remain unknown. We examined stomach contents from a total of 109 Catoprion individuals collected from rivers in eastern Guyana. Scales ingested by Catoprion were matched against a reference library made from scales collected from potential host fishes living in their community, in order to 1) identify host preference and 2) test whether Catoprion targets hosts with larger scales (i.e., scales with larger surface areas) or scales that require little force to dislodge. For this latter question, we quantified the force needed to dislodge scales from fishes using a handheld force transducer. In addition, we estimated the trophic position of Catoprion, in relation to potential host, and other fish in its community, using stable isotope analysis of carbon and nitrogen. Stomach content analysis revealed Catoprion frequently consumed scales from top- and mesopredatory fishes, including erythrinids and anostomids, which have large scales, relative to other syntopic fishes. Stable isotope ratios inferred Catoprion as feeding at the highest trophic position within this diverse neotropical fish assemblage. We propose that Catoprion may select hosts based on scale size or overall body size, rather than the mechanical ease of scale removal, highlighting a potential trade-off between foraging efficiency and scale profitability. Dean A. Hendrickson
567: Understanding the obligate relationship between freshwater unionid mussels and the host fish(es) of their larvae (glochidia) is key to the conservation of this generally threatened fauna. A significant challenge in determining these relationships is demonstrating the connection in nature. This study aimed to make a definitive link in the wild between the endangered Hickorynut mussel and its putative host fish the Lake Sturgeon, while also examining other potential fish-mussel connections. Hundreds of Lake Sturgeon and other fishes were captured over three field seasons (summer & fall) between 2021-2023 in the Ottawa River and the fluvial St. Lawrence. Glochidia were confirmed on 17 wild-caught fishes of five species from the Ottawa River: Burbot, Lake Sturgeon, Sauger, Walleye, and Yellow Perch. Morphological and genetic “keys” for glochidia were developed in-house from expert-identified adult females of the 10 mussel species distributed in the lac Coulonge region of the Ottawa River. Individual (not pooled) control and encysted glochidia on wild-caught fishes were quantified for four linear measurements and a larval hinge character and sequenced for mtDNA COI. Morphological identifications were confirmed using PCA and 3D plotting while genetic identifications were confirmed with phylogenetic and distancebased methods. We also examined historical museum and provincial fish collections for evidence of glochidia, with success in confirmation of mussel glochidia on fluid-preserved specimens. Approximately one-third of all freshwater mussels in Canada are at risk; identifying the life history requirement of which fish species can harbor their developing larvae in nature is critical to the development of conservation plans. Yuval Itescu Neri Blas(University of Haifa); Ryan Appler(San Diego State University); Kinsey Brock(San Diego State University); Yuval
568: The Neotropical catfish family Trichomycteridae contains parasite fishes that include scale and mucus-feeders (Subfamily Stegophilinae) and blood feeders (i.e., the Candirus;Vandelliinae). While parasitic fishes may be an important link in food webs, their role in trophic interaction and the dynamics on freshwater food webs are mostly unknown. Most ecological information on the feeding ecology of freshwater parasite catfishes have been based on visual observation of their diets via stomach content analysis, a method that might not provide enough resolution to determine the origin of food ingested, trophic positions, and overall trophic interactions. We used stable isotope analysis of carbon (13C) and nitrogen (15N) to explore the vertical trophic structure of a Neotropical riverine food web containing over 100 fish species including three species of trichomycterid catfishes. These parasitic catfishes exhibited the highest trophic position in food chain followed by piscivore and carnivore fishes. Contrary to the pattern seen across fishes of an increase in trophic position (TP) with body size, we demonstrated that TP does not correlate with the body size in tropical food containing parasitic trichomycterids. Compared to other fish species in our food webs, these parasitic catfishes were on average smaller in body size (~5 cm total length) compared to other fish species. Among the three species of parasitic catfishes examined, Ochmacanthus, the mucus-feeder, had greater 15N ratios enrichment compared to Paracanthopoma and Vandellia, both considered blood-feeder. Our findings from stable isotope analysis reveal that trichomycterid parasitic catfishes are top predators in these neotropical species-rich food webs. Carmen Montana
569: Assessing the success of marine protected areas requires determining whether fish abundances have increased since their delineation. Bahía de los Ángeles is one of the largest protected areas in the Gulf of California, Mexico. Still, since its creation, no formal monitoring has been conducted to assess fish assemblage trends and how the area succeeds in conserving them. In this work, the spatiotemporal trends of fish assemblages in the area were investigated between 2022-2023 using BRUVS. Monthly surveys were conducted across coastal sites and islands, covering multiple habitats, depths and management delineations. So far, 110 species from 53 families have been recorded. Serranidae had the highest richness among teleosts and Urotrygonidae among elasmobranchs. Species richness was highest in winter and summer, and lowest in spring. Low-complex sandy substrates were the dominant habitat, followed by rocky habitats with medium complexity. The highest species richness was recorded in highcomplexity rocky habitats. Twenty species represented 82.95% of the total relative abundance, with Microlepidotus inornatus (12.79%), Diplectrum pacificum (11.77%) and Balistes polylepis (11.50%) being the most abundant. Our results provide a baseline of fish assemblage trends in the area, which can inform management strategies within the protected area. Further, it demonstrates how using BRUVS can provide a systematic, cost-effective and fisheriesindependent monitoring. M. Christopher Norris
570: Deep tropical reef fishes are a poorly studied community due to their depths exceeding recreational SCUBA limits (40-300+ m). This has severely limited the knowledge on trophic relationships among deep reef fishes, and most of what we “know” about their diets is simply inferred from their shallow water relatives. However, deep reefs are ecologically distinct from shallow reefs with unique biotic and abiotic conditions that result in food webs that differ from those on shallow reefs. Nevertheless, trophic data for nearly all deep-reef fishes is nonexistent. This study seeks to examine the ratios of δ15N and δ13C in six common deep reef fishes and to map trophic relationships for the ecosystem. δ15N acts as a proxy for trophic position while δ13C tracks carbon sources and trophic plasticity. We used the submersible Curasub to collect specimens from six abundant species that occur on deep reef slopes in Curacao: Pronotogrammus martinicensis (Serranidae), Chrionema squamentum (Bembropidae), Symphysanodon beryi (Symphysanodontidae), Epigonus occidentalis (Epigonidae), Epigonus hexacanthus (Epigonidae) and Decodon puellaris (Labridae). Data from deep reef species will be compared to six abundant shallow water reef fishes from the same area: Stegastes diencaeus (Pomacentridae), Chaetodon capistratus (Chaetodontidae), Scarus iseri (Labridae), Myripristis jacobus (Holocentridae), Haemulon flavolineatum (Hemulidae), and Acanthurus tractus (Acanthuridae). Muscle and heart samples were taken to have a broader timespan of measurements as these tissues have distinct cell turnover rates. These values will be compared with samples from invertebrates and primary producers to begin to build a scaffold for food webs on Caribbean deep reefs. Sean Rovito
571: The idea of a periodic table of niches was first introduced by Robert MacArthur and elaborated by E.R. Pianka in his textbook Evolutionary Ecology. The concept was advanced by Winemiller et al. (2015, Ecol. Lett. 18:737) who proposed methodologies for its construction and tested them using a Neotropical fish traits dataset. This talk will explore the feasibility of developing a periodic table of niches for Neotropical fishes. Key to a periodic table are data of suitable quality at appropriate scales of resolution for traits associated with five niche dimensions (habitat, life history, trophic, defense, metabolic). At a coarse scale of resolution, there is greater likelihood of revealing niche convergence and a simpler classification scheme. A fine scale of trait resolution would result in more taxon uniqueness and a more complex scheme. A traits database for Neotropical fishes, Ecomatrix (Albert et al., 2025, Scientific Data 12:1127), codes species according to 12 traits, including body length, habitat use, trophic guilds, migratory behavior, and physiological traits such as electroreception, viviparity, and venom. To support analyses for producing a periodic table of niches, data are needed for more traits, especially for life history, defense and metabolic dimensions, information currently lacking for most Neotropical fishes. Traits data appear in other databases (e.g., Fishbase) for certain Neotropical species. Is construction of periodic tables of niches worth a collective effort from the scientific community? Discussed are research topics and conservation applications that could be advanced with periodic tables of niches. Megan Winton
572: The genus Mystus (family Bagridae) represents a diverse group of freshwater catfishes distributed across South and Southeast Asia, with limited occurrence in West Asia. Despite this wide distribution, species of Mystus show relatively low morphological differentiation, making taxonomy challenging and obscuring their evolutionary relationships. Previous phylogenetic studies have also produced conflicting results regarding the monophyly and systematic placement of the genus. In this study, we examined evolutionary relationships within Mystus using genome-wide restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RADseq). Phylogenomic analyses recovered Mystus as largely monophyletic, except for Mystus leucophasis, which was placed outside the core Mystus clade. The widely distributed species Mystus gulio was recovered as potentially monophyletic across its geographic range. All the Sri Lankan Mystus species were recovered as distinct evolutionary lineages. Overall, Mystus lineages were structured into two major clades. Within one clade, the Middle Eastern Mystus species formed a monophyletic subgroup. These findings provide phylogenomic support for the monophyly of Mystus sensu stricto, clarify relationships among major Mystus lineages, and highlight potential taxonomic inconsistencies within the genus. This study improves our understanding of Mystus evolutionary history and establishes a framework for future systematic and taxonomic revisions within the family Bagridae. João Marcelo Abreu
573: The sciaenid fish genus Corvula is known for its absence of canines and a narrow band of teeth, contrasting with long canines and single band of teeth found in Odontoscion. However, phylogenetic and species delimitation analyses have raised concerns about these characters and suggest that Corvula should be designated a junior synonym of Odontoscion. Here, focusing on Pacific Ocean species, we present morphological data suggesting a close relationship between these genera. Ontogenetic series demonstrate that C. macrops and O. xanthops exhibit distinct patterns of line and fin coloration. Odontoscion eurymesops can also be easily distinguished from the other two species by its several faint lines and the absence of conspicuous stripes, which are found in the juveniles of the other two species. Additionally, principal component analysis reveals distinct morphospace occupation between these genera, though there is some overlap between C. macrops and O. eurymesops. Therefore, we propose that both genera warrant recognition. A recent diagnosis of Odontoscion agrees that presence or absence of canines and spines on the preopercle are not reliable characters for supporting these genera. We argue that a phylogenetic analysis would improve these diagnosis and address uncertainties, particularly those concerning Corvula. Alyssa M. Andres
574: Silver Carp Hypophthalmichthys molitrix and Bighead Carp H. nobilis (collectively bigheaded carp) are aquatic invasive species in the United States with established populations throughout the Mississippi River basin. Bigheaded carp typically spawn when water temperatures exceed 18°C and water velocities reach 0.7 m/s. These deep, fast-flowing channels of the Mississippi and Missouri rivers may not be as conducive to bigheaded carp reproduction compared to tributaries with more suitable habitat. Yet, little is known about their reproductive readiness in shallower tributary systems such as the Platte River, a major tributary to the Missouri River. Currently for this study, approximately 900 bigheaded carp were collected in 2025. Gonadosomatic index (GSI) was calculated for 195 females and 407 males and compared across months and localities. We found a peak in female GSI in June followed by a steady decline through the end of summer into fall. In males, we found an early peak in GSI values in April and May followed by a progressive decline through October. Male and female GSI values followed a similar trend when grouped by locality, where GSI increased in populations further from the PlatteMissouri confluence, potentially indicative of density-dependent constraints on body condition and reproductive readiness. Data collection and analysis will continue in 2026 to verify and expand on our current findings. The results of our study will provide insight into bigheaded carp reproductive patterns that will ultimately allow resource managers to determine best removal and control practices in these shallow-water systems. Grace A. Casselberry Grace Casselberry; Chris Juredin; Emily Buchalter; Kitty Daniels; Amy Morrison; Kendyl Bernā; Schuyler Weiss;
575: Diversification patterns reflect shifts in ecological interactions and morphology of organisms and often studied at evolutionary scales. Cichlids exemplify these patterns, with cranial element plasticity and diverse feeding mechanics and strategies driving their divergence, even within guilds (ecological groups) or tribes (taxonomic groups). Parachromis, a genus of five Neotropical cichlid species, is widespread across Middle America with some species having overlapping distributions. This genus has been broadly categorized as predatory, with species showing patterns of morphological variability. However, there is no consensus on what predatory strategies each species uses, nor whether their morphological feeding traits are conserved, raising questions about ecological similarity among species in the genus. We used an integrative approach to compare ecomorphological traits and isotopic space occupied by all species of Parachromis to investigate patterns of ecomorphological diversification. We quantified body shape and morphological disparity using standardized measurements and 2D geometric morphometrics based on museum specimens from all five species. We then focused on traits related to feeding, including adductor muscles, mouth protrusion and gape size, and lower pharyngeal jaw morphology, and explored their correlation with carbon and nitrogen stable isotopes as proxy for their trophic position. We analyze our data within a phylogenomic framework to test if ecomorphologies and isotopic space are conserved across phylogeny. We hypothesize low phylogenetic signal for ecomorphological traits and isopace occupied, suggesting that ecology played a strong role during the diversification of Parachromis. Overall, we test if Parachromis exhibits ecomorphological divergence more closely linked to ecological characteristics rather than phylogenetic patterns. Matthew Fujita
576: The family Bagridae (Bleeker 1858) is a widely dispersed clade of catfishes comprised of 225 species belonging to 15 Asian genera and one African genus. Nomenclatural credit is attributed to Bleeker’s 1858 tribe Bagrini, although the group is thought to have been first conceptualized with Cuvier’s 1816 “les Bagre.” Since its inception, Bagridae has been a revolving door of taxa due to the use of plesiomorphic characters in early diagnoses. Taxa belonging to 17 present-day catfish families have been variably assigned to Bagridae under different definitions of the group. Our current understanding of Bagridae is based on morphological systematics from the most recent revision of the family by Mo in 1991. Though a few bagrids have been included in order-level analyses, there has been no dedicated molecular study of Bagridae at the family level. Monophyly of the modern Bagridae has yet to be validated. Phylogenetic analysis of molecular data available on GenBank shows that current sampling is insufficient to address this problem. Only 126 bagrid species are represented on GenBank, of which only 35 are sampled at genomic or even mitogenomic scales and the remainder are largely represented by one or only a few single gene sequences. Additional tissue samples reflecting broader taxonomic sampling are required to facilitate a genomic approach to inferring the bagrid phylogeny. Here we present our current understanding of a molecular phylogeny of Bagridae and ask for contributors and collaborators on a more complete work to resolve the relationships of this long-overlooked catfish family. Joshua M Hall
577: The family Sciaenidae comprises approximately 300 species and 70 genera globally, and the IndoWest Pacific (IWP) region has the greatest concentration of Sciaenidae species diversity. However, the taxonomic status of many species in the IWP region remains unsolved, and recent phylogenetic analyses suggested a revision of the genus Nibea in particular. Nibea Jordan & Thompson, 1911 is a polyphyletic genus with currently 10 recognized species. In this study, we present the most comprehensive phylogenetic relationships of IWP sciaenids using COI and RAG1 genes and utilize integrated taxonomic methods to review the taxonomy of the genus Nibea. Our results confirm the monophyly of the genus Nibea, restricting it to only six valid species: N. mitsukurii, N. albiflora, N. semifasciata, N. muelleri, N. chui, and N. soldado. We also confirm that Nibea leptolepis is a valid species, but a junior synonym of N. muelleri. Nibea coibor, previously considered a senior synonym of Bola coibor Hamilton, 1822 is herein represented as an invalid species, and B. coibor with three anal-fin spines, is not from the family Sciaenidae, and its taxonomic placement requires further investigation. Based on mental pores, scales on second dorsal-fin rays and anal fin, sagittal otolith, swim bladder, and molecular data, we establish three new monotypic genera for three species formerly assigned to Nibea as Indonibea maculata comb. nov., Pseudonibea microgenys comb. nov. and Neonibea squamosa comb. nov.. These findings assist in clarifying the diverse and essential biodiversity of the IWP region with key implications for conservation and fisheries management. Alexis Lindsey
578: The Beryciformes and Trachichthyiformes (Acanthomorpha) represent a historically unstable assemblage of acanthomorph fishes that has undergone extensive taxonomic revision since the early cladistic era. As recognized here, the Beryciformes includes 216 species in nine families, whereas the Trachichthyiformes includes 73 species in five families. Members of these clades exhibit striking morphological diversity, including bacteriamediated bioluminescent organs in subocular, dentary, and perianal regions, extreme sexual dimorphism, modified intermuscular bones forming enlarged tympanic plates, extensive dermal armoring, and an extreme proliferation of rod opsin genes. These lineages have long been considered close relatives of Percomorpha yet competing molecular and morphological hypotheses have obscured their limits, internal relationships, and broader evolutionary history. Here we use genome-scale nuclear sequence data, mitochondrial genomes, and a newly constructed morphological dataset of ~300 discrete characters spanning hard- and soft-tissue, otolith, and larval anatomy to resolve the phylogenetic relationships of the closest relatives of the Percomorpha. Our results establish the monophyly of both the Trachichthyiformes and Beryciformes, with the Trachichthyiformes (spinyfins, fangtooths, flashlight fishes, roughies, pinecone fishes) recovered as the sister lineage to a clade comprising the Beryciformes (alfonsinos, pricklefishes, ridgeheads, squirrelfishes, whalefishes) and the Percomorpha. These results provide a revised phylogenetic framework for early acanthomorph evolution and establish a foundation for future work on character evolution across percomorph and related lineages. Christopher Malinowski Chris Malinowski; Gregg Poulakis; Dean Grubbs; Matthew Smukall; Ashley Dawdy; Carolyn Cray; Jeny Soto; Ally
579: The genus Schistura is recognized as containing 324 species (Fricke et al. 2026) even though it is universally accepted as being a paraphyletic assemblage. The Schistura cincticauda complex is a genetically, morphologically, and geographically distinct group of species found in southern Myanmar, western Thailand, and peninsular Thailand. Integrated taxonomic techniques were applied to determine the status of the group. A new genus name, Tanaser, is assigned and diagnosed by possessing modally 7½ branched dorsal fin rays and a pair of distinctive black blotches on the lower lip. Schistura udomritthiruji is considered the most basal member of the genus rather than sister to it. Tanaser amplia, sp. nov., is distinguished from other species in the genus genetically, by its large size (to 75 mm), and the combination of a pelvic lobe, a large black spot anteriorly on the dorsal fin base, and an uninterrupted black bar at the caudal fin base. It is known from one locality in a mountainous headwater stream of the Pachi River in the Mae Klong basin, Thailand. Tanaser erubesca, sp. nov., is distinguished from other species in the genus genetically and by the combination of no black bar at the caudal fin base, no large black spot at the dorsal fin base, 2–3 broad and diffuse grey bars below the dorsal fin, red color on the posterior half of the body, and a pelvic lobe. It is found in several mountainous streams in the Pachi River basin, Thailand.
580: According to the IUCN, there are roughly 40,000 species that are at risk of extinction, and 21% of those are reptile species. The Rough-footed Mud Turtle, Kinosternon hirtipes, is mostly endemic to Mexico, with one subspecies, the Mexican Plateau Mud Turtle (K. h. murrayi), extending into Texas. Anthropogenic factors, such as the introduction of feral pigs, the increase in raccoon populations, and the draining of natural draws for ranch land, have greatly decreased the population, making the Mexican Plateau Mud Turtle critically imperiled in the U.S. Much about their life history is understudied, and there is minimal information available about the diet of these turtles. A previous study examined fecal samples under dissecting scopes. While this method provided great insight into the diet, there is a bias toward food items that are less digestible, so soft-bodied insects and plants remain unknown. To obtain a comprehensive diet composition of Mexican Plateau Mud Turtles, DNA metabarcoding will be performed on 17 fecal samples collected from three locations near Big Bend Ranch State Park. This is the first effort to use molecular techniques to describe the diet of the Mexican Plateau Mud Turtle. Resulting sequences will be compared to reference libraries, and statistical analyses will be conducted between sites and sexes. It is likely that K. h. murrayi will require management, and the results from this study will allow researchers to better understand the dietary needs of this vulnerable subspecies. Gianna Busala Gianna Busala
581: The study of body temperature is fundamental to understanding the ecology of ectothermic organisms. Exploring how variation in temperature affects animals’ physiology allows us to predict local extinctions and range shifts and supports effective conservation planning. However, obtaining continuous and accurate body temperature measurements can be time-consuming, costly, and detrimental to the health of the study organisms. This necessitates creation of a method of monitoring body temperature that is both continuous and accurate, but also minimally invasive. One non-invasive method involves predicting body temperature using a temperature sensor on a collar or otherwise externally attached to the animal; however, these measurements become less accurate as sensors are exposed to bright sunlight. To improve the ability of these sensors to monitor body temperature, we created a model to calibrate externally mounted temperature sensors attached to two species of terrestrial turtle, the Eastern box turtle (T. carolina), and the wood turtle (G. insculpta). By integrating sensor temperature and light data with ambient conditions and in situ field measurements, we developed a model that enhances the accuracy and temporal resolution of turtle body temperature estimates across both species. This approach provides a practical framework for calibrating external sensors and continuously monitoring ectotherm body temperatures in variable environments, facilitating broader insights into these animals’ ability to persist and adapt to climate change. Danielle McAree
582: The Lesser Siren (Siren intermedia) is an aquatic caudate found in swamps, ponds, and other stagnant wetlands across the southern and central United States. There is relatively little published information on the ecology of S. intermedia, and no studies have used radio telemetry to track its movement. This project aims to better understand the cryptic life history of S. intermedia by observing aestivation, measuring movement, and estimating home range through the repeated relocation of individuals. A total of 23 S. intermedia were captured using steel minnow traps between 6/19/25 – 8/3/25 in two wetlands in Edwardsville, Illinois. Each individual was implanted with a 7 mm passive integrated transponder (PIT) tag inserted into its tail and 18 individuals were also surgically implanted with radio transmitters. After monitoring for recovery from surgery, individuals were released at their respective points of capture. Each S. intermedia was tracked using radio telemetry and GPS locations were recorded 3–4 times per week until entering aestivation. Movement ranged from 0 to 178.8 m between successive relocations. Home ranges were estimated using minimum convex polygons (MCPs), kernel density estimation (KDE), and autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE), with mean sizes of 450.3 m2, 5,390.5 m2, and 2,139.5 m2, respectively. This study provides a better understanding of S. intermedia life history and spatial ecology to help inform conservation strategies for Lesser Sirens and their associated aquatic communities. Maria Ojeda Nathan Burkett-Cadena; Lawrence Reeves; Maria Ojeda-Rojas; Eric Suarez; Miles McCollum; Tanise Stenn;
583: The hawksbill sea turtle (Eretmochelys imbricata) is a Critically Endangered spongivore whose microbiome remains virtually uncharacterized, and no prior study has examined body-site-specific microbial communities in wild Atlantic hawksbills, leaving host–microbe associations and potential links to spongivory unresolved. We collected buccal, cloacal, and skin swabs from 14 nesting adult females and 11 hatchlings on Mona Island, Puerto Rico. DNA was extracted using ZymoBIOMICS kits and the 16S rRNA V4 region was sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq. Reads were processed in QIIME 2 with DADA2, including decontamination via extraction controls. We analyzed alpha diversity (Shannon, observed richness), beta diversity (Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA with strata for repeated measures), indicator species, co-occurrence networks, phylogenetic community structure (NTI), and predicted functional profiling (PICRUSt2). Body site explained 20.2% of community variation (PERMANOVA R² = 0.202, p = 0.001), and skin harbored the highest diversity (Shannon 4.54 ± 0.20). The cloaca lacked core taxa entirely and exhibited discrete community states, while within-individual distances were significantly lower than between-individual distances (Wilcoxon p < 0.001), indicating individual identity also structures community composition. Hatchling communities did not differ from environmental controls. Wild adult hawksbills maintain distinct, body-site-specific microbial communities not previously described in any sea turtle: the skin hosts a structured phototrophic biofilm convergent across individuals, while the cloaca exhibits individualized communities, a pattern also seen in captive hawksbills fed non-sponge diets, suggesting a conserved host–microbe association. All methods were IACUC-approved. Funding: NSF #2334779. Ramses Rosales
584: Snakes can be difficult to study due to low population densities across wide ranges, crypsis, and secretive behavior. Survey methods such as artificial cover objects and live trap/drift fence systems are effective but require significant sampling effort in the field. The Adapted-Hunt Drift Technique (AHDriFT) combines drift fences with camera traps and has potential to reduce effort and resources required to sample snakes. We investigated whether landscape and weather variables influenced the number of Common Gartersnakes (Thamnophis sirtalis) detections using the AHDriFT system. We installed three-camera, Y-shaped, omnidirectional arrays in grassland habitat near wetlands at 12 sites across Northern Indiana that we sampled from mid-April through mid-October of 2024. We report on the influence of landscape variables, weather, and seasonality on snake detection. Results suggest that area of cultivated croplands, temperature, humidity, cloud cover, and time of year are predictive of T. sirtalis detections. This research aims to shed light on patterns in snake activity and population dynamics as well as potential biases associated with AHDriFT as a method for sampling snakes. Max Seldes
585: As invasive species continue to spread throughout Florida, it has become increasingly important to determine how community structure and diversity affect invasibility (susceptibility to invasion) in relatively undisturbed habitats. The Asian Swamp Eel (Monopterus albus/javanensis) is a relatively new invader in Florida, estimated to have been introduced in 1997 in the central-west and southeast. By early 2024, this invasive species, alongside others, has become well-established at Rainey Slough, an aquatic community in Glades County, Florida. In the 1970s, Rainey Slough hosted high amphibian and reptile biodiversity and biomass, but drastic herpetofaunal declines have occurred over the past 50 years, likely driven by competition and predation from nonnative fish species, like the Asian Swamp Eel. We used δ15N and δ13C stable isotope analysis to construct relative trophic niches of native and nonnative species sampled from 1967-2025, obtained from preserved specimens and fresh tissue. We tested two contrasting hypotheses which may have contributed to the success of these aquatic invaders: the Vacant Niche Hypothesis and the Niche Competition Hypothesis. By constructing Bayesian ellipses and assessing proportional overlap in trophic niche space, we can not only understand how nonnative species like the Asian Swamp Eel isotopically “fit” within the aquatic community, but which functional groups and specific native species may be the most vulnerable to new competitors and predators. Use of museum specimens for long-term food web analyses provides valuable insight into potential competitive interactions and changes in resource use over time following the introduction of nonnative species into a novel community. Brett Sweezey
586: Eradication of non-native species is unlikely once establishment has occurred beyond a small spatial area. Identifying areas that could support non-native species is crucial to prevent establishment and expansion, loss of native species, and reduced functional diversity. Increased connectivity between natural and artificial aquatic habitats results in greater abundances of non-native species. Compared to other clades of herpetofauna, crocodylians are infrequently introduced to novel regions. Salt-tolerant crocodylians might have a competitive advantage over stenohaline species because they can use a variety of aquatic habitats along the freshwater to seawater continuum. Therefore, determining whether or not the southeastern USA is suitable to additional salt-tolerant crocodylians is crucial, as establishment of novel species could further disrupt coexistence between native crocodylians. I used Bayesian integrative species distribution models to quantify the similarity in environmental variables of the southeastern USA and native localities of salt-tolerant species of crocodylians. Even if most habitats across the southeastern USA are suitable for salt-tolerant species, invasion risk is unlikely to be comparable across crocodylians. Trade increases likelihood of escape or release of individuals, increasing propagule pressure. Because nearly all salt-tolerant crocodylians have been traded in or out of the USA within the last 25 years, I used an index of relative invasiveness incorporating variables related to trade and natural history. Combined, these metrics identify salt-tolerant species of greatest concern for establishment and provide state and federal managers species in need of stricter trade regulations. Shannan Yates
587: Amphibian fences are used as population sampling devices, site exclusion tools and roadkill mitigation measures. Researchers have been studying fence design effectiveness at blocking amphibians since the 1990’s, however most studies were performed in the field and focused on single designs. We performed a series of experiments to compare amphibian fence designs in controlled conditions in order to determine the most effective ones. Amphibians were put in the unattractive departure compartment of an experimental arena at sunset, and had until sunrise to cross the tested fence to join an attractive arrival compartment. Trials were recorded using cameras to quantify interactions with the fence. Tested fence materials were concrete, galvanised steel panels, wire meshing, polyethylene meshing, and polyethylene tarp. Fences were tested with and without a 10 cm overhang at their top. Tested taxa included newts, toads, frogs and tree frogs to account for the diverse modes of locomotion of amphibians. Every amphibian could cross wire meshing and polyethylene netting fences without overhangs. Runner and short distance jumpers could be stopped by 20-25 cm high non-climbable fences (slick materials or overhangs). Long distance jumpers needed 60 cm high non-climbable fences to be stopped. Tree frogs could not jump over 35 cm fences, and were blocked by overhangs. Amphibians interacted less with the fences when they were dry, and made of slick, opaque materials. Our results highlighted the key importance of overhangs, which made any material effective at blocking amphibians, allowing to prioritise cost-efficient and practical materials.
588: Vulnerability assessments are commonly used to highlight the relative vulnerabilities of target species or taxonomic groups to climate change. Because land use changes, invasive species, and disease also threaten much of the world’s biota, traditional climate change vulnerability assessments (CCVA) likely underestimate the true vulnerability of species to multiple, interacting threats. We describe a new integrated vulnerability dataset for 320 native amphibian species across the continental USA (CONUS). This dataset includes projected exposure of native species to a range of future water deficit (i.e., drought) conditions, future land use development, current threats from key invasive species, and predicted habitat suitability for the pathogenic fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd). We then summarize sensitivity and adaptive capacities for each species based on life history traits, habitat preferences, and historical exposure to a range of water deficit conditions. To estimate integrated vulnerability, we multiplied exposure and sensitivity scores. The four major threat exposures varied in magnitude geographically and across taxonomic families. Combined high exposure hotspots were projected for the Appalachian Mountains, Florida, the Sierra Nevada Mountains, and coastal regions of the western seaboard. Caudates, and particularly species in Plethodontidae, had the highest sensitivity scores, which ultimately led to higher integrated vulnerabilities. Species with the highest vulnerability scores occurred in areas without or with very limited land protection. This gap suggests that creative conservation solutions are needed to protect and limit exposure for the most vulnerable amphibians across CONUS. Daniel Coffey
589: Invasive species present one of the most challenging threats to native biodiversity, particularly when they hybridize with imperiled native taxa. In California, hybridization between the endangered California tiger salamander (“CTS,” Ambystoma californiense) and the invasive barred tiger salamander (“BTS,” Ambystoma mavortium) is one of the best understood examples of this management challenge. Reclusive life history and cryptic hybridization, often on private land, render eradication programs difficult or impossible. This study evaluates hydroperiod management as a tool to conserve and maintain native CTS populations threatened by hybridization. We adapt a recent, empirically informed Bayesian integral projection model (IPM) for CTS to incorporate new results that link genotype and ecology to fitness, and use this individual-based model to evaluate alternative management scenarios. We found overwhelming support for the importance of hydrology in both native and hybrid populations, where a 10-day increase in hydroperiod can increase population growth rate (λ) 17% and triple the carrying-capacity (K). We assess hydroperiod management as a strategy to control and contain non-native introgression, and offer suggestions on the most cost-effective solutions. This study demonstrates the value of integrating demographic, genetic, and ecological information to evaluate strategies for endangered species management, and may serve as modeling framework for a wide variety of imperiled species. Hadley Copeland Hadley Copeland; Rachael Bryson; John Maerz; Elizabeth McCarty; Peter Hazelton
590: Knowledge of species traits is critical for conservation. Many large databases of species traits are available, but their use is often limited by data completeness, taxonomic coverage, and/or specificity of traits being assessed. We produced a database of traits for amphibian species native to the continental USA, reducing the total number of traits presented by other databases while increasing the total completeness and scope of data. The database includes 14 traits related to species’ growth, reproduction, and habitat use, compiled from existing published data repositories. This database presents a refined, more complete view of traits for amphibians and identifies current knowledge gaps in fundamental knowledge of species. Zeanna Graves
591: The Streamside Salamander (Ambystoma barbouri) has a disjunct distribution, with an isolated range concentrated in Tennessee’s Central Basin. These populations are both genetically distinct from the rest of the species’ range and have the greatest genetic diversity. The Tennessee populations of this species are also associated with the unique, and declining, limestone cedar glade ecosystem. These populations—and their unique genetics— are threatened by the rapid urbanization of the Nashville metropolitan area. The growth of this urban center, coupled with the difficulty in protecting intermittent streams, has resulted in extensive habitat loss for Streamside Salamander populations. Where breeding streams do remain, many have either been directly modified (e.g., armored, or put in culverts) or indirectly modified as the amount of impervious surfaces in the watershed increase. In many cases, these modifications lead to the major “symptoms” of Urban Stream Syndrome, such as increased temperature, increased scour, and decreased channel complexity. These impacts are also coupled with the loss of non-breeding habitat due to limited stream buffer protections. To understand how these changes are impacting Tennessee's Streamside Salamander populations, we surveyed streams with varying levels of urban impact to quantify reproductive success. We also surveyed the condition of the streams using a rapid bioassessment protocol for intermittent streams. Further, we have used land cover data to quantify the degree of urbanization and impervious surfaces in buffers and watersheds. In this presentation, we will provide our initial findings on the impacts of urbanization on Streamside Salamander populations in Tennessee. Kale Humphries
592: Calling is the first step in a complex series of behaviors and processes necessary for reproduction in anurans. Changes in call characteristics associated with human-associated disturbances may disrupt the reproductive process, impacting individual and, ultimately, population fitness. We investigated the effects of human disturbances, particularly anthropogenic noise, on the call characteristics of anurans in eastern Texas. Calls of five species, including Spring Peepers, Gray Treefrogs, Cope’s Gray Treefrogs, Green Treefrogs, and Gulf Coast Toads, were recorded at urban and rural sites that varied in noise levels, light levels, and presence of invasive species. Changes associated with anthropogenic noise were found in at least one call characteristic, including call frequency, call duration, and call rate, in most species. Spring peepers exhibited lower dominant frequency and higher call rate at more urbanized sites. Call rate of Green Treefrogs was lower an urban site, and Gulf Coast Toads had higher dominant frequencies and lower call rate at urban sites. Cope’s Gray Treefrogs had lower dominant frequencies at urban sites. Higher dominant frequency in Gray Treefrogs was associated with higher light levels, but not noise levels. Additionally, current study suggests invasive plant species, which are more prevalent in urbanized areas, affect calls in treefrogs. These data may help explain the absence of some species from urban sites as human disturbances may have disrupted calling enough to cause population decline. Alexandra Kwiatkowski
593: Genetic rescue is a conservation strategy by which fitness and genetic variation is increased in small, imperiled populations by supplementing with individuals from other populations, often using captive breeding methods. The Santa Cruz long-toed salamander, Ambystoma macrodactylum croceum, is state and federally listed as endangered and has a range limited to a small area along California’s central coast. The proliferation of commercial agriculture in the region, expansion of development, salinization of breeding ponds, and introduction of non-native species have led to population declines, inbreeding, and loss of genetic diversity. This loss of diversity can lead to an ‘extinction vortex’, wherein small populations can spiral to extinction. To counter this risk, we initiated a captive breeding program aimed at increasing genetic diversity in wild populations of this salamander. We used an admixture design, breeding across various populations and releasing the resultant larvae into shrinking populations and newly constructed ponds. We tracked the reproductive and survival success of released individuals using genetic mark-recapture techniques and a genetic pedigree analysis using newly developed microhaplotype markers. These markers have been used to validate parent-offspring relationships in our breeding program and examine reproductive strategies in the species. Preliminary results from microhaplotype development indicate the confirmation of multiple paternity in our system. Field surveys suggest that larval introductions have led to breeding success in a few ponds. Continued evaluations using the pedigree analysis will assess the program's efficacy at increasing genetic diversity and reducing extinction risk. Kendall Pargot
594: Translocation is used increasingly to conserve and manage declining wildlife populations. The fully aquatic Eastern Hellbender is North America’s largest salamander, which has declined considerably over the past two decades. These declines have led to the consideration of translocation as a conservation strategy. We synthesized results from three studies in Tennessee that included a wild-to-wild translocation and two head-started translocations to reveal patterns of success and potential avenues for best management practices. Wild-to-wild translocations showed that success was strongly dependent on release site habitat. Survival ranged from 33% to 100% and was greatest in streams with abundant boulder cover and prey availability. Individuals in habitats with greater habitat connectivity exhibited greater site fidelity and smaller home ranges, whereas those in less connected habitats dispersed widely. Survival from the zoo head-start studies ranged from 14% to 67% among years. Conditioning protocols, including exposure to natural prey and use of a fungal prophylaxis increased survival. Headstarted individuals displayed increased movement and exploration, particularly after successively greater time in the wild. Across these studies, boulder density emerged as a key driver of habitat selection, likely serving as a settlement cue. Overall, we recommend: (1) rigorous pre-release habitat assessments that emphasize adequate habitat, connectivity, and prey availability; (2) environmental conditioning for captive-reared individuals; (3) longterm telemetry-based monitoring; (4) matching translocation strategy to population context; and (5) integrating habitat restoration where possible. Our findings demonstrate that translocation can be effective when habitat quality, animal conditioning, and monitoring are aligned within an adaptive management framework. Natalie Swearingen
595: For inland recreational fisheries, harvest pressure is typically concentrated in and around urban centers. In an era of climate change, the status of fisheries may also vary latitudinally. However, due to the lack of data required to conduct formal stock assessments, how climate change impacts and human population growth interact to shape trends in the status of recreational fisheries remains poorly understood. The midwestern United States represents a unique situation where multiple decades of fisheries independent surveys and interviews with anglers conducted by local state officials have generated extensive datasets that can be used to conduct length-based population assessments for hundreds of lakes subjected to recreational fishing and, in some cases, tribal harvest. Here we evaluate over 500 populations of seven harvested species and identify spatial and temporal predictors of status. Our results show that Walleye, a popular sportfish, had the highest proportion of overfished populations within the study area, whilst Bluegill had the lowest proportion of overfished populations. In general, population status exhibited weak temporal trends and strong spatial patterns. Specifically, local human population density was the best predictor of status, with the most overfished populations occurring in proximity to urban centers. Although we found evidence of latitudinal patterns in status, these relationships did not conform to predictions based on thermal preference and climate resiliency. Data limited stock assessment of inland recreational fisheries is a valuable and underutilized tool to guide population-specific management. Gracey Brouillard
596: Parasites play a key role in regulating wildlife populations by influencing host behavior, body condition, and survival; however, baseline data on parasite communities in wild snakes remain limited, constraining applications in conservation medicine, captive management, and zoonotic risk assessment. Here, we investigated endoparasites of Chinese cobras (Naja atra) in central Taiwan and evaluated factors shaping parasite communities, including habitat structure, seasonal variation, diet, host condition, and parasite interspecific interactions. A total of 104 snakes were examined, with an overall endoparasite prevalence of 89.4%, and parasites were classified into five major groups: cestodes, trematodes, nematodes, acanthocephalans, and pentastomes. Host snout-vent length was positively associated with infection probability, while infection intensity peaked at intermediate body condition; snakes consuming reptilian prey were more likely to harbor reptile-associated pentastomes, suggesting trophic transmission. Positive associations were observed among nematode species with direct life cycles, but not among species with indirect life cycles, indicating potential shared environmental or host-related drivers. Overall, host condition and diet had stronger effects on parasite community structure than habitat or seasonal variation. These findings highlight the importance of host traits and trophic ecology in shaping parasite assemblages and provide essential baseline data for understanding parasitism in wild snake populations. Taylor chapple Taylor Chapple; David Cade; Austin Flanigan; Jeremy Goldbogen; Nick Masset; Nicholas Payne; Josh Stewart;
597: Anthropogenic disturbances that result in extensive habitat losses and structural alterations to habitat are a leading cause of global biodiversity loss. The borderland of South Texas, USA is a uniquely biodiverse region that has been heavily modified by anthropogenic activities, including urban development and agriculture. Potentially compounding these issues, the U.S.-MX international border barrier has been of heightened geopolitical and ecological concern in recent decades. Herpetofauna are vulnerable to anthropogenic disturbances, and habitat requirements for many species are not well understood. The Texas Indigo snake (Drymarchon melanurus erebennus) is an under-studied colubrid snake and a hallmark species of the thornscrub brushlands of southern Texas and northeast Mexico. Although downlisted from state threatened in 2020, development of natural areas and impermeable barrier infrastructure may threaten future populations. Therefore, we sought to estimate both suitable habitats and functionally connected habitat networks for D. m. erebennus using ensemble habitat suitability modeling and graph theoretical landscape analysis in Cameron, Hidalgo, Starr, and Zapata counties. Suitable habitats occur in moist, vegetated lowlands, and those habitats were fragmented into numerous small patches. Connectivity modeling identified urbanization as the greatest impact to habitat connectivity for D. m. erebennus. Habitat networks in Starr County are the most vulnerable to proposed barrier construction. Our study is the first to examine habitat requirements for D. m. erebennus to aid in future studies on this snake and can inform conservation efforts focused on mitigating long-term ecological impacts posed by the border barrier in South Texas. Anthony DiMeglio
598: Urbanization imposes novel selective pressures on wildlife, including chronic exposure to heavy metal pollutants such as lead (Pb). Although lead is highly toxic to most vertebrates, brown anoles (Anolis sagrei) in New Orleans tolerate exceptionally high blood lead levels without apparent impairment, raising the question of whether such tolerance is unique or shared across the genus. Here, I examine responses to lead contamination in the native green anole (Anolis carolinensis), a co-occurring species that occupies a more arboreal niche. I tested two hypotheses: (1) green anoles experience lower lead exposure due to reduced contact with contaminated soils, and (2) green and brown anoles differ in physiological tolerance to lead, reflecting differences in exposure history. I quantified blood lead levels in field-collected anoles across New Orleans and conducted controlled laboratory dosing experiments. Green anoles exhibited significantly lower blood lead concentrations than brown anoles at the same sites (two-way ANOVA, species effect: F₁,₁₆₄ = 237.7, p < 2 × 10⁻¹⁶). In laboratory trials, green anoles also showed reduced tolerance to lead exposure relative to brown anoles (G-test, p < 0.05). These findings suggest that both exposure to and tolerance of heavy metal pollution are shaped by ecological niche, highlighting how cooccurring species can follow divergent evolutionary trajectories in response to shared anthropogenic stressors. César E. Fuentes-Montejo César Fuentes-Montejo; Diego Elias; Wilfredo Matamoros; Prosanta Chakrabarty; Miquel Gonzalez-Meler; Caleb
599: The Island Fence Lizard (Sceloporus becki) is highly genetically and morphologically divergent from its mainland sister species, S. occidentalis.
