This taxon inhabits three of the Northern Channel Islands (San Miguel, Santa Rosa, Santa Cruz Islands), which lie 20–44 km off the coast of Southern California. These islands have never been connected to the mainland and formed a single island, ‘Santarosae,’ as recently as 10–12 ka. Landscapes across these islands differ in solar radiation, cloud cover, and substrate type, contributing to climatic variation. Our goals were to quantify genetic diversity and connectivity within and among islands and investigate the geological and contemporary landscape drivers of population differentiation. We analyzed an individual-based RADseq dataset containing 274 individuals and nearly 32,000 SNP loci to estimate population genomic parameters and test landscape genomic hypotheses within a spatial graph-theoretic framework. We found low effective population sizes and genetic diversity, as well as weak structure within each island, with strong differentiation among islands. Landscape genetics analyses emphasized the role of local climate in driving population structure and showed that each population exhibits a different relationship with the environment and may require specific management plans. Combined, our analyses show that this island endemic has been deeply influenced by isolation due to geologic and landscape changes and requires conservation attention. Madden Haag
600: The northwestern pond turtle (Actinemys marmorata: NWPT) is one of three freshwater turtle species native to the West Coast of the United States. Despite its expansive range, the NWPT is experiencing a drastic population decline, warranting state-level protection and consideration for federal protection. There is no single clear cause of decline; however, in populations in the state of Washington, the fungal pathogen Emydomyces testavorans (Emte) is increasingly associated with shell disease in pond turtles. This form of shell disease manifests as both internal and external lesions. Both forms of lesions can have detrimental effects on individuals’ health and may contribute to the ongoing population decline. Although NWPT’s can be found across the three West Coast states, Emte seems to be disproportionately found in Washington. Currently, NWPT populations in Washington are supplemented through captive breeding programs, raising concerns about their genetic diversity. This presentation compares the immunogenetic diversity of individuals from Washington and California using blood samples from NWPT across the range, and next-generation sequencing. Our aim is to describe 1) interstate immunogenetic diversity, 2) the relationship between host immunogenetic diversity and pathogen load, and 3) the relationship between host immunogenetic diversity and disease severity. This work will provide insight into the power of genomic research in developing captive breeding programs and species management plans. Luke Johnson
601: River herring, including Alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus) and Blueback Herring (A. aestivalis), were once the among the most valuable food fishes in Virginia. These species experienced decline in their value to the fisheries resources of Virginia, and as early as the 1970s a significant decline in the stocks of these fishes throughout their range was noted. This range-wide decline culminated in the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission requiring moratoria on fisheries unless stocks within a jurisdiction were shown to be sustainable. Virginia enacted a moratorium in 2012 and soon after the Virginia Institute of Marine Science began annual monitoring of the spawning stock of river herring. Here we present relative abundance data for river herring species in the Rappahannock River of Virginia. Data indicate that abundance of Alewife and Blueback Herring have fluctuated, but have shown an overall positive trend since 2018. Climate change in Chesapeake Bay has shown that the seasonal change from winter temperatures to summer temperatures is occurring earlier and faster than the previous decades. We explore how the rate of increasing temperatures affects the spawning stock index for both river herring species in the Rappahannock River. The degree of warming can change both the time needed to migrate to suitable spawning habitat and the amount of time spent at spawning locations. Jimmy McGuire Jimmy A. McGuire
602: Biological invasions provide powerful natural experiments to understand the evolutionary and ecological processes that shape populations during rapid range expansion. Introduced populations often experience demographic bottlenecks, founder effects, and novel selective pressures that cause declines in genetic diversity that can shape evolutionary trajectories and patterns of genetic variation within and among populations through time. However, genetic bottlenecks do not always result in reduced fitness, as species can rapidly expand despite low initial diversity, suggesting that rapid adaptation, admixture, and spatial sorting may compensate for losses of genetic diversity. For this study, we will focus on a non-native lizard (Argentine tegus – Salvator merianae) that was introduced to Florida in the early 2000s from its native range in South America. The objective of this study is to investigate the population genomics of the introduced tegus to gain a more complete understanding of the demographic history, dispersal, and genetic variability of populations associated with the expansion. We used nextGen population genomic approaches to investigate how tegus are responding to ecological opportunities and constraints with genome-wide resolution. We analyzed the population history, number of independent introductions, genetic diversity, population structure, and levels of connectivity among the populations of tegus across Florida. We found that there are 4 distinct populations likely stemming from 3 independent introductions and one secondary expansion and that there is currently limited gene flow among populations. However, as their ranges expand there is high potential for hybridization which may accelerate their expansion as has been seen in other lizards in FL.
603: Historically, in vivo gene editing has been extremely difficult in reptiles. But with the advancement of oocyte based micro-injections of CRISPR-Cas9, three species of squamates (snakes and lizards) have successfully been gene edited: brown anoles, corn snakes, and Madagascar ground geckos. Here, we discuss how to apply these methods to additional species while also showing results from three new species of geckos: mourning geckos (Lepidodactylus lugubris), leopard geckos (Eublepharis macularius), and crested geckos (Correlophus ciliatus). We also demonstrate how gene editing can be leveraged to answer questions about the biology and evolution of interesting traits such as color and pattern. Specifically, we targeted the TFEC gene which is known to be necessary for iridophore production in Anolis lizards via functional studies. We tested if TFEC function is conserved between anoles and geckos by using CRISPR-Cas9 to disrupt TFEC function in both E. macularius and C. ciliatus. Anat Belasen (she/her) Anat Belasen; Anna Savage; Michael Campana; Kevin Mulder; Kevin Amses; Melissa Kemp; Robert Fleischer;
604: Anthropogenic modifications can disrupt gene flow among populations, thereby affecting population dynamics and structure. In riverine systems, modifications such as dams are beneficial for human activities but may act as barriers to gene flow for aquatic organisms. In the Pearl River of Louisiana and Mississippi, USA, at least four potential barriers to gene flow exist: three low-head dams on the main channel in the upper, middle, and lower reaches of the river, and the Ross Barnett Dam, a large earthen dam in Jackson, Mississippi. We investigated the effects of these barriers on gene flow and genetic structure in the Gulf Longear Sunfish (Lepomis solis) and the Gulf Darter (Etheostoma swaini), both widespread, non-migratory species that occur throughout the Pearl River basin. We hypothesized, based on differences in life-history traits, that L. solis would exhibit greater patterns of admixture and less population structure relative to E. swaini. To address this, we sampled 105 L. solis individuals from 19 sites and 44 E. swaini individuals from 7 sites in the Pearl River basin using backpack electrofishing and seining. We genotyped single-nucleotide polymorphic loci (SNPs) from double-digest restriction-site associated DNA (ddRAD) sequences. We used multivariate analyses to estimate patterns of genetic diversity, structure, and rates of gene flow among subpopulations in the study basin. Our findings provide an overview of population genetic structure and connectivity and indicate that barriers within the fragmented Pearl River system do not significantly affect gene flow of the two study species. Danielle Deutsch
605: Parthenogenetic vertebrates offer a rare opportunity to investigate the genomic consequences of hybridization and asexual reproduction. Building on molecular studies from recent decades that first identified the putative parental species of Lepidodactylus lugubris, we use modern genomic approaches and complete nuclear genomes to test these hypotheses and estimate the timing of the hybridization event. Here, we present the first chromosome-scale genome assemblies for both parental species of the gecko complex L. moestus (maternal) and L. pantai (paternal), alongside the subgenomes of their diploid parthenogenetic descendant, L. lugubris. All three species yielded highly complete assemblies (>97% BUSCO completeness) spanning 22 chromosomes. To generate the distinct subgenomes, trio binning was used during assembly, capturing ~99% of the conserved BUSCO genes present in each respective parent. Pairwise synteny analyses revealed largely conserved genome structure across parental and hybrid lineages, although some localized structural variants were detected. Demographic reconstructions using PSMC and β-PSMC revealed broadly parallel population size trajectories for both parental species, consistent with a shared phylogeographic history of Pacific island dispersal. Together, these data provide a comprehensive genomic framework for confirming parental ancestry, dating the hybridization event, and understanding subgenome stability and the maintenance of obligate parthenogenesis in vertebrates. Taylor L. Fisher
606: Viviparity, or bearing live young, has independently evolved many times throughout the vertebrate tree of life, leading to questions regarding the molecular mechanisms underlying the evolution of this trait. Caecilians display multiple reproductive modes, with some branches having undergone shifts from oviparity (egglaying) to viviparity. Here, we used a comparative genomic approach to test for signatures of selection associated with viviparity in the Gaboon Caecilian (Geotrypetes seraphini). Using publicly available data, we identified orthologous regions in the genomes of Geotrypetes seraphini and three oviparous caecilian species (Ichthyophis bannanicus, Rhinatrema bivittatum, and Microcaecilia unicolor). We aligned sequences and calculated ratios of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) to identify patterns of selection. Our findings provide insight into the evolution of viviparity in caecilians, and contribute to our understanding of the molecular basis of viviparity more broadly. Maria Gabriela Diaz Gonzalez
607: Understanding the mechanisms by which organs and tissues evolve new physiological functions is central to understanding the evolution of novelty. This is interesting in the context of related tissues that evolve specialized, yet complementary functions. Snake venom glands are an attractive system to test hypotheses related to the evolution and specialization of novel physiological function, as these modified salivary glands have evolved over ~60 MY to synthesize and store venom. Front-fanged venomous snakes (elapids and viperids) possess two types of venom glands: the main and accessory glands. The larger main gland produces greater quantities of venom toxins and has been studied extensively, while the smaller accessory gland has received less attention. Here, we explore gene expression differences between main and accessory venom glands across three rattlesnake species (Crotalus cerberus, C. oreganus concolor, and C. viridis). Our findings indicate that accessory glands express most venom genes at significantly lower levels than the main gland, with a few exceptions that may represent biologically relevant contributions of accessory glands to venom. The two glands also exhibit distinct trans-regulatory environments that we link to key differences in their underlying physiology and secretory roles. Our results further suggest that two signaling pathways that regulate venom, the unfolded protein response (UPR) and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), show significantly lower activation in the accessory gland. These findings provide insight into the physiological and functional diversification of snake venom systems, highlighting how distinct glandular systems have evolved contrasting and complementary roles, driven by distinct physiological and regulatory mechanisms. Kyle King
608: Femoral glands mediate chemical communication in many lizards, yet the gene regulatory architecture underlying gland function remains poorly understood, especially across major evolutionary transitions such as shifts in reproductive mode. Whiptail lizards (Aspidoscelis) include closely related sexual and obligately parthenogenetic lineages that retain broadly conserved gland morphology. We combined a femoral gland transcriptome atlas, differential expression analyses, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to test whether signaling divergence reflects regulatory rewiring or quantitative modulation of conserved networks. Femoral glands were transcriptionally distinct from non-glandular skin and enriched for gland development, secretion, lipid metabolism, and immune processes. Sex and reproductive mode affected expression of a limited subset of genes, whereas most gland-associated programs were conserved across species, sexes, and reproductive modes. Coexpression analyses revealed a shared modular architecture anchored by conserved hub genes involved in lipid processing, membrane dynamics, detoxification, and epithelial function. Together, these results indicate that femoral gland diversity in Aspidoscelis arises primarily through evolutionary tinkering—quantitative modulation within conserved regulatory networks—rather than extensive rewiring, highlighting regulatory constraint in the evolution of complex chemical signaling traits. Elise Rivera
609: We investigate whether genetic variation is associated with environmental heterogeneity and whether these patterns reflect local adaptation in the island fence lizard (Sceloporus becki), a species restricted to three of California’s Northern Channel Islands, which span a natural climatic gradient. To test for adaptive variation, we integrate environmental data (temperature loggers and remotely sensed variables), phenotypic traits (e.g., scale counts and field body temperature), and whole-genome sequencing from five populations across three islands. Using this framework, we conducted genotype–environment and genotype–phenotype association analyses, along with phenotype–environment comparisons, to link genomic variation with environmental conditions and organismal traits. Preliminary results reveal significant associations between genomic variation and environmental variables after accounting for population structure, with signals distributed across the genome, consistent with polygenic adaptation. Although field body temperature shows only a weak and nonsignificant trend across environments, overlap in a few candidate genes identified by both genotype–environment and genotype–phenotype analyses suggests a possible shared genetic basis linking environmental variation to phenotypic differences. Together, these findings suggest that S. becki populations are responding to local climatic conditions. Zandria Stanfield
610: Milksnakes (Lampropeltis triangulum species complex) are a group of closely-related lineages whose species status has been long debated. Previous work has identified a hybrid zone in eastern Kansas where two of these lineages, Lampropeltis triangulum and L. gentilis, are in secondary contact, providing an excellent opportunity to examine processes of divergences and better understand genetic barriers that have maintained these lineages. To estimate the hybrid ancestry of individuals and identify loci potentially under selection, we generated whole genome resequence data from 32 individuals across the hybrid zone and compared patterns of genomic differentiation between and within lineages. We identified most admixed individuals towards the center of the hybrid zone as latestage hybrids with some backcrossing with parentals. We also identified asymmetric gene flow with more contribution from the western lineage than the eastern. Regions of highest divergence between lineages seem to be driven primarily by recurrent local selection rather than barrier loci that resist migration, suggesting a strong role for ecological selection in maintaining lineage identity rather than intrinsic genomic incompatibilities. Brandon Welty Brandon Welty; Max Jones; Samantha Smith; Matthew Metcalf; Christina Romagosa; Daniel Haro; Mark Sandfoss;
611: Amphibians are often considered solely freshwater organisms unable to persist in saline habitats, yet evidence for their tolerance to saltwater is scattered across species, life stages, and experimental conditions. We conducted a meta-analysis of experimental studies to address three questions: (1) how salt tolerance varies across amphibian life stages and species, (2) how salt type and exposure duration influence survival, and (3) whether plasma osmolality predicts tolerance to salinity. Across the compiled dataset, embryos were the most salt-sensitive life stage, followed by larvae and adults. In larvae, chronic exposure (>96 h) caused substantially greater mortality than acute exposure, and NaCl-based road salts reduced survival far more than natural or synthetic sea salts. Although saltwater exposure consistently increased plasma osmolality, these changes were not associated with improved survival. Phylogenetic patterns were modest and largely limited to early life stages. Together, these results show that amphibian responses to salinity are context dependent and cannot be predicted using single physiological metrics or fixed tolerance thresholds. Wyatt Albert
612: Noise pollution may negatively impact fishes that depend on sound for spawning, feeding, and predator avoidance. High ambient noise can damage hair cells in the saccule of the ear and influence fish behavior. Still, less is understood about noise impacts on fish metabolism and stress responses. In this study, we examined whether elevated ambient noise affected the oxygen consumption, cortisol levels, and auditory system of Atlantic croaker (Micropogonias undulatus). We measured oxygen uptake over 30 hours with intermittent-flow respirometry, with the last 24 hours under control conditions (120 dB re: 1 µPa) or exposed to white noise at 150 dB re: 1µPa. Water samples were collected at the start and end of each period to assess cortisol release rates. At the end, plasma was sampled for cortisol, and ears were sampled to evaluate hair cell damage. Preliminary data showed an immediate rise in oxygen uptake during noise exposure, but no changes in standard, routine, or peak oxygen consumption over 24 hours. Cortisol levels in plasma and water cortisol release rates did not differ between control and noise-exposed fish. Therefore, while elevated noise instantly increases oxygen uptake, it does not affect sustained aerobic metabolism or plasma cortisol in Atlantic croaker. Ongoing analyses will investigate hair cell damage. Natalie Alonzo
613: Marine heatwaves are increasing in frequency and intensity, posing significant challenges to marine ectotherms. Here, we aimed to determine how juvenile pinfish (Lagodon rhomboides), an abundant and ecologically relevant coastal species, respond to repeated events of acute warming using an integrative multi-omics framework. Over a six-month period, juvenile pinfish were maintained under control conditions (23°C) or exposed to either a single simulated heatwave (SH) or multiple heatwave cycles (MH) of 31°C. We integrated transcriptomic, metabolomic, and epigenomic data to test whether repeated heatwave exposure confers a molecular advantage compared to a single heatwave event. We found that elevated temperature induced coordinated molecular responses, as both SH and MH individuals exhibited upregulation of genes associated with protein turnover and cellular stress responses. However, clear divergence emerged across treatments as SH individuals showed evidence of heat stress, including shifts in lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and redox signaling across all -omics layers. In contrast, MH individuals displayed small differences in gene expression compared to control individuals, and no significant metabolomic differences. Functional patterns in MH fish suggested cellular reorganization and maintenance rather than widespread stress, through epigenetics and gene expression. Together, these findings demonstrate that while warming elicits a conserved molecular stress response, the frequency and duration of heat exposure shape the resulting molecular and physiological responses. Repeated heat exposure appears to promote molecular signatures consistent with physiological adjustment, indicating the potential resilience of pinfish under increasingly variable thermal environments. Mikayla Beeson
614: Most marine fishes are ectotherms, which means that environmental temperatures play key role in their behavior, physiological processes and life-history traits. Ocean warming is expected to affect key physiological processes in fishes, affecting their abundance and distribution. This means that understanding the susceptibility of species, as well as the molecular mechanisms activated in response to warming, are critical for marine fishes. Recent studies have highlighted the ecological relevance of marine cryptobenthic species in coastal food webs and nutrient cycling. Despite these advances, questions remain on the responses of cryptobenthic species to acute and prolonged warming. In this presentation we will present advances on the thermal tolerance of five species of cryptobenthic fishes of the Atlantic, across three different sites. The results from this study show stark differences in tolerance among species with overlapping ranges and habitats. Further, we will present preliminary analyses of liver gene expression for the Molly Miller (Scartella cristata, Blenniidae) and the Frillfin goby (Bathygobius soporator, Gobiidae) exposed to a time series experiment. These analyses indicate mechanisms of protection are activated in gobies early on when confronted with acute heat stress, which could be a key element of their high thermal tolerance. These findings can help us predict how marine species of key ecological relevance will respond to predicted ocean warming in coming years.
615: Coastal urbanization is expanding rapidly, causing an increase in the frequency and magnitude of salinity fluctuations in tidal creek systems. Urbanization transforms coastal ecosystems: switching from vegetation to impervious surfaces. The latter increases freshwater runoff during precipitation events, producing extreme osmotic shifts. While many species today are only able to survive in forested sites, the Gulf killifish (Fundulus grandis) is consistently found in both reference and urbanized tidal creek systems. In this project, we conducted a reciprocal transplant experiment with individuals from two sites in the northern GoM: a reference creek (Long Bayou, AL) and an urbanized creek (Weakley Bayou, FL). The main idea was to evaluate the response to salinity stress in populations with different salinity regimes, low fluctuations (reference sites) or fast fluctuations (urbanized sites). Individuals from each population were subjected to a simulated tide event (low fluctuation) and a tide/runoff event (high fluctuation) over an acute period to assess responses via gill gene expression (RNA-seq). The analyses revealed 112 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with 31% of the variance being attributed to salinity treatment and 13% to population origin. The urbanized population displayed more than 20x DEGs than the reference population, suggesting greater transcriptional plasticity under fluctuating salinity. Analyses of transcriptome-derived single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) indicated small but significant genetic differentiation between the two populations, with five candidate genes under divergent natural selection. This study shows how adaptation and plasticity can act in concert to shape responses to abiotic variability in coastal environments at small spatial scales. Abby Clark
616: Metabolites are small biomolecules which are the end products of gene expression in cells. Quantification and analysis of the total metabolite profile, known as metabolomics, is a rapidly developing field in systems biology and has been used in ecology and evolution to link phenotype and genotype. Here, we analyze the metabolome of several threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) populations, leveraging a conservation translocation experiment where sticklebacks from populations were reintroduced into different lakes in Alaska. We identify and annotate various metabolites present in the stickleback system; then, we attempt to track metabolic signatures that would indicate 1) heritable metabolites from source to destination lakes, 2) plastic response to environmental changes, especially between benthic and limnetic lakes, and 3) other individual-level differences such as sex. Jack Dirck
617: Research in recent decades has greatly expanded our knowledge of the diversity of feeding behavior in fishes, particularly regarding the anatomical and functional correlates of prey capture by biting fishes. Few studies, however, have directly compared modulation between biting and suction feeding within the same species. This study compares the kinematics of feeding behavior in the red-bellied piranha, Pygocentrus nattereri, while capturing prey by both suction feeding and by biting. Surprisingly, both the sequence and extent of movement of the cranial bones is similar between the two behaviors, with skull movements slightly more expansive during bites on squid than on suction strikes on pellets. Squid bites are also generally faster than suction strikes, reaching peak displacement of the cranial bones in less time. As the drop in intraoral pressure during aquatic feeding is directly related to both the degree and speed of skull expansion, these results suggest, counterintuitively, that more suction is created during piranha bites than during piranha suction strikes. Similar analyses on Piaractus and Metynnis, both serrasalmids and so closely related to piranhas, are more consistent with expectations that suction strikes should be faster and more expansive than bites, so Pygocentrus bites are unusual. Fishes generate suction not just for prey capture but also for transport of ingested items during swallowing. The fast, expansive bite of Pygocentrus may be advantageous to rapidly swallow a mouthful of prey that requires little further processing while surrounded by hungry schoolmates who are all looking for their la bouffe.
618: Skeletal muscle is integral to a wide range of biological processes in fishes, including locomotion, feeding, and reproduction, and is functionally diverse, consisting of slow oxidative fibers that support sustained, aerobic activity and fast glycolytic fibers specialized for rapid, anaerobic bursts. In ectothermic organisms such as fishes, skeletal muscle performance is strongly influenced by temperature, typically following a thermal performance curve. Species with broad geographic distributions are therefore ideal for examining how temperature shapes muscle function. The black sea bass, Centropristis striata, ranges from the Gulf of Mexico to Maine, encountering diverse thermal regimes. We hypothesized that muscles supporting different functional roles would exhibit similar acclimation responses to temperature. To test this, individuals were collected from Long Island Sound and acclimated to 15 °C and 20 °C for two weeks. We then isolated myotomal muscle (locomotion), adductor mandibulae (jaw closing), and abductor superficialis (station holding), and quantified contraction kinetics using a muscle ergometer at both temperatures. Tissues were subsequently processed for immunohistochemical analysis to characterize fiber-type composition and thermal remodeling. Our results show that contraction kinetics differ significantly among muscle types and that acclimation responses are not uniform, indicating functional specialization in thermal plasticity. These findings highlight the importance of muscle-specific responses to temperature and provide insight into performance limits in a commercially important and emerging aquaculture species. Maddox Moran
619: Limb reduction has evolved many times across the squamate tree of life and has been particularly prevalent in the Family Scincidae. Within Scincidae several genera, including Scelotes, are represented by species that are limbed, limb reduced, and limbless. Scelotes are fossorial and semi-fossorial skinks distributed primarily across southern Africa. Although the genus provides an excellent opportunity to investigate patterns of limb loss within a group of closely related species, to date there have been no genus-wide phylogenetic studies. We provide a divergence dating phylogenetic analysis of Scelotes incorporating 18 of 22 recognized species and conduct ancestral state reconstruction to examine patterns of limb loss across the genus. We find that eastern and western species are not reciprocally monophyletic and that diversification within major clades may be related to complex geomorphological and climate changes that occurred in southern Africa, primarily in the Miocene. Ancestral state reconstructions suggest that there were multiple independent instances of limb loss in the genus, and potential limb gain, although there are caveats associated with this result, including difficulties capturing developmental complexities underlying trait evolution in model parameters. Kirsten Bauer Kirsten Bauer; Jeremy Higgs; Jill Hendon; Paul Grammer; William Slack; Dara Wilber; Mark Peterson; Michael
620: The emergence and maintenance of variation among intraspecific lineages is fundamental to the process of speciation. This is of particular interest in leuciscid fishes, the most diverse group of freshwater fishes in North America. Rhinichthys obtusus, the Western Blacknose Dace, offers unique opportunities to examine this process in situ. R. obtusus is a riffle-dwelling stream minnow with a broad distribution between the Appalachians and the Mississippi River to the east and west, and from the Hudson Bay drainage to the Mobile Bay drainage to the north and south. In this presentation, we will discuss the growing body of evidence for multiple, evolutionarilydistinct lineages within the species through the lens of genetic, genomic, and phylogenomic analyses. We will also explore the biogeographic processes associated with post-glacial recolonization that may explain the current distribution of these lineages. Together, these data enhance our understanding of the considerable diversity observed among leuciscid fishes in North America. Tim Earley
621: An investigation of community structuring can reveal the impact of historic and current biogeographical processes on the distribution and evolution of species. Okinawa, the largest of the Ryukyu Islands, is the ideal location for studying these complex dynamics due its exceptionally rich marine biodiversity, endemism, and resilience. Additionally, the Ryukyu Islands, which span 1,200 km from southern Japan to Taiwan, represent the northern border of the Coral Triangle, often noted as the global hotspot of marine biodiversity. In this study, we aim to examine the influence of community structure on the variation in morphological traits and genetic diversity of coral reef fishes found across Okinawa. Using robust morphometrics data, static video surveys across various reef substrates, a comprehensive trait database, and whole genome SNP analyses, we test hypotheses about community associations with benthic habitat and geographic patterns of trait and genetic variation. We hypothesize that there will be distinct fish communities associated with each substrate type and that more complex benthic habitats will maintain communities with more trait and genetic diversity. The results of this project provide insight into the underlying patterns of biodiversity across this island, and will form the framework for further work examination of population connectivity and dispersal capabilities of coral reef fishes and the impact of historic disturbances on community structuring across the Ryukyu Islands. Jill Nash
622: Why do some fishes occur in temperate regions of both hemispheres, yet are absent from the tropics in between? These “anti-tropical” distributions have fascinated biogeographers for more than a century and remain the focus of competing explanations, including dispersal across the equator during cooler climatic intervals, extinction within the tropics, or ecological constraints tied to ocean structure. Until recently, the resolution and dimensionality of available data and models limited our ability to test these ideas explicitly. Here I revisit this enigma with new tools to model species' suitable abiotic conditions in three dimensions and project them through deep time. By combining depth-explicit ecological niche models of several species with Cenozoic paleoceanographic reconstructions, I track how suitable habitats for anti-tropical fishes have shifted across both latitude and depth. This framework allows us to ask whether equatorial corridors of suitable habitat opened and closed in step with ocean climate change, and how they may have shifted in depth. Preliminary results indicate equatorial connections were not static, but fluctuated with the changing oceans. Although not universal for all the species modeled, these shifts may have provided rare opportunities for some fishes to disperse across the tropics. More broadly, this work demonstrates how integrating 3D ecological modeling with paleoenvironmental data can reveal the dynamic processes underlying disjunct distributions and yield new insights into one of biogeography's enduring puzzles. Andrew Pagan
623: Catfishes (Order Siluriformes) represent one of the most diverse and globally distributed groups of teleost fishes, comprising more than 4,000 species across 41 families. Although predominantly associated with freshwater habitats, a few lineages have successfully recolonized brackish and marine environments. Their geographic distribution across all continents, combined with limited dispersal ability across marine barriers in most lineages, makes catfishes an ideal system to investigate the roles of vicariance, habitat transitions, and long-distance dispersal in shaping global biodiversity patterns. Although current evidence supports a South American freshwater origin for catfishes, the pathways and processes underlying their global dispersal remain poorly understood, largely due to unresolved phylogenetic relationships among major lineages. Here, we aim to elucidate the evolutionary history of catfishes by integrating phylogenomics, divergence time estimation, and historical biogeography. We assembled the most comprehensive dataset to date for this group, including genomic data from ~700 species (~17% of described diversity), representing all families and approximately 75% of genera, along with 94 fossil calibrations. Using this time-calibrated phylogeny, we reconstructed catfishes’ ancestral ranges (continents) and habitat (freshwater, brackish, and marine). This framework will allow us to infer the timing and routes of dispersal and assess how habitat transitions have contributed to the global expansion of catfishes. Blanca Alicia Santoyo Cerón
624: The Upper Guinea Forests are considered a biodiversity hotspot containing many endemic terrestrial and freshwater species. The Guinean Range forms the backbone of the region spanning from the Fouta Djallon highlands, in central Guinea, to Mount Nimba in southeastern Guinea. This range of highlands separates two distinct biogeographical regions; to the west, the Upper Guinea region with rivers flowing west directly into the ocean, and the Nilo-Sudan region, with major rivers drainages, like the Niger and Senegal, flowing east and then back west into the Atlantic Ocean. This Guinean Range is proposed to serve as a barrier to species crossing from one region to the other, but there are species that are reported to occur on both sides of the range. Recent studies on these putative amphi-Guinean species reveal that many of these groups are likely complexes of species; many of which are endemic to individual basins within the region. Here the processes that may have facilitated the diversification of freshwater fishes in the area are discussed. Using Digital Elevation Maps (DEMs) to infer ongoing drainage evolution in the region allows comparison to recent phylogenetic reconstructions for several different amphiGuinean species. The study suggests that the dynamic drainage evolution along the Guinean Range and the relatively stable environment of the region have promoted high levels of diversification in several groups of fishes. The results from several ongoing studies in these fishes will also be presented.
625: For effective conservation, it is important to develop an understanding of the evolutionary history of sensitive species and the spatial distribution of their contemporary genomic diversity. Lungless salamanders (family Plethodontidae) are highly diverse and recent systematic studies have revealed distinct evolutionary lineages within wide-ranging species. Here, we examine the phylogeography of the wide-ranging and evolutionarily distinct fourtoed salamander (Hemidactylium scutatum) in the Eastern United States and Canada. We used range-wide four-toed salamander samples and generated SNP data using 2RAD sequencing. We then conducted analyses to assess the phylogenetic relationships, geographic population structure and admixture, and the spatial distribution of genetic diversity in this species. We found substantial phylogeographic structure across the range of four-toed salamanders, only some of which was concordant with previous patterns inferred from mitochondrial DNA sequence data (e.g., a distinct group present only in the vicinity of the Great Smoky Mountains). However, we also found evidence for extensive admixture along contact zones between different groups. Many of these contact zones are in southern Appalachia, where both individual-level genomic diversity and phylogeographic lineage diversity are highest. Together, our results help characterize the complex spatial genetic structure in this species and confirm the importance of Appalachia as both the geographic origin of phylogeographic lineages and center of current genomic diversity within these lineages. Cordon Wade
626: Diet information elucidates a species’ trophic role and its prey spectrum and is crucial for the development of ecosystem approaches to fisheries management. The Sand Tiger Shark (Carcharius taurus) is a cosmopolitan, upper-trophic level predator that ranges from Maine to Florida in the Western North Atlantic; however, diet studies are limited, especially in the southern part this range. Here, we employed a non-invasive technique to quantify the recent diet of Sand Tiger Sharks off North and South Carolina. Cloacal and fecal swabs were obtained from adult and juvenile sharks during fishing expeditions and profiled using eDNA metabarcoding with MiFish and cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (CO1) primers. Results were filtered to exclude non-marine species, and prey was analyzed based on a presence-absence basis. We found variable results in diet composition (%FO) between collection methods among 94 paired fecal and cloacal samples. Eighty-one total taxa were documented, mainly fishes. Of these, 69 (85.1%) total taxa and 26 exclusive taxa were identified in fecal samples, whereas and 54 (66.7%) total taxa and 11 exclusive taxa were identified from cloacal samples. %FO among prey taxa varied considerably between collection methods, with consistent result for only 8 (17.0%) samples. More prey items were documented from fecal samples (n=311)) compared to cloaca samples (n-189). These differences likely reflect the more complete dietary information available from fecal samples and the potential environmental contamination of cloacal samples. Using fecal samples (n = 104), intraspecific dietary variation was explored among several variables (location, sex, length, maturity stage). Corinthia Black
627: Central place foraging is a widespread behavioral strategy among mobile species, characterized by periodic, often predictable transitions between foraging excursions and returns to a central refuge. In many cases, the central place is shared among individuals, resulting in the formation of fission-fusion social groups. Here, we evaluate the extent to which juvenile white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) at a nearshore aggregation site in San Diego behave as central place foragers. We first used a fine-scale acoustic positioning system and depth-sensor data to generate a three-dimensional, meter-and-minute level resolution tracking dataset for 28 individual sharks (137274 cm total length) over a 6-month period. We then integrated shark tracking data into flexible state-space models designed to identify the timing, location, and drivers of shark movement behaviors. Our results provide strong support for juvenile white sharks acting as central place foragers at this aggregation site. Within the monitored area, sharks exhibited clear fission-fusion dynamics across the diel cycle, maintaining area-restricted movements around a central habitat feature during the day and more exploratory movements at night. We also observed diel variation in nursery emigration rates, with clear peaks during crepuscular periods that may reflect foraging excursions further offshore. Together, these findings provide management-relevant insights into the nursery behaviors of a recovering top predator, while also highlighting the utility of emerging statistical frameworks in understanding the dynamics of complex coastal ecosystems. Jack Elstner
628: Anthropogenic microparticle ingestion, including microplastics, in marine organisms is a growing concern. Yet, its prevalence in sharks of the Northeast Pacific remains largely unexplored. One species ideally suited to address this knowledge gap is the salmon shark (Lamna ditropis). Salmon sharks are regionally endothermic predators in the North Pacific and may be vulnerable to microparticle ingestion due to their high energetic demands, broad diet, and exploitation of coastal and offshore habitats known to contain relatively high amounts of pollution. To assess exposure in this species, we analyzed stomachs from 18 salmon sharks collected from the Oregon coast between 2022 and 2024. Anthropogenic particles were found in every stomach (100% detection frequency), with a total of 435 microparticles from 17 individuals (mean ± SD of 25.6 ± 23.0 particles per stomach). Particles were dominated by fibers (54.7%) and fragments (25.5%). μFTIR spectroscopy confirmed that ~16% of particles were synthetic polymers, primarily polyethylene, polypropylene, and nylon, while the remainder were largely anthropogenic cellulose (most often cotton). Microplastics were detected in all but three stomachs, yielding an 82.4% detection frequency of plastics. Relative to other elasmobranch studies, salmon sharks exhibited universally high detection frequencies and elevated particle burdens. This study provides the first evidence of microplastics and anthropogenic microparticle ingestion in salmon sharks and contributes to the growing body of literature documenting exposure in large pelagic predators.
629: Scalloped (Sphyrna lewini) and Carolina hammerheads (S. gilberti) are sympatric cryptic species, with neonates and young-of-year (YOY) being well sampled in overlapping coastal and estuarine nursery areas along the US Southeast Coast. By contrast, highly mobile juveniles and mature individuals are relatively elusive. Therefore, habitat use and movement patterns of older individuals of both species are difficult to discern through traditional movement ecology techniques. Trace element concentrations were collected across transects of previously aged scalloped and Carolina hammerhead vertebrae with LA-ICP-MS. Elemental concentrations were analyzed by life stages (prenatal, young-of-year, early juvenile, late juvenile and adult) to examine habitat utilization from birth through the terminal age of each shark, with prenatal vertebral elemental composition providing insight into the habitats occupied by gestating females. Patterns in trace elements across life stages indicate scalloped and Carolina hammerheads exhibit different habitat as juveniles and adults, with Carolina hammerheads potentially migrating farther offshore and at a younger age compared to scalloped hammerheads. Heather Galloway
630: The Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae) is a small coastal species distributed from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico, though individuals are most commonly encountered between Florida and the Carolinas. Genetic analyses have identified distinct stocks in the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico, and most research to date has focused on adult habitat use for the Gulf stock using survey data. The acoustic telemetry research that has been done has focused on juvenile nursery habitats. Consequently, a key data gap exists regarding adult habitat use and movement patterns in the Atlantic stock. To address this gap, 23 adult Atlantic sharpnose sharks were collected off the coast of Virginia using longline gear and fitted with acoustic tags from June to August 2024. An additional seven sharks were collected and tagged off the coast of South Carolina in November 2024. Results from this work will improve understanding of movement patterns and habitat occupancy for adult Atlantic sharpnose sharks, expand knowledge of their life history, and identify potential spatial overlap between shark habitat use and shrimp trawling activity. Emily R. Gray
631: Precise, fine-scale foraging behaviors are a crucial missing component in ecological monitoring of some large, mobile predators. However, using animal-borne sensors, we can closely observe predators as they carry out natural behaviors. Previously, we determined that combining multiple data streams from an animal-borne tag allowed us to detect and describe foraging and prey processing in Aetobatus narinari. Now, after recording feeding bouts from multiple individuals, we can explore the spatiotemporal distributions of these behaviors and their ecological context. A biologging tag package (CATS-Cam), equipped with an onboard inertial measurement unit, video camera, and hydrophone, was deployed on wild A. narinari, captured on sight in a tangle net. Video and audio data were manually labeled and then modeled to detect continuous diel, tidal, and spatial effects on foraging effort and success. Twenty-eight deployments on 27 adult individuals (13 female, 15 male), with disc widths ranging from 92 to 196 cm, were recovered and analyzed. Successful foraging events were confirmed through audio data (n = 206) in Bermuda and two Florida estuaries. Feeding occurred at depths of up to nearly 10 m and at all times of day, but with substantial variation among individuals. Prey type (infaunal or epifaunal) was identified through video or predicted based on the occurrence of audible “digging” behavior prior to prey processing. Using this unprecedented window into their lives, we describe patterns in foraging behavior across sexes, individuals, times, and locations in a large, mobile, and elusive durophagous predator. Catherine Hanks
632: Florida’s Big Bend region is a semi-enclosed basin in the Northern Gulf, composed of a pristine seagrass system, home to diverse assemblages of organisms with considerable stocks of commercially important fish and highly mobile species. Exploring diet composition of coastal predators such as sharks is important in mitigating ecosystem-wide effects of both commercial and recreational fisheries under changing environmental parameters. As fishing efforts, climate change, and human pressures affect species abundance and distributions, understanding the role of diet through food webs and species interactions is critical in conservation and management strategies. This invaluable prey information can be used by providing data for sustainable fisheries to support the continuation and growth of fishing-driven tourism and activities. Traditional methods of dietary sampling are lethal or largely invasive and provide many unknowns, resulting in vague dietary knowledge, especially for rare and endangered species. To investigate a new approach eliminating some challenges associated with traditional dietary sampling methods, the aim of this study is to create an effective sampling apparatus that maintains sample integrity through swabbing coastal shark species' stomachs for dna analysis and comparing results to contemporary, historical, and direct stomach content analysis. In observing elasmobranch diet within Florida’s big bend region, this study can shed light on potential top-down and species-specific driven effects on the system, elucidate prey fish assemblages, and aid in redefining suitable habitat for many commercial and recreational targeted teleost and elasmobranch species. Ayushi Jain
633: Knowledge of both horizontal and vertical movements of marine animals allows understanding of their habitat use, biotic and abiotic interactions, overall niche and may shed light on interactions with human activities. Hammerhead sharks are a group of animals with documented long distance horizontal movements including regular and repeated dives to considerable depths. However, vertical habitat use and dive behaviors of smooth hammerheads (Sphyrna zygaena) are poorly understood in comparison to other large hammerhead species, despite the importance of these movements for their survival and understanding of their biology in light of concern about declining populations. We used high-resolution satellite transmitters to track vertical movements of smooth hammerheads in waters off Long Island, NY. Tracked sharks exhibited very surface-oriented depths distributions (< 10 m), with 45.5% of depth records less than 2 m. Sharks were slightly deeper at night and spent the majority of time within a relatively narrow temperature range (20-24 °C). Sharks engaged in both V-shaped and U-shaped dives, likely indicating different behaviors such as foraging. The rate of dive descent was significantly faster than the rate of ascent, possibly indicative of energetic-related behaviors. Although smooth hammerheads tracked in our study were mostly surface oriented, they regularly dove throughout the water column. Our study sheds light on the vertical movements and biology of this species, providing information that will better inform investigations of anthropogenic threats in this region. Zoe Johnson
634: We applied a Bayesian multinomial logistic regression to investigate the probability of food preference of 227 Naru Eagle ray (Aetobatus narutobiei) in the Ariake Bay. For newborn individuals (L0 = 35-38 cm DW), the probability of food categories was bivalves (0.46), gastropods (0.43), and unidentifiable mollusks (0.10). When the Naru Eagle ray reaches size maturity (DW50%), the probability of the preferences for bivalves is 0.90 and 0.93 for males (DW50%= 76.42 cm) and females (DW50% = 95.20 cm), respectively. We further examined species-level preferences within bivalves. The bivalve species recorded were Anadara kagoshimensis (Ak), Crassostrea gigas (Cg), Ruditapes philippinarum (Rp), Atrina pectinata (Ap), and Anadara globosa (Ag), and their dietary preferences changed with body size. The preference for Ak showed a dome-shaped pattern, decreasing with increasing size. In contrast, the preference for Rp and Cg was higher at small sizes and declined exponentially as individuals grew. For newborn individuals, the probabilities of food items were Ak (0.52), Cg (0.42), and Rp (0.05). At the size at maturity, males showed probabilities of 0.28 for Ak, 0.58 for Cg, and 0.13 for Rp, whereas females showed probabilities of 0.46 for Ak, 0.48 for Cg, and 0.05 for Rp. These results are consistent with and complement the isotopic signals reported in previous studies for the species. This study demonstrates that reliance on commercially important bivalves is generally low and increases only at intermediate sizes, providing a quantitative basis for evaluating the actual impact of Naru eagle rays on fisheries resources. Benjamin Marsaly
635: Sharks play a critical role in maintaining marine ecosystem structure and resilience, yet many populations have declined due to overfishing and environmental change. In Texas, long-term trends in shark distribution and abundance across estuarine, nearshore, and offshore environments remain poorly understood. This study integrated three complementary fishery-independent surveys spanning ~40 years (1983–2023), leveraging distinct datasets to improve understanding of cross-shelf elasmobranch assemblage structure and evaluate temporal and environmental drivers of relative abundance for 12 shark species. Generalised additive models (GAMs) were used to quantify species- and environment-specific trends. This multi-dataset approach captured a broad range of environments and life stages, reducing bias associated with single-survey analyses. Of the 12 species examined, relative abundance of seven species increased in at least one environment, three species showed no temporal change and two species declined. Blacktip Sharks and Bonnetheads exhibited the most consistent multi-environment increases, while Bull, Spinner, Finetooth Sharks and Scalloped Hammerheads increased primarily in estuaries, and Great Hammerheads increased in nearshore areas. In contrast, Lemon Sharks showed persistent declines in estuaries and very low nearshore abundance, and Atlantic Sharpnose Sharks declined across all environments. Temperature, salinity and depth emerged as the most influential environmental predictors. Overall, these findings provide empirical support for reported increases in shark encounters by fishers, while also identifying species-specific declines that warrant concern. By establishing a unified, long-term baseline across environments, this study offers critical context for fisheries interactions and contributes valuable guidance for adaptive, evidence-based shark management in Texas waters. Roberto E. Reis
636: Juvenile blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) are abundant in the mangrove-fringed bays of the Galapagos, utilizing these habitats as nursery grounds. Due to spatial variation in factors including temperature and larval connectivity fish species richness is higher in the eastern portion of the Archipelago. Predator diets often reflect regional prey availability, leading us to hypothesize that juvenile blacktip sharks in the eastern Galapagos would have greater prey taxa richness than those in the west. To describe and quantify the juvenile blacktip’s diet, we used DNA metabarcoding of fecal matter collected via non-lethal cloacal swabs. We collected samples from 107 sharks across 240 km, spanning 14 bays on four islands, and released all sharks alive. The most common prey taxa identified were Thoburn’s mullet (Mugil thoburni; 20.0%, based on percent of occurrence), followed by fishes in the genus Abudefduf (sergeant-majors; 13.4%), Galapagos ringtail damselfish (Stegastes beebei; 12.7%), and scalloped hammerhead shark (Sphyrna lewini; 11.7%). Prey taxa richness was highest among sharks sampled in the bays of San Cristobal, possibly due to geographic variation in prey availability. Additionally, sharks sampled during a La Niña event in 2021 had higher prey taxa richness than those sampled during an El Niño event in 2023, which could be due to El Niño-induced declines in species richness and abundance resulting from shifts in primary productivity and upwelling. A deeper understanding of shark diets can improve our ability to predict how changes in food web dynamics and prey availability affect shark populations. Anne C. Sabol Anne Sabol; Catherine Alton; Catherine Hanks; Hyunseo Raphael Yang; Sarah Pepperman; Kelly Diamond; Sinlan
637: The development of animal-borne conductivity, temperature, and depth (CTD) recording tags has led to the establishment of marine animals as contributors to the global ocean observing system (GOOS). Over the past several decades, CTD tagging efforts have primarily focused on air-breathing marine animals, given that their need to surface for breathing permits regular transmission of data. More recently, many sharks have demonstrated similar potential as ocean observing platforms, facilitated by their vertical movement behavior and semiregular surfacing events. However, the variability of sharks’ diving and surfacing behaviors requires greater investigation to optimize CTD tag performance. CTD tags collect upcast profiles conditionally, based on the detections of dive terminus and time windows between GPS locations identified at the surface. The spatial and temporal scales of a tagged shark’s diving and surfacing behaviors directly affects the number of profiles a CTD tag transmits and the confidence in profile location, both factors with direct consequences on the operational utility of shark-collected profiles in the GOOS. We conducted a sensitivity analysis using previously collected vertical movement data from tagged sharks with emulation software that generates theoretical CTD tag performance in response to supplied pressure-depth time series. Tag performance was evaluated across defined biologically relevant programming conditions and spatiotemporal scales to identify how individual and species-specific variability in vertical movements impacts profile generation and transmission. Kristoffer Wild Kristoffer Wild; Julia Riley; Daniel Warner; Tobias Uller; Wei-Guo Du; Geoff While; Daniel Noble; Michael
638: A major challenge of fisheries management is determining the rate of species mortality, especially natural mortality. This can be especially true for highly migratory species such as sharks and some rays due to their wide distributions, highly mobile behavior, and poorly-understood trophic interactions. We used acoustic telemetry detections of Atlantic cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus, 58 adults, 35 juveniles), juvenile dusky sharks (Carcharhinus obscurus, 29 individuals), and adult smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis, 21 individuals) to test criteria for potential mortalities, estimate annual mortality rates, and identify potential sources of mortality based on timing and location of the last confirmed detections. Criteria for potential mortality included gaps in detection between the last confirmed tag detection and the tag expiration date that exceeded the mean time between detections, abnormal movements in comparison to other individuals of the same species, and apparent stationarity within receiver arrays. Estimated mortality rates were compared with published mortality rates derived from fishery stock assessments and other sources. To identify temporal and spatial trends in mortality, we plotted and mapped the dates and locations of final confirmed tag detections for individuals identified as potential mortalities. These times and dates were compared with available data on fishing activity, seasonal distributions of potential predators, and other possible sources of mortality. Our analysis will assess the utility of acoustic telemetry data in answering questions about mortality in highly migratory elasmobranchs. Nancy Barahona
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
639: Matrotrophic elasmobranchs concentrate 90% of maternal investment into gestation, yet the metabolic cost of this strategy remains unquantified. We measured standard metabolic rate (SMR) via 24-hour intermittent-flow respirometry across 64 trials in 22 mature female Atlantic stingrays (Hypanus sabinus) classified as non-pregnant, pregnant, or post-partum. Trials were conducted at Florida State University and Coastal Laboratory over a 6-month period. H. sabinus exhibits lipid histotrophy, secreting nutrient-rich histotroph through specialized uterine trophonemata to support embryonic organic matter increases exceeding over 860% and up to 1250% a fourmonth gestation. We predicted pregnant females would show elevated SMR reflecting the cumulative demands of histotroph production, uterine remodeling, and embryonic provisioning. Generalized additive mixed models controlling for body mass and habituation effects revealed no significant difference in SMR between pregnant and non-pregnant females, suggesting histotrophic provisioning operates through energetic reallocation rather than elevated metabolic intensity. We found there was a 38.8% reduction in SMR in post-partum females relative to the non-pregnant baseline group, a pronounced metabolic suppression persisting up to 55 days after parturition. This depression could reflect depletion of maternal reserves during gestation and suggests a necessary recovery period restoration of maternal resources after birth. These results demonstrate that the primary energetic cost of reproduction in this matrotrophic manifests as prolonged post-partum metabolic suppression. This extended recovery window represents an unrecognized period of vulnerability with direct conservation implications. We encourage conservation management programs to consider post-partum females in a critical phase where they are physiologically compromised and at risk. Annais Bonilla Annais Muschett-Bonilla; Kat Mowle; Linda Penfold
640: Genetic diversity is critical to long-term survival of species but can be eroded by population declines driven by human pressures. Temporal genetic monitoring of threatened species can reveal changes in genetic diversity over time, providing key data for conservation actions. Sawfish rostra from natural history collections were used to assess changes in genetic diversity in the Critically Endangered largetooth sawfish Pristis pristis. Historically, P. pristis had a circumtropical range, but following massive declines, is now primarily found in Australia with limited depleted populations elsewhere (e.g. Brazil). Genetic data (815-base pairs of the mitochondrial control region) from 87 specimens from across its historical range revealed significant population structure, with the Indo-West Pacific and the Atlantic/Eastern Pacific comprising distinct lineages. Comparisons between historical (~1878–2000) and contemporary populations (2001–2014) revealed genetic diversity loss, with only six of 35 historical haplotypes represented in contemporary populations. Most of the lost haplotypes were from the Atlantic/Eastern Pacific, which is at risk of further genetic erosion. Genetic diversity in Australia appears stable since ~1960s; however, Brazil showed a marked loss although contemporary diversity estimates are similar to those in Australia. These findings highlight the need to conserve remaining genetic diversity in P. pristis and emphasize the role of securing a population stronghold in the Atlantic/Eastern Pacific. Chris Feldman
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
641: A skate tagging programme was established in the Ross Sea region to improve skate knowledge and validate the utility of caudal thorn band counts for ageing Antarctic Starry Skate (Amblyraja georgiana). Since 2019/20, 11,647 skates were tagged and released across the Ross Sea, Amundsen Sea, and Bellingshausen Sea, including ~2,400 individuals chemically marked with either oxytetracycline (OTC) or strontium chloride (SrCl). Between 2019/20 and 2024/25, 183 skates were recaptured and returned for laboratory analysis, remaining at liberty from 3 days to 22 years (mean: 4.5 years). Recapture distances ranged from 0.5 to 142 km, with 54% recaptured within 30 km of release, indicating limited movement. Of the recaptured skates, 38 were chemically marked (OTC n=27; SrCl n=11). Chemically marked skates were at liberty for up to five years, and four OTC-marked skates showed confirmed chemical uptake into caudal thorns. However, minimal post-injection thorn growth and a lack of consistent band deposition prevented validation of annual band formation. Growth rates did not differ between chemically marked and unmarked skates, ranging from 0–5.7 cm/year (mean: 1.1 cm/year). Recaptured immature individuals at liberty for up to 17 years support previous estimates that this species reaches maturity ~20 years of age. These findings indicate that A. georgiana is a slow-growing, and likely long-lived, species with limited spatial movement. While OTC incorporation was confirmed, thorn banding does not appear to form annually. Future work should investigate elemental or isotopic signatures linked to strong seasonal sea-ice cycles. Grace First
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
642: The Bull Shark, Carcharhinus leucas, is widely distributed throughout the U.S. western North Atlantic waters, including the Gulf of Mexico (GoM) and is prominent in both commercial and recreational fisheries. However, limited research has been conducted on the life history of C. leucas within this region. The current study examined a total of 330 C. leucas (190 females: 55.0 – 232.8 cm fork length and 140 males: 49.5 – 214.0 cm fork length) collected between 2009 and 2025 to better characterize the reproductive biology of this species in the GoM. Females exhibited a slightly larger size-at-maturity (L50 = 178.4 cm fork length; a = -33.10, b = 0.01; n = 176) compared to males (L50 = 174.9 cm fork length; a = -17.42, b = 0.01; n = 140). Carcharhinus leucas also exhibited biennial reproductive periodicity as vitellogenesis and gestation occurred consecutively. Further, examination of reproductive metrics indicated that mating occurred during late spring/early summer, followed by an approximate year-long gestation period with parturition occurring during May and June. The observed average brood size was 8.30 (± 1.79) embryos with an estimated size-at-parturition of 74.8 (± 4.19) cm stretch total length. These results, in conjunction with the findings from our concurrent age and growth study, will aid in future management efforts of this species within the U.S. waters of the western North Atlantic Ocean. Gretchen Hilt
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
643: Depredation—the partial or whole removal of a fish from fishing gear by a predator—has reportedly increased along the southeastern coast of the United States, posing challenges to recreational fisheries through reduced target catch and gear loss. Magnetic shark deterrents, such as the Sharkbanz Zeppelin, have been proposed as non-lethal mitigation strategies, though their effectiveness remains uncertain. This study evaluated the efficacy of the Zeppelin in Gulf of Mexico recreational reef-fish hook-and-line fisheries using controlled experimental trials and applied field (charter) trials. Deterrent performance was assessed by testing active and inactive (control) devices with in-line underwater cameras to document: (1) shark behavioral responses, (2) catch per unit effort (CPUE) of target species, and (3) identification of depredating species. In experimental trials, depredation rates were lower with the active Zeppelin (0.01 per hook-hour; 91 hook-hours) than with control treatments (0.10 per hook-hour; 92.3 hook-hours), and shark depredation occurred only on control treatments (0.03 per hook-hour). Sharks exhibited behavioral responses in 58% of interactions with the active deterrent compared to 20% in controls. Additionally, the Zeppelin did not significantly affect CPUE for all teleost species, including red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus). In applied field trials, depredation occurred at a rate of 0.02 per hook-hour (4,079.12 hook-hours) on public angler lines, with sharks accounting for 66% of events and 31% attributed to unknown depredators. Results suggest magnetic deterrents may help reduce shark depredation without diminishing target catch; however, continued research is needed to evaluate performance across fisheries and support sustainable recreational fisheries management. Ella Kinney
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
644: Incidental capture and discard of non-target species (bycatch) can represent a substantial source of fishing mortality, particularly for elasmobranchs that are overfished or highly sensitive to capture-related stress. Spatiotemporal avoidance strategies that identify and mitigate areas of high interaction potential (i.e., bycatch hot spots) provide a proactive means of reducing these impacts. Here, we present a flexible analytical tool designed to identify bycatch hot spots by quantifying the spatiotemporal overlap between fishing effort and species relative abundance. The approach integrates publicly available datasets, normalizes fishing effort and abundance to estimate fishery-interaction potential, and applies spatial statistics to delineate hot spots while also quantifying whether fishing effort or species abundance primarily drives each area of elevated interaction risk. We demonstrate the utility of this tool through a case study of thorny skate (Amblyraja radiata), an overfished species with prohibited retention in the U.S. Northeast, focusing on three major commercial fisheries in which it is captured: Northeast multispecies groundfish, monkfish, and Atlantic sea scallop. Vessel Monitoring System data were processed using gear- and fishery-specific rules to distinguish fishing effort from transit and other non-fishing activity, while thorny skate abundance was estimated from fishery-independent surveys and observer program data. Monthly and annual analyses revealed numerous hot spots across fisheries, including areas associated with smaller thorny skate that experience elevated discard mortality. These results provide insight into potential bycatch mitigation strategies for thorny skate and highlight the broader applicability of this tool for identifying bycatch hot spots across species and fisheries of management concern. William Koehler
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
645: Historically, the American Cownose Ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) was considered the only Rhinopterid present within the Gulf of Mexico (GoM); however, the externally identical Brazilian Cownose Ray (R. brasiliensis), has now been genetically confirmed to occur in this region. Due to these external similarities, previous studies may have inadvertently included both species, and as such, species-specific life history parameters are needed. From 2016-2025, 377 R. bonasus (171 females and 206 males) and 109 R. brasiliensis (39 females and 70 males) were collected from across the northern GoM to define size-at-maturity, reproductive timing, periodicity, parturition date, and size-at-birth for each species. Results indicate that both sexes of R. brasiliensis (females: 754 mm disc width; males: 733 mm disc width) mature at a larger size than R. bonasus (females: 649 mm disc width; males: 669 mm disc width). Through monthly examination of male and female reproductive structures, both species show a peak in reproductive metrics in spring to prepare for summer mating. Females of both species exhibit annual periodicity based on the simultaneous presence of vitellogenic ovarian follicles and near-term embryos. Examination of embryonic growth (R. bonasus: 57-364 mm disc width, n=59; R. brasiliensis: 207-418 mm disc width, n=18) across months indicates parturition of one pup in June following an 11-12 month gestation for both species, with R. brasiliensis exhibiting a larger size-at-birth than R. bonasus. The results of this study will provide species-specific life history data for conservation and management of these two species. Melissa Miller
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
646: Atlantic sharpnose sharks (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae) are one of the smallest and historically most abundant highly migratory small coastal shark species along the eastern coast of the United States and throughout the Gulf of Mexico. While small and prone to mortality from predation as well as commercial and recreational fisheries, known life history characteristics such as relatively fast growth rates, early maturation, and high annual reproductive output were thought to provide reasonable stability for populations. Catch data collected by multiple regional long-term fishery-independent surveys were used to model juvenile and adult trends in relative abundance by gear type and region. Additionally, relative abundance of potential predators and environmental variables were evaluated to explore which factors were most influential as predictors of relative abundance. Overall declines in relative abundance were observed, emphasizing the need for updated stock assessments and potential management action. Andressa Viol Andressa Viol; Justin Lee; Theron Harris; Alison Davis Rabosky
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
647: The freshwater (or largetooth) sawfish (Pristis pristis) is a diadromous ray which once had the largest geographic range of all sawfishes, but their abundance has declined >60% from overfishing and habitat loss. Now rare across most of their former range, and listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List, the Fitzroy River in the Kimberly region of north-western Australia is one of the last known nursery habitats for this species. The Fitzroy River is large (~100,00 km2), highly dynamic, and relatively pristine due to its remoteness and lack of both coastal development and fishing pressure. This highly dynamic river system has distinct wet and dry seasons that are known to heavily influence freshwater sawfish recruitment; however, the Fitzroy River is now being considered for water resource development. To better understand sawfish dispersal, recruitment, and philopatry, we analyzed ~150 DNA samples collected from juvenile freshwater sawfish in the Fitzroy River over the past two decades using single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). We uncovered numerous pairs of both first- and secondorder kin, with high relatedness and patterning indicative of long-term seasonal philopatry to this area. This strategy can have a negative effect on genetic diversity, which is a known buffer against extinction risk. By better understanding freshwater sawfish reproductive ecology in the Fitzroy River, we can provide managers with information crucial to effective conservation and management strategies of this at-risk species. Dylan Yakich Sarah Torre; Matthew Ajemian; Andrew Wooley; Lukas Heath; Dylan Yakich; Liberty Boyd; Michael McCallister;
AES Life History / Fisheries Recruitment / Genetics
648: Atlantic (Hypanus sabinus) and Bluntnose (Hypanus say) stingrays are two benthic species found in coastal waters in the western Atlantic Ocean, including estuaries and lagoons. While both species appear abundant in their respective ranges, the IUCN evaluated both populations as decreasing. Basic life-history information concerning H. sabinus and H. say is also lacking or incomplete. This project will assess the age, growth, maturity, and reproductive patterns of H. sabinus and H. say stingray populations. Specimens have been collected monthly since July 2023 from the Indian River Lagoon, an estuarine ecosystem located along the east coast of Florida, via a collaboration with Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s (FWC) Fisheries Independent Monitoring program (FIM). Age and growth models will be developed using vertebral band counts and corresponding morphometric measurements including disk width and total weight. Stage of maturity for each specimen is assessed based on extragonadal tract development, vas deferens coiling, and clasper length and calcification in males, and tract development and ovarian/uterine tract development in females. Collections to date include 156 H. sabinus (female: n=82, 100 to 316 mm DW; male: n=74, 112 to 379 mm DW) and 134 H. say (female: n=68, 156 to 575 mm DW; male: n=66, 110 to 451 mm DW). The results of this study will increase our understanding of these two species and provide the information required for their increased conservation. J. Jaime Zúñiga-Vega J. Jaime Zúñiga-Vega; Sharon Valdez-Carbajal; Eugenia Zandonà; Karla Kruesi; Israel Solano-Zavaleta; Vianey
