649: Fish biodiversity is a key indicator in measuring environmental and ecological health of an environment. Augusta, GA is an urban city, with high levels of contaminants and turbidity in local waterways that drain into the Savannah River. There exists a large gap in the known fish biodiversity of Augusta. After analysis of data from natural history aggregators like GBIF and iDigBio, it was discovered that many waterways in Augusta either don’t have any sampling data, or the current data is very old, and does not reflect the modern impacts of the urbanization. Additionally, there is very little fish diversity sampling data on the Georgia coast. This project aims to fill the gaps in knowledge about the species composition of the local waterways of Augusta, and coastal GA. Sampling was conducted throughout the Central Savannah River Area (CSRA), and along the coast of Georgia. In conjunction with this, sampling data from local DNR branches and coastal research groups were requested and are being analyzed. Various correlations between different aspects, such as biodiversity in urban areas vs. rural areas, or in clean streams vs. polluted streams, will be analyzed. These results will aid in the understanding of the various human impacts in the CSRA, and how they affect fish diversity. Some fishes sampled were kept in the Augusta University Aquarium for further study, and at the end of their life were accessioned into the Augusta University Zoological Collections. These specimens will be digitized and added to natural history data aggregators. Emilie Barenghien
650: The relative importance of different abiotic factors in shaping species distributions remains a central question in the ecology of freshwater fishes. Within darters (Percidae:Etheostomatinae), a group of benthic freshwater fishes endemic to North America, some species exhibit exceptionally narrow distributions congruent with spatial variation in abiotic landscape variables. However, we lack a systematic characterization of predominant abiotic predictors for darter species distributions and to what extent these predictors vary across species. Here, we use a comparative approach to evaluate the relative importance of hydrologic, climatic, landcover, and topographic variables in predicting darter species distributions. We additionally examined whether niche breadth and the degree of ecological specialization vary across genera and identified factors responsible for these differences. To do so, we compiled open-sourced (Fishnet2; GBIF) species locality records and quality controlled the georeferencing. Then, we linked locality information to National Hydrologic Database (NHD) flowlines (version 2) and extracted environmental variables from the EPA’s Stream-Catchment database (StreamCat). Our workflow extracts environmental variables along river networks and avoids the use of raster-based environmental variables often used when investigating terrestrial organisms. Our results indicate that many darter species exhibit a high degree of specialization, but that the three genera significantly differ in the degree of habitat specialization. Additionally, the relative importance of topographic, hydrologic, and climatic habitat variables for predicting species distributions differed significantly across genera. These findings highlight how multiple abiotic dimensions within the geologically and hydrologically diverse landscapes of southeastern North America shape freshwater fish species distributions. Matt Davis
651: The marine waters off the US state of Alaska are some of the most productive areas for commercial fishing globally and are home to a diverse and abundant ichthyofauna. Alaskan waters are unique in that they (i) are situated at the interface of the temperate Pacific Ocean and the cold Arctic Ocean, (ii) possess high habitat heterogeneity, (iii) have a complex palaeoceanographic and geologic history, and (iv) are highly productive. These factors may interact with one another to produce unique patterns of fish biodiversity not seen in other parts of the world. However, despite the region’s economic importance, we lack a thorough understanding of the patterns and processes that have generated the substantial diversity of fishes found in Alaskan waters. Here, we leverage decades of data from trawl surveys conducted by the NOAA Alaska Fisheries Science Center to examine the dynamics of Alaskan fish biodiversity through three diversity metrics: taxonomic, phylogenetic, and functional diversity. Specifically, we use species distribution modelling (sdmTMB) to spatially map each diversity metric across Alaskan waters, and identify regions, lineages, and combinations of ecological traits that significantly contribute to biodiversity. By investigating the relationship and interplay of biodiversity facets in Alaskan waters, we can better understand groundfish communities in this ecologically, biogeographically, and economically important region. Aanchal Garg
652: Northern species of mole salamanders spend most of their life within the fossorial zone of forests. Visual inputs in this zone are limited, and little is known about how the Ambystoma laterale complex responds to different olfactory cues. Understanding how forest salamanders respond to predator and conspecific cues is an important component of ecosystem dynamics. To address how blue-spotted salamanders might respond to olfactory cues, we conducted experiments testing the behavioral choices of salamanders, including trials with predator odor, conspecific alarm, and non-alarm cues. Results indicated a strong behavioral avoidance of shrew (Blarina brevicauda) odors, choosing the control area 64% of the time, and a similar avoidance of the alarm secretion, choosing the control at a 67% rate. No significant avoidance of garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis) fecal cues was detected. Salamanders were attracted to conspecific odors and spent 66% of their time in conspecific odor areas but did not discriminate between their own odor and conspecifics’. The escape response rate of the salamanders to shrew odor was 90% but was only about 14% to snake odor. This study indicates a stronger avoidance of mammalian odors compared to reptilian cues and attraction to conspecific odors, but no discrimination between conspecific cues. These findings suggest that predation pressure on northern salamander populations may be driven more by endothermic predators such as shrews than by reptilian threats. Moreover, conspecific markings and alarm pheromones may serve the salamanders as identification of safe refugia, potential aggregations, and alerts to potential threats, rather than individual recognition. Paulina Gutierrez-Trejo Paulina Gutierrez-Trejo; Natalie Claunch; Eric Tillman; Bryan Kluever; Anthony Wilmes; Juan Rodriguez; Dustin
653: Prairie rattlesnakes (Crotalus viridis) in Colorado inhabit a mega-den occupied by large numbers of snakes year-round. The opportunity to observe rattlesnakes naturally in a mega-den via a 24/7 live-streaming camera (Project RattleCam) allows scientists and the public to observe rattlesnakes without impacting their behavior. The camera not only shows us the snakes’ daily lives, but also shows how the den can provide resources for other species. Using the livestream chat, where viewers comment in real-time on what they observe, we documented the numerous species of insects that use the den for an entire active season for shelter, nutrition, and reproduction. The livestream documented several novel interactions between insects and rattlesnakes, including cave crickets eating shed skin, phlebotomine flies feeding and mating on snakes at night, yellowjacket wasps biting newborn snakes, and beetles feeding upon carrion in the den. The huge number of snakes inhabiting the den year-round provides a stable resource for the insects. Cameras like the one on this den can give unique insights into new rattlesnake or other species' unobserved behavior and niches while also giving a glimpse into the thriving invertebrate world that would otherwise not be visible to us. Rebecca Hardman Rebecca Hardman; Theresa Cody; Micah Bakenhaster; Yasu Kiryu; Tiffany Nicholson; Eric Fortman; Josh Black;
654: Vertebral deformities such as abnormal curvatures and shapes may influence kinematics of fishes during swimming. Our study examines the vertebral deformities of hatchery-reared lumpfish (Cyclopterus lumpus) to better understand the effects of vertebral deformity on swimming kinematics. We recorded and analyzed videos of 50 juvenile lumpfish that were being raised as cleaner fish for salmonid farms. Each lumpfish was observed in 10second video intervals and then euthanized for X-ray visualization of the skeleton. We used midline tracking to calculate speed, tailbeat amplitude, stride length, tailbeat frequency, and tail curvature during volitional swimming. Body shape analysis using 2D landmarking and principal component analysis showed that there was a significant relationship between the number of deformities and body shape from a dorsal view. We also found that body shape from a lateral view was a significant predictor of speed and stride length. We expected that an increase in deformity would cause a change in tail curvature and a decrease in speed, stride length, tailbeat frequency, and tail amplitude. Instead, we found that the lumpfish swimming was mostly unaffected by the deformity. There was only a significant relationship between tailbeat amplitude and the number of early compressed vertebrae. Since vertebral deformities had a significant relationship with body shape, there was also an indirect effect of deformity on swimming speed. Kady Lyons
655: Lizards constitute over 80% of established non-native reptiles in Florida. Two notable invaders are the Cuban brown anole (Anolis sagrei) and the Peters’s rock agama (Agama picticauda). In areas of sympatry, agamas have been documented consuming brown anoles. Brown anoles are frequent hosts for vector mosquitoes that transmit arboviruses and function as dilution hosts for these mosquito-borne diseases. In contrast, Peters’s rock agamas rarely serve as mosquito hosts. As Peters’s rock agamas are voracious predators, often existing at high densities in Florida, we hypothesize that agamas may mediate transmission of mosquito-borne viruses through predation, and subsequent reduction, of brown anoles. To evaluate this, we experimentally removed Peters’s rock agamas at three sites in St. Lucie County, FL, with one unmanipulated control site. We monitored agama and anole abundance at each site pre and post agama-removal and sampled mosquitoes at each site during the study. Mosquito bloodmeal hosts were identified by DNA barcoding. When comparing treatment and control sites, we found that agama removal resulted in higher brown anole abundance and corresponding bloodmeal analyses showed a shift in host species utilized by mosquitoes; with an increased frequency of bloodmeals from brown anoles and less on birds, the primary amplifying hosts of arboviruses. Our results demonstrate that invasive reptiles can indirectly impact the transmission ecology of mosquito-borne pathogens, including those that are zoonotic, with implications for wildlife and public health. Segun Oladipo
656: Noise pollution impacts vary among marine animal species that differ in auditory morphology and hearing acuity. For fishes, noise can induce behavioral changes, damage tissues, and reduce hearing sensitivity. Estuarine species are at particular risk because noise pollution is concentrated along coasts. Further, species with sound pressure sensitivity may be affected by noise differently. We conducted a controlled laboratory experiment with artificial vessel noise to investigate how Silver Perch, (Bairdiella chrysoura), a common western North Atlantic estuarine species, is impacted by noise. This species possesses a unique anatomy of ear end organs (lagena, saccule, utricle) and a close association of the ear and swim bladder that, together, are hypothesized to detect sound pressure. We used histology to measure impacts to the end ear organ maculae immediately after noise exposure and after five quiet recovery days. Additionally, we estimated hearing thresholds with auditory evoked potentials across 7 frequencies (300-3,200 Hz) after noise exposure. Generalized linear mixed-effects models showed a 14% reduction (p < 0.01) in hair cell density immediately after noise exposure in the lagena and a 9.5% reduction (p = 0.03) in the saccule five days post noise exposure, indicating onset of damage is not consistent in time or effect between end organs. Notably, hearing thresholds did not shift significantly post noise exposure. This work shows anthopogenic noise pollution can damage hair cells in the ear of coastal fishes with sound pressure sensitivity and the onset of these impacts may vary in time and among end organs. Rebecca Pritt
657: Fish otoliths can be utilized by managers to understand exposure to pollutants and trace fish habitat movements. Otoliths are calcified structures in otic capsules of fishes that aid in movement, sensation, and hearing. Otoliths grow throughout the lifespan of a fish and trace elements get incorporated into the structure during formation. We aimed to use element concentrations in otoliths to test the hypothesis that fishes experience variation in pollutants throughout their life. We predicted that trace elements As, Ba, Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Mn, Pb, Se, Sr, Zn would differ across the otolith from the inner core, formed earlier in life, to outer edge, more recently formed. We selected three species, Red Snapper (Lutjanus campechanus), Tomtate (Haemulon aurolineatum), and Hardhead Catfish (Ariopsis felis), from artificial reefs located offshore of Orange Beach, Alabama. Otoliths were cross sectioned, polished, and aged. We used an Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometer coupled to a laser to ablate the surfaces. Rate of ablation and otolith ring formation created a timeline of element exposure. Red Snappers were 0-1, Tomtates 0-4, Hardhead Catfish 2-16 years old. Ba and Mn differed between inner core and edge of the otolith in Tomtate, and Mn and Zn differed for Hardhead Catfish. Element concentration did not differ for otolith location in Red Snapper. Element concentrations for one Hardhead Catfish indicated plausible exposure to a period of intense pollution. We show that otoliths provide a record of pollutant exposure, and that element incorporation may vary by species, age, and/or habitat use. Sam Schenker
658: Determining species occurrence and the conditions under which species can be detected is crucial for developing monitoring and conservation planning strategies. Gila monsters (Heloderma suspectum) are notoriously cryptic and difficult to observe directly due to their minimal above ground activity and patchy spatial distribution. The status of many Gila monster populations remains unclear, due to a lack of standardized, repeatable methods for assessing populations at scales relevant to conservation and land-use planning. We used single-season occupancy models to estimate occupancy and detection probability of Gila monsters across six sites in Washington County, Utah, during the 2025 active season. Surveys consisted of 1-km time-constrained line transects (n = 500), with siteand survey-level covariates used to inform occupancy and detection. Despite survey effort, all detections were based on tracks or sign rather than visual encounters. Occupancy varied among sites and was associated with habitat characteristics including substrate structure and shrub density. Detection probability was strongly influenced by environmental conditions, such as substrate, wind speed, and air temperature. The best-fit model estimated a mean occupancy of 0.83 (CI: 0.45–0.97), and mean detection probability of 0.026 (CI: 0.0–0.05). Higher-quality habitats were associated with higher site occupancy probabilities and were characterized by structurally complex, rocky habitats and moderate shrub cover. Our findings highlight the challenges of surveying cryptic species and importance of accounting for detection in monitoring strategies. Our results may also inform future conservation planning efforts for Gila monsters by demonstrating how environmental drivers of occupancy can inform habitat prioritization. Jeonghyo Song
659: Body shape is a fundamental metric of functional diversity across the tree of life. In aquatic animals, body shape and size strongly influence physiology and behavior, predicting ecological and life-history traits, evolutionary patterns, and conservation risk. Fishes provide an excellent system for examining how whole-body phenotypes structure ecological dynamics, spatial distributions, and conservation outcomes. Nowhere is this more evident than in Neotropical freshwater fishes, the most species-rich continental vertebrate fauna on Earth, which offer exceptional insight into morphological and ecological diversification. Here, we applied 3D photogrammetry, geometric morphometrics, and principal components analysis (PCA) to quantify shape variation in South American freshwater fishes. We generated digital 3D models representing 1,045 species (18% of South American fish species), in 425 genera (63%) and 74 (88%) families, sampled across seven major river basins (Amazon, Chubut, Colorado, Lake Titicaca, Magdalena, Orinoco, Paraná-Paraguay). We used PCA to construct a 3D morphospace and quantify disparity across taxa and basins. We estimated hypervolumes in PC space to measure morphospace occupancy for each clade and compared these to ecospace occupancy using a dataset of 42 ecotraits per species. Our analyses reveal differences in morphospace occupancy among basins, with tropical systems occupying larger and more diverse regions than temperate systems. Disparity is unevenly distributed across clades, with few lineages contributing disproportionately to shape diversity. Comparisons between morphospace and ecospace indicate partial decoupling between form and function. Together, these findings highlight the value of integrating morphological and ecological data to understand biodiversity patterns and inform freshwater conservation. Sarah Torre
660: The larval fishes of Humboldt Bay, the second largest bay in California, were first surveyed in 1969. However, recent surveys, from 2016 onward, have not been made publicly available. As such, there is now a large gap in available knowledge of ichthyoplankton assemblages of Humboldt Bay. I resurveyed the same sites from the 1969-70 and 2016-17 surveys during 2025-26 in order to compare how ichthyoplankton assemblages have shifted over the past fifty-five years. Morphological characteristics and DNA barcoding were used to identify larvae down to the lowest possible taxon. I then compared 2016-17 and 2025-26 assemblages against assemblages from the offshore Trinidad Head Line (THL) of the same years, to examine potential differences between offshore and Bay communities. Several species of special interest are found in Humboldt Bay: most notably, the threatened Longfin Smelt (Spirinchus thaleichthys) and economically important species such as Pacific Herring (Clupea pallasii). Additionally, the invasive Yellowfin Goby (Acanthogobius flavimanus) has recently been introduced to Humboldt Bay, and it is critical to monitor its dispersal patterns to know where else in the Bay and along the California coastline it might settle. As incoming anthropogenic impacts, such as an offshore wind turbine manufacturing facility, pose potential risk to existing larval fish communities in Humboldt Bay, it is important to establish a baseline understanding of modern populations, and how those assemblages have already changed through time. Wayne Wang
661: Characidae sensu lato (s.l.) is a clade of Neotropical freshwater fishes comprising about 1,300 described species distributed across four families: Stevardiidae, Acestrorhamphidae, Spintherobolidae, and Characidae sensu stricto (s.s.). In addition to their remarkable species richness, characids exhibit great morphological diversity, particularly in coloration, life history strategies, and ecomorphology. However, the macroevolutionary patterns of this ecomorphological diversity remain unexplored. Here, we investigate the evolutionary patterns of ecomorphological diversity in Characidae s.l. We collected 21 ecomorphological traits associated with habitat use and diet from 1,056 museum specimens representing 121 genera and 327 species. Using the most representative phylogenomic hypothesis of Characidae s.l., we conducted a phylogenetic Principal Component Analysis (phyloPCA) to identify major axes of ecomorphological variation. We also examined whether traits evolved under Brownian Motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU), or Early Burst models, and we calculated disparity through time (DTT) for Characidae s.l. and each family. Our phyloPCA suggests that Stevardiidae, Acestrorhamphidae, and Characidae s.s. occupy a large portion of the ecomorphospace with considerable overlap, with only a few regions occupied exclusively by a single family. The first two principal components, capturing the most variation, were mostly influenced by traits related to habitat use and were best fitted to an OU model. DTT analyses reveal a steady decline in observed disparity through time for Characidae s.l. and Acestrorhamphidae, whereas Stevardiidae and Characidae s.s. show an early plateau followed by a decline and a subsequent gradual increase toward the present. Madelyn Albritton
662: Located along the Colombian–Venezuelan frontier at the confluence of the clearwater Orinoco, blackwater Atabapo, and whitewater Inírida rivers, the Inírida River Star (IRS) is one of the most physicochemically and biologically heterogeneous freshwater ecosystems in South America. Across this environmental mosaic, the recently erected suckermouth armored catfish genus Iriancistrus has radiated into four currently recognized species differentiated by variably blue, orange, or green color patterns. All are heavily exploited for the ornamental aquarium fish trade. The phantom pleco (Iriancistrus subviridis) occurs as two phenotypically distinct, allopatric ecotypes: a green form inhabiting sediment- and tannin-poor waters upstream of the IRS, and a blue form occupying physicochemically mixed waters downstream. Using genome-wide SNP data and demographic model-testing for I. subviridis and congeners I. beggini and I. guahibrorum, we evaluated whether divergence within I. subviridis is primarily driven by isolation-by-environment (water chemistry) or alternative demographic processes. We recovered three allopatric, genomically distinct populations of I. subviridis associated with disjunct bedrock shoal habitats: one blue downstream population and two green upstream populations, one centered on the Ventuari River and the other on the Casiquiare. Two geographically intermediate hybrid populations were also identified. Demographic inference indicates that this diversity arose through near-simultaneous, geologically driven subdivision during the Andes uplift (~3 Ma), followed by restricted gene flow shaped by combined effects of isolation by distance and environment. These findings highlight the IRS as a natural laboratory for investigating how geography and environmental heterogeneity interact to generate diverse tropical river faunas. Patrick Baca
663: Sexual size dimorphism (SSD) is often attributed to behavioral sexual selection, life history specializations, or habitat/trophic partitioning. While body size SSD is common among vertebrates, extreme dimorphism in oral jaw and cranial morphology is relatively rare. Here we examine these traits in gymnotiform electric fishes, which exhibit a remarkable diversity of body and jaw SSD. Two clades, Compsaraia and Parapteronotus have irreversible, terminal male phenotypes with extreme oral jaw morphologies more than 3x longer than that of mature females. In several other clades, terminal male oral jaw length is more than twice that of females; Apteronotus leptorhynchus and “A.” bonapartii clades. Other gymnotiform clades exhibit dimorphism in tooth morphology and position, body and head size and shape, tail morphology, and in electric organs and their discharges. We map the phylogenetic distribution of these traits across Gymnotiformes using a newly updated inventory of relevant phenotypes and a time-calibrated phylogeny. We find extreme jaw dimorphism spatially concentrated in the Western Amazon, a geographic center of phenotypic disparity, with lesser snout SSD outside this region. We compare these extreme phenotypes to conditions across vertebrates, including examples from sharks, mammals, birds, and other teleosts, and find jaw size dimorphism in apteronotids is exceeded only by deep-sea anglerfishes. To our knowledge, no other craniates, extant or extinct, exhibit similar degrees of jaw dimorphism, suggesting the developmental and ecological pathways permitting extreme SSD are rare. These phenotypes are largely attributable to mate courtship and combat behaviors, and not trophic or other reproductive behaviors. Matthew R. Brander
664: The large rivers of tropical South America are home to seven valid species of electric fishes in the genus Porotergus sensu lato. Here we present morphological and molecular data to support the monophyly of Porotergus, a clade with unusually high phenotypic disparity such that species had previously been assigned to two genera; two species with short snout and gracile oral jaws in Porotergus, and five species with a long snout and robust oral jaw in the genus Apteronotus. We used micro-CT imaging of >100 specimens representing all valid species, landmark-based 3D geometric morphometrics, and multivariate statistics (PCA) to examine differences in skull morphology in the context of a time-calibrated phylogeny estimated from a combination of molecular and morphological datasets. Specimens were selected to include variation of ontogenetic size series based on different levels of ossification, and sex identification was considered to account for sexual dimorphism. Study of the type materials indicates that the nominal species A. macrolepis is a junior synonym of A. bonapartii, and that A. ellisi is a junior synonym of A. paranaensis. We report osteological synapomorphies supporting the following clades: P. bonapartii, P. sp. "ringtail" and P. paranaensis; P. gimbeli; P. gymnotus and P. apurensis; P. duende. Diversification in Porotergus is due to mostly allopatric speciation events with several species coexisting in secondary sympatry. Here we defined Porotergus sensu lato taxonomy to understand patterns of diversification, systematics, evolution, and biogeographic patterns of deep-channel ghost electric fishes. Jessé Figueiredo
665: Accurately delimited freshwater ecoregions are essential for understanding biodiversity and evolutionary processes in continental systems. In Southern Brazil, the Tramandaí-Mampituba ecoregion (Maquiné, Três Forquilhas, Mampituba, and Araranguá river basins) and Southeastern Atlantic Forest ecoregion (Tubarão and other coastal basins) are understood primarily based on ichthyofaunal composition. However, recent evidence suggests possible inconsistencies in these ecoregions with the Tubarão River basin potentially belonging to the Tramandai-Mampituba ecoregion. This study aims to comparatively evaluate and compare fish biodiversity in each of these ecoregions to investigate a potential shift of the Tubarão River drainage to the Tramandai-Mampituba ecoregion. Data from scientific collections and digital databases were compiled and analyses of faunal composition similarity were conducted. Results were then compared with previously done population studies to explore evolutionary patterns in the region. A total of 104 species were recorded in the Tramandaí-Mampituba ecoregion, 112 in the Southeastern Atlantic Forest as a whole, and 77 in the Tubarão River basin alone. 52 out of the 77 species present in the Tubarao basin are also found in other basins within the Southeastern Atlantic ecoregion. Analyses revealed greater ichthyofaunal similarity between the Tubarão basin and the Tramandaí-Mampituba ecoregion (63%) compared to the relationship between Tubarão basin and the other basins in the Southeastern Atlantic Forest (49%). This is also corroborated by a high number of species endemic to the Tubarão and Tramandaí-Mampituba. These results indicate that the Tubarão River basin has greater biogeographical proximity to the TramandaíMampituba ecoregion, reflecting historical connections associated with a shared Pleistocene paleodrainage. M.Laura Habegger
666: Amazonian rivers exhibit diverse water chemistry profiles that affect fish physiology, ecology, and evolution. These rivers are grouped into three broad categories based on color, sediment load, dissolved organic carbon (DOC), pH, and electrical conductivity (a proxy for dissolved ions). Clearwaters originate from basic granitic or calcium-rich limestone parent rocks, have high transparency due to low sediment load and DOC, have nearneutral pH, and contain few dissolved ions resulting in low conductivity and limited nutrient availability. Blackwaters arise from aluminum-rich soils under primary rainforests, have high DOC and low pH, nutrients, sediments, and dissolved ions. Whitewaters come from geologically young soils of Andean origin characterized by high sediment load, dissolved ions, low transparency, high nutrients, near-neutral pH, and often elevated DOC. This study examines evolutionary transitions patterns among fish clades across these river types using Ancestral State Estimation and ecotrace analyses. The water-chemistry origins of South American fish clades are roughly divided into three categories: about one-third from clearwaters, one-third from estuarine or marine environments, and onethird from other water types. However, most (73.5%) South American fish species belong to clades that originated in the clearwaters of the Brazilian and Guiana Shields, while only about 10% are derived from marine lineages. Notably, a general evolutionary trend among large clades is a shift from eurytopic water chemistry tolerances to specialization within a single water chemistry profile. Overall, results highlight clearwater origins dominance and evolutionary shifts toward specialized water chemistry adaptation. Eric Haddad
667: Lithoxancistrus is a small genus (3 species) of suckermouth armored catfish (Siluriformes: Loricariidae: Hypostominae) from Guiana Shield portions of the Orinoco River Basin. A morphometric analysis of the genus was conducted, including all three described species as well as individuals potentially representing new species. Data collected supports the distinction of the three recognized species. Additionally, certain individuals from across the range of the genus exhibited unique traits suggestive of previously unrecognized species-level diversity. Observed patterns of variation provide a basis for additional evaluation of these specimens warranting further taxonomic study. Tucker Heptinstall
668: Originally described in 1929 as a subgenus of Leporinus containing species with downturned mouths, Hypomasticus has undergone a complex taxonomic history of synonymization and revalidation. Recent molecular analyses support the validity of Hypomasticus but also reveal substantial variation in mouth position within the genus; the clade clearly includes species originally assigned to other genera because of their terminal mouth positions. The newly reformulated Hypomasticus now spans much of the breadth of oral and cranial morphology observed across the family. This remarkable variability raises important evolutionary and ecological questions, such as how many times mouth position has changed in the clade, whether different positions reflect distinct diets and if position differences facilitate congeneric sympatry. Here, we investigate character evolution and ecomorphology in Hypomasticus using molecular data, micro-computed tomography, radiography, morphometric analyses, and stomach content examination. Radiographic measurements show significant differences in mouth angle among morphotypes, with well-defined quantitative distinctions and minimal overlap between subterminal and inferior conditions. Ancestral character state reconstructions indicate that the most recent common ancestor of Hypomasticus likely possessed a terminal mouth, that inferior mouths evolved twice within the genus, while the subterminal condition arose at least three times. Sympatric species with distinct oral morphotypes appear to occupy different ecological niches, with shifts in mouth position extending beyond the oral apparatus to other anterior skeletal elements. These results suggest a prominent role for character displacement or ecomorphological divergence in the diversification of Hypomasticus, and maybe Anostomidae as a whole. Cole J. Ivie
669: This project is a comparative osteological analysis of the three valid species of Steatogenys (S. elegans, S. duidae, and S. ocellatus) with an emphasis on skull morphology. This presentation describes osteological differences among the species to investigate whether allopatric speciation, especially the Amazon-Orinoco drainage divide, has influenced diversification in Steatogenys. Using CT-derived 3D models of specimens from the Amazon, Orinoco, and Essequibo river basins, homologous landmarks and semi landmarks were collected across an ontogenetic size series. These data were analyzed in 3D Slicer using PCA to quantify shape variation. Static allometry was evaluated by examining size-related shape changes within species, while phylogenetic allometry was assessed by comparing scaling patterns among species and basin-specific lineages. Environmental data were integrated to test associations between cranial morphology, river basins, habitat type, and water chemistry. Genetic data suggest that S. elegans comprises at least two distinct lineages, leading to the hypothesis of historical isolation due to major geological changes such as the Andean uplift and subsequent redirection of the Amazon and Orinoco drainage systems. Results indicate that skull morphology varies both interspecifically and geographically, with evidence of basin-structured variation in S. elegans, consistent with genetic hypotheses of multiple lineages. Allometric patterns reveal ontogenetic shifts in cranial elements with differences in scaling among habitats. Additionally, broader comparative analyses suggest that the western Amazon exhibits elevated morphological variation, likely reflecting complex hydrological history and habitat heterogeneity. Together, these findings support a combined role of historical biogeography, ecological divergence, and allometric scaling in shaping diversification within Steatogenys. Kersten Plicner
670: South American freshwater fishes are the world's most diverse continental fauna, yet their ecological diversity remains poorly understood geographically. River size and trophic position drive eco- evolutionary diversification, with origins in small rivers at small body sizes and convergent evolution toward larger sizes in larger rivers, but links to ecospace occupancy remain unexplored. Here we quantify the biogeographic structure of body size and ecological traits (ecotraits) across major South American bioregions. We analyzed 6,354 freshwater fish species assigned to nine bioregions using a matrix of 41 ecotraits spanning macro-, meso-, and microhabitat, diet, life history, and behavior, plus body size (as maximum SL cm). We performed PCAs for the ecotrait matrix, computing convex hull volumes in multidimensional space. Linear regressions of ecospace volume with species richness, geographic area, and mean body size, show strong correlations with unique habitats types (largest rivers with distinct channel/floodplain fauna), and paleography, being now or formerly part of the SubAndean foreland. PCA recovered a core-periphery patterns in both species richness and ecospace volume, with differences associated with the presence of large rivers. Trans-Andean has a lower, and Orinoco and Brazilian Shield higher ecospace volumes than predicted by their species richness values. These results indicate that ecological diversity and species richness in Neotropical freshwater fishes are similar but distinct, both exhibiting a core-periphery patterns, but with somewhat different responses to paleogeographic history since the Late Miocene formation of the modern continental drainage basins. Edgardo Rosado
671: Neotropical catfishes (Siluriformes) comprise more than one-third of the fish diversity in rivers of the Guiana Shield, South America. They exhibit broad variations in their feeding ecology and functional traits, making them suitable for assessing their ecological roles and informing effective conservation practices. In this study, we investigated the trophic ecology of catfishes in two rivers in Guyana and quantified isotopic niche variation using carbon (δ¹3C) and nitrogen (δ¹⁵N) stable isotope analysis (SIA). Furthermore, we examined the relationship between body size and δ¹⁵NField surveys were conducted in May 2023 (Rupununi) and May 2024 (Essequibo), coinciding with the start of the region’s rainy season. In both rivers, fishes were collected from floodplain lakes and main channel habitats using a variety of fishing gears. A total of 40 catfish species from Rupununi and 23 from Essequibo were used for SIA. Differences in carbon and nitrogen ratios were found in catfish assemblages between habitats of the Rupununi and Essequibo. However, no differences were observed between habitats within each river. There was 74% isotopic niche overlap between catfish assemblages of the two rivers. Within rivers, catfish assemblages in the Rupununi showed high overlap (73%) between floodplain lake and main channel habitats, compared to the Essequibo River (54%). Among catfish families, the isotopic niches of the seven families in the Rupununi exhibited higher overlap compared to the Essequibo. Finally, a positive and significant relationship between body size and δ¹⁵N ratios was observed only for catfishes in the Rupununi. Our findings highlight relevant aspects of the trophic ecology and dynamics of neotropical catfishes that have not been previously studied. Further research should focus on assessing catfish isotopic niches across seasons to better understand isotopic niche diversity and differentiation, and to provide critical information for sustainable management of these species in the Guiana Shield. Donald B. Shepard
672: Feeding is crucial for most organisms‘ survival and fitness. Therefore, trophic niche divergence is often an important axis of variation underlying diversification. Trophic divergence includes not only specialization in resource utilization (e.g., detritivory, insectivory, piscivory), but also along elemental, nutritional, and ecological niche gradients. Even in seemingly trophic generalists, particularly in groups of sympatrically occurring species such as Limia, an island radiation of livebearers from the Caribbean, small differences in niche use could allow coexistence and subsequently promote lineage diversification. Diet data on Limia is scarce, but recent studies have shed light on their potential trophic niche partitioning (Rodriguez-Silva et al., 2021). Although not conclusive on whether diet specializations may drive speciation in Limia, these findings support that trophic ecology might be a factor to consider when exploring the causes of diversification in this group. I have collected muscle tissues of 8 species of Limia and related species, in various locations along their range in Hispaniola, for Stable Isotopes Analysis to study their trophic ecology. Preliminary analysis suggests significant differences in isotopic signal between the species analyzed, which could be related to fine-scale variation in diet. In this work, I expand on this dataset, adding new samples as well as incorporating morphological data and new tools such as mixing models and baseline-standardized isotopic vector analysis (Black and Armbruster, 2021) to test trophic niche divergence in Limia. Samantha Trame
673: Freshwater fishes in order Characiformes have independently evolved gigantism in multiple lineages, providing a framework for comparing the molecular mechanisms underlying convergent extreme body size evolution. Within family Serrasalmidae (pacus, piranhas), pronounced and repeated increases in body size occur across lineages. In subfamily Colossomatinae, the tambaqui Colossoma macropomum of 1.1 m contrasts with the smaller pacu-caranha Piaractus mesopotamicus (40 cm), while in Serrasalminae, redeye-piranha Serrasalmus rhombeus (45 cm) is substantially larger than silver-dollar Metynnis hypsauchen (15 cm) and other relatives. This study investigates the genomic correlates of gigantism leveraging the six high-quality serrasalmid genome assemblies available on NCBI, encompassing this size spectrum. Genomes are annotated using BRAKER2 with protein homology evidence. Predicted orthologs are used to assess gene family expansion and contraction using CAFE and to test for signatures of positive selection based on dN/dS ratios. These analyses target convergent genomic signals in large-bodied taxa, particularly growth-related pathways previously implicated in fish gigantism (e.g., in Arapaima gigas). We further expanded the dataset to include all available characiform reference genomes and reconstructed phylogenetic relationships using basic universal single copy orthologs (BUSCOs), comparing resulting topologies with those from alternative datasets. Our results begin to reveal candidate genes and gene families associated with extreme body size and provide insight into the genomic architecture of gigantism in serrasalmids. This work also enables evaluation of phylogenetic signals across genomic datasets and supports future comparative analyses of gigantism across Characiformes to better understand the genomic mechanisms driving convergent body size evolution in fishes. Eli Warshaw
674: Desert environments are vulnerable to climate change, and desert reptiles face potential extinction risk yet most species lack sufficient data for robust conservation assessment. Here, we use species distribution models (SDMs) to estimate the current distribution of two Arabian Peninsula lizards and project future shifts in suitable habitat. Using multiple global circulation models (GCMs), climate scenarios, and time frames, we project habitat shifts up to the 2080s, and assess how current and future suitable habitat overlaps with protected areas in Saudi Arabia. Additionally, we report lizard body temperatures from several sites and compare field-collected microclimate data with WorldClim data used to train SDMs. We find that suitable habitat for both species decreases with future climate change: 33.4–73.8% for the spiny-tailed lizard, Uromastyx aegyptia; 20.3–33.7% for the toadheaded agama, Phrynocephalus arabicus. Currently, 22.2% and 18.0% of suitable habitat for U. aegpytia and P. arabicus, respectively, falls within protected areas in Saudi Arabia. Under future scenarios, 11.6–13.2% of suitable habitat will overlap protected areas for P. arabicus. By contrast, for U. aegpytia, proportion of suitable habitat within protected areas increases by 31.5–56.2%, due to more suitable habitat projected in protected areas in northern Saudi Arabia. We observed small discrepancies between field and WorldClim data, and lizard body temperatures were consistently lower than substrate, supporting active thermoregulation and emphasizing the importance of microenvironments. SDMs are valuable tools for conservation, especially for data-deficient species, yet they could be improved by including microclimate data or microclimate proxies, especially for desert species. Haley Altadonna
675: The Eastern Massasauga is a globally imperiled viper declining across its range, yet past conservation translocations have been met with suboptimal outcomes. A review of snake translocations identified tactics associated with positive translocation outcomes, the application of which might improve snake translocations. That study also recommended investigating the effect of prerelease conditioning (e.g., artificial hibernation) on postrelease survival of captive-reared snakes. In 2024 we conducted an experimental translocation with 21 two-yearold Massasaugas at Canada’s Southernmost population (Ojibway Prairie) to determine if the application of beneficial translocation tactics would result in positive outcomes related to movement behaviour, site fidelity, and survival. The snakes were divided into two treatment groups based on exposure to one or two winters of artificial hibernation prerelease, and  radiotracked from release in late August until spring emergence. Average home range size was significantly larger, and closer to “normal”, for snakes in the two winter group. Overall, 60% of snakes chose hibernacula at the 0.5 ha release site, yet only 27% returned to their specific delayed release pen to hibernate (with significantly better outcomes for the one-winter group). Overall, post-release survival to spring emergence was 38%, with slightly better, but non-significant, outcomes for the two-winter group (44%) compared to the one-winter group (33%). Snake translocations should aim for ≥ 50% post-release survival and site fidelity, therefore, release protocols will be refined to improve outcomes. This study was part of ongoing Massasauga recovery efforts in Canada, and results will inform future snake translocations more widely. Eva Chukwudi
676: We present preliminary findings from the assessment of Mesoamerican snakes and lizards conducted as part of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Global Reptile Assessment 2. This effort evaluated a total of 596 species against the IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria, drawing on the most up-to-date published data, relevant grey literature, and extensive input from regional and taxonomic experts during a dedicated Red List review workshop held in 2025. While several species were assessed for the first time, the majority underwent reassessment, enabling the comparison of extinction risk status over time and providing an important second data point for trend analysis. The inaugural Global Reptile Assessment, published in 2012, delivered essential baseline data on many threatened species; however, numerous taxa are now overdue for reassessment, with the IUCN’s goal of updating species status at least once every decade. Mesoamerica, recognized globally as a biodiversity hotspot with high levels of reptile endemism, was identified as a priority region for this global initiative. Completion of the entire Global Reptile Assessment 2 is anticipated in 2030. These preliminary results will help elucidate the major drivers of extinction risk in Central American reptiles, track shifts in Red List status, and highlight priority conservation measures. Collectively, this work underscores the urgent need for targeted, evidencebased conservation action to safeguard the region’s diverse and ecologically significant assemblage of snakes and lizards. Jon Hoffman-Vinje Jon Hoffman; Dylan DeBaun; Mozes Blom; Carlos Pavón-Vázquez; Uri García-Vázquez; Adrián Nieto-Montes de
677: Reptiles evoke emotions ranging from fascination and reverence to fear and disgust, and are often portrayed in media as either villainous predators or misunderstood victims of environmental harm. While prior research has examined ophidiophobia and general wildlife attitudes, fewer studies have directly compared how visual imagery shapes anthropomorphic values across reptilian groups or evaluated how reptiles are perceived relative to other taxa within an invasive species framework. We conducted two complementary online Qualtrics surveys (n = 50n = 1,000) to investigate: (1) perceptions of reptiles compared to other invasive taxa such as feral cats; (2) willingness to support eradication of invasive reptilian species versus other taxa; (3) how background, personal experience, religion, and popular culture influence perceptions of snakes, including willingness to handle or kill them; and (4) how imagery influences perceptions and salient visual features. Using images of six snake species (five native, one non-native) from the southeastern United States, we incorporated diverse photographic contexts— head-on and side profiles, close-up facial imagery, size comparisons, feeding events, nurturing interactions, and defensive displays—to test how framing alters emotional, aesthetic, and moral responses. Participants also evaluated invasive species across taxa, enabling direct comparison of anthropomorphic values such as beauty, intelligence, danger, and cultural importance and their influence on eradication support. Across surveys, reptiles—particularly snakes—elicited stronger fear-based and moralized responses than mammals, even when behaviors were held constant. Anthropomorphic values significantly predicted management support, with perceived beauty and cultural importance reducing willingness to kill. Notably, many participants expressed admiration for snakes despite fear, especially for colorful venomous species. These findings underscore the influence of imagery, experience, and cultural narratives in shaping reptile conservation attitudes. Alina Hussey
678: Rodenticides are widely used to control pest populations. The most common rodenticides are anticoagulant compounds that cause death from excessive internal bleeding, typically 4–14 days after baits are ingested. Prior research has shown that exposure to anticoagulant rodenticides (ARs) can be a major conservation concern in some predatory mammals and raptors. Only a handful of studies globally, however, have examined the potential that snakes may also get exposed to ARs by preying upon poisoned rodents. Here, we test for exposure to ARs in multiple snake species in California. Tested specimens had been previously collected as roadkill or were euthanized by outside parties as part of rattlesnake removal efforts. We tested 113 individuals, spanning 15 species. Rodenticides were detected in 38% of tested snakes. Six different ARs were detected, with 21% of snakes exposed to multiple ARs. Rodenticides were found in ten snake species. For the remaining snake species tested, only 1–3 specimens were available, and we suspect that testing more individuals would similarly reveal that they are sometimes exposed to rodenticides. Specimens were collected between 2001 and 2025, allowing us to examine whether recent state-wide bans have reduced secondary poisonings of predatory species. Unfortunately, we do not find evidence that these bans are decreasing exposure rates, suggesting that further efforts are needed to protect nontarget species from rodenticide exposure. This work highlights the need for further studies examining impacts and conservation threats of rodenticide exposure in reptiles. Gregory B. Pauly
679: Open-canopied longleaf pine (Pinus palustris) forests support a diverse array of squamate species. However, this ecosystem has widely declined over the past four centuries due to fire suppression and overharvesting. Alongside habitat loss, the emergence of novel pathogens poses a significant threat to squamate populations. In recent decades, a fungal pathogen, Ophidiomyces ophidiicola (Oo), has been detected in wild snake populations throughout much of the eastern United States. Oo is one of the primary infectious agents responsible for Ophidiomycosis (commonly known as “Snake Fungal Disease”). The combination of habitat loss and novel pathogen emergence has created important questions for land managers seeking to conserve diverse squamate assemblages. The United States Forest Service is restoring longleaf pine forests across the southern range of the William B. Bankhead National Forest. To monitor how herpetofaunal communities are responding to these efforts, we deployed 16 drift fence arrays with both funnel and pitfall traps across a chronosequence of longleaf pine restoration. Traps were open from May to August in 2021-2024. Rare habitat specialists, such as Pituophis melanoleucus, were more commonly detected in managed stands with a lower basal area and extensive burn history. In 2023 and 2024, we collected skin swabs to monitor for the presence of Oo. Out of 417 total samples, representing 19 species and 387 individuals, Oo was detected in approximately 17% of snakes. Prevalence of Oo had a significant positive correlation with stand humidity levels and was greatest among Lampropeltis elapsoides, Crotalus horridus, Pituophis melanoleucus, and Pantherophis alleghaniensis. Ian Robinson
680: Invasive species present substantial challenges to preserving biodiversity and ecosystem function, necessitating adaptive management approaches. Efficient management of invasive Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus) in South Florida has been hindered by their low detectability and high adult survivorship. To address these challenges, we introduce the Weighted Removal Index (WRI), a quantitative technique designed to enhance the effectiveness of python management by prioritizing removals based on demographic characteristics. Specifically, WRI targets demographics, which disproportionately influence population growth through high survivorship and reproductive potential, such as large females. Utilizing data from the South Florida Water Management District's Python Elimination Program, we evaluated the WRI through three modeling approaches, Generalized Additive Models (GAM), Boosted Regression Trees (BRT), and Neural Networks (NN), to robustly assess the ability of analytical frameworks to predict this derived metric. The NN model demonstrated superior predictive capacity to the other models, achieving a positive predictive value of 47.86% and a mean absolute error of 2.31. Additionally, linear regression analysis of contractor performance revealed a strong positive relationship between contractor-specific coefficients and mean aggregate survey WRI (R² = 0.59, p = 0.01), underscoring the critical role of contractor skill and experience in removal impacts. Our findings emphasize the utility of integrating demographic weighting with predictive modeling, enabling management programs to target removals that disproportionately contribute to population growth. This informatic approach offers a data-driven framework for informing invasive species removal efforts, particularly for species with low detectability and natural mortality. Alejandro Romero Henry Gallo; Oscar Barbosa; Alejandro Romero-Figueroa; Omar Melo-Ortiz; Alexander Urbano-Bonilla; Wilmer
681: Biodiversity has decreased globally over the past several centuries, largely driven by human activities. Amphibians and reptiles are among the most at-risk with 33% of amphibian and 20% of reptile species threatened with extinction. Brazil is a global hotspot for amphibian and reptile diversity, but many areas have been impacted by deforestation, livestock grazing, farming, and anthropogenic fire. The semi-arid Caatinga biome covers >800,000 km² in northeastern Brazil and harbors many amphibian and reptile species, approximately 22% of which are endemic (~53% of lizards). Ongoing land-use change and threats associated with global climate change are predicted to significantly impact Caatinga biodiversity in the future. How the distributions of Caatinga amphibians and reptiles will respond to climate-induced vegetation changes is a critical question. Towards this, we made species distribution models for 25 frog and 38 squamate species endemic to the Caatinga and forecast species distributions at two timepoints (2041 and 2061) under optimistic and pessimistic climate-change scenarios. Our models predicted complete or near-complete loss of 21 of 25 (84%) endemic frog species and 28 of 38 (74%) endemic squamate species under both scenarios. Only 3 frogs and 3 squamates were predicted to remain stable or expand their distributions. With ~6% of Caatinga land area currently in protected areas, strategic expansion of protected areas in the region is likely needed if there is any hope of conserving these endemic species. Abbey Shields
682: Large-scale anthropogenic habitat modifications, such as the damming of rivers, have the potential to significantly impact range restricted taxa. The conversion of riverine habitat to lacustrine habitat drastically alters ecological conditions with downstream effects on disease dynamics, population connectivity, and habitat availability. Our work examines the status of reservoir-dwelling Nerodia harteri, a species of threatened riverine watersnake endemic to the Brazos and Colorado river drainages of north-central Texas. Using minnow traps and traditional hand capture methods we sampled and tagged hundreds of N. harteri and congeners (N. erythrogaster and N. rhombifer) and employed site-consistent biannual monitoring and mark-recapture techniques to investigate spatial and temporal dynamics across species, seasons, and reservoirs. To examine patterns of disease prevalence we assessed snakes for parasitic helminths (oral trematodes and nodule-forming nematodes) and fungal pathogens (Ophidiomyces ophiodiicola) and found that infection prevalence was driven largely by host identity, seasonality, and micro-habitat characteristics. We also used radiotelemetry tracking of select individuals in combination with geospatial analyses and site-specific belt transects, to glean fine-scale habitat use and behavior data and found distinct ecological differences and unique behaviors (e.g., basking in trees) between presently occupied and unoccupied historic N. harteri sites. Our results highlight the importance of shoreline habitat preservation in lacustrine systems, the utility of tagging and telemetry methods in the tracking and frequent monitoring of elusive, range restricted taxa, and the complexity of disease dynamics and habitat requirements in a shifting landscape.
683: The conservation of imperiled species is a pressing challenge in maintaining global biodiversity, particularly for organisms that face multi-faceted threats and are no longer recoverable by in-field conservation methods. Captive breeding and headstarting programs play a pivotal role in preserving imperiled species by offering a viable solution for boosting population size, providing genetic rescue, and increasing resiliency to anthropogenic stressors, like climate change. We explore the key steps in implementing a successful captive propagation and headstarting conservation program for native, endemic herpetofauna that are typically considered non-charismatic and have low public support. Critical components necessary for establishing such a program include partnerships with wildlife agencies, proper facility design, and the development of protocols for breeding, rearing, and releasing animals. Using giant garter snakes, Thamnophis gigas, and Santa Cruz long-toed salamanders, Ambystoma macrodactylum croceum, as case studies, we address key program goals: ensuring that breeding practices are informed by data, evaluating captive breeding efficacy on species recovery, and testing how these efforts contribute to increasing the resiliency, redundancy, and representation of wild populations. We also show how a non-profit program can work closely with collaborators to design both practical experiments and large-scale research projects that benefit scientific understanding as well as broader conservation goals. Collaborative, science-driven conservation efforts can support both immediate population needs and long-term recovery to conserve highly imperiled species. Max Sprute
684: The dunes sagebrush lizard (DSL; Sceloporus arenicolus) is a habitat specialist endemic to the Mescalero-Monahans shinnery-sands ecosystem of west Texas and southeastern New Mexico, over which land-use practices have contributed to fragmentation and loss of habitat. We created a fine-scale, continuous habitat suitability model for the DSL in Texas to support conservation actions. We used generalized linear (GLM) and spatially weighted generalized additive models (GAM) to predict DSL occurrence. We included sand cover, shinnery oak cover, binned rugosity, and mean maximum rugosity as covariates. We replicated our model selection analysis and our spatial prediction analysis across a random sample of pseudo-absence data, then selected the best ranking model, defined as the model having the highest frequency being ranked first across 1,000 replications. Finally, we used the averaged prediction, from the replicated model prediction runs (n=1,000), as our estimate of occurrence for each grid cell. The highest-ranked model was the mean maximum rugosity and percent cover shinnery oak interaction model. The distribution of predicted occurrence captured Winkler County well in the GLM, but Andrews County had a lower predicted probability than expected. The GAM accounted for DSL spatial dynamics; thus, we see a higher occurrence probability in Andrews County and a much lower occurrence probability in Crane County compared to the GLM. The GLM is important for identifying areas of potential DSL habitat, allowing us to identify areas for future surveys. The GAM could determine areas for high-value conservation actions, such as protecting dune habitat from further development.
685: Long-term surveillance of wildlife populations can provide novel opportunities to investigate changes in population dynamics over time. As many taxa are experiencing widespread declines globally, sustained multiyear datasets are of increasing importance to examine how wildlife populations respond over time to stressors such as climate change, invasive species, habitat loss and degradation, pollutants, pathogens, and overexploitation. Documented declines in reptiles, particularly snakes, are occurring worldwide at alarming rates with many of the aforementioned stressors implicated. To assess long-term population trends of native snake species in Everglades National Park (ENP), Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties, FL, we examined a large dataset amassed from weekly standardized vehicle surveys conducted within ENP during 2014 – 2024 as part of our Everglades Invasive Reptile and Amphibian Monitoring Program, an initiative aimed to increase detection, monitoring, and removal of nonnative wildlife while concurrently documenting native wildlife observations. We identified declines of several native snake species over this period, particularly for watersnakes, and we discuss the potential influence of stressors such as invasive species, altered hydroperiods, pathogens, and changes in prey availability, as the primary drivers of snake declines. Connor White
686: Historical genomics can provide insights into wildlife responses to stressors through time, with applications to future conservation efforts. For example, predicting future susceptibility to the frog-killing fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) is difficult in amphibians that show widely variable disease outcomes. Historical responses of amphibian populations to Bd outbreaks may reveal signals of future susceptibility in naive populations. In the Lowland Leopard Frog, Rana yavapaiensis, both genetic and environmental factors may drive observed variation in Bd susceptibility across the species' extant range in Arizona. A number of genetic loci, some of which are known to mediate immune function, may play significant roles in Bd susceptibility in R. yavapaiensis and other amphibian species. If populations that survived historical Bd outbreaks exhibit selection or allelic shifts at these loci, this could validate their use as signals of future Bd susceptibility. In our study, we address this need for empirical validation using a “museomics” approach: we leverage historical museum collections and molecular methods designed for historical and ancient DNA to test for genetic responses to historical Bd outbreaks. Using sequence capture with custom RNA baits, we sequenced ~1400 candidate Bd response genes and random genome-wide markers in R. yavapaiensis specimens collected as far back as 1946. Our preliminary results indicate that several key immunity loci and pathways vary among populations that were extirpated following historical Bd outbreaks vs. those that survived and persist today. We anticipate that our findings will improve prediction and mitigation of disease outbreaks in vulnerable wild amphibian populations. Rayna C. Bell
687: Haemogregarine parasites are widespread blood parasites of freshwater turtles, yet the relative roles of host taxonomy and environmental factors in shaping infection patterns remain unclear. This study evaluated haemogregarine prevalence and parasite intensity in three turtle species (Apalone spinifera, Pseudemys gorzugi, and Trachemys gaigeae) across the upper, middle, and lower regions of the Rio Grande Basin and in two of its major tributaries, the Pecos and Devils rivers. A total of 1,424 turtles were sampled, with an overall haemogregarine prevalence of 35% across the Rio Grande Basin. Blood samples were screened using quantitative PCR targeting the 18S rRNA gene, and prevalence and parasite intensity were analyzed using generalized linear models. Across all regions, host species emerged as the strongest predictor of both infection prevalence and parasite intensity. Trachemys gaigeae consistently exhibited the highest prevalence and parasite intensity, Pseudemys gorzugi showed intermediate prevalence, and Apalone spinifera had the lowest infection rates. In contrast, regional effects were weak, indicating that differences among river systems contributed less to infection patterns than host taxonomy. These findings demonstrate that host-specific traits are the primary drivers of haemogregarine infection dynamics in this system. Todd R. Clardy
688: Susceptibility to infection is an urgent issue in global wildlife health, making the characterization of immune responses essential for developing effective conservation strategies. The opportunistic bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila is commonly present in the amphibian microbiota, but can become pathogenic in immunocompromised hosts, often leading to death. While host–pathogen interactions involving fungal and viral agents have been extensively studied, much less is known about the amphibian immune responses to lethal bacteria. We generated a de novo transcriptome of Rhinella diptycha toads (Anura: Bufonidae) to characterize early immune responses to A. hydrophila across major immune organs and identify tissue-specific differential gene expression following bacterial stimuli. Toads were injected with heat-killed A. hydrophila, and RNA-seq was performed on spleen and liver tissues six hours post-injection. Preliminary results reveal higher tissue-specific differential gene expression in the spleen compared to the liver, indicating organ-specific immune activation during systemic bacterial infection. Ongoing functional enrichment analyses will identify tissue-specific signaling cascades and gene families involved in this response. Our results provide a multi-tissue transcriptomic framework for understanding amphibian immune responses to A. hydrophila. Because these pathogens are present in healthy hosts, immune activation may depend on host condition, offering insight into mechanisms underlying susceptibility and survival. Felipe Floreste Felipe Floreste; Hongyuan Chen; Tsering Chan; Gregory Brown; Vania Assis; Fernando Gomes; Richard Shine; Lee
689: Pathogens shape host ecology and evolution, but population declines driven by emerging infectious diseases have heightened their importance for wildlife conservation. A critical question for both basic disease ecology and conservation is: how does pathogen exposure dose influence host outcomes? Although exposure dose is widely assumed to influence infection success and disease severity, dose–response relationships remain poorly characterized for most wildlife pathogens. Snake fungal disease, caused by Ophidiomyces ophidiicola (Oo), has been linked to snake declines across Europe and North America, yet the role of exposure dose in shaping infection dynamics and host responses has not been experimentally tested. Here, we conducted an experimental infection using corn snakes (Pantherophis guttatus) to examine how increasing doses of Oo influences infection dynamics, host responses, and disease outcomes. We applied dose–response models to quantify infection probability across increasing exposure doses. Infection prevalence, disease progression, and severity all increased with dose, demonstrating strong dose dependence in disease outcomes. Hosts mounted a defensive response via accelerated skin shedding and frequency that scaled strongly with exposure dose. Despite this, substantial heterogeneity in host responses persisted, potentially mediated by variation in shedding dynamics and host susceptibility. Notably, even low-dose exposure was sufficient to cause infection and disease in some individuals. Together, these findings demonstrate that exposure dose is a critical driver of pathogen establishment and disease progression in snake fungal disease, providing insight into mechanisms shaping infection risk and informing conservation strategies for wild snake populations. Amelia Harward
690: Turtle fraservirus 1 (TFV1) is an emerging pathogen that has been detected in multiple species of Florida’s native and nonnative freshwater turtles. The first mortalities associated with TFV1 may have been as early as January 2018 and statewide surveillance has been ongoing since March 2018. Given the recent discovery of TFV1, the epidemiology of the virus remains poorly characterized, with limited baseline information on which species are affected, where detections occur, and when infections are observed. This study builds on past surveillance to characterize the epidemiology of TFV1. To better understand host species, spatiotemporal distribution, and detection context, we analyzed aggregated surveillance data derived largely from opportunistic sampling associated with wildlife rehabilitation, mortality investigations, confiscations, and periodic monitoring. Molecular detection of TFV1 was performed on multiple sample types collected from necropsied carcasses and live turtles, including oral/cloacal swabs, liver, kidney, and urine from free-ranging, rehabilitated, and confiscated individuals. A total of 1,023 turtles were tested for TFV1, of which 55 tested positive with at least one sample type. TFV1 was detected in 10 Florida counties, with most detections occurring in east-central and southwest Florida. Detection peaked in late winter through early spring, which is consistent with previous observations. However, detections also occurred during summer and fall. TFV1 was detected in seven host species, and surveillance expanded the known host species to include diamondback terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin) and gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus). Continued surveillance is essential for improving our understanding of TFV1 epidemiology and its impacts on wild turtle populations. Jackie Kerler
691: Fungal dermatomycoses are an increasing concern for wild snake populations, yet surveillance to date has focused primarily on Ophidiomyces ophidiicola, the etiologic agent of ophidiomycosis. In contrast, the prevalence and distribution of other onygenalean fungi, including Paranannizziopsis spp. and Nannizziopsis spp., remain poorly characterized in free-ranging snakes. This study used a validated multiplex quantitative PCR assay to screen skin swabs from 1,394 wild snakes for O. ophidiicola, Paranannizziopsis spp. and Nannizziopsis spp. The objectives were to estimate pathogen-specific prevalence, describe geographic and host associations, and evaluate evidence of coinfection and alternative fungal etiologies for skin lesions in wild snakes. Samples were collected from free-ranging snakes found on military installations throughout the U.S. and represented 79 species sampled across 36 states and Puerto Rico. The prevalence of O. ophidiicola was 19.2% (95% CI: 12.2-21.4%) across a broad geographic and taxonomic range. Results were largely consistent with prior surveys, although ophidiomycosis was detected in Nevada for the first time. Paranannizziopsis spp. were detected at low prevalence (0.5%; 95% CI: 0.21.0%) across seven states, including first detections in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, Oklahoma, Texas, Wisconsin, and in previously unreported host species (Agkistrodon piscivorus, Phyllorhynchus decurtatus). Nannizziopsis spp. were not detected. Coinfections were rare (n = 1). Multiplex screening did not identify other fungal pathogens in lesion-positive individuals previously negative for O. ophidiicola by singleplex qPCR, indicating that unexplained skin lesions were not attributable to Paranannizziopsis or Nannizziopsis spp. Associations between O. ophidiicola detection and geographic, taxonomic, and demographic variables were consistent with prior studies, while no significant associations were identified for Paranannizziopsis spp. These findings reinforce O. ophidiicola as the predominant fungal pathogen affecting wild snakes in North America and demonstrate the value of multiplex qPCR for wildlife pathogen surveillance. Christopher G. Lowe
692: Parasites can provide insights into the ecology of their hosts. For instance, digenean trematodes (“flukes”) have obligate multi-host life cycles. Many flukes infect a gastropod as an intermediate host before relying on one or more trophic transmissions to infect a vertebrate definitive host. This life history strategy allows flukes to be relatively abundant and easily sampled during early life stages. Moreover, flukes typically rely on less abundant definitive hosts for dispersal so their population genetic structure can be congruent with their hosts’, which may be rare or more difficult to sample. We investigated the population genetic structure of the “terrapin fluke”, Pleurogonius malaclemys, which infects an intermediate snail host (Ilyanassa obsoleta) and then diamondback terrapins (Malaclemys terrapin) as the definitive hosts. We hypothesized that high population genetic structure would be detected across fluke populations due to the limited dispersal and low population connectivity of their terrapin hosts. Pleurogonius malaclemys was collected from Cape Cod, Massachusetts to northeast Florida on the Atlantic coast of the United States. Fluke mtDNA was sequenced at the COI marker, providing a 620bp fragment which was then used for population genetics analyses. Analyses revealed high levels of structure and diversity that broadly correspond with metrics of terrapin population ecology found in previous studies. Our study is a valuable contribution towards understanding the life history, diversity, and ecology of the terrapin fluke, and makes an important step towards establishing them as a new tool for terrapin conservation. Cara McElroy
693: In a changing world amphibians face multiple stressors which affect their survival, behavior, and sublethal body condition independently and in conjunction. Among these stressors is the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd). Bd is now present in amphibian populations across the globe, where its affects range from sublethal to lethal. Sublethal responses are often moderated by the environmental context in which the pathogen interacts with its anuran hosts, which some environmental conditions substantially exacerbating the effects of Bd. To better understand the interaction between host, pathogen, and the environment, we have exposed American toad (Anaxyrus americanus) metamorphs to Bd across ecologically relevant temperature, moisture, and UVB gradients. We found that temperature had an independent effect on A. americanus during their first terrestrial season, but both temperature and Bd had strong effects on overwinter survival for this species. Soil moisture regimes interacted with both Bd and the host to alter infection dynamics. Finally, UVB has a strong fatal effect on the pathogen, but zoospores which survive exposure to UVB can still infect hosts. Despite this, our results suggest that high UVB intensity on the pathogen may result in low enough exposure intensity for hosts to survive and clear the infection. These results in conjunction offer critical insights into the effect that multiple stressors can have on anurans.
