694: The Burmese python (Python molurus bivittatus), introduced to the Florida Everglades, has cointroduced a nonnative tongueworm, the pentastomid Raillietiella orientalis. Since its introduction, R. orientalis has spilled over from pythons to infect approximately half of Florida’s native snake species; and with rapid spread, it can now be found outside of the pythons’ range. While robust studies linking the effects of R. orientalis infection on snake hosts are lacking, anecdotal reports suggest hosts are adversely impacted. However, it is unknown whether native snakes are showing any signs of resilience to infection over time. Understanding temporal variation of parasite prevalence and infection intensity can help us gauge the resiliency of native snakes to R. orientalis infection as snake hosts may exhibit heterogenous responses. We compared historic data of prevalence and intensity of native snake species collected in southern Florida during 2012 - 2016 to recent data for these metrics collected during 2024 - 2025 from dead-on-road (DOR) snakes obtained during vehicle surveys. Preliminary results are discussed in regard to temporal trends of infection dynamics and what these data may indicate regarding the resiliency of native snakes to to infection by a novel tongueworm. Ryan Miller
695: Aquatic environments in African urban waterways impacted by anthropogenic activities are increasingly recognized as reservoirs of microbial dysbiosis, antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), and virulence determinants. This study investigated whether trophic ecology shapes gut microbial dynamics in wild-caught fish across environmental gradients by analyzing three species with distinct feeding strategies: Mugil cephalus (detritivore/omnivore), Trachinotus blochii (benthic carnivore), and Sphyraena barracuda (piscivore), collected from low- and high-impact sites influenced by human activities within an African lagoon system. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was used to characterize microbial diversity, functional pathways, resistomes, and virulence profiles. Result showed that individuals from high-impact sites exhibited reduced alpha diversity and lower community evenness, with microbiomes dominated by Proteobacteria and Fusobacteria, consistent with pollution-associated dysbiosis, whereas fish from low-impact sites showed more balanced communities. Microbiome composition further reflected feeding ecology, with M. cephalus (detritivore/omnivore) enriched in sediment-associated microbes, while carnivorous (T. blochii ) and piscivorous (S. barracuda) species exhibited microbiomes linked to protein-rich diets and higher trophic transfer. Functional analyses revealed conserved metabolic pathways alongside environment- and trophic-specific signatures, with individuals from high-impact sites enriched in anaerobic metabolism, xenobiotic degradation, and stress response pathways. Resistome profiling indicated higher diversity and abundance of ARGs in high-impact sites, including tetracycline, macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin, and β-lactam resistance genes, with greater accumulation observed in higher trophic level species. Virulence factors associated with stress response, quorum sensing, and metal resistance were also enriched in high-impact sites. These findings demonstrate that trophic ecology and urban environmental pressures jointly shape fish gut microbiomes, highlighting African urban waterways as hotspots for antimicrobial resistance and underscoring the need for integrative, microbiomebased monitoring frameworks Diana Verónica Nolasco Diana Nolasco Flores; Luz Saldaña Ruiz; Omar Valencia Méndez; Oscar Sosa Nishizaki; Emiliano García
696: Ranaviruses (genus Ranavirus, family Iridoviridae) are an emerging and widespread group of pathogens that infect reptiles, amphibians, and fish and are capable of causing mass mortality events. In Florida, USA, ranavirus is well documented in amphibian die-offs; however, its epidemiology in wild chelonian populations remains poorly understood. This study aimed to address the knowledge gap of ranavirus epidemiology in Florida chelonians using surveillance data collected from multiple sources. To understand the disease prevalence, host species, and spatial and temporal patterns, we analyzed opportunistic samples aggregated from wildlife rehabilitation facilities, mortality investigations, and biological health sampling. Molecular detection via quantitative PCR was performed on a variety of sample types for individuals both ante- and postmortem. Out of 1401 samples collected, 28 were confirmed ranavirus positive, representing eight chelonian species, with detections primarily occurring in the southwest and north-central regions of Florida. In addition to confirming known host species, this study also identified three new host species in Florida: striped mud turtle (Kinosternon baurii), coastal plain cooter (Pseudemys floridana), and Florida red-bellied cooter (Pseudemys nelsoni). Most ranavirus detections occurred in winter and early spring, suggesting a likely pattern of seasonality in infection dynamics. Continued surveillance is essential for improving our understanding of ranavirus epidemiology in Florida chelonians and assessing its potential effects on wild populations. Hannah Owens
697: Coinfections are increasingly recognized as important drivers of disease dynamics. In snake populations, diseases including mycosis and raillietielliasis have been linked to severe pathology, mortality, and population declines. The pygmy rattlesnake (Sistrurus miliarius) in Florida exhibits infection with mycosis caused by Paranannizziopsis spp. and Ophidiomyces ophidiicola along with raillietielliasis caused by the invasive pentastome, Raillietiella orientalis. The spatial and temporal patterns of coinfection and their potential impacts on survival are unknown. As part of a long-term study, we surveyed S. milarius across 12 sites in the Florida panhandle and peninsula to assess variation in infection prevalence, severity, and coinfection dynamics. Here, we discuss findings from the first three years of the study. Raillietiella orientalis is present in nine sites and in 19% of snakes (n=451), while clinical signs consistent with mycosis were observed at all sites and in 40% of individuals (n=831). Coinfections were detected at six sites, with prevalence ranging from 3 to 50% (mean=8%). Temporal patterns suggest that mycosis prevalence and severity may increase following wetter conditions associated with active hurricane seasons, while declining during drought periods. Ongoing analyses will evaluate how environmental variation shapes coinfection risk and disease outcomes. Given the empirical and anecdotal evidence of declines in S. miliarius along with the diversity of host species affected by these pathogens and the potential for co-infection, it is critical to investigate the dynamics of coinfections in S. miliarius to understand the conservation implications.
698: Disease effects are a significant conservation concern for both aquatic and terrestrial chelonians, including North American tortoises (Gopherus spp.). Although upper respiratory tract disease (URTD) is common and sometimes causes mortality in Gopher Tortoises (G. polyphemus), relationships among infection/co-infection, clinical signs, and long-term health outcomes are poorly understood. We recently detected the first severe cases of URTD in Gopher Tortoises at Archbold Biological Station, providing a unique opportunity to investigate disease dynamics in concert with long-term demographic research. In spring-summer 2025, we collected oral-cloacal swabs for diagnostic testing (Fluidigm qPCR; n = 62) and initiated frequent visual health assessments and behavioral monitoring of a representative subset of 48 radio-tagged adults. Pathogen prevalence based on PCR was 44% for Tortoise Helicobacter sp., 13% for Mycoplasmopsis agassizii, and 6% for Emydomyces testavorans. Six of eight Mycoplasmopsis-positive tortoises were co-infected with Helicobacter. Preliminary logistic regression models indicated younger adults (≤ 15 yr old) were more likely to be PCR-positive than older adults, whether the binomial response was detection of any pathogen or just M. agassizii. Tortoises that were Mycoplasmopsis-positive (of which all but one were co-infected with Helicobacter) used smaller areas and changed burrows less frequently in the ensuing mating season. Prevalence of nasal discharge increased throughout the mating season and remained at a higher level through winter, though even the most severely affected tortoises survived and resumed activity in spring. Further analyses and ongoing monitoring of disease prevalence and effects in this sentinel population will aid development of appropriate management responses. Isaiah Rothschild
699: As human activity accelerates the spread of pathogens and other invasive species, reconstructing the cryptic early dynamics of undetected invasions has become a central challenge in disease ecology and invasion biology. We used museum specimens to reconstruct invasion of Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), a fungal panzootic driving global amphibian biodiversity loss, across historically enigmatic declines in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Two hypotheses have been proposed to explain Bd’s historical dynamics in this region: (1) Bd is enzootic, with historically stable prevalence, or (2) Bd is a recent epizootic invader, driving regional amphibian declines. Using PCR-based molecular screening, histopathology, and SNP-based genotyping of museum and modern specimens, we find no evidence of Bd infection prior to the decline, followed by widespread infection immediately thereafter. Only the global panzootic lineage (Bd-GPL) was detected during the initial post-decline period, implicating its invasion in driving regional losses. Infection prevalence varied among species following the decline, likely reflecting species-specific interactions between baseline susceptibility and ecological exposure risk. Contemporary host populations exhibit more uniform prevalence regardless of decline history, consistent with the evolution of pathogen tolerance under enzootic conditions. Together, these results provide the first site-specific evidence linking Bd-GPL invasion to enigmatic amphibian declines in Brazil and demonstrate the power of museum collections for resolving detection lag dynamics in emerging infectious diseases. Jack Boyette

700: Among ophidiiform fishes, certain species of the genera Ophidion (Ophidiidae) and Onuxodon (Carapidae) possess a highly specialized mineralized structure traditionally referred to as the “rocker bone.” Located at the anterior end of the swimbladder, this structure serves as the insertion site for sonic muscles and transmits their contraction forces to the swimbladder wall during sound production. The rocker bone’s formation is therefore likely driven by muscle-induced mechanical stresses, although its evolutionary origin remains unclear. This study compares the rocker bone in these two genera to assess whether this structure may result from such mechanical stresses, and to test for a common mechanistic basis underlying its formation across families. We estimated sonic muscle-induced stresses and examined rocker bones using histology, backscattered scanning electron microscopy (BSE-SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) in Ophidion rochei and Onuxodon fowleri. We identified a consistent spherulitic mineralization pattern, indicating that the rocker bone originates from mineralization processes occurring within the swimbladder tissues. The similarities in the structural organization of rocker bones, built from the same tissues and under similar mechanical constraints, could point to a common developmental origin. 701: Damming of river systems is one of the most consequential forces impacting freshwater environments. The past two decades have seen an increased research focus on understanding the cascading effects artificial damming has upon these habitats, particularly in relation to anadromous fishes whose migration patterns are highly modified by anthropogenic change. To date, most studies investigating the morphological impacts of artificial damming focus on changes in 2D body shape, particularly in relation to functional implications for swimming and/or feeding. In this study, we conducted the first 3D geometric morphometrics analysis on a fish population impacted by intermittent damming: steelhead trout collected along the Eel River. We developed a microCT dataset using museum specimens and investigated shape differences in several skeletal regions within the skull: orbit, preoperculum, and cleithrum. We tested for both temporal and spatial differences across the seasonal barrier impounding this watershed. Our findings reveal some differences in specimens collected below and above Benbow Dam—most notably in the cleithrum—but other variables (size, specific locality, year collected) also impact morphological trends in all cranial regions. This data-rich 3D approach validates field-deployable 2D GMM findings on these same specimens, particularly along an environmental spatial axis. This research lays the foundation for future work to test hypotheses of morphological modularity, as well as skeletal estimates of biomechanical performance to estimate functional differences. These types of analyses will continue to enhance our understanding of the functional morphological shifts in freshwater fishes caused by human-built dams.

702: The Klamath Basin is a geologically old and complex system that experienced over a century of damming, resulting in major alterations to habitat connectivity and flow regimes. Although the basin supports numerous native fish species, relatively few have been systematically collected and archived in museum collections, limiting our ability to assess long-term morphological change. The Klamath Smallscale Sucker Catostomus rimiculus is distributed throughout the basin, occurring in tributaries, the mainstem Klamath River, as well as reservoirs and lakes. To investigate patterns of morphological variation, 3D geometric morphometrics was used to quantify skull shape in 77 CT-scanned specimens collected between 1945 and 2016. This shape dataset was used to evaluate temporal changes in skull shape, ontogenetic variation, and relationships between skull morphology and flow regime. We also assessed the influence of population connectivity, approximated by distance from the main stem and position relative to the dam complex. These analyses provide insight into how environmental variation and landscape fragmentation shape morphological diversity in a native Klamath Basin fish, highlighting the value of museum collections for understanding long-term ecological and evolutionary change. 703: Scansorial animals require firm contact with the substrate to induce sufficient forces during climbing to resist gravity. Anolis lizards accomplish this through their subdigital adhesive pads and claws which enhance interactions with the substrate through intermolecular adhesion, friction, and mechanical interlocking. Human-made structures and surfaces substantially alter the locomotor environment of Anolis lizards exploiting urban habitats, resulting in significant changes to morphology, performance, and behavior. Although several studies have discovered that urbanization significantly impacts climbing performance in Anolis, these studies have focused on ascending locomotion (i.e., anoles moving uphill). Descending locomotion (i.e., moving downhill) is an oftenoverlooked aspect of animal locomotion, imposing different physical demands and constraints on the organism. As such, urban and natural populations of Anolis may perform differently and/or use different strategies while descending from arboreal habitats. Here we studied the individual and interactive effects of substrate incline and running orientation on climbing performance in urban and natural populations of the green anole (Anolis carolinensis), as well as an urban population of an introduced competitor, the brown anole (Anolis sagrei). Our findings directly add to our understanding of how scansorial animals effectively move in ecologically relevant conditions and how human habitation and species introductions affect biological populations and communities.

704: The skull in teleost fishes exhibits remarkable variability, serving as a rich source of morphological innovation. Although our understanding of this complex structure continues to expand, many anatomical features remain understudied. Among these are the scleral ossicles (SO), bony elements that surround the eyes in many fishes. The functional role of SO remains unclear and their patchy distribution across teleost clades suggest that factors other than protection may influence their occurrence. Despite their close association with SO, the role of extrinsic eye muscles (EEM) in shaping SO morphology and function has not been investigated particularly with respect to how SO robustness correlates with muscle torque output. The goal of this study is to quantify these interactions and identify potential relationships that may explain variation in SO morphology. Because SO have been found predominantly in fast moving species, this study focused on pelagic fishes including Thunnus atlanticus (blackfin tuna), Coryphaena hippurus (mahi-mahi) and Acanthocybium solandri (wahoo). SO morphology was characterized, and EEM 3D force vectors were estimated for all species. Our data showed positive correlations between SO thickness and EEM force production, in addition to variation in muscle insertion that may contribute to species-specific eye movement. Results from this research will be contextualized within an ecological framework to better understand the functional significance of this musculoskeletal interaction and the role of SO in fishes. 705: The closure of the Isthmus of Panama ~3 million years ago created a natural experiment in evolutionary divergence, isolating marine populations into distinct ocean environments. The Caribbean’s warm, nutrient-poor waters and the Tropical Eastern Pacific’s (TEP) seasonally upwelling, nutrient-rich waters have likely driven trophic divergence in sister taxa. In this study, I examine the trophic adaptations of Abudefduf saxatilis (Caribbean) and Abudefduf troschelii (TEP), which diverged ~2.8 million years ago, to determine how dietary plasticity, trophic morphology, and physiological traits reflect their distinct environmental histories. Specifically, I compare interspecific differences in trophic adaptations while also assessing intraspecific variation within the TEP across the Gulf of Panama (upwelling) and the Gulf of Chiriquí (non-upwelling). To capture developmental changes in trophic ecology, I take an ontogenetic approach, analyzing dietary and morphological variation across size classes. By integrating dietary (visual and metabarcoding analysis), physiological (gut length, stable isotope analysis), and morphological data (jaw mechanics, muscle mass, head structure) with high-resolution Micro-CT scanning, I test whether A. troschelii exhibits traits favoring suction-feeding for pelagic prey, while A. saxatilis prioritizes traits for biting and handling prey items. This research will provide insights into how environmental differences shape trophic specialization and plasticity across ontogeny, contributing to a broader understanding of how marine species respond to shifts in nutrient availability and oceanographic conditions. Katie Van Hise

706: The Tubesnout Aulorhynchus flavidus (Aulorhynchidae, Gasterosteales) is a common schooling fish that inhabits nearshore habitats on the Pacific Coast of North America. Breeding males have been observed excreting a glue-like substance from their vents to create nests in kelp and eelgrass. Aulorhynchus is the only nonstickleback within the Gasterosteales known to exhibit this trait. Glue-production also occurs in all of the stickleback members of the Gasterosteales, and the genomic and morphological source of the glue, as well as the amino acid structures of the substance itself, has been described in the literature. In Aulorhynchus, the substance is assumed to be sourced from genes and structures homologous with those of gasterosteids, but to date, this has not been tested. In this study, gross dissection, histology, in-situ hybridization, peptide fingerprinting, and computed tomography were performed to characterize glue production in Aulorhynchus. Ancestral state reconstructions using recent topologies of the Gasterosteales were also performed to place the clade’s glue-production trait in a phylogenetic context. The renal morphology of breeding male Aulorhynchus includes greatly hypertrophied kidneys, bladders, and kidney tubules, similar to the condition found in breeding male sticklebacks. Additionally, the genes responsible for glueproduction are close genetic matches to known stickleback glue-genes, suggesting homology of these genetic and anatomical mechanisms. Combined with ancestral state estimations, this may indicate that glue-production arose in the common ancestor of the Gasterosteales. Rachel Keeffe

707: Single-locus DNA barcodes often lack resolution in recent evolutionary radiations, where shallow divergence, introgression, and shared haplotypes obscure species boundaries. Rockfishes (Sebastes), with ca. 100 described species worldwide and representing one of the most species-rich marine fish genera in the northeastern Pacific, exemplify the limitations of standard markers (COI, 12S, 16S), which rarely resolve relationships among the 58 species distributed in southern California. To address this gap, we used low-coverage (~5X) whole genome sequencing for 41 Sebastes species to identify candidate multilocus genomic markers for eDNA species-level detection. First, we inferred a phylogeny from 1,132 exonic loci harvested from genome skims for all Sebastes species and two outgroups (Sebastolobus alascanus and Hexagrammos decagrammus), confirming the presence of a rapid radiation consisting of very short internodes. Second, using a k-mer-based maximum likelihood method (Krepp), we estimated distance-based metrics to evaluate candidate markers from filtered 80 bp regions with less than 10% masked or low-quality bases across both mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Candidate markers were benchmarked using in silico targeted sequencing simulations (CapSim). Further performance evaluation was conducted via in vitro capture probe testing against available metagenomic long and short read sequences from the 2019 Rockfish Recruitment and Ecosystem Assessment Survey. These genomic markers provide a scalable resource for eDNA-based monitoring of rockfishes diversity and fisheries management in southern California. Jill B.K. Leonard

708: While competitive interactions promote phenotypic divergence in sympatric species (competitive character displacement), interactions with predators promote phenotypic convergence in poisonous species (Müllerian mimicry). Thus, poisonous sympatric species may experience complex, opposing selective pressures on their phenotypes. We investigate this dynamic in the sympatric zone between rough skinned newts, Taricha granulosa, and California newts, T. torosa. These species are distinguished by color patterning and eyeball size, however, diagnostic characters are continuously distributed and sometimes intermediate in sympatric animals. T. torosa and T. granulosa are poisonous, raising the possibility that phenotypic convergence is the result of Müllerian mimicry. Furthermore, they coexist in ponds and streams during the breeding season and return to those breeding sites every year, which may place them in consistent competition. Work in nonpoisonous Plethodon salamanders shows that cranial morphology exhibits competitive character displacement when species are in sympatry. We are employing a 2D geometric morphometrics approach to evaluate T. torosa and T. granulosa head and jaw shape divergence in sympatric and allopatric populations. Additionally, we are quantitatively characterizing color patterning convergence in these populations. Our preliminary findings show that differences in head shape between species are driven by allometry and are consistent in and out of sympatry, suggesting that newt head shape is not experiencing competitive character displacement. However, sympatric newts do show increased variance in head shape, a pattern known to occur in admixing species. Future work will couple morphological data with RadCAP genotyping to evaluate admixture between sympatric T. torosa and T. granulosa. Jen Terry

709: Reproductive pheromones are used in chemosensory communication across taxa and diverse environments to convey information on species, sex, and status. Salamanders express pheromones during multisensory courtship rituals. Pheromones are produced by specialized courtship glands, which are typically only found in males. The most well studied of these glands are the mental and caudal glands which exhibit seasonal periods of hypertrophy and atrophy. A similar pattern can be seen in the external nasal glands of plethodontid salamanders. However, unlike confirmed courtship glands, external nasal glands are also found in females. Both sexes exhibit similar histological reactions and staining to that of other courtship pheromone producing glands signifying that these are likely courtship glands. Using light microscopy of serially sectioned heads we tracked the external nasal glands of various species of plethodontid salamanders and noted changes in morphology. To our knowledge, this is the first study done across a family of salamanders comparing changing morphology in a courtship gland utilizing both male and female specimens. Our results showed that biphasic metamorphs exhibited the most well-developed glands and fully aquatic paedomorphs lost the gland altogether. Cave and tropical salamanders appear to have specialized characters in comparison to other salamanders of the same life history. This study highlights the importance of taking into account both the life history and ecology of an organism when tracking secondary sexual characteristics within a clade. Spencer N. Trimpe

710: The Flathead Catfish (Pylodictis olivaris) is a large, benthic freshwater fish species that is widely distributed across North America. The genus Pylodictis is monotypic and, despite its widespread distribution, very little is known about intraspecific variation apart from a single mitochondrial DNA study. Using that as a starting point, we address this knowledge gap by conducting a study combining phylogeographic and population genomic techniques to examine genome-wide genetic divergence, structure, and variation across the species’ native range. In collaboration with state and university partners in Iowa, Wisconsin, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama, we collected data on 102 individuals. We genotyped single-nucleotide polymorphic (SNP) loci from the nuclear DNA of our individuals using double digest restriction site-associated sequencing (ddRADseq) and analyzed the data with a suite of population genetic and phylogenetic approaches. Our results indicate that there are genetically distinct population clusters across the native range of Flathead Catfish. Specifically, our results suggest an east-west genetic split across the Mississippi river. Pairwise FST estimates range from 0.02-0.52, and both PCA and sNMF plots recover similar patterns of geographic structure. These findings suggest long-term geographic or ecological isolation within the species and provide a foundation for research concerning their evolutionary history and management. Nick Whitney

711: Male secondary sexual traits in frogs provide an opportunity for integrating phylogenetic, behavioral, anatomical, genetic, and other tools to study morphological novelties. Here, I will present what is known of the elongate third finger in males of the African frog genera Arthroleptis and Cardioglossa (family Arthroleptidae). Hyperelongation of the third manual digit evolved in the ancestor of these two genera and was both elaborated and reduced multiple times. Males of at least two species are known to use these digits in male-male wrestling, including rapidly vibrating and wiping the fingers across the dorsum of competing males. The elongation of this digit is associated with sexual maturity and is hypothesized to be driven by androgens. Elongation of the distal cartilaginous epiphysis of the phalanges, metacarpal, and radioulna contribute to creating a longer forearm and third finger. This hypertrophy and subsequent ossification create a composite skeletal element that is unique among anurans, and likely co-opts existing developmental mechanisms. I will present preliminary evidence for how these bones experience stress and how their associated muscles differ from other frogs, as well as a hypothesis for why larger bodied species exhibit limited sexual dimorphism in the third finger. An integrated, organismal approach allows us to begin making sense of the evolution and function of novel traits in these poorly studied frogs. Emily Blackwell
712: Amphibian secretions serve several functions, including communication, respiration, and defense against predators and harmful microbes. They have also been considered for various biomedical uses. Eastern Tennessee is a hotspot for salamander diversity, and within one family (Plethodontidae), the stickiness and volume of secretion released by a salamander when agitated varies greatly among species. Stickiness (“biological glue”) has a defensive function, but it might be metabolically expensive, resulting in a tradeoff. Protein synthesis compriseis a major portion of cellular energy budgets. This study utilizes a BCA Assay to quantify the protein concentrations within salamander secretions collected in three locations in Eastern Tennessee to test the hypothesis that stickier secretions contain a higher proportion of protein by volume. The results of the BCA protein assay revealed that salamander species, most notably Plethodon glutinosus, that secrete quantifiably stickier secretions, have a higher protein concentration than species such as Plethodon serratus, that are smaller and secrete a less sticky substance. The results of this study could point to chemical differences in specialized glands, and different levels of investment in secretions between species in the family Plethodontidae . 713: Coloration in animals often reflects a balance between conflicting evolutionary forces, with sexual selection favoring conspicuous traits for mate attraction and natural selection favoring cryptic traits for predator avoidance. The Eastern Indigo Snake (Drymarchon couperi), a federally threatened species, is predominantly black but displays color variation on its head and ventral scales. The function of this variation remains unknown. In this study, we investigated whether coloration in Eastern Indigo Snakes is cryptic or conspicuous relative to the environmental background, comparing males versus females and juveniles versus adults, as well as conditions before and after habitat burns. Using color data from captive-bred snakes and paired environmental measurements, we assessed whether observed variation in coloration may serve roles in predator evasion or sexual signaling. We used color spectrometry to characterize important aspects of color in two ways: by examining overall color differences across the entire color spectrum, and by comparing differences within the ultraviolet, yellow, and red colorbands. This research will contribute to understanding of color function in reptiles and applied efforts to inform captive breeding and repatriation strategies for species recovery. Marie Del Vicario
714: Pit-tagging is a widely used marking method for monitoring amphibians, but the invasive procedure comes with an inherent stress response from individuals. Pattern recognition offers strong potential for identifying animals based on their unique markings (e.g., spots) and can be effective without the need for invasive methods. However, while large mammals can be photographed from a distance, aquatic amphibians must be captured and arranged in a fashion to acquire suitable pictures for use with image recognition software. Pit tag recaptures are unambiguous and instantly recorded without need for extensive handling. We collected corticosterone through water borne hormone methods to compare the accumulated corticosterone response of initial and subsequent recaptures using image recognition versus pit tagging on the lesser siren (Siren intermedia). Corticosterone was collected following initial processing and after each recapture for both techniques. Mark and recapture corticosterone levels were integrated over several recaptures to identify when and if either approach minimizes the accumulated physiological stress response. Our assessment of these marking techniques provides a comparison of individual stress response in a field setting to gain insight to wild animal welfare. Cali Falkenstein
715: Embryonic temperature influences developmental trajectories in all organisms. Oviparous ectotherms are particularly amenable to thermal developmental plasticity because eggs are often left in thermally variable environments. Some levels of thermal variation, such as differences in mean temperature or in minimum and maximum temperatures, induce substantial variation in physiology, morphology, and performance. However, it is unclear how the stochastic variation inherent in real environments might influence phenotypic variance independent of mean differences in temperature. We incubated eggs of the brown anole (Anolis sagrei) in three treatments that differed in levels of variation: constant temperature, repeated sine waves, and a natural treatment which allowed temperature fluctuations to change daily. These were repeated across two mean temperatures in a 2 by 3 factorial design. This allowed us to determine how different levels of thermal variation impact phenotypes. We constructed linear mixed models and compared them with AICc to determine how treatments influenced phenotypic variation in hatchling morphology, physiology, and performance. Results varied greatly by phenotype, but in no case did we observe greater levels of trait variation in response to the naturally-fluctuating treatment. Our results demonstrate that relations between thermal variation and phenotypic variance are highly context-dependent for developmentally plastic traits. We suggest that some, not all levels of thermal variation meaningfully contribute to population-level trait variance. As global climate change progresses, it will be critical to determine the levels of thermal variation which most strongly correlate with trait variation. Brian J. Halstead
716: Since their inception in the mid 1800’s as treatments for diphtheria and tetanus, antivenoms have proven their efficacy as the only effective treatment for life threatening snake envenomation’s. The production of antivenoms begins with the immunization of large animals to a target toxin or venom, before high titer plasma is collected and variably processed; while this methodology has been refined since inception, the general process remains largely unaltered. Modern antivenoms are typically designed to target a geographic region or taxonomic group of medically significant species, with variation in the refinement of antibodies influencing the distribution of active molecules within a patient once administered. Due to the complex and varied composition of venoms, this often results in antivenoms containing antibodies for non-medically significant toxins and other proteins, increasing the number of vials required for a given treatment and leading to an increase of the financial burden caused by snakebite. To combat these challenges, a new generation of antivenoms using smaller, more specific nanobodies produced in bioreactors to create modular treatments has been the focus of an international collaboration recently featured in Nature. In conjunction with more effective antivenoms, the repurposing of small molecules has proved promising in the development of cheap, accessible, and orally available first aids for snakebite as prehospital treatments, the first of their kind. Here, we will discuss the benefits and shortcomings of modern antivenoms, and how future innovations are working to improve patient outcomes in both developing and developed regions. Raymond Kidder
717: Greater Siren, Siren lacertina, are abundant large aquatic salamanders that are underappreciated for their roles in aquatic ecosystems. Here we present the results of demographic data from an 11-year mark-recapture study on a closed population of greater sirens in a 5-ha isolated Carolina Bay wetland in Aiken, SC. From 20062016, we recorded 831 S. lacertina captures, including 466 new individuals that were PIT-tagged and released, and 350 recaptures of marked individuals. We used spatial capture recapture models that were parameterized for trapping effort in the first three years of sampling (2006, 2007, 2008) to estimate survival, population size and density. Survivorship increased with length and mass and showed a strongly sigmoidal increase with body condition index. We leveraged growth rate models derived from this population and historical records of drought-induced size class gaps to provide the most thorough age estimation of wild greater sirens to date. Even across several years, recaptures largely occurred within a few meters of their original capture (spatial scale of detection, Sigma, estimated to be 2.85 ±0.06m SE). Although not occurring at the same population densities as other highly abundant salamanders, the biomass per unit area of greater sirens in this population readily exceeded that of red-backed salamanders and high density estimates for white-tailed deer biomass in North American forests. These data clearly point to the potential for sirenids to exert strong ecological roles.
718: Venomous snakes, in particular rattlesnakes, possess a myriad of adaptations that can serve as models for exploring diverse biological phenomena. These include production and storage of toxic, unstable biological weapons, easily induced complex systems for exploring mechanisms of genetic regulation, AI-assisted design of toxin inhibitors and sources of novel therapeutics. However, the distribution and conservation status is poorly known for many species, and is likely changing over time, so basic fieldwork is required in order to obtain a better understanding of present status. These surveys also allow sampling across species’ ranges and provide the raw material for analyses of genetic regulation mechanisms leading to venom proteome variation. This presentation will underscore the importance of fieldwork to providing the materials needed for these “higher order” analyses, highlighting some of the patterns observed in venom variation among members of the Western Rattlesnake clade and discussing some of the mechanisms of regulation of venom expression. The utility of in silico design of novel compounds followed by in vitro expression of minibinder antitoxins to treat snakebite is yet another example of how snakes and their venoms can serve as a model system for new approaches to treating a variety of human diseases. By utilizing a combination of “old school” methods and cutting-edge technologies, a more complete understanding of the evolution and diversification of venomous snakes is possible, leading to better treatments for snakebite victims and to advancing knowledge of regulatory mechanisms common to vertebrates (including humans).
719: Reptile immune performance has been historically understudied despite its essential role in assessing the health of wild populations, including survival and reproductive potential. Further, fitness traits (e.g., body size, condition) hold potential for explaining reproductive life-history within ecoimmunological contexts. Our study examined the influence of body size, sex, and parasitism on immunocompetence in a population of red-sided garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis) in Manitoba, Canada. Garter snakes exhibit significant sexual size dimorphism, and males in multiple populations often have overt signs of parasitism (e.g., shortened, swollen tails caused by trematode infection). During the spring breeding season (May 2024) at a well-studied hibernaculum, we opportunistically collected unmated females (n=37), normal males (n=25), and infected males (n=25) actively engaged in breeding. From blood samples, we conducted pathogen killing assays (PKAs) with plasma and total cell (Ilastik; AI-based software) and manual counts (heterophils, lymphocytes, monocytic cells) of smears. We saw no effect of parasitism on immunity, therefore males were collapsed for between-sex comparisons. We found pronounced sex differences, with females having greater immune cell counts and stronger PKAs than males in addition to body size and condition effects within each sex. Our study is unique in that all snakes were sampled during the peak of the breeding season within a single week. We demonstrate a clear reproduction-immunity tradeoff in a mating system where males invest heavily in prolonged activity in spring at the expense of immunocompetence while females dedicate energy to defenses, perhaps to safeguard summer gestation and parturition. Elyse Parker Elyse Parker; Benedicte Garmann-Aarhus; Jarl Andreas Anmarkrud; Chi-Hing Christina Cheng; Hauke Flores; Mario La Mesa; Felix Mark; Ekaterina Nikolaeva; Elie Poulin; Luca Schiavon; Audun Schrøder-Nielsen; Nicolas Straube; Torsten Struck; Lisbeth Thorbek; Thomas Near; Thomas Desvignes; Santiago Ceballos; Chiara Papetti;
720: Biofluorescence is a phenomenon wherein part of an organism absorbs light at one wavelength and re-emits it at another, usually longer wavelength. Biofluorescence is common in nature but has only recently been documented in amphibians where it appears to be widespread, but the sources and functions of biofluorescence are not well understood in salamanders. The salamander genus Plethodon contains 61 species, yet only three of these species (P. cinereus, P. metcalfi, and P. shermani) are known to biofluoresce. From these, we have gleaned three broad facts: Biofluorescence is associated with ventral serous 1 glands, is sexually dimorphic (with larger and more numerous biofluorescent glands found in males), and appears to coincide with the onset of sexual maturity. The three species fall into different clades, suggesting that biofluorescence and perhaps sexual dimorphism are widespread. Our research sought to discover if these facts hold true across the genus by documenting its presence and patterns in seven species, covering a large range of the Plethodon phylogeny. Biofluorescent gland density and size were measured across three major body regions and compared between different age classes, sexes, and species. Our results suggest that biofluorescence is widespread in the genus and sexual dimorphism is common, though our species are not uniform in their degree of biofluorescence expression. In addition, several species displayed novel non-glandular fluorescent patterns. This study provides a foundation for advancing our understanding of the ecological and behavioral significance of biofluorescence, contributing to a comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon. Naomi Scott
721: Understanding how organisms respond to rising temperatures is crucial for predicting species persistence under climate change. Two general mechanisms can buffer populations against rapid warming: phenotypic plasticity and evolutionary adaptation. While both are well documented at the whole-organism level, little is known about gamete level responses, even though reproduction, and sperm function in particular, is often compromised by heat stress. To address this gap, we first tested whether sperm in the brown anole (Anolis sagrei) exhibits adaptive thermal plasticity. We evaluated both pre-ejaculate plasticity, in which males acclimated to warm environments produce more heat-tolerant sperm, and post-ejaculate plasticity, in which ejaculated sperm exposed to sublethal heat stress trigger increased tolerance. We found neither mechanism was supported. Acclimation did not improve sperm heat tolerance, and mild heat shocks on ejaculated sperm did not enhance post-ejaculate performance. We then examined evolutionary responses across 25 lizard species using a phylogenetic comparative framework. We found that sperm heat tolerance varied substantially among species and was strongly aligned with adult thermal physiology, consistent with adaptive divergence. Moreover, sperm heat tolerance evolved more rapidly than adult heat tolerance. Together, these results indicate that sperm thermal tolerance has limited plastic capacity to buffer against rapid warming but retains evolutionary potential, highlighting the dual vulnerability and adaptability of male reproductive traits, with important implications for predicting species resilience under climate change. Xiaojun Wang
722: Sex chromosomes have evolved repeatedly in animals. Evolution of sex chromosomes is particularly interesting in reptiles, as they have frequent transitions among systems, with transitions between XX/XY and ZZ/ZW systems as well as changes to which chromosomes in the genome are acting as sex chromosomes. However, we lack data for many reptile species. The Mediterranean house gecko (Hemidactylus turcicus), for example, is an invasive gecko that is now found across the globe. While we know both its karyotype (2n=44) and sex determination system (XX/XY sex chromosomes), we have until now not been able to identify which chromosomes in the genome are the sex chromosomes. To address this, we assembled and annotated a high-quality reference genome for a male H. turcicus using PacBio HiFi, Hi-C sequencing, and multi-tissue RNASeq for annotation. We used this reference genome, in combination with RADSeq of 7 males and 7 females and Illumina resequencing of 3 males and 3 females, to identify the previously unknown sex chromosomes. This genome assembly is a critical resource for studying the genomics of sex-specific patterns of aging, as sex chromosomes likely contribute to sex-specific aging.
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
723: The genus Salvadora comprises a group of colubrid snakes characterized by an enlarged, free-edged rostral scale and, in most cases, longitudinal striping. The genus inhabits the southwestern deserts in the United States and much of northern to central Mexico, a region with a complex geological and hydrological history that has likely contributed to genetic structure and diversification in many arid-adapted taxa. Consistent with the complex natural history of their range and a sparse distribution, these snakes are not easily sampled in high densities. Taxonomic assignments within Salvadora have relied largely on morphological assessment since the genus was described in 1853. Because of this, it is still unclear if these morphology-based taxonomic assignments are concordant with genetic variation. To address this knowledge gap, we used ddRAD sequencing on samples obtained from the southwestern deserts in the United States representing four clades within the grahamiae group. The resulting sequences were used to construct phylogenetic trees using both maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference to investigate the validity of the currently accepted taxonomy within Salvadora. We interpreted the topologies alongside fixation indices, which were calculated among the resulting clades. Our results provide molecular evidence for the retention of S. deserticola as a species designation and suggest that S. g. lineata should remain a subspecies of S. grahamiae. We also genetically confirmed a suspected hybrid of S. hexalepis and S. deserticola which was originally identified as a hybrid when captured. Felipe Floreste
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
724: The southeastern crowned snakes (Colubridae: Tantilla) are a group of morphologically conserved, centipede-eating snakes native to the southeastern United States. Three species are currently recognized: Tantilla coronata (southeastern crowned snake), T. oolitica (rim rock crowned snake), and T. relicta (Florida crowned snake), the latter of which contains three subspecies. Tantilla oolitica and T. relicta were both described in 1966 based on scalation and color pattern, but analysis of the cytochrome b (Cyt b) gene region suggested significant discordance between these historical classifications and genetic clades. We sought to evaluate these discrepancies by generating genome-wide SNP data with thorough geographic coverage, sampling all named taxa, all major Cyt b clades, and putative contact zones. Analyses of these data found that neither T. coronata nor T. relicta are monophyletic, and further, that T. oolitica is wholly nested within a subclade of T. relicta. We found evidence that diversification in this group was driven by Pleistocene refugia corresponding to ancient sand ridges in the Florida peninsula and regions of the Atlantic seaboard and gulf coastal plain. We also found evidence of significant gene flow between lineages in the Florida peninsula, but with major rivers and their associated floodplains constituting significant biogeographic barriers. Tantilla oolitica is threatened and was proposed as federally endangered. Thus, the results of this study and subsequent taxonomic implications may impact conservation measures.
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
725: Interspecific hybridization and introgression have been shown to be more widespread in vertebrates than traditionally considered. However, it remains unclear how the prevalence and magnitude of introgression correlate with different historical scenarios related to the geographic ranges of hybridizing taxa. Here, we integrate phylogenomic network inference with time-stratified historical biogeography to explicitly test how geographic range compatibility and dispersal connectivity influence introgression within the toothy skinks (genus: Plestiodon). Using whole-genome data from 57 individuals representing 37 species (73.6%), we inferred species relationships, estimated phylogenetic networks, and reconstructed ancestral ranges under alternative dispersal hypotheses. We identified six reticulation events spanning the Late Miocene through the Pleistocene, including five instances of asymmetric introgression and one consistent with homoploid hybrid speciation for P. fasciatus. Then, we derived quantitative, node-informed geographic predictors of introgression magnitude (γ), including range overlap, range adjacency, and connectivity via dispersal between donor and recipient lineages. We find that introgression occurred primarily among closely related lineages historically occurring in adjacent regions, consistent with hybridization along shifting parapatric boundaries rather than strict, long-term sympatry. Parapatric geographic situations were positively associated with γ, whereas direct overlap showed no relationship and dispersal-weighted connectivity exhibited a model-dependent effect. By linking phylogenomic estimates of introgression to explicit, time-stratified geographic models, this study demonstrates that reticulate evolution is likely structured by dynamic dispersal connectivity rather than static range overlap alone. Matthew L Holding
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
726: The all-female lineage of salamanders in the genus Ambystoma reproduce by “stealing” sperm packets from sympatric males, through a process called kleptogenesis. These salamanders have many combinations of nuclear chromosomes, known as biotypes, and how this influences their phenotypes is an ongoing area of study. Salamanders produce diverse bioactive peptides in their skin secretions, which influence the community of microbes that persist on an individual. The structure of these peptides is heavily influenced by the number, and diversity of genes, which vary in these unisexual Ambystoma salamanders. I collected skin swab samples from 20 male smallmouth salamanders (Ambystoma texanum) and 80 unisexual Ambystoma salamanders across six sites. I took tail clips from all female salamanders to confirm biotypes through the genotyping process of microsatellite loci. At each site, I took a soil and water sample to account for transient environmental microbes that may still have been on the individual. I extracted bacterial DNA from the skin swabs and environmental samples. Then I amplified the v4 multivariate region of the 16s rRNA gene and sent it off to be sequenced. I processed the raw sequence information using QIIME2 to generate a feature table, which I then quantified using diversity metrics and finally visualized using PCoA plots. The results of this research reveal how genetic diversity can influence host-microbe relationships and potentially help explain the co-existence of unisexual and sexual salamanders. Chloe Kaelin
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
727: Island ecosystems often host organisms distinct from mainland counterparts in physiology, behavior, and morphology. The Channel Islands, off the coast of California, are home to several endemic species exhibiting reduced body sizes relative to the mainland. Morphological data from three Islands (Santa Cruz, Santa Rosa, and Santa Catalina) along with three mainland California locations have demonstrated that relative to mainland, the island populations of Southern Alligator Lizard (Elgaria multicarinata) are 14% smaller and Santa Cruz Island Gopher Snake (Pituophis catenifer pumilis) are 30% smaller. We characterize the genetic divergence between island and mainland populations for these two species using mitochondrial genomes (mtGenomes) from 102 P. catenifer and 98 E. multicarinata across islands and mainland locations. Analyzing the demographic history at the level of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from mtGenomes in P. catenifer, we find that each island population has its own unique haplogroups, as does each mainland site. We see evidence of multiple introductions onto the island system, suggesting each island population was colonized independently. In contrast, E. multicarinata haplogroups are not distinguished on Santa Rosa and Santa Cruz Islands, suggesting they may have arrived on the super island Santarosae before it split into the modern Northern Channel Islands, but the southern Catalina Island had a unique haplogroup. Together, these data contribute to our understanding of genetic uniqueness of these island populations, with implications for different colonization histories across different species. Future work will use nuclear data to further elucidate these genetic histories and link genetic divergence to variation in morphologies. Lin Lindstrom Lin Lindstrom; Brett Riffel; Jerod Thomas; Molly Russell; Parker Binns; Shania Burkhead-Harris; Krista Ward;
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
728: Environmental conditions and evolutionary history both shape organismal traits, but their relative influence remains unclear. We tested whether trait evolution is driven more strongly by environmental selection or phylogenetic history using barking geckos (Ptenopus), a semi-fossorial group distributed across arid regions of Namibia, Botswana, and South Africa. A recent taxonomic revision expanded the genus from three to nine species, with species boundaries often corresponding to distinct soil types, providing a natural framework to disentangle environmental and phylogenetic effects on evolution. Ptenopus exhibits traits likely under environmental selection, including simple morphological features such as toe flange number and density, as well as more complex traits such as burrow architecture. We quantified variation in these traits across six Ptenopus species and compared observed patterns to expectations derived from phylogenetic relationships and environmental similarity. By contrasting simple and complex traits across environmental conditions, this study evaluates how trait complexity and function interact with ancestral biases and environmental limitations. Our results show that simple traits are less constrained by phylogenetic history, whereas complex traits are more strongly shaped by ancestral condition, while still being limited by environmental limitations. These findings highlight how trait complexity mediates the balance between environmental adaptation and evolutionary constraint. Tobit Liyandja
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
729: Understanding the process of lineage divergence and speciation is central in evolutionary biology. Greater Antilles Anolis have long been studied as a classic example of adaptive radiation, yet few studies have used this group to study the causes of population genetic divergence. Previous work focused on A. opalinus of Jamaica has demonstrated two divergent mitochondrial lineages that are the result of ancient mtDNA genome capture. Here we increase geographic sampling across the island of Jamaica and incorporate additional mtDNA and genomic sequence data. Genomic sequence data were used to assess gene flow between these two distinct mtDNA lineages and to test whether geographic distance and environmental variables are, in part, responsible for genetic divergence. From these data it was corroborated that two genetically distinct populations of A. opalinus exist on the island, with little admixture between them. One population is restricted to the Blue Mountains in the east part of the island, while the other population was found to be distributed across the rest of the island at lower elevations. Ancient introgression events within A. opalinus are important to understanding local adaptation and the process of speciation within A. opalinus.
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
730: Squamate species vary immensely not only in the rate at which they form, but also in how they accumulate in space: some establish sympatry rather quickly in the divergence process, whereas others exist solely as geographic replacements of one another. This is important for the buildup of biodiversity as the evolution of sympatry may serve as a rate-limiting control in resetting the ‘speciation cycle.’ We characterized the tempo and mode of speciation and the evolution of sympatry among various squamate clades and tested how closely-related allopatric species (‘allospecies’) impact our inference of speciation rates. We found that clades vary widely in the degree to which they produce allospecies, spatially segregate, and achieve intraclade sympatry. Our results suggest that some clades differ fundamentally in their biological properties (e.g., ecological versatility), which impacts their proclivity to accumulate species in space and may constrain diversification. We discuss these insights and consider their implications for understanding the mechanisms underlying diversification and governing the spatiotemporal accumulation of biodiversity. Olivia Schuitema
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
731: In reptiles, body-size evolution is shaped by selective pressures—often amplified on islands—such as temperature, resource availability, and diet. Vegetation changes on the California Channel Islands resulting from human occupation type and density have altered ecosystem dynamics. Island Night Lizards (Xantusia riversiana), endemic to three Channel Islands, provide a unique opportunity to identify the abiotic and ecological mechanisms driving body-size evolution. These omnivorous lizards have a rich ~1500-yr subfossil record and experienced welldocumented shifts in climate, diet, and habitat. We are testing how abiotic and ecological variation influences bodysize and diet evolution of X. riversiana, based on the subfossil record from Santa Barbara Island and contemporary data (museum and live specimens) from all occupied islands. We hypothesize that larger body sizes and higher rates of herbivory are selected by warmer, wetter climates and higher plant densities, which promote greater availability of high-quality foods (e.g., fruits, flowers). Similarly, reductions in herbivory and body size are selected by cold, dry periods, punctuated with prolonged droughts and habitat disturbances. Preliminary results suggest cyclical body-size fluctuations, largely concordant with temperature variation. In warmer periods, lizards were larger, and vice versa, supporting our prediction. Future lab and field work will refine radiocarbon dates, reconstruct diet histories using stable isotopes and DNA metabarcoding, and measure body sizes. Our interdisciplinary study provides a long-term record of vertebrate morphological change on the Channel Islands, advancing our understanding of island evolution and informing conservation efforts of X. riversiana and other insular endemics under future climate change. Yucheol Shin
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
732: The genus Hyperolius (Rapp, 1842) is the most speciose amphibian genus in sub-Saharan Africa. Many species of Hyperolius have a complex taxonomic history because of their extensive intraspecific morphological variation, large geographic distributions, gaps in sampling, and the discovery of cryptic genetic diversity within many of these taxa. The goal of this study is to elucidate the systematics of one such widespread taxon, Hyperolius langi, via an integrative taxonomic approach that combines molecular, morphological, and bioacoustics data. Two mitochondrial genes (16S and cyt b) and one nuclear gene (RAG1) were used to construct phylogenetic trees in the H. langi complex, employing maximum likelihood (IQ-TREE) and Bayesian inference methods (BEAST). Maximum Likelihood analyses recovered four strongly supported clades, and molecular and morphological evidence support the recognition of two new cryptic species. Future work should reconcile the taxonomic status of a well-supported subclade of H. langi sensu stricto from Irangi and Bitale in South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo (known from only 1 male and 4 females) and a unique lineage, H. sp. Mitwaba, known from only one male specimen collected near Upemba National Park in southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo Ibrahim M Turki
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
733: Urban centres are considerably hotter than their rural counterparts, which can lead to differences in the thermal physiology of urban and rural populations (Luber and McGeehin 2008, Hajat and Kosatky 2010, Diamond and Martin 2021). Urban and rural areas can also differ in temporal temperature fluctuations (Bennett et al. 1992), which can potentially select for differences in thermal plasticity (Diamond et al. 2017), though this effect of urbanization is little studied. To address this gap in knowledge, I tested for differences in the thermal tolerance plasticity of urban and rural populations of the green anole lizard (Anolis carolinensis) in New Orleans, Louisiana. I focus on diel and seasonal plasticity and investigate the following questions: (a) does the thermal tolerance of animals differ between the day andnight, (b) does the thermal tolerance of animals differ between the spring and summer, and (c) are there differences in diel and seasonal plasticity between urban and rural animals. I predicted that (a) lizards would be more heat tolerant but less cold tolerance during the day compared to night, (b) lizards would be more cold tolerant but less heat tolerant in the spring than in the summer and (c) urban lizards would show reduced plasticity in cold tolerance, but greater heat tolerance plasticity compared to rural lizards. For diel patterns, I measured thermal tolerances of 32 lizards from each of four sites (two urban, two rural). Each animal had either their heat or cold tolerance measured twice, once during the day and once at night. Half the animals were measured first at night, while the other half were measured first during the day, with a 36-hour recovery period between measurements. To assess seasonality, heat and cold tolerance were measured during the spring and summer. Cold tolerance and heat tolerance were measured with dynamic assays that cooled or heated animals at a constant rate, respectively. Data were analysed using linear mixed effects models in R. As predicted, animals were more cold tolerant at night (P < 0.01), but we found no habitat × time of day interaction (p = 0.62)(Fig 1A). Therefore, urban and rural animals do not differ in diel cold tolerance plasticity. As predicted, animals were more heat tolerant during the summer, and we found a significant seasonal × habitat interaction (p < 0.01), as the heat tolerance of rural animals changed more than urban animals (Fig 1B). We found differences in plasticity between urban and rural lizards in some, but not all scenarios. Further studies are needed to understand if the difference in seasonal plasticity is genetic or because there are less seasonal changes in urban habitats. Emily Yeager Emily Yeager; Amber Ringle; Katherine Polatcheck; Katherine Wilson; Colin Foord; Christian Pankow; Julia
SSAR Siebert Award: Evolution and Genetics
734: The “spinning fish” phenomenon has been documented by FWC at low prevalence since 1997, but in late 2023 a series of public reports originating from the Lower Florida Keys marked the beginning of a spinning fish event that was unprecedented in its temporospatial scale and was further noteworthy because of numerous mortalities of smalltooth sawfish Pristis pectinata. Here we provide preliminary findings based on solicited public reports and our own observations. Public reporting rates of spinning fish peaked in spring of 2024, dropped precipitously by that summer, and stayed low until a lesser peak in spring of 2025 followed again by a rapid decline in with the onset of summer. Ultimately, spinning fish were observed throughout the Florida Keys. Affected fish belonged to at least 70 species. Generally, affected specimens cooccurred with unaffected fish, and they were remarkable only for their dysfunctional swimming behavior (i.e., “spinning”). These behaviors sometimes were triggered by, or intensified in response to, strong artificial lights or other external stimuli. Most reports were of abnormal behavior absent extensive mortality, and widespread fish kills were not characteristic of the event. Smalltooth sawfish were apparently more likely to die than other species. Irregularities in benthic algal communities and preliminary toxicological studies indicate that further investigation of a phytotoxic etiology is warranted. In the 1970’s, benthic algal toxins were also implicated in an earlier spinning fish event dubbed the “Dance of Death”, which resulted in the brief closure of southern Biscayne Bay to fishing and boating. McKinley Baker McKinley Baker; Kya Whiting; Baylee Christensen; Syrus Miner; Reagan McKee; David Bean; Alexander Everett;
735: Fish exhibiting erratic behavior (e.g., spinning) and mortalities were observed in the lower Florida Keys in winter 2023 and spring 2024. Examination of water samples did not reveal the presence of any likely stressors (i.e., red tide, low oxygen, pollutants) and red tide toxins (brevetoxins) were not detected in fish tissue samples. The toxigenic benthic dinoflagellate, Gambierdiscus, was reported at concentrations of 1,000 cells L-1, far above baseline levels measured by the authors over the previous ten years sampling in the Florida Keys (averaging 39 cells L-1). Over 50 taxa of fish affected, coupled with the lack of other potential stressors and potentially elevated levels of Gambierdiscus, a more extensive survey was undertaken in the lower Keys to determine if a “benthic bloom” of Gambierdiscus was occurring. Over one thousand seagrass (Thalassia testudinum), macroalgae (Dictyota, Halimeda, and Laurencia), and water samples were collected and examined to quantify Gambierdiscus cell densities in addition to other, co-occurring benthic dinoflagellates. A comparison of samples collected in spring 2024 with baseline samples (2011 – 2023) collected elsewhere in the Keys indicated that Gambierdiscus cell densities were up to 7 times higher on average at sites exhibiting erratic behavior versus baseline levels. Gambierdiscus densities returned to baseline levels in summer 2024, but a second, less severe scenario was observed in the middle Keys in conjunction with observations of spinning fish in the region in 2025, suggesting a prolonged cascade of events may be occurring. Bloom causation is still unknown and further research is ongoing. Josephine Caton
736: Fishing guides function as distributed observational assets within coastal ecosystems, and their continuous on-water presence, broad spatial coverage, and species-level familiarity position them to detect ecological disturbances in near real time. In 2023, professional guides across the Florida Keys began documenting recurring behavioral abnormalities in multiple nearshore fish species, including disorientation and erratic spinning. Recognizing the potential ecological significance, the Key West & Lower Keys Fishing Guides Association (dba Lower Keys Guides Association or LKGA) established the Guide Rapid Response Network (GRRN), a structured, guide-led monitoring and response framework designed to support rapid detection, documentation, and scientific investigation of marine anomalies. LKGA recruited and trained more than 30 professional guides across the island chain, equipping them with standardized protocols for documenting observations, collecting environmental water samples, obtaining tissue specimens when appropriate, and coordinating vessel-based access for agency and academic partners. In its first year, the GRRN contributed 127 documented hours of field effort and established five strategically located freezer depots from Key West to Key Largo to maintain sample integrity and chain-of-custody continuity. The network represents the first organized, guide-driven rapid response models of its kind in the United States, linking practitioner-based observation with formal scientific inquiry. Since its inception, the GRRN has expanded to include members of other professional guide organizations increasing spatial coverage across the sanctuary. This model demonstrates how stakeholder-based monitoring can strengthen adaptive management, improve data collection, and enhance resilience in coastal marine systems. Madeline E. Denman
737: The 2024 Florida Keys Unusual Sawfish Mortality Event (UME) resulted in catastrophic losses of the endangered smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata), with 56 confirmed mortalities and over 200 individuals documented exhibiting distinctive “spinning behaviors” characterized by disoriented swimming, impaired equilibrium, and erratic movements across a region supporting the last remaining U.S. population of this species. In response, an emergency multidisciplinary team of veterinarians, biologists, researchers, and pathologists undertook an unprecedented effort to bring a live, clinically affected smalltooth sawfish into managed rehabilitation care. This presentation will describe the clinical approach and conservation context of the intervention, including the decisionmaking framework used under emergency conditions, challenges unique to sawfish anatomy and physiology, and handling and transport protocols developed in real time. It will also review the diagnostic methods employed and treatment strategies trialed throughout the rehabilitation period. Clinical findings, outcomes, and the animal’s physiological responses will be discussed in the context of what they suggest about the etiology and pathophysiology of the affected sawfish observed across the broader UME. Although the animal did not survive, this case generated important baseline clinical information for the species, expanded current understanding of elasmobranch rehabilitation medicine, and informed triage and response considerations for future events, with implications for conservation of this Critically Endangered species. Kathryn Greiner-Ferris
738: In late 2023, reports began of unusual, widespread “spinning” swimming behaviors exhibited by over 80 species of fish in the lower Florida Keys. Most individuals and most species recovered; however, at least 65 large juvenile or adult endangered smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata, died. On 28 January 2024, the U.S. Sawfish Recovery Hotline received the first report of what became an Unusual Sawfish Mortality Event. Over the winter and early spring of both 2024 and 2025, 297 reports were received of large sawfish (>10 feet total length), observed swimming in circles, beaching themselves, or exhibiting other unusual behaviors. Reports peaked in March and April of 2024, with as many as nine individual spinning sawfish reported in a single day. We responded to 134 of these reports, attempting to observe and, if possible, tag and obtain biological samples from each individual. Various wounds on their fins and ventral surface were frequently observed, as well as abnormal sensitivity of the rostrum to touch. Among the live spinning sawfish and recovered carcasses, thirteen had been previously tagged, seven as small juveniles. Others were acoustically tagged during the event response. Most of these were only detected for a few days after release and have not been detected since, while others were found dead a few days later. Response to these spinning sawfish and ongoing analysis of samples collected during these unprecedented events has helped us learn more about sawfish life history, reproduction, and physiology, and contributes to our investigation of this spinning fish phenomenon. Jens Hegg
739: Shark and ray (elasmobranch fish) skeletons feature an unmineralized cartilage core encased by a layer of mineralized tiles (tesserae). This lightweight composite architecture is not without trade-offs: cartilage has poor repair capabilities, making it counterintuitive how elasmobranch species can live for decades or even centuries when their skeletons cannot self-repair like bone. Here we present an injury response observed in several individuals of wild-caught sawfish (Pristis pectinata), characterizing the mineralization of both normal and injured jaws using high-resolution µCT imaging. Sawfish jaw structure in undamaged areas was like that described for other elasmobranchs, with a continuous and defined tesserae layer overlain by a fibrous perichondrium. Defects were conspicuous localized disruptions to the skeletal architecture, forming bulbous calluses (in one case visible externally, bulging against the skin). Within defects, tesserae were displaced and in disarray, enveloped within a porous and poorly organized, mineralized matrix, intruding into the cartilage and perichondrium. Massive radioopaque mineral deposits peppered the callus matrix, considerably larger and more cuboidal than tesserae. Undamaged sections of the tesserae layer were visible within and emerging from the callus. The callus’ matrix appears to function like a ceramic filler bridging the zone of damage. This suggests a secondary mineralization process distinct from normal tessellated growth, possibly a reparative response to tissue trauma, allowing mechanical reinforcement despite loss of the skeletal cortex. Our findings demonstrate a phenomenon of plasticity and reconfiguration in the sawfish jaw skeleton, offering insights into tissue development and health, and injuryinduced remodeling in cartilaginous fishes. Aryanne Sonnier
740: The smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) is one of the most imperiled marine fishes in the United States, having experienced drastic declines in both abundance and range. Once relatively common from Texas to North Carolina, sawfish were gone from most of their former range by the late 20th century due to fisheries bycatch mortality and habitat loss. Now regularly found only in south Florida, the U.S. population was listed as Endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in 2003. After 20 years of ESA protection, the population appeared to be stable, and possibly increasing at localized scales with recurrence in some areas of its former range. A new threat emerged in the winter of 2023-2024, and recurred in winter 2024-2025, as over 80 invertebrate and fish species were observed spinning erratically in the Florida Keys. Smalltooth sawfish were among the species observed spinning and, while other species were not dying in large numbers, sawfish mortalities were documented at unprecedented levels. Symposium speakers will present results from field observations, environmental sampling, biological testing, and other findings from these “spinning fish events” and sawfish “unusual mortality events”. These events represent a significant threat that potentially reversed two decades of conservation progress and could further imperil an already fragile U.S. smalltooth sawfish population or push it to extinction. During a post-symposium forum, participants will synthesize the results presented to discuss possible mitigation measures and determine future research and management priorities. Krystan A Wilkinson Krystan Wilkinson; Gretchen Lovewell; Sydney Haas; Devin Jordan; Jason Allen; Kylee DiMaggio; Jonathan
741: In 2024, reports of “spinning” and dead smalltooth sawfish in the lower Florida Keys increased from the end of January through February. By 1 March, given the seriousness of the event, the decision was made to begin planning an attempt to rescue a spinning sawfish from the wild, rehabilitate it under veterinary care, and release it back into the wild. Under the guidance of NOAA Fisheries and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, a large interdisciplinary team planned the logistics of this unprecedented task. On 22 March, permission was granted from NOAA Fisheries to attempt a rescue if the opportunity occurred. In the late afternoon of 5 April, an 11-foot total length male was reported exhibiting spinning behaviors in a canal on Cudjoe Key. Researchers responded, captured, and transported it to a holding facility on nearby Summerland Key. This presentation will highlight the logistical challenges of planning, capturing, and moving a large sawfish into captivity, and serves as an introduction for a subsequent talk on the captive care it received. Andrew Wooley
742: Blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) are a coastal shark species common through much of the Southeast United States. The Florida Keys is at the transition zone between two oceanic basins, the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean, in which Blacktip sharks are managed as two stocks. Blacktip Sharks are known to undergo migrations, especially along the Southeast Coast of Florida. However, the movement patterns of individuals from the Florida Keys is not well documented, and if these sharks do migrate to where. The Florida Keys may facilitate connectivity between the two currently recognized stocks. Mature individuals of both sexes (n = 19) were surgically implanted with Innovasea V16 passive acoustic telemetry tags to determine residency, habitat use, and dispersal throughout the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary. Sharks were detected transiting along both the east and west coasts of Florida, suggesting the Florida Keys is an area of connectivity for the species.
