Continued monitoring will be used to determine residency and movement patterns across multiple years, and the influence of biotic and abiotic factors. James S. Albert
743: Kings Bay and its associated Crystal River represent the second largest natural Floridan spring system and a unique elasmobranch nursery: the first spring system confirmed as an active bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas) nursery and thermal refuge. Young-of-the-year bull sharks use thermally stable freshwater spring habitat as refugia to survive winter cold snaps that are lethal to juveniles in open coastal waters—a function undocumented in any estuarine or riverine nursery otherwise characterizing this species’ early life history. Using monthly fisheriesindependent shark surveys and passive acoustic monitoring, the Crystal River Bull Shark Project (CRBSP) examines presence, abundance, movement, habitat use, and environmental associations across the springs-bay-river continuum (75 surveyed bull sharks, August 2023–April 2026; 29 acoustically tagged individuals). Evidence supporting nursery function is strong and consistent across datasets. Neonates and young-of-the-year comprise 82% of survey catches and occur across all four seasons; individuals from neonate through juvenile stages use the full springs-river continuum seasonally; all young-of-the-year cohorts remain in the system through the following spring; and repeated detections across nearly three annual cycles demonstrate strong site fidelity and cohort return. Evidence for thermal refuge function is similarly robust and complementary. Acoustic tracking shows young-of-the-year overwintering during their first year, with consistent winter habitat contraction into Kings Bay springs (November– March) and individual variation in range extent. Paired thermal and detection data demonstrate that these springs buffer cold stress events linked to cold-stunning mortality in coastal Florida populations. Collectively, these findings formally characterize Crystal River/Kings Bay as both an active bull shark nursery and a thermally critical overwintering refuge. Greg Aniolek Gregory Aniolek; Paige Powell; Jane Zheltov; Melissa Walker; Stefanie Whitmire; Peter van Den Hurk; Bryan
744: The Bull Shark (Carcharhinus leucas) is a large, euryhaline, coastal species that is distributed globally in tropical and subtropical regions. They are commonly encountered in Mississippi Coastal Waters, but their seasonal movement patterns and spatial use have not been well documented in this region. Between 2017 and 2018, 20 V16 Innovasea acoustic transmitters were deployed in neonate and young juvenile Bull Sharks (48.3 – 98.0 cm fork-length) in St. Louis Bay, Mississippi to investigate movement, site fidelity, and potential dynamics with other acoustically tagged sharks within the system. Tagged Bull Sharks were monitored using a passive acoustic telemetry array through 2025. All 20 tagged individuals were detected within the array, and 12 were detected across multiple years. Overall, the Bull Sharks followed similar seasonal movements with very few detections within the system in December, January, or February, likely driven by seasonal variation in environmental parameters. In 2021, the acoustic array was expanded to provide better coverage at the Mississippi Barrier Islands allowing for observation of ontogenetic related movement shifts. Over time, detections shifted from being predominantly within St. Louis Bay and mid-Mississippi Sound waters to being around the Mississippi Barrier Islands. To examine potential overlap in species distribution we examined Bull Shark and Lemon Shark detection densities within the different barrier islands. Both species occur in similar regions, suggesting interaction between the two species is likely during this stage. Results from this study can help to better characterize drivers of Bull Shark movements and understand shifting spatial use over time. Edison Bonilla
745: Tiger sharks, Galeocerdo cuvier, are a global marine predator inhabiting a wide range of environments from coastal to pelagic ecosystems. Aggregations of these sharks in association with large fishing piers are increasingly common in the panhandle of Florida; however, our understanding of why these aggregations occur remains limited. We used satellite and acoustic telemetry to elucidate fine scale habitat use of tiger sharks at a model pier in Ft. Walton Beach, FL and investigated the broad scale movements of tiger sharks away from these aggregations. Tiger sharks (n = 34) were tagged near the pier between 2022-2025 with acoustic transmitters (V16, Innovasea Inc.) and satellite tags (SPOT, Wildlife Computers; FastGPS, Lotek). Acoustic receivers were maintained at the site year-round, with an acoustic positioning system deployed in 2024 and 2025 to examine behavior around the pier structure. We assessed the effect of temporal, environmental and biological factors on probability of presence at the aggregation (GAMM), and habitat use both at the pier and at large throughout the Gulf using KDEs. Preliminary results suggest interannual fidelity to the aggregation is high and strongly influenced by season, occurring from June-August. Additionally, there was a diel pattern in presence at the pier, indicating aggregation occurs during daylight hours. When absent from the pier, tiger sharks were detected throughout the Gulf, showing differential spatial distribution based on maturity and sex. Our results suggest that this aggregation serves as a seasonal foraging hotspot, drawing tiger sharks of multiple demographics whose movement behaviors rarely overlap otherwise. Maddisyn Braun
746: Long-term fishery-independent monitoring provides a unique opportunity to evaluate how coastal predator communities respond to environmental variability over decadal timescales. Standardized gillnet survey data collected by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department from 1976-2022 were used to quantify changes in shark assemblage structure, size distributions, and size-environment relationships across major Texas estuarine systems. These estuaries serve as critical nursery habitats for multiple shark species, making them ideal for detecting longterm ecological and demographic change. Shark assemblages exhibited dynamic yet structured reorganization over time, reflecting persistent, non-random shifts in community composition among bays and across decades rather than stationary assemblages. Multivariate analyses indicated that assemblage variability was significantly associated with environmental gradients—including temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, and turbidity—highlighting a strong role for environmental filtering. These compositional shifts were accompanied by species-specific changes in size structure. Body size increased for blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus), spinner sharks (C. brevipinna), and bonnetheads (Sphyrna tiburo), whereas Atlantic sharpnose sharks (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae) declined in size. In contrast, bull shark (C. leucas) size structure remained relatively stable, consistent with continued estuarine nursery use despite broader assemblage change. Size distributions were significantly associated with environmental conditions, with nonlinear responses and strong temporal effects indicating that long-term demographic trends are not solely explained by short-term variability. Together, these results demonstrate concurrent compositional and demographic restructuring in northwestern Gulf of Mexico shark assemblages, highlighting divergent, speciesspecific responses to changing estuarine environments. Caroline Collatos
747: Estuarine ecosystems function as critical nursery areas for many marine species, with some species exhibiting selective occupancy driven by environmental conditions, biotic interactions, and life-stage transitions. The bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas) is a circum-global euryhaline predator, that utilizes estuarine nurseries to complete their life cycle, but spatiotemporal patterns of movement and habitat use remain poorly understood in many northern Gulf estuaries. We used passive acoustic telemetry to track 39 juvenile bull sharks across an array of approximately 100 receivers throughout Lake Pontchartrain, an approximately 1,600 km² oligohaline estuary that connects to the Gulf of Mexico through several tidal passes to the east. Over six years of monitoring, we characterized estuarine residency dynamics including timing of arrival and departure, duration of residency, and interannual philopatry. We employed a spatiotemporal modeling framework to estimate the probability of shark presence as a function of spatial, temporal, and environmental covariates. Models were then used to develop predictive maps to identify potentially important habitats for bull sharks within the estuary. Using network analysis, we further examined how sharks move through the system to identify movement corridors and examine whether individuals exhibit coordinated movement patterns. This work provides a multi-scale assessment of juvenile bull shark nursery use in Lake Pontchartrain with implications for identifying and prioritizing estuarine habitats critical for elasmobranch conservation in the northern Gulf of Mexico. Mel Walker Melissa Walker; Paige Powell; Zachary Padgett; Greg Aniolek; Kylie Artosky; Evgenia Zheltov; Jessica Schulte; Ethan Personius; Jessica Donaldson; Divia Feinstein; Sora Kim; Joseph Bisesi; John Bowden; Meghan Holst; Taylor
748: Captive breeding and release programs are increasingly instrumental strategies for preserving at-risk species from extinction. In order to promote their success, it is important to understand what changes an individual may experience after being released and evaluate the impact of their captive environment, since these consequences can greatly influence survival ex-situ. To explore this, we conducted a mock-release study with yearling dusky gopher frogs (Lithobates sevosus), a critically endangered frog species, bred and raised in captivity as part of Memphis Zoo’s reintroduction program. Half of the frogs were released as the experimental group into an outdoor pond made to resemble their native habitat, while the other half remained inside as the control, living in the glass tanks the population is normally raised in prior to reintroduction. We evaluated three main categories: 1. Body condition through snout-vent length and mass measurements, 2. Physical endurance through distance, length of time, and distance the frog jumped in a locomotion trial, and 3. Response to stress through water-borne corticosterone concentration. Evaluation periods occurred at the beginning of the study, after the first and second month, and again after six months.This study presents potential changes captive bred frogs experience when released outdoors, as well as comparative morphology and locomotion between indoor and outdoor frogs over time. By further understanding these effects, conservationists can make better informed decisions on strategies to raise and release captive bred amphibians to better survive ex-situ and improve reintroduction program success. Eva Alvarado
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 1
749: Herpetological staff in zoological institutions have the opportunity to contribute to research and conservation on many levels. Participating in valuable conservation efforts both at the institution and beyond are important component of modern zoological institutions. At the Philadelphia Zoo, we are dedicated to contributing to the field, both from a collection management and welfare standpoint as well as from a research and conservation purview. Furthermore, we aim to collaborate widely to enhance our data sets and magnify our efforts. Herein, I will present on the multifaceted approach to herpetoculture and Herpetology we embody at the Philadelphia Zoo. From studying the impacts of heat provisioning on snakes to leading the AZA Cuban crocodile SAFE program and studying free-living chelonians in Guatemala, we aim to utilize our resources to best fill gaps in knowledge and contribute to the evolution of the field. Johnathan G. Austin
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 1
750: Captive breeding and reintroduction programs aim to conserve and restore endangered species. Soft releases, where animals are allowed to gradually acclimatize to their new environment, often within an artificial enclosure, can improve reintroduction success by allowing animals to gain necessary experiences while ensuring their protection. The dusky gopher frog is a critically endangered species, with a species recovery plan that includes efforts to restore historical habitats (longleaf pine forests) and annual reintroductions from captive breeding populations. The aim of this study is to quantify if soft-releasing frogs could increase the chances of survival by improving locomotor performance. We predicted that frogs released into artificial ponds would have improved jumping performance (longer and higher jumps and higher endurance) compared to frogs that remained in a laboratory environment. We also predicted that differences between groups would increase as our experimental group spends more time in the outdoor ponds. To test these predictions, we compared the jumping performance of soft-release frogs to lab-reared frogs over the course of a year. Metrics collected included endurance, jump height, and jump length. While both groups had indistinguishable jumping performance at the start of the experiment, our lab-reared control frogs had higher endurance than their soft-released siblings. Results from this study could inform the current captive breeding programs concerning best practices for future clutches of dusky gopher frogs. Claire E. Dietrich
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 1
751: Despite criticisms from biologists, ex-situ research conducted on animals in zoos has been substantial and provided crucial information otherwise impossible or unlikely to have been collected in situ. In herpetology, a few innovative researchers established the field. Their work, and the work they inspired, has led to important contributions in fields as disparate as behavior, genetics, and natural history, and biomechanics. There will be nongratuitous name-dropping in this presentation. Robert W. Mendyk
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 1
752: The Center for Conservation & Research (CCR) at San Antonio Zoo has worked with multiple threatened and endangered reptile, amphibian, fish, and invertebrate species since its founding in 2013. Ex situ research involves the establishment of husbandry and breeding protocols for understudied species, such as the Salado salamander (Eurycea chisholmensis), the reticulated flatwoods salamander (Ambystoma bishopi), and the Mexican blind catfish (Prietella phreatophila). These efforts have resulted in the first documented captive breeding events for both the Salado and reticulated flatwoods salamander, thus providing valuable insight into their developmental and reproductive biology. In addition, the CCR conducts in situ research in the form of eDNA sampling and targeted trapping, to detect the presence of the Mexican blind catfish (Prietella phreatophila) and widemouth catfish (Satan eurystomus), and by conducting cave and karst surveys to better determine their range and ecology. Lastly, the CCR’s Texas Horned Lizard Reintroduction Project has shown successful reintroduction of the Texas horned lizard (Phrynosoma cornutum) with the establishment of two distinct genetic maternal lineages on the release site. These projects demonstrate how collaborative research in a zoological institution can fill key knowledge gaps, and strengthen advocacy for vulnerable species and their habitats. Aidan O’Brien Aidan O'Brien; David Cook; Stacy Martinelli; Michael Fawcett; Leyna Stemle; Arianne Messerman; Christopher
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 1
753: Zoos and aquariums have long been recognized for their pivotal role in public education and access to nature and biodiversity. The majority of zoos and aquariums are located in densely populated areas and are often the first point of contact for those interested in biological sciences. However, living collections in zoos and aquariums have only recently been recognized for their value in basic scientific discovery and their impact on conservation. The vast amount of data present in zoo and aquarium collections — encompassing birth or point of collection, major life history events (growth and maturity, reproduction, death), medical history (diet, nutrition, disease, etc.), welfare, and behavioral observations — and the impacts zoos and aquariums can have through their ex situ and in situ conservation programs make them a powerful, but underutilized resource for scientific research and discovery. This symposium highlights the unique and diverse research and conservation projects conducted at zoos and aquariums, both ex situ, with living collections, and in situ, using resources and expertise at these institutions. Here, we give an overview of the types of living collections research conducted at the Memphis Zoo as an example of the wide breadth of research questions that can be pursued in living collections organizations, such as zoos and aquariums. Joseph Post
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 1
754: Life is distributed non-randomly along Earth. An important determinant of where species occur in space is the geographic variation in climate. However, the microhabitat that species occupy mediates how they experience climate. Here we use anurans—wet-skinned ectotherms that occur in a variety of microhabitats globally—as a model system to investigate how microhabitat influences climatic niche evolution. We build on a global database of anuran microhabitats and use phylogenetic comparative methods to investigate the evolution of different climatic variables among different microhabitat categories (arboreal, terrestrial, burrowing and aquatic). Emilie Barenghien
755: Cryptic species are being discovered at an unprecedented rate, especially in understudied biodiversity hotspot regions such as Southeast Asia. Most of these discoveries rely on molecular approaches that employ treeand distance-based methods, assuming that gene flow is absent. To test the validity of these methods, we used genomic data to investigate one of the most celebrated examples of cryptic species in Southeast Asia—Bornean Fanged Frogs (Limnonectes kuhlii complex), which has been split into more than 18 species, most of which are morphologically indistinguishable. We showed that most lineages fall within the gray zone of the speciation continuum, where gene flow is prevalent, causing tree- and distance-based methods to overestimate species. Recognizing the central role of gene flow reframes our understanding of cryptic species; rather than being considered as genetically distinct units that failed to evolve morphological differentiation, they can be manifestations of continuous diversification in the gray zone. This shift in perspective offers a new and dynamic evolutionary framework for identifying and interpreting cryptic biodiversity across the Tree of Life. Lauren M. Chan
756: Neotropical salamanders possess gigantic genomes ranging from approximately 12 to 87 Gb, comprising at least 50% transposable elements (TEs). Genome size evolution may be explained by the interplay between TE proliferation and host silencing mechanisms that counteract the negative effects of transposition. This interaction can be described by the “arms race” coevolutionary model. Interestingly, patterns across neotropical salamanders suggest that larger genomes harbor mainly ancient TE activity, whereas species with smaller genomes tend to show more recent TE activity. In this context, the piRNA pathway—a mechanism predominantly active in the germline—represents a central component of host defenses against recent TE activity. In this study, we aim to determine whether species with smaller genomes exhibiting recent TE activity show high TE transcriptional activity and reduced piRNA pathway activity. Using two species of plethodontid salamanders with contrasting genome sizes and TE activity profiles, we analyze low-coverage genomes and germline transcriptomes to characterize TE landscapes and explore correlations between recent TE activity and TE transcription. We also evaluate the expression levels of piRNA pathway-associated elements, expecting to observe weak piRNA-mediated silencing in the smaller genome, as a consequence of TE escape from suppression, evidenced by recent TE activity and high TE transcriptional activity. This study provides insights into genome size evolution, suggesting that weak silencing may enable ongoing genomic expansion through the coevolutionary dynamics between TEs and host silencing mechanisms. Massmo Gulino
757: How adaptive divergence is maintained despite hybridization remains a central question in evolutionary biology. We investigate this in two closely related salamanders, Ambystoma barbouri and Ambystoma texanum, which differ in breeding habitat, reproductive traits, and larval pigmentation. Using controlled crosses, we show that the two species can hybridize, with heterospecific pairings producing offspring at rates comparable to conspecific crosses. Across multiple traits—including oviposition behavior, clutch size, and larval pigmentation responses to ultraviolet radiation (UVR)—hybrids most often resembled the maternal phenotype, with occasional intermediate expression. Despite this divergence, hybrid fitness did not differ from parental forms, as measured by survival to metamorphosis. Genome-wide SNP data reveal two well-defined genetic clusters corresponding to each species, with admixture largely confined to contact zones. Patterns of asymmetric gene flow indicate ongoing hybridization but limited genomic homogenization. Together, these results show that although hybridization is common and produces viable offspring, species boundaries remain intact. Divergence is maintained through ecological selection on key traits and strong maternal effects that bias hybrid phenotypes, limiting the homogenizing effects of gene flow. Dom Jimenez
758: Hybridization between closely related lineages can reduce species differentiation, especially in systems with partially conserved phenotypes such as communication signals and morphology. We investigated whether hybridization occurs between Bokermannohyla nanuzae and B. feioi, two Neotropical hylid frogs with similar morphology and calls. We analyzed acoustic, morphological and genetic differences across their geographic range in the mountains of southeastern Brazil. We measured seven call parameters from 58 individuals and 12 morphometric traits from 130 individuals. We then used ca. 9000 SNP markers for 150 individuals across the geographic range to analyze genetic structure and hybridization. We found two well-defined, species-specific genetic clusters, but five individuals in different populations showed mixed ancestry, were unequivocally assigned as F2 hybrids, and occupied expected positions for hybrids in a triangle plot. The phenotypic analyses revealed moderate but consistent differentiation among species and populations, with gradients associated with spectral parameters of calls, body size, and forearm thickness, traits commonly under sexual selection and potentially important for maintaining species boundaries. Hybrid phenotypes were either intermediate or coincided with those of pure species in the multivariate space. Our results indicate that B. nanuzae and B. feioi constitute distinct evolutionary lineages, maintained primarily by reproductive barriers that are not totally effective. These results reinforce the importance of integrative approaches for understanding speciation and gene flow processes in amphibians, including hybridization. Renato Nali Matheus Neves; Ramon Dominato; Davi Bang; Luís Gustavo Boa Morte; Anat Belasen; Kelly Zamudio; Renato
759: Recent taxonomic revisions driven by a growing understanding of cryptic diversity and advancements in genomic technology have increased the number of known southern Appalachian salamander species significantly, raising questions about biogeography and community structure. Recently described species in the Desmognathus quadramaculatus-marmoratus complex are morphologically cryptic but diagnosable by mitochondrial DNA. The complex includes multiple species within each of two distinct ecomorphs, the highly aquatic ‘shovel-nosed’ (SN) ecomorph and the semi-aquatic ‘black-bellied’ (BB) ecomorph. Using mitochondrial DNA we show more extensive co-occurrence of two cryptic species of the black-bellied ecomorph than previously recognized. Our results are also consistent with earlier work indicating shared variation between ecomorphs within one clade, drawing into question their present status as distinct species. Joseph Sheffield Joseph Sheffield; Anastasia Umstott; Adair Hernandez; Stephanie Fox; Madison Nguyen; Megan Hobratschk;
760: Conservation resources are finite, yet management for long-lived vertebrates often targets incorrect vital rates. Turtles counter low fecundity with increased longevity, accumulating reproductive output across decades, but elevated adult mortality eliminates decades of potential reproduction. The spotted turtle (Clemmys guttata), a state-endangered wetland species at the western edge of its North American range in Illinois, exemplifies the challenge. Long-term mark-recapture surveys documented the last populations in the urban greater Chicago region annually since 1987, producing a long record of demographic data. We constructed integral projection models from data incorporating size-structured vital rates (growth, survival, and fecundity) using hierarchical Bayesian models. Population growth rates at both sites fell below replacement, indicating decline. Elasticity analysis revealed adult survival as the dominant demographic driver, contributing far more to population growth rate than fecundity or juvenile survival. Stochastic projections confirmed substantial extinction risk under current conditions, particularly at the smaller population, where adult survival is also lower. Taken together, the IPM results strongly support a management approach focused on reducing adult mortality. Nest protection and headstarting programs, widely used in turtle conservation, showed minimal elasticity and should be treated as supplemental rather than primary strategies. The IPM approach and elasticity-guided management apply broadly to other long-lived, low-fecundity vertebrates where adult survival dominates population dynamics. Marcus Drymon Marcus Drymon; Tobey Curtis; Matthew Ajemian; Kesley Gibson-Banks; Grace Casselberry; Daniel Coffey; Andy Danylchuk; Paula Dominguez Rein-Loring; Amanda Jargowsky; Kyle King; Jeff Kneebone; Michael McCallister;
761: Much has been written about the importance of improving inferential rigor in science including ecology. Most attention has focused on improving observation and statistical analyses. There has been far less attention to how authors treat the literature. The breakdown of careful and critical use of the published literature leads to biases and distortions in scientific belief. I used a critique of the claim that diamond-backed terrapins are keystone species within salt marshes to demonstrate how scientific distortions begin, why they may be perpetuated and exaggerated, and how they grow from hypothesis to fact without any primary empirical support. I identified 524 journal publications, book chapters, theses, and technical reports about terrapins, 90 % of which were published between 1979 and 2025. There were 25 unique primary sources that were cited by 39 secondary sources as evidence that terrapins “might be” or “are” important/keystone species in salt marshes; however, there were actually only four primary sources that presented data on the potential influence of terrapins on salt marsh ecosystems (one master’s thesis testing top-down control on snails, one peer-reviewed publication estimating energy transfer to terrestrial habitats through egg deposition, and two peer-reviewed publications demonstrating seed dispersal). Of the 21 other sources, twelve had little or nothing to do with terrapins and provided no data related to terrapin influences on salt marshes. One primary source was cited independently by 35 of the 39 papers that discussed terrapins as keystone predators but that paper did not present any data on terrapins. There was an increase over time in the number of secondary sources making claims about terrapins as important or keystone predators and the claim evolved from a “likely” hypothesis to fact via citation transmutation, misrepresentation, and exaggeration. In more recent secondary sources, statements about terrapins as keystone predators were expanded to claims about their value as regulators of saltmarsh health and as a key motivator for terrapin research and conservation. Of the 39 secondary publications that mentioned or discussed the influence of terrapins in saltmarsh ecology, nearly all (92%) had foci not related to the ecological roles of terrapins. The potential causes of the citation cascade and distortion were insufficient precision by primary authors representing their work including overgeneralization and wording hypotheses as inferences, and secondary authors not critically reading the primary or secondary sources and engaging in “apparent citation” by passing along statements from secondary sources but citing primary sources the authors likely had not read. The mistreatment of the literature and subsequent cascade of citation distortion is a breakdown in a fundamental element of the scientific process, even when the distortion or misrepresentation is tangential to the aims of a paper. The increasing volume and varied rigor of papers and journals makes critical treatment of the literature more important and more challenging. However, that challenge cannot be used to justify a lack of careful and critical representations of facts. Recommendations on how authors, reviewers, editors, and journals can improve the rigor of literature citations are presented. Alex Maile
762: Highly mobile marine megafauna such as sea turtles, often attract fish entourages commonly called hitchhikers. The fidelity of these relationships varies; some species are association-obligate during certain life history stages while others accompany turtles only briefly. This study used remotely operated vehicle and camera tag imagery recorded between 2008 and 2023 to document the fish hitchhiker communities accompanying 74 loggerhead (Caretta caretta) and 57 leatherback sea turtles (Dermochelys coriacea) in continental shelf waters of the Northwest Atlantic Ocean (Northeast Scotian Shelf, Southern New England, and the Mid-Atlantic Bight). A total of 598 fish representing 15 genera were observed, of which 10 have similar global distributions to loggerheads and leatherbacks. Seven hitchhiker species were observed foraging alongside leatherbacks as they consumed jellyfish. Leatherback hitchhikers preyed upon other fishes (primarily butterfish, Peprilus triacanthus, and whiting, Merlangius merlangus) found hitchhiking with jellyfishes (moon jelly, Aurelia aurita, sea nettle, Chrysaora spp., and lion’s mane, Cyanea capillata) at probabilities of encounter as high as 0.25 ± 0.13 (mean ± SE) fish per jellyfish eaten. Intraspecific competition was high among turtle hitchhikers and interspecies competition was mainly observed within the Carangidae family. Greater amberjack and crevalle jack (Seriola dumerili and Caranx hippos) made the most foraging attempts, while network analysis showed that juvenile banded rudderfish (S. zonata) competed with the broadest range of other species. Collectively, our results show that hitchhiking with sea turtles is an advantageous behavior for fishes, conferring protection, long-distance dispersal, school meeting places, and foraging opportunities, although with a risk of expatriation.
763: Freshwater turtles are among the most imperiled vertebrates globally, yet their ecology and population dynamics remain poorly documented across much of Central America. To address this gap, we established a longterm mark–recapture study in 2021 at the Belize Foundation for Research and Environmental Education (BFREE) reserve in the Maya Mountains of southern Belize. Using standardized trapping, hand captures, and snorkeling surveys across diverse aquatic habitats, we uniquely marked all individuals via marginal scute notching and passive integrated transponder (PIT) tagging and recorded morphometric data to establish demographic baselines. Over five years (2021–2025), we captured and marked approximately 1,100 individuals representing eight of Belize's nine native freshwater turtle species — the most comprehensive assemblage survey conducted in the region to date. Captures were dominated by Kinosternon leucostomum (>500) and K. acutum (~300), with lower numbers of Trachemys venusta (>80), K. scorpioides (>70), Staurotypus triporcatus (~60), Claudius angustatus (25), Rhinoclemmys areolata (>20), and Chelydra rossignonii (8). Species richness and relative abundance varied markedly across habitats. Notably, our records of C. angustatus confirm a viable breeding population and extend the verified range of this species in southern Belize. These data substantially expand distributional records for multiple taxa and provide the most detailed demographic baseline for freshwater turtles in southern Belize yet assembled. Ongoing monitoring will enable robust estimation of population size, survival, and recruitment, supporting regional conservation management and deepening our understanding of Neotropical freshwater turtle assemblages. Alissa Murphy
764: Few freshwater turtles spend time in saline environments aside from the Emydid Diamond-backed Terrapin (Malaclemys terrapin) of North America’s brackish-water Atlantic and Gulf Coasts. It is thus surprising that vibrant and widespread populations of the declining Northwestern Pond Turtle (Actinemys marmorata) are found in the brackish waters of Suisun Marsh in the San Franscisco Bay Estuary of California, USA. The marsh has salinities that vary from freshwater to seawater, fluctuating daily with tides, seasonally with dry Mediterranean summers, and annually depending on climate. In a lab study, we found that pond turtles from the marsh lost more mass than did those from inland after two weeks of exposure to 15 ppt salinity, but they were better able to maintain blood plasma osmolalities near field values, presumably because turtles from the marsh forwent feeding and drinking to manage blood solutes. Using telemetry trackers on turtles in the marsh, we found they increased home range areas and moved away from a site where tides were restored to a previously dammed portion of the marsh, with smaller turtles disappearing altogether. Finally, from surveys across the 470 km2 marsh, we found that pond turtle occupancy decreased as salinity increased, with an inflection around 10 ppt salinity. Our work highlights the limits some freshwater species face in dynamic coastal environments where sea level rise, droughts, and diversion of freshwater all converge to increase salinities in coming decades. Laura Todd
765: Ranavirus (Rv), Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), and amphibian Perkinsea (Pr) have been documented in most climates across the US, temperate and subtropical anuran assemblages seem to host Bd more often. While ranavirus is known to demonstrate higher occurrence and virulence during the warmer seasons and locations with overall higher temperatures in the southeastern US, studies have shown co-occurrence and coinfection cases with both Bd and Pr in central Florida during cooler months. These co-infections were recorded during cooler months with Pr dominating the infection system, suggesting a preference for cooler seasons in subtropical climates. Georgia has a range of habitats from subtropical humid to temperate mountainous habitats. The north Georgia mountains support a diverse assemblage of amphibian communities, with the region being known as a salamander diversity hotspot. This isolated temperate region is nested within the humid subtropical state of Georgia. This dynamic influences unique shifts in seasonal temperatures, precipitation, and humidity. In turn, the region experiences climatic conditions through the year which can support Bd, Rv, and Pr infections. Bd and Rv have both been documented in this region in high quantities. While Pr has not yet been detected in the North Georgia mountains, climate change may increase habitat suitability for the pathogen and/or weaken amphibian immune systems and introduce susceptibility. Data generated by the IPCC has demonstrated that the region has begun and will continue to experience more dramatic shifts in temperature, precipitation, and humidity. Climate change in Northern Georgia, for these reasons, could favor the transition of diseases that are normally enzootic to epizootic states, possibly leading to local extirpations or even extinction of amphibians endemic to these mountains. The North Georgia sampling site, Charles H. Wharton Conservation Center (CHWCC), serves as an optimal habitat to study seasonal disease dynamics amongst a diverse amphibian community. This 129 acre property is located in the Southern Nantahala Wilderness portion of the Chattahoochee National Forest at the cusp of the Blue Ridge Mountain and the Appalachian Mountain formations, two global hotspots for amphibian diversity, especially salamanders. With elevations ranging from 2480ft to 3200ft, the climate displays summer maximums of 80.7 F and winter minimums of 26.4 F with an average of 66” of precipitation annually, making this a temperate ecosystem. This diverse mosaic of habitats supports over 22 species of amphibians (8 frogs and 14 salamanders) many of which have been tested positive for Bd and Rv in these communities. With this, I have begun to quantify the seasonal occurrence and intensity of co-infection and pathogen virulence of Bd, Rv, and Pr in this amphibian community. Ariel Alonso
766: Recent studies have shown that Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are effective for monitoring crocodylians' abundance in Africa and Asia. Despite that, UAVs have not been used as a monitoring tool in the Greater Everglades, presenting an opportunity for novel research on American alligator management. Herein, we present preliminary results from an ongoing monitoring project comparing drone-based surveys with traditional spotlight surveys. The study involves repeated drone flights over the course of a year, paired with spotlight surveys on the same day, to evaluate the effectiveness of each method. During the first month of sampling (January 2026), we conducted five drone flights, which resulted in 70 crocodylian observations (53 American alligators and 17 American crocodiles), averaging 14 ± 6.03 detections per flight. The observed size range for alligators was from 1.5 m to 2.75 m, and for crocodiles from 0.75 m to 2.75 m. The highest counts (20 individuals), comprising 17 alligators and 3 crocodiles, occurred during midday flights, when the sun was more than 42° above the horizon and solar radiation exceeded 750 W/m2. The lowest count was observed in the first flight, with four crocodylians observed when the sun's position was 7.1 degrees, and the sunlight was 66.3 W/m2. We recorded a total of 35 crocodylians during the Spotlight survey (16 alligators, seven crocodiles, and 12 additional eyeshine detections). Sizes ranged from 0.25 m to 2.75 m for crocodiles, and 1.25 m to 2.75 m for alligators. Ongoing data collection will broaden sampling across various environmental conditions, enabling us to identify optimal survey setups and enhance the integration of UAVs into standard crocodilian monitoring protocols. Annais Bonilla
767: Urbanization encompasses a suite of changes to landscapes that shift selective pressures and resulting traits of organisms living in urban habitats. Lizards may be particularly vulnerable to impacts from urbanization as they are ectotherms, are sensitive to changes to substrates and climbing surfaces, and rely on food resources that may also be sensitive to urbanization (e.g., arthropods). Habitat changes associated with urbanization such as increased temperatures, decreased vegetation, changes to arthropod communities, and the presence of artificial substrates are therefore expected to affect urban lizard populations. In this study, we compared morphological features in the common side-blotched lizard (Uta stansburiana) and the ornate tree lizard (Urosaurus ornatus) from urban and rural environments in the Phoenix metropolitan area in Arizona, United States. Measurements of morphological features included mass, snout-vent length (SVL), head length and width, leg lengths (femur, tibia, foot, and toe), arm lengths (arm, forearm, hand, and finger), tail length, and total length, along with various proportional comparisons between related traits. Mass was greater for urban individuals in both species as compared to those from rural sites. Urban individuals from both species also had lower limb lengths relative to their SVLs. In common side-blotched lizards, urban individuals also had relatively shorter and thinner heads as compared to rural individuals. We propose that the morphological changes we observe in urban environments may result from selective pressures associated with changes in temperature, artificial substrates, and prey availability that occur in urban environments. Tyler Brock
768: Environmental Niche Modeling is a tool used to predict and model species distributions by relating species presence data with environmental variables. It can be utilized to estimate possible invasive potential of species by assessing their range of environmental suitabilities. In some cases, asexual reproduction can allow species to be better suited for a larger range of habitats than sexual ones. These populations can increase quickly and thrive in less ideal environments due to different resource and energy allocation than sexual species. Asexual reproduction occurs in select species of whiptail lizards (genus Aspidoscelis) via parthenogenesis, which only occurs in species produced through hybridization. Over the past fifteen years, evidence of introduced asexual whiptail lizard species across the Southwest United States has been found, displaying their potential to invade. In this study, we aim to identify if asexual whiptail species show any difference in habitat suitability ranges compared to sexual species. We utilized the flexsdm package in RStudio to create Environmental Niche Models, which provides information about the range of suitabilities of each whiptail species and possible differences in invasive potential between sexual and asexual species. We show that asexual species are suited to a broader range of environments than their parent, sexual species. By identifying their distributions, we can draw conclusions about the possible invasive potential between asexual and sexual species. Jonathan D. Choquette
769: Charles Frederick Hartt (1840–1878) was a Canadian-American naturalist whose work in Brazil helped the understanding of Neotropical geology and paleontology. Among his lesser-known contributions are fish collections from the 1870-1871 Morgan Expeditions to Brazil. Most of this material was deposited at the Cornell University Museum, now Cornell University Museum of Vertebrates (CUMV). The collection currently comprises 92 specimens of 75 species with incomplete locality and collection data, including type material, which is about onethird of the 280 specimens originally cataloged in the late 1800s. The goal of this project was to reconstruct locality and collection data and to determine the destination of the missing specimens using Hartt’s correspondence and publications, Cornell Zoology Department and Museum records, and the CUMV database. Most specimens were collected in 1870 in the state of Pará, Brazil. Archival evidence indicates that 71 of the missing specimens were transferred to other institutions, including the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History and Harvard Museum of Comparative Zoology, between 1881 and 1886. Specimens collected by Hartt also included material acquired later through gift or exchange from the 1865-1866 Thayer Expedition led by Louis Agassiz. These specimens were fixed and preserved in alcohol and are potentially suitable for molecular studies. Hartt’s collection is one of the oldest series at CUMV and is a valuable historical record of Brazilian fish diversity.Charles Frederick Hartt (1840–1878) foi um naturalista canadense-americano cujo trabalho no Brasil ajudou a compreensão da geologia e paleontologia neotropical. Entre suas contribuições menos conhecidas estão coleções de peixes das Expedições Morgan ao Brasil, entre 1870 e 1871. A maior parte desse material foi depositada no Museu da Cornell University, atualmente o Museu de Vertebrados da Cornell University (CUMV). A coleção atualmente compreende 92 espécimes de 75 espécies, com dados de localidade e coleta incompletos, incluindo material tipo, o que representa cerca de um terço dos 280 espécimes originalmente catalogados no final dos anos 1800s. O objetivo deste projeto foi reconstruir os dados de localidade e coleta e determinar o destino dos espécimes perdidos utilizando a correspondência e as publicações de Hartt, registros do Departamento de Zoologia e do Museu de Cornell, e o banco de dados do CUMV. A maioria dos espécimes foi coletada em 1870 no estado do Pará, Brasil. Evidência arquivística indica que 71 dos exemplares perdidos foram transferidos para outras instituições, incluindo o Museu Nacional de História Natural do Smithsonian e o Museu de Zoologia Comparada de Harvard, entre 1881 e 1886. Os exemplares coletados por Hartt também incluem material adquirido posteriormente por doação ou troca, proveniente da Expedição Thayer em 1865–1866, liderada por Louis Agassiz. Esses exemplares foram fixados e preservados em álcool e são potencialmente adequados para estudos moleculares. A coleção de Hartt é uma das séries mais antigas do CUMV e constitui um valioso registro histórico da diversidade de peixes do Brasil. Dylan DeBaun
770: The winter skate, Leucoraja ocellata, is a large, slow maturing species that can be found along the western Atlantic coast from the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence in Canada to North Carolina, U.S. (Sulikowski et al., 2003). They are categorized as part of the Northeast Skate Complex and monitored by the New England Fishery Management Council (NOAA, 2025). Since the winter skate is commercially harvested, understanding such biological parameters, such as growth rates, are necessary components of the fishery management process. Past research on this species has indicated a relatively slow (female k value = 0.059 and male k = 0.074) growth rate which makes this species susceptible to overfishing (Sulikowski et al. 2003). The goal of this study is to determine if age at size and growth rate has changed since Sulikowski et al. (2003), and if so, what are possible fishery implications. Sixty-eight females (465 mm – 885 mm TL) and 69 males (590 mm – 990 mm TL) were used for interpreting annular counts on vertebral centra. The oldest age estimates collected for L. ocellata were 18 years (990 mm TL) for males and 15 years (859 mm TL) for females. Preliminary analyses suggest slightly elevated size at age in both female and male winter skate relative to historical estimates (Sulikowski et al., 2003), potentially reflecting environmental or density-dependent changes. James Emerson
771: The Winter Skate (Leucoraja ocellata) is a commercially viable species distributed throughout the Northwest Atlantic. The species is slow growing and reaches sexual maturity later in life, making it particularly vulnerable to overfishing. Fully understanding their life history parameters is essential to assessing stock health and retaining the current Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) certification of the fishery. The last comprehensive study of growth and maturity for this species was done two decades ago. This means there is a gap in understanding of what, if any, changes have occurred within the population since. The objective of this study was to assess whether size at sexual maturity has changed since Sulikowski et al. (2005) by comparing contemporary reproductive metrics with historical maturity ogives. Sexual maturity in males and females was determined through macroscopic examination of reproductive organs during systematic dissections. Size at 50% maturity (L₅₀) for each sex was estimated using logistic regression, and contemporary estimates were statistically compared (p= 0.8326 for males, p = 0.6221 for females) with historical datasets. Preliminary results indicate that while increases in total length occurred, by 7 mm in males and by 11 mm in females, these differences are not statistically significant. Ongoing work will incorporate vertebral age analysis to better place changes to maturity in context and assess their implications for the sustainable management of the fishery. 772: Sphoeroides is a genus of pufferfishes primarily distributed in coastal North and South America (19 of 21 species). Sphoeroides dorsalis Longley 1934, commonly known as the Marbled Pufferfish, occurs at moderate depths (20-100 m) along the eastern coast of the United States. Sphoeroides dorsalis is one of the least known pufferfishes in the Atlantic Ocean, with limited information about its life history, reproductive biology, and toxicity. It is the only species of Sphoeroides with external sexual dimorphism in its coloration, yet there are knowledge gaps in how coloration relates to the stage of maturity and varies among specimens of the same sex. The original description of S. dorsalis described the type specimen as having “pale blue vertical pencilings upon the cheek”, although the sex of the specimen is not recorded. Identification guides consistently describe S. dorsalis as sexually dimorphic in its coloration, yet it is unclear where the data came from. Similarly, there is no information on the maturation and reproduction of S. dorsalis, with spawning data existing only for related species. While several pufferfishes have been studied for their toxicity—human consumption can be lethal—the toxicity of S. dorsalis is poorly understood, as the only previous study showed variable results. Through photographs and reproductive information from confirmed individuals and new data on depth and distribution, we characterized the natural history of S. dorsalis. Our new data provides a framework for future analyses to verify the toxicity of S. dorsalis and investigate the connection between toxicity and maturity. Mei Lin McLaughlin
773: High rates of diversification are observed to occur within biodiversity hotspots, making these key study regions for investigating drivers of species diversity. However, the rapid radiation of species within these hotspots can pose challenges for investigating their evolutionary histories. Incomplete coalescence and hybridization can obscure species boundaries and result in phylogenetic discordance that misrepresents the true species diversity. This raises a series of foundational questions, including how species boundaries are maintained in the presence of gene flow, how gene flow may contribute to or even drive divergence, and how to achieve conservation in the face of uncertain or porous boundaries among species. The map turtles, Graptemys, are a clade of river endemics that form a central component of the global biodiversity hotspot for turtles in the southeast of North America. The clade has allopatrically radiated into at least fifteen lineages within the last 1.5 million years. Despite prior molecular and morphological studies that have examined the evolutionary relationships among Graptemys lineages, their species boundaries remain poorly understood. The objectives for this study are to resolve the species boundaries, patterns of gene flow, and investigate processes of diversification within Graptemys. Genomic data was obtained for 144 specimens encompassing the geographic ranges of all described species. I used a combination of phylogenetic, network coalescent, and population genomic tests to resolve the evolutionary relationships among lineages and investigate introgressive hybridization in this clade. Daniella Mori
774: Developmental abnormalities in viviparous sharks, particularly among species prone to fisheries interactions, have been documented periodically in the scientific literature. In these cases, historical emphasis tended to be on gross morphological descriptions and two-dimensional x-ray imaging. The prevalence, degree of variability, and root causes of skeletal abnormalities are largely unknown, making each teratological specimen a potentially valuable point of comparison. Here, we present three-dimensional reconstructions of a vertebral deformity in an embryonic Blue Shark (Prionace glauca) using high-resolution, contrast-enhanced computed tomography. We offer preliminary insights into the disruption of embryonic development and highlight areas in which a larger sample size of similarly afflicted specimens might yield an enhanced understanding of selachian developmental and reproductive biology. 775: Island groups offer unique insights on evolutionary processes. The Greater Puerto Rican Area (including the islands of Mona, Monito, Desecheo, Puerto Rico, and Spanish, United States, and British Virgin Islands) boasts great diversity of miniaturized geckos. The Sphaerodactylus macrolepis species complex is found only in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. Recently, a combined analysis of molecular and morphological data resolved the relationships within this complex, classifying this group into four different species: S. grandisquamis in Puerto Rico, S. inigoi in Vieques and West Culebra, S. parvus in Aguilla, and S. macrolepis in East Culebra and the U.S. and British Virgin Islands including St. Croix. In this project, we study the variation within S. macrolepis among these clades. Coloration and pigmentation pattern is consistent in all geographic clusters identified with molecular data. Snout to vent length is also variable among these clades, showing a gradual increment across the Virgin Islands from West to East, with significant differences in sex and locality (Tukey’s multiple comparison test). It has been proposed that S. macrolepis can be differentiated from S. inigoi and S. grandisquamis by the lack of knoblike organs on dorsal scales, but this character needs to be corroborated examining more specimens, including comparison to outgroup S. parvus. We will continue looking at external characters and, osteology measurements using digital X-rays, and computed topographies to explore additional variation within the Virgin Islands populations. We hope to find that the morphological variation is consistent with the existing molecular analysis. Furthermore, we will use the morphological variation to describe new lineages. Griffin Nicholson
776: Semi-aquatic snakes play critical roles as both predators and prey in freshwater ecosystems, yet their diet in water-limited systems remains poorly studied. The Diamond-backed Watersnake (Nerodia rhombifer) and Plain-bellied Watersnake (Nerodia erythrogaster) commonly co-occur across Texas, including regions where reduced water availability may intensify interspecific interactions. The documented dietary overlap suggests there is potential for niche partitioning, allowing for coexistence, but reduced water availability seen in the West Texas area may intensify competition for resources or space. Addressing this gap is critical for understanding how the species thrive under spatial environmental constraints. This study investigates dietary composition and niche overlap between the two species in a water-scarce habitat in San Angelo, Texas. Fieldwork is beginning this spring semester at a site with a limited water source. Snakes will be captured using baited minnow traps, collapsible bait traps, or by hand, and handled following standardized protocols. DNA material will be collected using minimally invasive cloacal and external body swabs. Cloacal swabs will be used to characterize diet via DNA metabarcoding, while external swabs from the head, back, and belly scales will capture environmental DNA and provide insight into species interactions within the surrounding community. Diet analyses will be used to assess whether dietary differences exist between Nerodia rhombifer and Nerodia erythrogaster, allowing us to determine if one species is utilizing prey resources not consumed by the other. Together, these approaches will clarify whether dietary differentiation occurs despite shared habitats. Mariana Palencia Mariana Palencia-Martínez; Ángel Ayala-Leyva; Israel Solano-Zavaleta; Gonzalo Ramírez-Cruz; Stacey Weiss; A.
777: The movement patterns of cryptic aquatic species are often difficult to quantify, particularly when subjected to anthropogenic disturbance. This study utilizes a novel, custom-developed aquatic camera trap system to continuously monitor salamander activity in situ. By deploying these units in a highly studied area of known Eurycea sosorum abundance before, during, and after an on-going capture-recapture study, we aim to acquire high-resolution behavioral data as individuals pass beneath the sensor array. The study follows a three-week experimental timeline in which week 1 will establish a baseline of natural movement patterns, week 2 will observe salamander response during a high-intensity routine capture-recapture study involving three comprehensive habitat surveys, and week 3 will monitor the "recovery" period to track post-disturbance activity levels. We hypothesize that salamander movement will increase significantly during active habitat disturbance as individuals attempt to flee or find new refugia. Furthermore, we anticipate a lasting uptick in movement immediately following the survey, gradually returning to baseline levels within seven days. This research highlights the utility of noninvasive automated monitoring in aquatic ecology. By correlating movement frequency with specific disturbance events, we can inform and update survey protocols and conservation management strategies for this and other aquatic, endangered amphibians. In addition, this study will provide some baseline approaches on properly utilizing the camera trap system to assist or supplement an on-going capture-recapture study. Kamryn Richard
778: A new species of Gigantactis is described from a single female collected from the eastern North Pacific. As with others of this genus, this species is distinguished by its unique luring apparatus, most obviously through the presence of a relatively short illicium, bearing a secondary escal-like appendage. This specimen was collected during the first large scale community survey in the eastern Clarion Clipperton Zone, a region allocated for deep sea mining. Holden Diane Rierson
779: The scalloped hammerhead Sphyrna lewini, a Critically Endangered species, relies on coastal habitats that function as essential nursery areas. However, for more than two decades, the trophic ecology of juveniles in Santa Rosalía, Baja California Sur, has remained largely unknown, limiting our understanding of their ecological role in one of the most productive regions of the Mexican Pacific. This study examines the trophic dynamics of 136 juveniles using an integrative approach that combines stomach content analysis and stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N) in muscle and vertebrae, allowing dietary reconstruction across short- and long-term temporal scales. Isotopic niche structure was quantified using the Bayesian SIBER model. Juveniles exhibited a high trophic position (TP = 4.40) and a predominantly piscivorous diet dominated by teleost fishes (82.88% PSIRI). While the population displayed a generalist niche (Levins’ index, B = 0.64), individuals showed opportunistic specialization, reflecting intensive use of locally available prey. Vertebral isotopic signatures revealed sex-based differences in long-term trophic niche width, with females exhibiting greater trophic plasticity, as well as ontogenetic shifts characterized by increasing δ¹⁵N values and niche expansion with body size, indicating a transition toward higher trophic level prey. These findings identify Santa Rosalía as a critical nursery habitat and provide robust evidence to inform conservation strategies for this key predator. Alfonsus Saputro
780: Hybridization plays an integral part of salamander evolution, with at least 12.1% of salamander species known to hybridize. In the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, salamanders of the genus Plethodon form a gene flow network consisting of multiple hybridizing species. The endemic Red-cheeked Salamander (Plethodon jordani) hybridizes with every other large Plethodon species it contacts, including the Southern Gray-cheeked Salamander (P. metcalfi), Northern Slimy Salamander (P. glutinosus), and Southern Appalachian Salamander (P. teyahalee). Hybrids are viable and fertile, resulting in substantial backcrossing at these locations. The degree of hybridization where these species occur in sympatry appears to be spatially heterogeneous. In some areas, these species hybridize prolifically, resulting in broad hybrid zones with extensive backcrossing and introgression. However, in other areas, these species appear to co-occur with little if any hybridization. We present a preliminary analysis investigating how the prevalence of hybridization among different Plethodon species is influenced by local demographic, geographic, and environmental contexts. Ongoing analyses will further clarify how context-dependent hybridization contributes to adaptive gene flow dynamics across multispecies hybrid systems. Cel Velasquez
781: Acoustic communication plays a central role in amphibian reproduction, yet the spatial organization and behavioral dynamics of natural choruses remain poorly understood because individuals are difficult to track in dense habitats. We used a three-dimensional acoustic triangulation array to localize calling males of an arboreal reed frog (Hyperolius albomaculatus sp. nov) at a breeding pond in a Central African rainforest. Triangulated call positions were used to quantify spatial arrangement, movement behavior, and temporal interaction patterns among calling males. Frogs showed strong spatial structure within the chorus, typically maintaining 4–5 m spacing from neighboring males and calling from heights of approximately 2–4 m. Many individuals returned to the same microhabitats across nights, indicating site fidelity to specific calling locations. Hidden Markov modeling of vertical movements revealed three behavioral states, and demonstrated that most vertical movement occurred early in the evening, with frogs rapidly descending and then settling into stable calling positions. Analysis of call timing showed two distinct interaction modes within choruses: rapid response calls and slower alternation patterns, with the likelihood of rapid responses influenced by inter-male distance, chorus size, and the time a frog had been waiting to call. Together, these results show that frog choruses are spatially structured communication networks shaped by spacing behavior, movement dynamics, and socially mediated call timing.La communication acoustique joue un rôle central dans la reproduction des amphibiens, mais l'organisation spatiale et la dynamique comportementale des chœurs naturels restent mal comprises, car les individus sont difficiles à suivre dans les habitats denses. Nous avons utilisé un réseau de triangulation acoustique tridimensionnel pour localiser les mâles chanteurs d'une grenouille arboricole (Hyperolius albomaculatus sp. nov) dans un étang de reproduction situé dans une forêt tropicale d'Afrique centrale. Les positions triangulées des chants ont été utilisées pour quantifier la disposition spatiale, le comportement de déplacement et les schémas d'interaction temporelle entre les mâles chanteurs. Les grenouilles ont montré une forte structure spatiale au sein du chœur, maintenant généralement un espacement de 4 à 5 m entre les mâles voisins et chantant à une hauteur d'environ 2 à 4 m. De nombreux individus sont retournés dans les mêmes microhabitats au cours des nuits, indiquant une fidélité au site à des emplacements de chant spécifiques. La modélisation de Markov cachée des mouvements verticaux a révélé trois états comportementaux et a démontré que la plupart des mouvements verticaux se produisaient en début de soirée, les grenouilles descendant rapidement puis s'installant dans des positions de chant stables. L'analyse du timing des cris a montré deux modes d'interaction distincts au sein des chœurs : des cris de réponse rapide et des schémas d'alternance plus lents, la probabilité de réponses rapides étant influencée par la distance entre les mâles, la taille du chœur et le temps d'attente d'une grenouille avant de chanter. Ensemble, ces résultats montrent que les chœurs de grenouilles constituent des réseaux de communication structurés spatialement, façonnés par le comportement d'espacement, la dynamique des mouvements et le timing des cris, qui est influencé par les interactions sociales. Aaron M. Bauer
782: As global temperatures continue to rise, species range shifts are becoming increasingly common. Animal behavior, particularly consistent among-individual differences in behavior (i.e., animal personality), may play an important role in mediating colonization processes during range shifts because individuals with certain behavioral tendencies (e.g., increased boldness, exploration, or aggression) may be more likely to disperse and persist within newly colonized habitats. We asked whether consistent behavioral differences among individuals contribute to the ongoing range expansion of green treefrogs (Hyla cinerea) in the midwestern United States. We hypothesized that frogs from the historical range would differ behaviorally than those found in the expanded range (populations colonized within the last ~25 years). Specifically, we predicted that expanded populations would exhibit elevated dispersal-related behaviors, including boldness, exploration, and aggression, relative to historical populations. To test these predictions, we conducted a field playback experiment to assess aggression and repeated laboratory assays to quantify boldness and exploration using four expanded and four historical populations of frogs. Latency to exit (boldness), the number of jumping events, and latency to explore (exploration) were significantly repeatable. Additionally, expanded populations were significantly bolder as they exited sooner from a shelter and also showed higher jumping performance than historical populations. Although aggressive behavior did not show consistent among-individual variation, the proportion of aggressive calls relative to advertisement calls was significantly higher in expanded populations. Our findings suggest that behavioral traits associated with dispersal can diverge rapidly during contemporary range expansion, highlighting the importance of animal personality/behavior in driving colonization success. Diego J. Elías
783: The Cuban Treefrog (Osteopilus septentrionalis; CTF) is native to Cuba, the Bahamas, and the Cayman Islands and has expanded its invasive range throughout the Caribbean and peninsular Florida in recent decades. CTFs are dietary generalists, to the suspected detriment of their introduced ecosystem, consuming a variety of vertebrate and invertebrate prey including native amphibians and conspecifics. The first established population of CTFs in Louisiana was documented in 2017 at the Audubon Riverview Park and Audubon Zoo in New Orleans. To better understand the dietary habits of CTFs at the edge of their invasive range, we conducted a dietary analysis utilizing 1005 CTFs collected from this newly established population. CTFs were collected during visual encounter surveys and from artificial pipe refugia. The complete gastrointestinal tract (GI) was resected, sectioned, and present prey items were identified to the lowest practical taxonomic level. Various arthropod prey items were commonly found, whereas evidence of vertebrate predation was relatively rare (3.4%). Females exhibited a wider dietary breadth than males and were approximately twice as likely to consume vertebrate prey items; however, the latter observation was largely attributable to sex-based differences in body size. We determined that GI contents recovered from the stomach and large intestine, when compared to contents of the small intestine, were better representative of the entire GI content. These findings expand current understanding of the feeding behavior of a pervasive anuran exotic while providing meaningful methodological insight for future studies of anuran dietary composition. Jonathan Kim
784: Amphibians are key ecosystem indicators and are highly sensitive to environmental change, making them powerful models for understanding how behavior responds to ecological variation. However, behavioral data is still scarce for many arboreal species, limiting our ability to link individual behavior to ecological and evolutionary processes. Here, we characterize behavioral variation in the fringed leaf frog (Cruziohyla craspedopus), integrating personality traits and antipredator responses across developmental stages and ecological contexts. We quantified activity, exploration, and boldness using behavioral assays conducted under both laboratory and field conditions. Behavioral variation was structured along two primary axes: an activity axis associated with locomotion and exploration, and a boldness axis associated with emergence responses. These axes were independent, indicating a multidimensional organization of behavior. We detected clear ontogenetic differences, with juveniles showing lower activity and greater use of ground substrates, whereas adults exhibited higher activity and increased use of vertical structures. Field-collected individuals were also more active and emerged more rapidly than captive-raised individuals, highlighting the role of environmental experience. In addition to consistent individual differences in routine behavior, we observed context-dependent defensive responses. Individuals displayed a previously undescribed “twerking” posture under laboratory conditions, along with stress-induced color changes and the release of volatile compounds, suggesting multimodal antipredator strategies. Together, our findings reveal that both personality traits and defensive behaviors are shaped by life stage and environment, providing new insights into how behavioral strategies are organized and expressed in arboreal amphibians. Bruno Melo
785: The spread of invasive frogs may be resulting in acoustic interference that impacts communication in native frog species. To avoid interference, native frogs may alter the acoustic properties of their calls. However, shifts in call properties carry their own costs for frog communication and increase energy expenditure. To advance our understanding of how frogs respond to the calls of invasive frogs, we exposed Chiricahua Leopard Frogs to playbacks of American Bullfrog calls. These species have substantial spectral overlap in their vocalizations, with potential for acoustic interference. Furthermore, previous work found Chiricahua Leopard Frogs view bullfrog calls as potential mating cues. We recorded and compared the vocalizations of leopard frogs from control and experimental creek segments and before-after for segments where American Bullfrog vocalizations were introduced. We found that Chiricahua Leopard Frogs called at lower dominant frequencies when presented with bullfrog calls. We also found variation in temporal properties of leopard frog calls, but they did not avoid calling when bullfrog calls were broadcast. The decrease in dominant frequency was unexpected, as bullfrog calls are lower in frequency than Chiricahua Leopard Frog calls. We expected the opposite – an increase in dominant frequency to avoid acoustic interference. These results could be due to Chiricahua Leopard Frogs attempting to compete with calling bullfrogs rather than attempting to avoid acoustic interference.
786: As anthropogenic wildfires increase in frequency and intensity worldwide, there is a dire need to determine species’ vulnerabilities to changing fire regimes. Of key importance is understanding the pressures animals face in post-fire environments. Notably, fires burn vegetation leaving animals exposed on darkened substrates. This shift in habitat structure and coloration presumably increases predation risk, which could negatively affect fitness. However, animals in fire-prone habitats may have adaptations to reduce this risk. My lab has been studying the responses of western fence lizards (Sceloporus occidentalis) to post-fire stressors. Fence lizards occur across flammable habitats, are well-known to survive massive wildfires, and may have consequently evolved fireadapted traits. We have found that reduced vegetation cover due to fires associates with higher attack rates on clay lizard models, suggesting heightened risk. Behaviorally, lizards respond by reducing flight initiation distances, presumably to reduce detection by predators (i.e., rely more on crypsis). This reduced escape response is also associated with enhanced camouflage on darkened substrates suggesting that lizards in burned habitats may have adaptations to reduce detection by predators in post-fire environments. Increased openness in burned habitats did not associate with higher levels of circulating stress hormones (e.g., corticosterone), but some evidence suggest that lizards may experience more thermal stress (e.g., risk of overheating) in burned areas, and future work in the lab will quantify this. Overall, our work suggests that if fire return intervals continue to decrease, predation levels could remain elevated for longer periods of time, placing strong selective pressures on animals.
787: Biological clocks allow organisms to anticipate cyclical environmental changes, yet in high-latitude or deep-sea habitats, the diel cues that entrain these rhythms are often seasonally diminished or absent. Fishes of the order Perciformes have rapidly diversified and adapted to these arrhythmic ecosystems, suggesting that a reduced dependence on circadian systems may have contributed to their success as one of the most species-rich vertebrate orders. Here, we used a comparative genomic approach to investigate patterns of core biological clock gene loss across 96 perciform and five outgroup species. We found widespread and lineage-specific loss in core clock genes, particularly in the convergently evolving polar and deep-sea suborders Notothenioidei and Cottioidei. This trend of circadian gene loss was significantly amplified with higher-latitude species. To determine if these genomic signatures reflect a functional loss of rhythmicity, we performed metabolic phenotyping on three notothenioid species. We found a consistent lack of circadian metabolic oscillations during the late austral fall across all notothenioids, including the sub-Antarctic sister lineage to the cryonotothenioid adaptive radiation, Eleginops maclovinus. Experimental data across Perciformes, combined with suborder-wide patterns of gene loss, suggest that a release from circadian constraints occurred early in their diversification, potentially facilitating the repeated expansion of these fishes into polar and deep-sea habitats. Ben Dalton
788: Heterochrony, or changes to developmental timing, provides a classic descriptive framework that is used to understand skeletal diversification and adaptation. However, an underlying genetic and developmental basis for heterochronic shifts remains poorly understood. One form of heterochrony, pedomorphy, involves the retention of juvenile traits into adulthood through features such as delayed ossification, cartilage retention, and miniaturization. Skeletal pedomorphy has evolved multiple times independently within Cypriniformes, an order that includes zebrafish (Danio rerio) and the pedomorphic Danionella model organisms. Here, we combine comparative genomics with zebrafish experimental genetics to uncover the genetic basis of skeletal heterochrony. We generated chromosome-level genome assemblies for two pedomorphic species, Sundadanio goblinus and Danionella cerebrum. These genomes were integrated into a multiple genome alignment of 23 non-pedomorphic and six pedomorphic cypriniform species, representing three independent pedomorphic transitions: the genera Danionella, Paedocypris, and Sundadanio. We find that genome size has independently contracted in all three pedomorphic clades, coinciding with repeated loss of skeleton-associated genes. To test the functional relevance of lost genes, we used Crispr/Cas9 to disrupt two candidate genes, ccn4a (wisp1) and klf10 (tieg1), in a dual-reporter zebrafish line marking cartilage and bone (Tg(sox10:rfp,sp7:egfp)). Compared to age-matched controls, crispants exhibit altered bone development timing, disrupted cranial sutures, and reduced body size, phenotypes that parallel the skeletal changes in pedomorphic cyprinids. These results highlight candidate molecular levers driving parallel evolutionary shifts in skeletal heterochrony and provide a roadmap for genetic dissection of complex morphological transitions. Natalie Loftin Natalie Loftin; Veda Allen; Nicole Smolensky; Lauren Van Horn; Kathryn Steffen; Danielle Walkup; Wade
789: Ophichthys cuchia is a species of obligate air-breathing swamp eel from Southeast Asia that was discovered in Bayou St. John in New Orleans in the summer of 2019. It has proven difficult to monitor the abundance and spread of this potentially invasive species using traditional sampling methods (e.g., seines and throw traps) because Cuchia are nocturnal, fossorial, and occupy densely vegetated habitats. To overcome these difficulties, we are developing an eDNA protocol to detect the presence of Cuchia DNA in water samples collected from monitoring sites in Bayou St. John and adjacent water bodies. To create the eDNA assay, we designed species- specific primers and probes targeting ~150bp regions of the COI and Cytb genes. We are using PCR and qPCR to test sensitivity and specificity of these primers/probes using DNA isolated from tissue samples from Cuchia and other fish species caught in Bayou St. John, and swamp eel specimens from other populations established in Texas and Florida. We also determined the limit of detection for each primer/probe set, as well as how many days can pass after DNA is released into the water for the primer to remain effective. We will be conducting field testing to determine its effectiveness outside of a lab setting, and to try and determine the current range of Cuchia in Bayou St. John.
