Ideally, our eDNA protocol will provide fishery managers with an accurate and relatively inexpensive tool to monitor the invasion dynamics of Cuchia in Bayou St. John and beyond. Grant McCargar
790: Connectivity in reef-associated fishes emerges from processes occurring across multiple spatial and temporal scales, but these processes are rarely assessed together. Here, we combined genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) data with otolith elemental signatures to study connectivity in red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) and vermilion snapper (Rhomboplites aurorubens) across 14 shelf-edge sites in the northern Gulf of America. We evaluated whether genomic variation indicated population structure across geographic and depth gradients (shallow, upper mesophotic, and lower mesophotic). Additionally, we examined whether otolith chemistry detected fine-scale, site-specific environmental exposure and habitat use patterns not captured by genetic markers alone and how these complementary signals related to spatial variation in age structure and growth patterns. Genome-wide SNP data indicated limited genetic structure across the sampled banks for either species, while otolith microchemistry revealed strong site-related environmental structuring. Red snapper otolith signatures aligned with reef-associated habitats, whereas vermilion snapper showed more diverse elemental signatures, indicating exposure to a wider range of environments. Age structure and growth also varied across different areas, demonstrating that demographic differences can develop within a connected regional system. Overall, these findings suggest that gene flow can coexist with localized ecological and demographic differences, and that otolith chemistry provides important insights into post-settlement processes beyond what genetic markers alone can reveal. This integrated approach links evolutionary-scale connectivity with ecological and demographic factors influencing local population performance, offering a more complete understanding of resilience and guiding fisheries management in shelf-edge reef systems. Jackson Roberts Jackson Roberts; Travis Taggart; Edward Myers; Rafe Brown; Ana Motta; Mark Herr; Jeffrey Weinell; Kinn Chan;
791: Investigating transcriptional divergence within and between species provides insights into lineage divergence, adaptation to local environmental conditions, and functional differences between species. The Blacknose Dace complex, composed of Rhinichthys atratulus and R. obtusus, serves as a useful model for divergent transcriptional responses within two wide-ranging sister species across a latitudinal gradient. We quantified gene expression using RNA-seq and assessed differences between species, between intraspecies lineages, across latitudinal gradient, and between closely related populations. Additionally, we used clustering algorithms to test for grouping of transcriptional profiles by latitude, species, clade within R. obtusus, and geography. To understand the functional consequences of differential expression, we tested for functional enrichment of differentially expressed genes. This study emphasizes the importance of latitudinal gradient and phylogeny in determining gene expression in wild fishes and serves as a basis for future hypotheses about range-wide patterns of expression in non-model organisms. Rory S. Telemeco
792: Polyphenisms enable species to adapt to seasonal extremes through tissue remodeling, yet the mechanisms driving this functional plasticity remain poorly understood. Polar fish kidneys offer a prime example of this phenomenon. To survive in sub-zero oceans temperatures, some fish species produce antifreeze proteins to suppress fatal ice crystal formation. Importantly, these small antifreeze proteins (< 10 kDa) must be maintained at high blood concentrations (~20-30 mg/ml), making them susceptible to continuous loss through renal filtration or requiring energetically costly active reabsorption. To preserve antifreeze, some fishes permanently lose their glomeruli, the primary structural unit of filtration in the kidney. In contrast, limited reports suggest that cods retain these structures, relying instead on seasonal disruption of glomerular filtration. Here, we investigate seasonal renal plasticity in three species that rely heavily on winter antifreeze production: saffron cod (Eleginus gracilis), Atlantic cod, (Gadus morhua), and Greenland cod, (Gadus ogac). Histological comparisons between summer (8°C) and winter (0°C) conditions revealed substantial thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, podocyte effacement, and hypercellularity that mirror the conditions of late-stage renal failure in other vertebrates. To investigate the molecular mechanisms of seasonal polyphenism, we generated a new chromosome-level genome assembly for Greenland and improved the saffron cod assembly. Using RNA- and ATAC-seq, we have discovered distinct seasonal changes to gene expression patterns and cis-regulatory enhancer occupancy. Understanding how the vertebrate kidney responds to antifreeze production will address central questions to polar, evolutionary, biomedical, and developmental biology. Austin Wright
793: Morphological diversification can be influenced by environmental factors, functional constraints, and ecology. Typically, morphology requires some coordinated evolution to maintain biomechanical and ecological function, which may constrain morphological diversity. However, when parts of a system in an organism become decoupled, these limitations can be lifted, resulting in accelerated morphological divergence. In ray-finned fishes, the feeding apparatus is a classic example of a functionally decoupled system. Ray-finned fishes have a two-jaw system that separates the prey capture and prey processing mechanisms. This morphological and functional separation of the jaws allows fishes to bypass the mechanical constraints of a single-jaw system, which is subject to the typical force/velocity trade-offs. In addition to relaxing constraints between the two-jaw systems, factors such as diet type and prey-capture behavior can influence the form and function of the jaws, with the oral jaws associated with prey-capture mechanisms, whereas pharyngeal jaws may be correlated with how prey is processed. The minnows provide an ideal model to test for decoupling of the two-jaw system and determine how decoupling may influence ecological transitions. Minnows are ecomorphologically diverse, inhabiting a wide range of Holarctic freshwater environments and display variation in morphology which may be influenced by their ecologies. In this study, we use 3D geometric morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods to test for decoupling of the twojaw system and to assess the influence of ecology on the evolution of shape in minnows. Dave Blackburn
794: Local adaption and speciation are fundamental processes underlying biological diversity. They can result in functionally important geographic variation at large and small spatial scales. Many differences in physiology and behavior might go unobserved by humans. While of great interest to ecological and evolutionary biologists, such cryptic divergence raises challenges for conservation. In particular, when ecological restoration programs rely on exogenous sources for species reintroduction, there is a risk that different source populations might encounter two kinds of mismatches when translocated. Ecological mismatch occurs when local adaptation results in poor performance in the new environment, and genetic mismatch occurs when mixed source populations are not reproductively compatible. In the southern Appalachians, restoration of native Brook Trout often relies on mixing source populations to enhance genetic diversity of founders and avoid depleting sources. Managers generally try to source fish from nearby watersheds and similar environments (e.g., elevation), but choices are often limited. Here, we report on the admixture process in multiple restoration sites in the Great Smoky Mountains. Population density estimates indicate successful restoration in all sites. DNA analyses indicate successful admixture in all except one site. This site received propagules from the most divergent source lineages, which were released non-randomly across a 500m elevational gradient. Spatial genetic analysis indicates that a combination of ecological sorting and reproductive incompatibility has maintained two distinct, elevationally segregated subpopulations with limited interbreeding. Nora Flannery
795: Tropical rivers in Australia and New Guinea (AUNG) provide a rare natural experiment in vertebrate evolution: unlike other continental systems, their freshwater ichthyofaunas are composed almost entirely of marinederived lineages rather than primary freshwater fishes. This unique biogeographic setting enables replicated tests of why some marine-to-freshwater transitions give rise to extensive adaptive radiations while others remain speciespoor, and whether these outcomes reflect ecological opportunity or paleoenvironmental constraints. Using a densely sampled, time-calibrated phylogenomic framework spanning 2,303 teleost species, we identified a likely range of 27–34 marine-to-freshwater transitions across the Cenozoic, including a pronounced Middle Miocene peak (16–11 Ma). While ecological opportunity in AUNG rivers enabled repeated colonization in the absence of dominant primary freshwater incumbents, younger freshwater lineages nevertheless diversify faster than older ones, contradicting the expectation that early arrivers should undergo elevated diversification while accessing vacant niche space. Although some colonizations coincide with bursts of speciation consistent with adaptive radiation, many yielded few species despite long residence times. Functional trait analyses likewise revealed no consistent relationship between colonization timing, ecological breadth, or diversification rate, although expanded functional space characterizes previously proposed AUNG adaptive radiations. Comparisons with paleoenvironmental curves indicate that colonization success correlates with sea-level minima and low-oxygen conditions, suggesting that Earth history dynamics modulated when ecological opportunity was accessible. Together, these findings demonstrate that while ecological opportunity enabled repeated freshwater invasions into the AUNG region, diversification outcomes are governed by the interaction of paleoenvironmental dynamics and possibly lineage-specific traits, generating stark asymmetries in freshwater radiation potential. Joseph Medina
796: The Anabantiformes (gouramis, climbing perches, snakeheads, leaffishes) are a diverse clade of freshwater fishes native to Southeast Asia, exhibiting a wide array of body shapes, parental care strategies, and airbreathing capabilities. The genus Betta, with 78 recognized species, is the most speciose group in the clade. Bettas are small, vibrantly colored fishes that possess a vascularized bony structure in the posterior neurocranium known as a “labyrinth organ” which enables air-breathing and supports “bubble-nesting” behavior, where males build and guard mucus-based bubble-nests produced by the labyrinth organ. Mouthbrooding has also evolved independently multiple times in Betta, where males brood eggs orally and forgo eating for weeks at a time. This alternative behavior imposes increased functional demands on the parent, requiring coordination of feeding, ventilation, and brood care. These differing parental care modes may therefore drive alternate patterns of cranial integration and modularity. Since parental care is male-specific, male bettas may exhibit cranial morphologies more specialized for parental care than females. We microCT scanned over half of all Betta species, sampling both sexes from multiple bubble-nesting and mouthbrooding lineages. We then collected 3D geometric morphometric landmarks to quantify skull shape and test whether cranial integration and modularity varies by parental care mode and sex, and determine whether parental care influences sexual dimorphism. We predict greater skull shape disparity and modularity in bubble-nesters, and stronger integration in mouthbrooders; males and females are predicted to have stronger integration and modularity respectively. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation awards DEB2333683 and DEB-2333684. Betsie Rothermel
797: Body size is a fundamental biological trait tied to the ecology, evolution, and diversification of species. Leuciscidae, the true minnows, are one of the most speciose freshwater fish families, comprising over 600 species and exhibiting exceptional variation in body size, ranging from 26.8 to 1800 millimeters in total length. This wide range raises questions about how body size evolved in minnows and whether selection on this trait played a role in their diversification. To study this in minnows, we compiled maximum body size data for 635 minnow species across North America and Eurasia, representing roughly 90% of described species, and analyzed body size evolution for the 540 species with available sequence data. We also compiled standard and total length measurements for 1350 specimens across 42 genera to calculate genus-specific length ratios and standardize all size data to standard length. Previous research focusing on the evolution of Leuciscidae body size has been restricted to North American taxa, and our dataset extends this to Eurasian taxa, allowing for a more comprehensive analysis of the family. We tested for shifts in the dynamics of body size evolution across the family under multirate Brownian Motion and multi-peak Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models. We also tested the relationship between body size and speciation rates using QuaSSE. We repeatedly identified the importance of the benthic–pelagic shift within the Pogonichthyinae leading to shiners as an important shift in body size evolution. Future research explicitly incorporating ecology can be used to test if and how ecology drives body size evolution.
798: While occupying less than 1% of the world’s oceans, coral reefs house about a third of marine fish species. Why is fish diversity on reefs so high? Traditional explanations point to niche diversity resulting from complex reef habitats. We explored patterns of reef fish diversity from the standpoint of their feeding biology. Unlike other marine habitats, reefs are characterized by an abundance of hard surfaces that are colonized by a myriad of sessile life. At least 40% of reef fish species feed on these benthic, attached organisms. To do so, they use a range of biting and scraping mechanisms that differ fundamentally from suction feeding, the method most fish use to capture free swimming prey. In a morphospace based on functional traits from the feeding apparatus in 110 reef fish species, those that feed on attached prey occupy a multidimensional hypervolume that is 11.7 times greater than species that feed on mobile prey. In a kinematic space of jaw and head motions we measured from high-speed videos of feeding in 24 species, those that feed on attached prey roughly double the total hypervolume of reef fish although they are less diverse than species feeding on free moving prey because they show a limited range of jaw protrusion. The tremendous diversity of coral reef fishes is due in large measure to the diversifying effects of feeding on attached benthic prey, an abundant and diverse food resource that is common on reefs but rare elsewhere. Dylan Wainwright
799: Postmortem examination and biospecimen collection of aquatic wildlife offers a unique opportunity to generate large datasets that can improve diagnostic criteria, predict future health risk, and advance basic research. Our lab investigates how environmental stressors such as marine toxins, heavy metals, and plastics alter the normal function of the central nervous system. These exposures are widespread and relevant to both marine and terrestrial species. By combining toxicological findings with global effects on gene expression, protein function, and neural cell morphology in the brain, we can create a spatial map for global representations of brain that can be use for indepth investigations. We have recently applied this strategy to archived brain biospecimens collected from stranded dolphins. We created a large transcriptomic database for 20 dolphins to evaluate the effects of cyanobacterial toxin exposure and bloom season on the brain. Using this dataset, we were able to generate novel hypotheses about toxin exposure and brain health. Here we will review a potential application of ultramodern spatial transcriptomic techniques to necropsy brain biospecimens samples with a focus on dolphins, sawfish, and sharks. We will discuss selection criteria, tissue recovery, sample preparation, biospecimen storage, assay development, selection of controls and data collection, AI analysis, and dissemination of data. Connor Davison
800: During winter 2023 – spring 2024, the Florida Keys experienced a widespread phenomenon of neurologically inappropriate spinning behavior across varied teleost and elasmobranch taxa. This coincided with beaching and mortality of the endangered smalltooth sawfish. A multidisciplinary collaborative effort began for response and research including the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). Multiple objectives were identified in this response initiative which included evaluation of changes associated with blood profiles. The Fish and Wildlife Health subsection collected blood from affected fish during spring 2024, with a focus on mullet (Mugil sp, n=15). For comparison, we collected from normal mullet in early winter 2024 and spring 2025 from the same region (n=9), and from a control region (Tampa Bay, n=18). We performed blood smears and collected plasma banking the latter at -80C. We sent samples to the University of Miami Comparative Pathology Laboratory for blood chemistry profiles, plasma protein electrophoresis, and white blood cell (WBC) differentials. We performed preliminary analysis via PERMANOVAs to evaluate changes associated with the above three blood parameter groups for clinically spinning animals. We found significant effects of blood chemistries and WBCs driven by increased BUN and Uric Acid, decreased potassium, and decreased lymphocytes. Interpretation of these findings will be discussed. Blood collection from mullet will continue on a seasonal basis for normal fish and hopes to capture more abnormal fish. These data help characterize physiological parameters associated with this syndrome with the goal to identify an etiology and prevent or mitigate effects of this emerging disease. Daniel Haro
801: Starting in fall of 2023 and into the spring of 2024, the Lower Florida Keys experienced a mysterious spinning fish phenomenon that caused multiple fish species to swim in circles, become disoriented, and die. Most notably, the endangered Smalltooth Sawfish (Pristis pectinata) suffered over 50 reported deaths during this event. Many unknowns surrounding this event remain, and a critical question is how Smalltooth Sawfish and related elasmobranch species were physiologically impacted. For this study, we compared the health and physiological responses of symptomatic and non-symptomatic Smalltooth Sawfish recovered during the event, as well as cooccurring shark species including Nurse Sharks (Ginglymostoma cirratum), Lemon Sharks (Negaprion brevirostris), and Blacktip Sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) captured during the same time period. To assess oxidative stress and immune system function, four biomarkers were analyzed: reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS), glutathione peroxidase (GPX), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and glutathione S-transferase (GST). These biomarkers were selected because they reflect the body's antioxidant defense response and can indicate the degree of cellular damage occurring during physiological stress. Findings from these markers help shed light on the physiological burden experienced by these animals and advance our understanding of sublethal and lethal impacts on imperiled elasmobranch species exposed to conditions that caused this event. Sarah Mangia
802: The Charlotte Harbor estuarine system, in southwest Florida, is one of two federally designated critical habitat areas for juvenile smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata. Within the estuary, there are discreet high-use areas which have historically served as nursery grounds. Glover Bight, a small embayment at the mouth of the Caloosahatchee River, is one such area. The study area is composed of Glover Bight creek and Glover Bight proper, separated by a shallow sandbar. In 2023, following Hurricane Ian, a dredging project temporarily breached the sandbar to remove a derelict yacht, potentially altering nursery function. To evaluate potential impacts, a Vemco positioning system array was installed to analyze fine-scale movement and space use. Utilization distributions were estimated using a Bayesian state-space model with continuous-time correlated random walk. Preliminary results show age-0 individuals primarily using the creek. After age-1, they gradually shift to using Glover Bight proper. With continued growth, the frequency of returns to the high-use area decreases, and space use is restricted to the mouth of Glover Bight. Additionally, Glover Bight serves as a thermal refuge. During extreme cold snaps in 2010 and 2026, dozens of juveniles were observed in the study area. Of four tagged during the 2026 event, three stayed in Glover Bight for 2 to 22 days, while the smallest (120 cm) stayed longer than a month. While the dredging may have had initial impacts, these results show that Glover Bight continues to function as a critical nursery area and thermal refuge for juvenile smalltooth sawfish. Carmen Montana
803: The Florida Keys abnormal “fish spinning event” reportedly affected at least 70 fish species, 59 teleosts and 11 elasmobranchs, with peak impacts between November 2024 and June 2025. Prominent among affected species was the endangered smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata), which exhibited erratic swimming patterns, spinning at the surface, lethargy, and high mortality rates compared to other affected species. Of the over 60 reported sawfish mortalities, 43 specimens were necropsied, and tissues for histopathology were collected from 32 affected individuals. Central nervous system (brain, spinal cord) samples were taken from 17 animals: 14 at single brain locations (telencephalon (n=4), cerebellar corpus/pons (n=9), and medulla (n=1), one at multiple sites, and the entire brain was collected from 2 individuals. Histopathology using hematoxylin and eosin, luxol fast, and cresyl violet stains identified suspected myelin damage (n=12) characterized by white matter vacuolation, axonal swelling, myelin sheath rarefaction and splitting, and myelomacrophage foci. Suspected neuronal degeneration was identified in the cerebellum in five samples, specifically within the lateral folia of the corpus. While immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for myelin basic protein (MBP) was unsuccessful, likely due to a lack of antibody cross reactivity, glial fibrillary acid protein (GFAP) staining in two cases suggested reactive astrocytosis. Investigations into links between these lesions, microalgal toxins, and other undetermined etiologic factors are active. Ongoing serial evaluation through two whole brains from affected sawfish aims to fully characterize lesions across all brain regions and compare these changes with non-event sawfish. Lilly Nguyen
804: There is considerable inter- and intraspecific variation in brain size and organization (e.g., the relative size of major brain regions) across both teleost and cartilaginous fishes. These patterns are often linked to ecological and life history parameters, suggesting behavioral and sensory capacity varies between species and may shift across ontogeny. However, less is known about neuroanatomy in endangered species, due to their rarity, leaving gaps in our understanding of brain evolution. The endangered smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata, has experienced significant declines throughout its Atlantic range, with the U.S. population primarily restricted to southwest Florida, prompting research to better understand its biology and ecology. During 2024 and 2025, over 60 sawfish mortalities were observed in the Florida Keys, coupled with hundreds of accounts of a “fish spinning disease,” suggesting neural impairment, but lacking a causal explanation. Advanced bioimaging techniques, including magnetic resonance (MR) imaging, provide opportunities to advance our understanding of neuroanatomy nondestructively. This study acquired T1-weighted, contrast-enhanced brain MR images of opportunistically collected P. pectinata across its size range in healthy and “spinning” specimens. We demonstrate that the brain grows throughout ontogeny, with variation in size and regional complexity, which may inform behavioral and sensory specializations. These baseline data will be used to make qualitative and quantitative comparisons with brains from neurocompromised individuals in order to identify regional degeneration that informs functional deficiencies and better understand this unique spinning phenomenon. Rachel N Pikstein
805: The Florida Keys host a diverse ecosystem vital for subsistence, recreational, and commercial fisheries, contributing significantly to the local economy. However, climate-driven and human-induced disturbances have impacted these resources in the last few decades. Adding to these impacts, in Fall 2023, a myriad of behavioral abnormalities were documented in close to 80 fish species crossing many trophic and migratory guilds, initiating a response effort to determine the cause. During these events, significant mortalities of the critically endangered elasmobranch, Pristis pectinata, were observed, raising concerns about the long-term impacts of this species. Subsequent environmental sampling revealed elevated levels of Gambierdiscus and a complex suite of marine neurotoxins in the water. Fish necropsy results showed no consistent macroscopic effects in fish, however, subsequent toxin testing by in vitro neurotoxicity assay, targeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), gas-chromatorgaphy-mass spectrometry, inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry, and untargeted high resolution mass spectrometry revealed the bioactivity and presence of benthic algal toxins and other contaminants in a variety of environmental samples and in tissues of symptomatic sawfish. Subsequent chemical partitioning, assay-guided fractionation, and LC-HRMS analyses aided in toxin profiling in sawfish tissues, with differences observed between blood, gill, liver, brain, and muscle, highlighting a complex combined waterborne toxin exposure. Archived tissues and blood from sawfish recovered from prior years in the absence of behavioral abnormalities have served as important field controls, while algae and sediments collected from sawfish foraging habitat have further aided in uncovering data on the possible causes to this unprecedented event. Robert Robins
807: Blood is an accessible and dynamic sample matrix that is widely used to monitor health across taxa. As part of the coordinated response to “spinning” Smalltooth Sawfish (Pristis pectinata) in the Florida Keys in 2024, blood samples were collected from 11 affected fish to help determine the cause of the aberrant behavior and understand what physiology might be impacted. Because reference intervals from healthy sawfish were not available for comparison, a separate and ongoing effort to collect samples from apparently healthy fish began in parallel (n=67). Heparinized whole blood was collected from Smalltooth Sawfish and analyzed for toxic elements and hematology (whole blood) and for routine chemistry, protein electrophoresis, and trace minerals (plasma). Blood cell morphologic features were described using modified Wright-Giemsa stained blood films, cytochemical stains, and transmission electron microscopy. Lymphocytes were the predominant white cell type, followed by similar proportions of heterophils and eosinophils, few monocytes, and rare basophils. Reference intervals will be an important resource for current and future health monitoring of this recovering population. Jennifer Wyffels
808: The endangered smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) historically occupied much of Florida’s coastal waters, including the Indian River Lagoon in east-central Florida. However, the population and range severely declined throughout the 20th century mainly due to bycatch mortality. By the 1970s, the species was extirpated from the Indian River Lagoon estuarine system. After decades with few sightings of juveniles anywhere along Florida’s east coast, public encounter reports to the U.S. Sawfish Recovery Hotline began increasing in 2015 and peaked between 2020 and 2023. The St. Lucie River, which is a major tributary in the southern portion of the estuarine system, had a disproportionate number of reports, which prompted research to assess habitat use there. Ultimately, seven small juveniles were acoustically tagged between 2020 and 2023 and monitored within the St. Lucie River through 2024. The south fork of the St. Lucie River was identified as a perennial high-use area (87% of detection days were there), evidence that the southern Indian River Lagoon is functioning as a nursery again. Identifying highuse areas within the broader estuary, such as the upper St. Lucie River, is an important step toward safeguarding key habitats, and such habitat protection is essential for promoting reestablishment of this species into historical parts of its range. Atsuko Yamaguchi
809: The Mississippi barrier islands (BI) help support infaunal assemblages used by several species of fishes as their forage base, including cownose rays and Gulf Sturgeon (GS; Acipenser desotoi). Two morphologically conserved cownose ray species inhabit the Gulf of Mexico (GoM), the American Cownose Ray (Rhinoptera bonasus) and Brazilian Cownose Ray (R. brasiliensis). Both species are considered Vulnerable by the IUCN due to slow life history traits and declining populations, with R. brasiliensis further listed as a state species of concern due to data deficiency. Gulf Sturgeon, once prolific along the Gulf Coast, are now federally listed as “Threatened” due to overfishing and habitat alteration. Generally, it is believed that the seasonal use of BI habitats by GS is in response to a combination of environmental parameters and potential competition with other species during warmer months. Little data on the seasonal use of Mississippi BI habitat by cownose rays exists, so determining competition between these taxa with similar feeding habits is difficult to determine. Therefore, this study aims to explore the space overlap of taxa with similar diet breadth in relation to infaunal metrics. Cownose rays exhibited elevated use of the waters around Ship Island during late spring and summer, unlike GS. However, both taxa showed increased and overlapping use of the area during fall and early winter. Overall, these data can help determine locations important to both cownose rays and GS, addressing conservation data gaps for both taxa.
810: While shark populations are undergoing dramatic global declines, populations in French Polynesia, the world’s largest shark sanctuary, remain relatively robust and free from human pressures. There, island geomorphology has been shown as a highly influential driver of relative abundance of sharks, with atolls supporting average abundances ~3x greater than high islands. This disparity highlights the importance of atolls for conservation, but mangment efforts based on this finding will be limited by our poor understanding of the reasons for this pattern. One possible explanation is that since lagoons serve as nursery areas for several shark species, the large dynamic lagoons of atolls may boost shark populations in surrounding waters, however no study to date has explored this idea. Using the protected lagoon of Tetiaroa, French Polynesia, as a natural laboratory, we collected 5+ years of passive acoustic telemetry data (n > 1,170,000 detections) to examine habitat use across life stages of two sympatric reef shark species that are threatened with extinction: blacktip reef (Carcharhinus melanopterus) (n= 136) and sicklefin lemon (Negaprion acutidens) (n= 53). Our results show increasing spatial separation of species and sexes through ontogeny- with smaller sharks overlapping more in what are likely refugia areas- as well as differing yearly patterns of residency and habitat use by males and females, centered around a probable pulse in pupping. This emerging picture suggests that the dynamics of atoll lagoon shark nurseries are shaped by pressures from competition, reproduction, and predation risk that are molded by the lagoon landscape. Liz Farley
811: Understanding the demographic structure of predator-prey interactions—including size and life-stage relationships between predators and their prey—is important for interpreting the ecological dynamics of predation. The Sarasota Dolphin Research program has tracked shark-dolphin interactions and taken morphological measurements on resident bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) for several decades. 35.5% of Sarasota Bay dolphins exhibit shark bite scars, and while bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) are the most likely predators of the dolphin community, we still do not fully understand the size demographic of sharks biting the dolphins. To address this, we measured the interdental distance and bite circumference of fresh shark bites using photos of free-swimming dolphins and carcasses to estimate size and species of the shark responsible for the wound. Measurements of 27 bites were made using ImageJ and analyzed. Because a ruler for scale could not be placed in photos of free-swimming dolphins, each dolphin’s dorsal fin height was used as a scale, as previous work suggests this measurement is relatively stable over time; a ruler was used as a scale for necropsy photos. Estimated total length of bull sharks ranged from 1.26 m to 2.80 m, and tiger shark size ranged from 0.91 m to 3.45 m. This study provides an example of how such methodology could be used elsewhere to identify the species and sizes of sharks responsible for shark bite marks on cetaceans. Mateus Haas
812: The decline of wild sawfish populations occurred before much of the basic life-history of sawfish was known. Our understanding of life history diversity, population-scale movement patterns, and regionally unique ecology has been hampered by this lack of information and the paucity of extant fish. Our research shows that the teeth from the rostrum of critically endangered Largetooth Sawfish (Pristis pristis), frequently preserved in museum collections or seized from the illegal wildlife trade, store detailed movement records and potentially age and growth information in their chemistry and structure. Using laser-ablation ICPMS we analyzed the full isotopic and trace element records retained in 103 preserved Largetooth Sawfish rostral teeth to examine the movement and location of sawfish from the Brazilian Amazon coast. This population is thought to be the last stronghold of Pristis pristis in the Americas, yet very little is known about the population, its structure and distribution, or individual migratory lifehistory. Using a time-series approach our results reconstruct a detailed, temporally explicit record of movement both across salinity and within fresh water. These movements show significant individual life-history diversity as well as location and habitat specific chemical signatures including strong trace-element signatures previously associated with mangroves and other areas of high organic matter decay in the substrate. Jens Hegg Jens Hegg; Linh Truong; Brad Vega; Tommaso Giarrizzo; Patricia Charvet
813: In the eastern Pacific, Pacific Angel Sharks (Squatina californica) were overexploited in the 19701990s before California’s inshore gillnet ban was implemented in 1994. Currently listed as vulnerable in the IUCN, Pacific Angel Sharks are still landed in the commercial gillnet fishery and incidentally caught in California, yet no specific management strategy exists, and regional patterns of movement and habitat use remain poorly understood. This study sought to characterize movements and habitat use of Pacific Angel Sharks to identify key habitats for recovery and evaluate their use of southern California using fisheries-dependent (commercial landings) and independent (acoustic and satellite tracking, trawl surveys) data. Twelve Angel Sharks (TL: 93.4 ± 21.9 cm) were internally tagged with an acoustic transmitter (V13, Innovasea) and five sharks were double-tagged with a micro pop-up satellite archival transmitting tag (Wildlife Computers Inc.). Acoustic coastal detections were limited due to presumed limited time spent nearshore. Distances traveled over a 24 h period were similar among sex and maturity groups (~ 20 km). Satellite tags reported for three of the five sharks, although deployments were short (6.8 ± 3.8 d). Sharks made vertical movements at night and few vertical movements (i.e. < 1m) in the day, consistent with their benthic ambush strategy. The data presented here highlight the need for long-term monitoring and fill a critical knowledge gap in understanding the habitat use and seasonal movements of Pacific Angel Sharks. Daniela Pareja Mejia
814: The soupfin shark (Galeorhinus galeus) is a medium, critically endangered shark species that occurs seasonally in the nearshore and offshore waters off Oregon and Washington State (USA). To date, research on the migratory behavior of the soupfin shark in the Northeast Pacific has focused on females, which primarily inhabit the southern latitudes of their range (Baja to Central California), only sporadically venturing north to Oregon and Washington. The triennial migratory pattern observed in these females is likely sex-specific, correlating with their reproductive cycles and the gestational benefits of occupying warmer waters. Conversely, the migration patterns and habitat utilization of males, which occur with abundance in the Northern Latitudes of the Northeast Pacific, are likely mediated by different drivers that have yet to be explored. As a highly mobile species of greatest conservation need, identifying the timing, scale, and patterns of migratory behavior, site fidelity, and habitat utilization of the soupfin shark is crucial for the effective conservation and management of this species. Here, we present our findings on the migration timing, inshore site fidelity, and offshore habitat utilization of adult male soupfin sharks tagged with internal transmitting acoustic tags and external pop-off satellite tags in the Northeast Pacific. Kenna Peters
815: Atlantic guitarfish (Pseudobatos lentiginosus) are a vulnerable batoid species found in the Western Atlantic, with populations declining due to bycatch in commercial fisheries and habitat loss. Despite their Vulnerable status, limited information exists on their biology and ecology. This study evaluated the effectiveness of using individual spot patterns for individual photo-identification of wild Atlantic guitarfish to support minimallyinvasive monitoring of their movements and habitat use. Photographs of the rostrum were taken during field surveys in Palm Beach County, Florida, and processed using I³S Spot software to generate a database of unique individuals (n=200). The software demonstrated high accuracy, with a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve showing an area under the curve (AUC) value of 0.93, indicating strong sensitivity and specificity. This method provides a costeffective and minimally invasive alternative to traditional tagging techniques for studying guitarfish movement patterns. Initial resighting data revealed evidence of site fidelity and local movements, with several individuals documented at multiple study site locations. The successful implementation of photo-identification could enhance long-term monitoring efforts, inform management, and allow the incorporation of citizen science into the study of Atlantic guitarfish John Powers John Powers; Micheal Dreslik; Benjamin Jellen; Ethan Kessler; Andrew Kuhns; Christopher Phillips; Donald
816: Shark attacks are statistically rare but traumatic events that can undermine public support for shark conservation policies, particularly for species that represent a potential threat to public safety, such as the white shark (Carcharodon carcharias). In the aftermath of white shark attacks on humans, it has been suggested that smaller individuals are likely responsible because they are less skilled predators and are still learning how to successfully feed on pinniped prey. However, little empirical evidence exists to support this; interactions between individual white sharks and seals are difficult to directly observe repeatedly, and therefore the extent to which individual sharks hone their predatory abilities and any associated timeline remain unclear. The relatively recent emergence of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, as a seasonal aggregation site for the species in response to the local population recovery of grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) provides a unique opportunity to explore changes in individual shark’s predatory ability over time. The primary goal of this project is to mine an extensive photographic identification database of over 750 individuals to quantify the occurrence and extent of seal-inflicted injuries on white sharks encountered off Cape Cod from 2014 - 2024. These data will be used to identify individual- and sizespecific patterns of injuries resulting from prey handling, which we consider indirect but measurable proxies for predatory skill. The results will be used to determine whether there is evidence that white sharks’ predatory efficiency improves with experience and how that may translate to variable risk to recreational water users. Matt Wojtowicz
817: Texas horned lizards are listed as a species of greatest conservation need in the state of Oklahoma. This species once was very common throughout the state but over the past few decades, the population has seen significant decline and local extirpations due to habitat loss, invasive fire ants, pesticide use and changes in land management. Since 2008, the Oklahoma City Zoo (OKC Zoo) has been committed to supporting the conservation of this species through partnerships with the University of Oklahoma and Tinker Air Force Base (TAFB). The OKC Zoo has participated in a long-term mark and recapture study on TAFB and began a headstart program in 2019 for release back onto TAFB. This partnership has also provided several research projects for graduate students at the study site and at the OKC Zoo. The OKC Zoo is now transitioning to a breeding program that will raise hatchlings for release. Christopher K. Beachy
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 2
818: Extreme weather events associated with climate change are increasingly shaping the conservation trajectories of amphibian and reptile populations worldwide. While catastrophic events such as wildfires, cyclones, and prolonged droughts often precipitate rapid conservation action, many species experience extended periods of decline before such thresholds are reached. This presentation synthesizes case studies from multiple taxa, including Fiji iguanas, Arroyo toads, Houston toads, Texas watersnakes, and Texas horned lizards, to examine how zoo-based conservation programs respond across a continuum of acute and chronic climate-mediated threats. These case studies highlight contrasting conservation pathways, ranging from emergency interventions following sudden habitat loss to prolonged stakeholder deliberations and early-stage planning prior to population collapse. Comparative examples illustrate how differences in response timing influence available conservation pathways, from rapid postdisturbance intervention to prolonged periods of uncertainty and early-stage planning prior to population collapse. Some taxa exemplify long-term, cryptic declines without a singular triggering event, while others highlight systems where climate-driven changes in hydrology and habitat conditions are prompting proactive discussions of conservation escalation before irreversible declines occur. Collectively, these examples underscore the challenges of initiating conservation action under uncertainty and the risks of relying on catastrophic thresholds to justify intervention. Zoo-based contributions extend beyond captive assurance programs to include surrogate taxa research, natural history studies, field-based support, and adaptive decision frameworks. We argue that conservation planning must move beyond reactive models and incorporate early warning indicators, climate resilience strategies, and crossinstitutional collaboration to inform intervention before crisis thresholds are reached. Eva Greco
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 2
819: Glyptemys insculpta (wood turtles) in Massachusetts exhibit higher mortality rates than other aquatic turtle species due to increased predation rates. Wood turtles are considered endangered by the IUCN, a Species of Special Concern under the Massachusetts Endangered Species Act, and under evaluation for listing under the federal Endangered Species Act. Zoo New England has been monitoring and supplementing local wood turtle populations through headstarting efforts for several years. One goal of headstarting is to produce ‘predator-proof’ juvenile turtles which can be safely released into the wild. However, increased mortalities have disproportionately affected headstarted wood turtles in some of our field sites. To gain a better understanding of predation pressures affecting wood turtles and how to mitigate them, we investigated predator occurrence and behavior with motion-triggered wildlife cameras placed in wood turtle habitat. We recorded ten second videoclips with 36 cameras between May and November 2024 and 2025 in three different field sites. Each camera was paired with one of four treatments consisting of a visual and/or olfactory cue: 1) a realistic wood turtle model, 2) a scent tube infused with wood turtle scent, 3) a turtle model with a scent tube, 4) control treatment (no visual or olfactory cue). Video processing is still underway using volunteer and machine learning efforts. A subset of manually quantified video clips revealed 11 species of potential mammalian predators in wood turtle habitat, including several canids and mustelids. Raccoons were noticeably the most abundant predator species recorded and showed the most interactions with treatments. Desi Joseph
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 2
820: Emerging infectious diseases pose a major threat to amphibian conservation. While research has largely focused on chytrid fungi and ranaviruses, the protist Amphibian Perkinsea (Pr) remains understudied despite its significant impact on larval amphibian populations, particularly in the Southeast United States. The critically endangered dusky gopher frog Lithobates sevosus has experienced repeated mass mortality events (“MMEs”) linked to Pr. Here, we investigated the disease ecology of Pr across ponds critical to L. sevosus conservation, while concurrently monitoring breeding ponds for Pr-associated MMEs. We monitored 18 L. sevosus breeding ponds from January–August 2025, conducting 274 visits, sampling 1,450 tadpoles across seven species, and screening 680 individuals with a Pr-specific qPCR assay. Overall Pr prevalence was 17.5%, varying significantly by location, metapopulation, and month. Infection intensity varied by location and among species, with L. sevosus showing significantly higher pathogen loads than two co-occurring host species. Two MMEs were detected, including one resulting in near-complete loss of a L. sevosus cohort. Although MMEs were rare (~0.85% of visits), their demographic consequences were severe and were likely under detected. These results indicate that Pr is widespread, variable across space and time, and poses a significant, unpredictable threat to amphibians. For L. sevosus, Prassociated MMEs may substantially hinder recovery by causing severe cohort losses. Conservation strategies that incorporate disease surveillance, habitat restoration, and careful timing of translocations may help mitigate impacts. More broadly, these findings highlight the importance of understudied pathogens in global amphibian declines Chun Kamei
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 2
821: Zoo New England (ZNE) studies small, isolated populations of eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) near the northern edge of their range. We captive-rear (“headstart”) hatchlings for ~18 months before releasing them back to their natal populations, aiming to increase the probability of juvenile recruitment. The hatchlings are raised to a target weight of ≥160 g, outfitted with radiotransmitters, and tracked post-release. ZNE has tracked more than 20 headstarted box turtles for >100 turtle-years as they mature and explore their changing habitat, including pre- and post-construction of a solar array. We report here on the high survival and apparently successful acclimation of these headstarted turtles into the resident population, assessed through measures of growth, behavior, and stress physiology. We conducted baseline and stress-induced blood draws to test corticosterone response in both the headstarted juvenile box turtles and adult resident turtles, and tested our ability to measure chronic corticosterone from claw tips. We found that paired claw tips from the same individuals were fairly representative in the younger headstarted turtles (<10 years old,) but not as reliable with the resident adult box turtles. Inspired by protocols developed by the St. Louis Zoo, we conducted boldness tests on the individual box turtles (both headstarted and resident adults), measuring their latency to movement, which we compared to corticosterone measurements. The headstarted turtles are maturing into reproductive, apparently healthy adults, demonstrating long-term success of the intervention. Emily McFarland
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 2
822: San Antonio Zoo’s Center for Conservation & Research (CCR) has several labs designed to provide appropriate and specialized care to subterranean wildlife. Some of the species of focus include the Georgia Blind Salamander (Eurycea wallacei) and the Dougherty Plain Cave Crayfish (Cambarus cryptodytes). The CCR team works with wildlife departments in both Georgia and Florida to establish small populations of these species in the lab. Close collaborators on this project also include team members of the Niemiller Lab (University of Alabama in Huntsville) and several other subterranean salamander specialists from around the country. Project goals include the development of husbandry and breeding protocols before these species become critically threatened and/or federally listed. A written protocol for husbandry and breeding would serve as a conservation tool should the populations of either species continue to decline. Further goals include the documentation of reproductive behavior. Across the past 12 years, the team has improved husbandry practices with these species, bred them both for the first time ever in the lab, and have recorded remarkable reproductive behavior in the process. We report here on the experience of working with the Georgia Blind Salamander in the lab and provide some of the data that we have been able to assemble on clutch size, reproductive behavior, and lab-based husbandry practices. Breann Richey
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 2
823: Zoological institutions are designed to provide suitable habitats for collection animals, as well as providing aesthetically pleasing natural features to enhance guest experience. Animal husbandry practices, including feeding and habitat maintenance (e.g., water changes, vegetation landscaping), for collection animals may also provide suitable habitat for non-collection wildlife. We aimed to formally investigate a population of somewhat managed non-collection freshwater turtles that inhabit various exhibits and natural features at the Memphis Zoo, in Memphis, Tennessee, USA. Since 2021, we captured turtles for mark-recapture, recorded morphometrics, and collected blood samples annually? We assessed leukocyte populations and hemoparasite populations from blood smears, and microbial killing ability and endocrine function from blood-derived serum and buffy layer. We also estimated survival and capture probability with and without physiological metrics. We captured 36 individuals across three species, Pseudemys concinna, Trachemys scripta elegans, and Graptemys pseudographica kohnii in six areas of the zoo. Based on observations and keeper accounts, these wild turtles are somewhat managed due to routine husbandry practices for collection animals. We found that these turtles had higher and more consistent survival and capture probability rates than a less managed population in the same region. This study presents a unique opportunity to collect longitudinal data on individuals, assess how management practices influence physiological and population dynamics, and highlight academic and zoological collaborations. Stéphanie Tessier
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 2
824: Genital variation and coevolution directly impact reproduction, yet most studies focus on male genitalia. Here we use 3D geometric morphometrics and copulation recordings to quantify shape variation, genital allometry and copulatory fit in female and male genitalia in red-sided garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis). We examined shape differences in vaginal endocasts of live vs. deceased females and found that the vagina of live females is significantly narrower and thinner than in deceased females, suggesting that active muscular contraction from concentric smooth muscle fibers changes vaginal shape, and likely influences the outcome of copulation. Hemipene shape is no different when comparing specimens of each of two male mating strategies that have been described in this species (female mimics and non-mimics). Further, there was no directional asymmetry in hemipene shape or size, contrary to previous reports. Vaginal pouches are isometric with respect to SVL, while hemipenes are negatively allometric, growing at a slower rate than SVL, and they are significantly larger in volume than vaginas. This pattern of hemipene growth, likely allows even small males to succeed at copulating even with large females. High speed videos of copulations demonstrate that intromission occurs instantaneously, and males thrust their hemipenes into the pouch, while aligning their cloaca parallel and posterior to the female’s, placing their postcloacal region directly on top of the hemiclitoris, suggesting a role for copulatory stimulation, despite well known sexual conflict over copulation duration in this species.La coevolución y variación de los genitales impacta la reproducción directamente, pero la mayoría de estudios se centran en los machos. Aquí describimos la morfología geometrica en 3D y grabacion de copulas para estudiar la morfolgia y coevolución de los genitales de las hembras y machos de Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis. Examinamos las diferencias en la forma de modelos del lumen de las vaginas de hembras vivas vs. muertas, y encontramos que en las hembras vivas las vaginas son más estrechas y delgadas sugiriendo que la contracción de los músculos circunferenciales de la vagina afectan las interacciones copulatorias. En los machos no vimos diferencias en la forma de los hemipenes en las dos estrategias de apareamiento que han sido descritas en la especie (female mimics y non- mimics). Tampoco encontramos diferencias de la forma o el tamaño entre el hemipene derecho e izquierdo, contrario a lo que se ha reportado anteriormente. Las vaginas son isométricas con respecto al SVL mientras que los hemipenes son negativamente alométricos, y tienen en promedio un volumen más grande que las vaginas. Esto quiere decir que aun los hemipenes de machos pequeños pueden funcionar durante la cópula con hembras grandes. Con grabaciones usando una cámara de alta velocidad vimos que la intromisión es instantánea y el macho alinea su cuerpo posterior y paralelo a la cloaca de la hembra, just encima de los hemiclitores, sugiriendo un rol de la estimulación durante la cópula, aunque se conoce que hay conflicto sexual sobre la duración de la cópula. Patience Brennan
825: Rattlesnakes and their prey are understood to be in an ancient coevolutionary interacting pitting venom proteins against molecular resistance mechanisms. Rattlesnakes venoms are complex mixtures of proteins from 18 separate gene families, and include many paralogous gene duplications leading to additional functional novelty. Though we have a comprehensive understanding of rattlesnake venom composition, we know comparatively little about the molecular targets of venom proteins, and the molecular basis of venom resistance in prey. Is a complex venom resisted through complex molecular mechanisms or through generalist inhibitors? To address this question, we applied an unbiased, high throughput approach to identifying the targets of snake venom proteases: terminal amine isotopic labelling of substrates (TAILS). The TAILS approach identified a large suite of targets, several of which have not been previously reported to interact with snake venom proteases. Moreover, the specific cut sites within each prey protein are identified by the method, yielding information about substrate specificity and generating testable hypotheses concering where prey my evolve resistance through amino acid substitutions. Finally, we incoporate population genetic data to test the hypothesis that mammalian proteins that are targets of snake venom will be subject to diversifiying selection among populations. Overall, this work reveals that the venom/prey molecular "interactome" is highly complex, underscoring the power of snake/prey systems in the study of how coevolution generates life's complexity and diversity. Charlie Holguin
826: Diet is a fundamental component of animal ecology, but its representation is inherently difficult, requiring decisions about what to measure, how to measure, and at what scale food resources should be examined. As a trait, diet is inherently multidimensional and hierarchically structured. Thus, individual food items can be categorized under a variety of taxonomic, ecological, and functional criteria, each encompassing different axes of a trophic niche. These complexities are widely acknowledged yet difficult to implement in evolutionary studies, which typically employ coarse and univariate categories to represent diet. Here, we use a high-resolution trophic dataset of elapid snakes (Elapidae) to investigate whether downstream comparative analyses are affected by dietary categorization methods. We found significant differences in the number of trophic niche modalities across all major elapid groups. Some of these differences were consistent across categories, but most were impacted by categorization, leading to divergent and unpredictable inferences of diet breadth, niche states, and tip rates. Our results emphasize that single, univariate categories that lack hierarchical or relational context may paint an inadequate picture of a trophic niche. Consequently, we argue that using a combination of approaches for classifying food resources may lead to more biologically robust inferences and insights of dietary evolution. Justin Lee Justin Lee; Platon Yushchenko; Chatmongkon Suwannapoom; Parinya Pawangkhanant; L. Lee Grismer; Tan Nguyen; Veerappan Deepak; Surya Narayanan; Sandeep Das; Thy Neang; Hmar Lalremsanga; Jian-Huan Yang;
827: Adaptive radiation is often initiated by ecological opportunity, which is the availability of ecologically accessible resources that may be evolutionarily exploited. Ecological opportunity can be presented when a lineage colonizes a new area. When a lineage enters a new area, they are often exposed to novel pathogens, potentially creating a barrier to persistence and diversification in the new environment. Ecological opportunity through colonization is not limited to geographic dispersal, as transitions between climate zones, such as along elevational gradients, may similarly present new ecological niches. Therefore, ecological opportunities within a clade may be more numerous than simply looking at geographic dispersal may imply. Using pit vipers (Subfamily: Crotalinae) as a model, we conduct phylogenetic comparative methods to infer transitions between different climate affinities across the phylogeny to identify potential ecological opportunities. Furthermore, we harness pit viper genomes within a comparative framework to examine selection patterns of immune response genes in lineages that exploit these instances of ecological opportunity. Here, we clarify how immunogenomic evolution correlates with climatic transitions in pit vipers and provide a framework for integrating climate, geography, immunology, and genomics to better understand the underlying mechanisms that allow lineages to exploit ecological opportunity and diversify. Brittany Nunn
828: Adaptive radiations offer a powerful framework for understanding how phenotypic diversity evolves quickly in unique environments. Galápagos giant tortoises, with 15 species that diverged approximately 3 million years ago, represent an study system, as each species is characterized by distinct shell morphologies. Galápagos tortoises are generally classified into domed and saddle-backed, which evolved in response to distinct environmental pressures across the archipelago. For instance, domed shells have evolved in humid highland habitats, whereas saddle-backed shells have evolved in xeric lowland environments. While the ecological relevance of these morphotypes is well established, the genetic mechanisms underlying this variation remain largely unexplored. To address this, we used a comparative genomic approach across 13 species to identify genes evolving under positive selection using codon-based models of molecular evolution implemented in codeml (PAML), screening approximately 2,000 single-copy orthologs. These analyses found that around 200 orthogroups showed evidence of positive selection, and most positively selected genes were shared across shell morphotypes, suggesting a common adaptive core potentially related to general tortoise biology or island adaptation. However, a morphotype-specific subset of genes points to potential genomic drivers of specialized adaptation. Gene Ontology (GO) analyses revealed enrichment in broad biological processes, including development, metabolism, and cellular regulation, consistent with a complex, pleiotropic genetic architecture underlying shell evolution. Together, these results demonstrate that adaptive radiation can leave detectable genomic signatures over short evolutionary timescales and suggest that phenotypic diversity may arise through selection acting on broadly conserved developmental and physiological pathways.Las radiaciones adaptativas ofrecen una oportunidad para comprender cómo la diversidad fenotípica evoluciona rápidamente en condiciones únicas. Las tortugas gigantes de Galápagos, con 15 especies que divergieron hace aproximadamente 3 millones de años, representan un sistema de estudio excepcional, ya que cada especie presenta un caparazón distintivo. Históricamente, estas tortugas se han clasificado en dos morfotipos principales: caparazón abovedado y tipo “silla de montar”. Cada uno ha evolucionado en respuesta a distintas presiones ambientales a lo largo del archipiélago. Por ejemplo, los caparazones abovedados se asocian con ambientes húmedos de tierras altas, mientras que los tipo silla de montar predominan en ambientes más áridos. Aunque la importancia ecológica de estos morfotipos está bien establecida, los mecanismos genéticos subyacentes permanecen poco explorados. Para abordar esta pregunta, utilizamos un enfoque de genómica comparativa en 13 especies para identificar genes bajo selección positiva mediante modelos de evolución de codones en codeml (PAML), evaluando aproximadamente 2000 genes ortólogos de copia única. Nuestros resultados indican que cerca de 200 ortogrupos presentan evidencia de selección positiva. La mayoría de estos genes son compartidos entre morfotipos, lo que sugiere un núcleo adaptativo común. Sin embargo, también identificamos subconjuntos específicos por morfotipo, lo que apunta a mecanismos de adaptación especializada. Los análisis ontológicos de genes (GO) revelaron enriquecimiento en procesos de desarrollo, metabolismo y regulación celular. En conjunto, estos resultados sugieren que la radiación adaptativa deja señales genómicas detectables incluso en escalas evolutivas recientes. Lizzy Patton Lizzy Patton; Amanda Picelli; Luis Ceríaco; Maria Pacheco; Edward Netherlands; Matthew Heinicke; Ananias
829: New World elapids, including the brightly banded coral snakes of Micrurus and their sister lineage Micruroides, represent one of the most recognizable groups of highly venomous snakes in the Americas. Despite their extensive diversity, with more than 80 species of Micrurus distributed across the Americas, the group remains poorly understood due to limited taxonomic, phylogenetic, and molecular resources. In particular, the absence of high-quality reference genomes has limited investigations on the genes underlying phenotypic variation within the group, including variation in venom gene architecture and genomic factors driving lineage diversification. To address this gap, we generated the first PacBio long-read reference genome assemblies for New World elapids, with genomes produced for Micruroides euryxanthus, Micrurus fulvius, and Micrurus tener. We then integrated these genomic resources with venom gland transcriptomes to establish an initial comparative framework of the venom genes and their expression. The coral snake genome is ~1.66 Gb. The M. euryxanthus assembly recovered 494 contigs with 97.9% BUSCO genes. Micrurus fulvius and M. tener assemblies were scaffolded using Hi-C, yielding 106 scaffolds and 98% BUSCO for M. fulvius, and 128 scaffolds with 98.1% BUSCO for M. tener. Venom gland transcriptomes were dominated by three-finger toxins and phospholipase A2’s, but comparative analyses revealed lineage-specific differences in venom gene composition and expression. Together, these data establish foundational genomic resources for an understudied group of venomous snakes and provide a baseline for future work on venom evolution and the ecological factors shaping diversification in New World elapids. Fandresena Rakotoarimalala
830: Roadside habitats are exposed to many disturbances, from chemical and noise pollutions to the introduction of invasive species. However, in modified European landscapes such as intensive farmland, they represent rare semi-natural habitats attractive to squamates. Indeed, roadsides can offer a variety of open habitats with diverse vegetation and prey species. Squamates are therefore often observed in road verges, but the quality of these habitats for them is unknown. Do they support populations, only act as corridors, or are ecological traps for these species? To study habitat quality, squamate populations were monitored across transects placed at different distances from highways in three sites in eastern France. At each site, parallel transects were surveyed in farmland, natural open habitats and forests, from the roadside to 250 m away from the road. The species richness of squamates and preys, population dynamics, evidence of breeding, individual movements, body condition and autotomy rate were studied to inform on habitat quality. This monitoring showed that roadside habitats support sedentary, healthy and breeding populations of squamates. In natural open habitats, the species richness was as high in road verges as in distant habitats. In forests, squamates were more present and diverse in roadside habitats, and in farmlands they were only found in these road verges. These findings show that roadsides provide habitats for squamates, acting as refuges in modified landscapes. We hope this will guide road managers towards better consideration of roadsides as species habitats. Jennifer Deitloff
831: Although Florida is known for its Everglades marshes and coral reefs, most of its endemic species are associated with longleaf pine savannas, so-called uplands, defined by well-draining sandy soils and sparse trees. We questioned whether herpetofaunal species found in uplands are specialized to a particular upland community or if they are generalists. We examined the habitat associations of each species and the differences among assemblages found in each of five upland habitat/ecotone types. We tested which environmental factors were important for determining the occupancy of reptiles and amphibians in south-central Florida. We installed 60 triad drift fence arrays in the protected lands of Avon Park Air Force Range. Amphibians and reptiles were recorded through pitfall traps, funnel traps, array camera traps, and cameras facing gopher tortoise burrows. After 11 months of sampling, we recorded 34 species and 2948 individuals. The highest overall abundance was in the scrub whereas the lowest was in dry prairie. Diversity was similar among habitat types, but community compositions differed. We found large differences in the factors determining occupancy, such as fire history, percentage of sand, distance to roads, and other factors. Most species appear to be habitat generalists, with Scrub Lizards and Eastern Spadefoots as notable exceptions. Because the upland habitats share connectivity and similarity, most species occurred throughout the uplands, though abundances differed among upland habitats. The herpetofauna of the understudied upland habitats of Florida deserve more scientific attention because even the basic ecology of some of the species is still unknown. Kaci Dodd
832: Understanding the distribution and ecology of species with limited surface availability is fraught with difficulty, increasing uncertainty and hampering conservation decisions for rare species. Environmental DNA (eDNA) offers a potential solution because DNA might persist on surfaces after animals have retreated and are no longer available for visual detection. Methods for collection of terrestrial eDNA are still being developed, and few studies have evaluated its utility for detection of cryptic terrestrial species. We developed and tested a terrestrial eDNA protocol for limestone salamanders (Hydromantes brunus), a species with very limited surface availability for visual detection, and compared detection probabilities from eDNA and time-to-detection visual surveys using an integrated multi-scale occupancy model. We found substantial variability among sites in the availability of the salamanders for visual detection on the surface or under surface cover, and mean availability for visual detection was 0.59 (95% equal-tailed interval = 0.22–0.90) at occupied sites in November and March – April. The detection rate of salamanders was 0.03 (0.01 – 0.05), corresponding to 39 (18 – 70) min to detect the first salamander. Detection probabilities using eDNA were 0.56 (0.30 – 0.79) during the day and 0.78 (0.45 – 0.96) at night, corresponding to visual encounter survey durations of 29 and 53 min, respectively. Sampling terrestrial eDNA is a promising technique for detection of cryptic amphibians with limited surface availability. Maddie Hamlin
833: Blue spotted salamanders, Ambystoma laterale, and their associated polyploid unisexual hybrids are common species throughout eastern North America. These animals migrate to ponds in the spring for reproduction. While the forms in the species complex are common, they demonstrate considerable variability across populations in migration timing and demographic responses during migration. Northern populations are early spring migrators that must often deal with harsh weather. Further, many populations are impacted by human influences. At our study site, we have been monitoring movements of salamanders across a road for multiple years using an extensive student survey program. Our data shows a tendency toward early nighttime pulses of migration as well as strong photoperiod control of the migration overall, despite variable weather. Modeling of the abundance of migratory animals suggests strong reliance on wet substrate and localized temperatures, although the moisture may result from rain or snowmelt. Our data suggests significant resiliency to changing climate and environmental perturbation in the species complex. Jill B.K. Leonard
834: Movement influences how organisms interact with their environment shaping resource use, population dynamics, reproduction, and survival. Individual movement patterns are driven by a combination of factors including sex, resource availability, microhabitat conditions, and climate. Most ecological studies analyzing movement focus on large migration events, but even small-scale movements are a valuable, often understudied, component of movement ecology. Passive integrated transponder (PIT) tag telemetry has emerged as a powerful tool for tracking fine-scale movement in small-bodied organisms. The Eastern Red-Backed Salamander (Plethodon cinereus) is a small-bodied, terrestrial salamander that uses subterranean habitats. Having strong site fidelity and high sensitivity to environmental conditions, P. cinereus serves as an excellent model organism to understand finescale movement and space-use patterns. We employed PIT telemetry and high precision Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) location data to quantify individual home-range and assess how sex jointly interacts with season to shape movement metrics. Individuals (n=58; 35 M, 23 F) were monitored using a systematic survey design across three field sites during periods of peak survey activity (fall and spring). Preliminary results provide support for using PIT telemetry to successfully detect salamanders with our initial systematic surveys (n=8) having an average detection probability of 57.5%. Across a six-month sampling period, salamanders with ≥ 10 detections (n=20) had an average minimum convex polygon area of 17.51m2 ± 11.72m2. Results provide novel insight into understanding the fine-scale movement patterns and space use of small-bodied organisms that frequently use subterranean space. Katelyn Sewcharran
835: As climate change intensifies the atmospheric conditions of the planet, it is crucial to understand how populations of herpetofauna will respond to extreme weather events. Hurricane Helene, whose intensity has been attributed to climate change, brought unprecedented rainfall to the Southern Appalachian Mountains. This event likely represents a major biomass altering disturbance to many species, however the extent of its effects on populations are still being resolved. During the summer of 2025, I conducted a study to assess the impact of the extreme rainfall from Hurricane Helene on populations of Pisgah Black-bellied Salamander (Desmognathus mavrokoilius), Northern Shovel-nosed Salamander (Desmognathus marmoratus) and Blue Ridge Two-lined Salamander (Eurycea wilderae) in headwater streams of Western North Carolina and East Tennessee. I hypothesized that many of these salamanders were injured or killed in floodwaters during the hurricane. As adult salamanders may have exited the stream channel during flooding, I hypothesized that larval individuals, who are entirely aquatic, were lost at higher rates during the storm. I repeatedly surveyed 30 streams to model occupancy of larval and postmetamorphic salamanders across a rainfall gradient. Hurricane Helene cumulative rainfall ranged from 7.01 to 23.12 inches among sites. Contrary to my predictions, occupancy models indicate that Hurricane Helene had a certain negative impact only on adult Pisgah Black-bellied Salamander occupancy and not on any other group. This research demonstrates species and life stage dependent impacts from flood disturbance and indicates that climate change related extreme weather events may significantly alter community composition and ecology of riverine ecosystems. John P. Tyminski
836: Climate change imposes different pressures on organisms through both extreme pulse events and longer-term chronic changes. For ectotherms such as turtles and lizards, variation in temperature and water availability can alter development, behaviour, and physiology at key life stages, with effects that can scale up to population consequences. Nesting may be one of the most vulnerable stages in this process because population outcomes depend on multiple interacting aspects of the nesting processes, rather than any single factor. The conditions that permit female activity shape when nesting can occur, nest-site selection determines the thermal and hydric conditions embryos experience, and the conditions offspring emerge into can shape early post-hatch success. We lack a mechanistic framework that links how each of these changes will be impacted under future climate scenarios at a global scale. Here, we develop a biophysical modelling framework for turtles and lizards that integrates maternal activity, nest-site selection (depth, shade, and soil type), embryonic survival (temperature and water), and post-hatch opportunity. By simulating potential activity time and nest conditions across different microhabitats under 20-year climate windows, we identify when and where short-term extremes and longer-term climatic change create the greatest vulnerability under future climates. These data provide a mechanistic framework to test whether realistic variation in nesting ecology can buffer embryos and hatchlings from climate change, and to identify global hotspots of vulnerability. Chase Wild
837: The Leuciscidae is a Palearctic family of cyprinoid fishes with roughly equal number of species in the Old World and the New. Despite a wealth of phylogenetic studies, the movements of the fishes between the continents is still unclear with phylogenomic techniques revealing a monophyletic clade of North American subfamilies (minus Notemigonus) nested within the Eurasian species and Sanger sequence data suggesting a more complex scenario of movements, although relationships were poorly supported. Despite relative morphological similarity, Leuciscidae is the dominant family in terms of numbers of species in most areas in which they occur. In this preliminary study, we will examine the three-dimensional shapes of North American leuciscids using photogrammetry and analyzed using phylogenetic comparative methods. Sarah Arnette
838: Mid-Atlantic states have planned for development of offshore wind farms, expected to become the largest introduction of artificial infrastructure to the marine environment.
