This will likely cause changes in the distribution, connectivity, and behavior of marine fishes, including elasmobranchs. Non-extractive monitoring approaches are needed to document presence and/or abundance of fish before, during and after construction of offshore wind farms, to elucidate changes. Acoustic telemetry and environmental DNA (eDNA) are two nonextractive approaches becoming increasingly important in recent years. Both approaches are employed for biological monitoring independently, often within the same projects, yet each has biases. Studies combining these approaches and comparing the resulting datasets are scarce in the scientific literature. We combined data from concurrent fisheries monitoring efforts at offshore wind development sites employing acoustic telemetry and eDNA to compare patterns of presence and/or abundance in elasmobranch species detected. Elasmobranch species commonly encountered in NY/NJ waters were acoustically tagged and tracked within acoustic receiver arrays from two ongoing projects—Empire Wind and the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection's Research and Monitoring Initiative. Concurrently, surface water samples were taken for eDNA monitoring; the resulting DNA was analyzed and assigned to species level. We then compared acoustic telemetry detections for tagged fish at nearby acoustic receivers 24 hours before and after eDNA sampling with the species detected from eDNA samples. Here, we present and briefly discuss preliminary results of these comparisons and their implications for elasmobranch populations, assuming continued development of offshore wind across the region. Martin Benavides Martin Benavides; Ximena Velez-Zuazo; Bruno Vildoso; Robert Aguilar; Piero Guardales; Elizabeth Silva;
839: The fully aquatic, neotenic Barton Springs salamander (BSS; Eurycea sosorum) and Austin blind salamander (ABS; Eurycea waterlooensis) are found in the groundwater of the Barton Springs segment of the Edwards Aquifer, a karst aquifer in central Texas. While BSS is found at the springs, the species presumably reproduces in the aquifer where it is sympatric with the subterranean ABS. Despite decades of monitoring of the primary springs where BSS and the rare ABS visitor are found, courtship has not been observed in the wild. The City of Austin maintains assurance populations of these species to safeguard against extinction. While courtship and reproduction with viable offspring have been observed in both species in captivity, the spermatophore deposition has not been documented. To gain a better understanding of courtship behavior, we set up trials using 11 BSS and nine ABS male-female pairs and videotaped their behavior over 14-24 hours. Preliminary results are that courtship with spermatophore depositions occurred in four BSS and three ABS trials, with multiple spermatophores deposited in at least two trials of each species. In addition to observations of male behaviors described in the literature, we also observed females engaged in behaviors that indicate female choice may play a role. Our descriptions of courtship in these species will contribute to the broader knowledge of salamander courtship behavior, which is thought to be evolutionarily conserved. In addition, this information will help us better understand the reproduction needs of the species in the wild and in captivity. Chan Kin Onn
840: Amphibians around the world are threatened by the emerging infectious disease chytridiomycosis, caused by the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd). Some species and populations are able to resist Bd infections, while others are extremely susceptible. In order to better understand how amphibian immune systems respond to this pathogen, numerous studies have measured differential gene expression between infected and uninfected individuals. Through the varied expression of immunity-associated genes, these data have highlighted how some species or populations are able to resist Bd infections. While these results have proven to be extremely valuable for the handful of species used in these studies, comparing across studies is difficult and prevents extrapolation to other amphibians threatened by Bd. A single study can reveal hundreds of differentially expressed genes, meaning that often only those with the greatest differential expression are reported. Additionally, depending on the reference used to annotate genes, orthologs of the same gene can be named differently across studies, further complicating comparisons. To determine if the amphibian immune system responds similarly to Bd across species, we re-analyzed publicly available raw sequence data for 14 amphibian species across 11 studies. This analysis ensures comparability across studies and common gene naming schemes. Using this dataset, we will perform a meta-analysis to determine which factors, including species identity, contribute most to host gene expression during a Bd infection. Determining if there is a common host response to Bd, or if response is completely species-specific, will aid in our understanding of how some amphibians resist Bd infection. Daniela García Cobos Daniela Garcia Cobos; Priscila Santos Carvalho; Diego Santana; Dylan DeBaun; Agusto Luzuriaga-Neira; Fernando
841: Sexual dimorphism is well documented in snakes; a prominent example is tail shape and size differences associated with the location of the reproductive organs. Sexual dimorphism may be further influenced by competitive displacement, leading to body size differences between sexes or skull size due to differences in feeding ecology. Sea snakes have a suite of specialized adaptations for marine environments, including those associated with consuming marine prey, which is generally a unique ecological strategy among snakes. Using micro-CT scanning, we compared the skeletal morphology between the sexes across five species of sea snakes to test for sexual differences across a broad set of morphological traits. Based on previous findings, we predicted that Aipysurus laevis and Emydocephalus annulatus will show sexually dimorphic traits, while Hydrophis platurus, H. cyanocinctus, and H. fasciatus will not have sexually dimorphic traits. We found that sexual dimorphism of species within the aipysurine lineage does extend past the external (head) measurements and body size. Hydrophis species have sexual size dimorphism (SSD), but their internal skeletal morphology was not dimorphic when corrected for body size. Because cranial skeletal dimorphism is rare in snakes compared to SSD and tail size dimorphism, sexual dimorphism in sea snake skull morphology may represent an evolutionary innovation with important links to variation in sex-biased ecological pressures. Quang-Hai Francis Dinh
842: Cranial telescoping is a phenomenon in which cranial bones develop an extensive sutural overlap and proximity, especially in bones of the anterior part of the skull. Cranial telescoping has been observed in various squamate groups, such as sphaerodactylid geckos, pygopods, and some anguimorphs, including mosasaurids. However, it is unknown as to how this phenomenon convergently evolved in multiple lineages and the function of it. While cranial telescoping has been observed in these select groups, a concrete categorization of the degrees of telescoping between groups has not yet been developed. Thus, it is important to determine what constitutes cranial telescoping in each group, as well as which species can be classified as having a slight or extensive sutural overlap between certain bony elements. By using computed tomography (CT) scans to segment the skulls of specimens and quantify the extent of overlapping, we expect to be able to classify degrees of telescoping in model species within each group. Maureen A Donnelly
843: Critical thermal limits for Mediterranean geckos are published from west Texas and from multiple sites along the Gulf Coast, but those studies were done decades apart and with different protocols. A group of five teams from four states set out to determine if we would find the same patterns as previous work, or similar limits across sites, if we all used replicate equipment and the same protocols. We are coordinating quarterly sampling sessions and aim to measure 15 adults and 15 subadults per season. We have sites in Mississippi, Alabama, north Texas, and Oklahoma. We have now met multiple times via Zoom and conducted the spring sampling session. While collecting geckos for physiology, we are also collecting gecko tail tips to look at fine-scale population genetic structure using protocols developed over the last ten years in Oklahoma. We are already gaining insights from the collaboration process. Preliminary data from Mississippi found a lower thermal minimum and comparable maximum, although there is not enough data yet to draw conclusions about effects of geography or life stage on gecko thermal limits. Roman Ferraro
844: The coastal waters of North Carolina are among the most biologically and geographically dynamic regions along the U.S. East Coast. Yet despite their ecological richness and role as a migratory corridor for numerous shark species, the state remains a data-deficient region for elasmobranch science. To address this gap, the North Carolina Shark Conservancy (NCSC) was founded in 2025 as a nonprofit organization dedicated to advancing shark research, education, and conservation across the state’s coastal and nearshore ecosystems. The early development of NCSC underscores the importance of community-driven conservation models, particularly in regions where formal shark monitoring frameworks are limited, through the launch of multiple complementary research, monitoring, and outreach initiatives, including North Carolina’s first dedicated Shark Stranding Network. This project was designed to focus on three key initiatives: 1) scientific accessibility, 2) community collaboration, and 3) education and outreach to serve as the foundation for long-term datasets, supporting both conservation assessments and academic research collaborations. We recognize that conservation success depends on both scientific rigor and community engagement; thus, our programs are designed to integrate professional research with citizen participation and public education. The long-term vision for NCSC’s stranding network is to investigate the underlying causes of mortality events, expanding beyond fishing-related trauma, while providing researchers with unique opportunities to collect valuable biological samples. Blake Hossack Blake Hossack; Philip Gould; Kenzi Stemp; Brian Tornabene; Bruce Christman; Niall Clancy; Wendy Estes-Zumpf; Caren Goldberg; Erim Gomez; Brandon Holton; Pieter Johnson; Michael Lucid; Audrey Owens; James Rorabaugh;
845: Reintroductions and other conservation translocations are often challenging, resource intensive and may have limited success rates. However, this conservation technique has helped save many species from extinction, and it is frequently employed when other conservation options are unavailable. Some of the earliest documented endangered species conservation efforts utilized translocations over 100 years ago. For example, the earliest conservation translocations are often cited as being done with birds or mammals, such as the 1907 reintroduction of Bison in Oklahoma, USA. Surprisingly, historical translocations of reptiles and amphibians for conservation purposes also began in the late 19th and early 20th century including multiple conservation translocations of Tuatara (Sphenodon punctatus) in New Zealand. This project aims to provide the first systematic review of early reptile and amphibian conservation translocations that occurred prior to the year 1980. The earliest translocations for each major group of reptile and amphibian will be discussed. Due to the obscurity and often small-scale nature of many early herpetological conservation efforts, a solicitation for additional data on historical translocations will be made. Ethan Livingston
846: Acoustic telemetry data provides essential information on marine species distribution, habitat use, and connectivity, aiding the implementation and assessment of marine zoning. Individual researchers typically deploy and maintain localized receiver arrays that are project-specific, with limited data sharing capabilities. For highly mobile species, the lack of infrastructure to share detections across research programs limits the power of acoustic telemetry methodologies. While acoustic data sharing networks are well established along other US coastlines, the West Coast has lagged behind. The Northeast Pacific Acoustic Telemetry Node (N-PAcT; npact.aoos.org) was established in 2025 and aims to shift perspectives from localized efforts to national and international collaboration to better understand animal movements and support effective management of mobile species. N-PAcT serves as a platform to integrate data from a multitude of researchers across jurisdictions spanning from Alaska, USA, to Baja California, Mexico. N-PAcT is interoperable with the Ocean Tracking Network (OTN), which has well-established infrastructure to enable data sharing across research groups, including detection matching with other nodes and affiliated networks,and rigorous quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) of ingested data. This collective approach will break down geographical and logistical barriers, thereby transforming individual studies into powerful, cohesive projects by providing a clearer, more complete picture of animal movement in the northeastern Pacific Ocean. Participation in N-PAcT can provide numerous benefits to researchers through data sharing across research groups, with utility of the N-PAcT database highlighted through several case studies. Andrew Lyons
847: Small populations are vulnerable to extirpation through factors including environmental stochasticity, reduced genetic variation, and susceptibility to stressors such as disease. Yet small populations can be important to species persistence across a landscape. Small populations may act as stepping-stones providing connectivity among populations in a larger-scale metapopulation, and act as reservoirs maintaining genetic variation. Amphibian decline and the reduction of populations of amphibians across landscapes highlights the importance of small populations. However, precise estimates can be elusive because, by definition, a small population has few individuals and data may be sparse. Nevertheless, insights into population dynamics in these populations can be useful, especially if the small population in question represents a threatened species that managers are particularly concerned about. Management actions may be easier to implement in small populations, but similarly, effects may be more difficult to detect. We provide an example of insights gained by long-term monitoring and the assessment of one management strategy, using two decades of capture-mark-recapture data from a small, but apparently stable, population of boreal toads in Rocky Mountain National Park. The population is persisting, and recruitment is increasing, but survival in recent years is declining. Our data do not reveal an effect of the implemented management action on population estimates. Larger confidence intervals in recent estimates likely reflect reduced monitoring effort. This work illustrates the value of a concerted effort to maintain multi-visit monitoring particularly in small populations where management may be crucial and identifies the need for additional monitoring focused on juvenile lifestages. Caden Myers
848: Many lizards have evolved long or otherwise conspicuous tails that are capable of autotomizing which may serve to redirect attacks away from vital areas. Prior work has investigated the effect of conspicuous tail coloration on predation, but the effects of tail length on predation risk in lizards remains unknown. Here, I will use clay replicas of Aspidoscelis sexlineatus created with variable tail lengths (± 20% typical length) to test the hypothesis that longer tails will result in a relative decrease in attacks by birds on vital areas such as the body and head. Clay replicas will be painted to closely mimic wild A. sexlineatus, using spectral analysis and color matching through visual modeling, to ensure emulation as viable prey to UV-sensitive predators. Replicas along with generic clay balls that serve as controls will be deployed in both longleaf pine stands and conservation-managed stands for the Florida Scrub Jay within Ocala National Forest, Florida, USA. After 72 hours of deployment, replicas and controls will be retrieved and examined for bird attacks and recorded for each body section. I expect overall predation rates to stay consistent with historical reports in the Ocala National Forest, yet hope to see a bias skewed toward tail regions of longer-tailed replicas. In this study, I aim to explore the evolutionary and behavioral drivers of lizard tail length with an emphasis on predator avoidance. Lily Orton Lily Orton; Keith Keel; Kim Titterington; David Steen; Kuttichantran Subramaniam; Laura Adamovicz; Matthew
849: Maine Big Night: Amphibian Migration Monitoring Project (MBN) is the only state-wide community-based conservation initiative designed to document and protect migratory amphibian populations during their annual spring breeding movements. This citizen science driven non-profit organization organizes volunteers to adopt sites and assist animals across the road while gathering valuable data helpful in informing conservation efforts. MBN has grown exponentially in its first eight years, with 17,570 amphibians recorded across 335 sites in 2025, and 51,738 amphibians documented overall. This project integrates citizen science with ecological monitoring to collect data on amphibian abundance, species distribution, and road mortality hotspots across the state. Volunteers are trained to identify species, safely assist amphibians across roadways, and use a phone app to record standardized observations, including weather conditions, timing, and traffic levels. Data collected contributes to a growing database used to assess population trends and inform mitigation strategies. Preliminary findings indicate that traffic volume is a major predictor of amphibian mortality (24.6% mortality overall in 2025), with certain crossing sites experiencing disproportionately high losses. These are priority conservation areas, leading to ongoing targeted interventions such as public awareness campaigns and a current study on retrofitting culverts for amphibians. By combining grassroots participation with scientific rigor, MBN enhances our ecological understanding of Maine’s amphibians, fosters environmental stewardship, and demonstrates the effectiveness of citizen science in addressing conservation challenges for species vulnerable to habitat fragmentation and climate variability. Vane Parra
850: Hammerhead sharks (family Sphyrnidae) are widely recognized for their dramatic head shape, also known as the cephalofoil. Dispersed across the cephalofoil are specialized sensory organs called ampullae of Lorenzini that aid in navigation, pursuit of prey, and detection of conspecifics. The bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo)—a smaller member of the hammerhead family—is distinguished by its round, scoop-like head shape, unlike the exaggerated laterally-extended cephalofoil seen in other hammerhead species. Bonnethead sharks exhibit sexual dimorphism in head shape, where males present a more distinct rostral point in comparison to females, who exhibit a more rounded rostrum. Prior research has identified porefield patterns in various elasmobranchs that differ across species but few studies separate patterns by sex. This research aims to assess differences in porefields between male and female bonnethead sharks as well as explore locality-related morphological patterns. Location-based differences will be investigated for bonnethead sharks obtained across Florida, USA (Tampa Bay, Biscayne Bay, and Long Key Bight). Body measurements were acquired and a standardized grid board was used to collect ventral and dorsal photo data. ImageJ was used to quantify head morphology measurements, pore counts, and porefield morphometrics. We aim to assess differences in porefield distribution between male and female bonnethead sharks from three locations across Central and South Florida. In our next steps, we aim to explore porefield morphometrics between sexes of other elasmobranchs. Sienna Solis-Stokes
851: This project examines the incorporation of invasive zebra mussels (Dreissena polymorpha) into the dietary habits of the Texas Map Turtle (Graptemys versa) population in Lake Nasworthy, San Angelo, Texas. Because female map turtles are typically specialists in mollusks and there are limited native mollusks in this area, this newly introduced zebra mussel may represent a new potential food source. To assess this possibility, we will collect fecal samples from wild-captured turtles, and we will utilize quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis to document and quantify the presence of zebra mussel DNA. This project adds to our knowledge of the potential effects of an invasive species on these turtles and may provide evidence of some ecological benefit of the invasion in a setting where it is not normally considered. Sydney Stanley
852: The Malagasy spider tortoise (Pyxis arachnoides) is a critically endangered tortoise species native to southern coastal Madagascar that is subject to intense pressures from habitat destruction as well as poaching for the international pet trade. Three subspecies are currently recognized (P. a. arachnoides, P. a. oblonga, P. a. brygooi). It is one of several surviving members of a broader western Indian Ocean tortoise assemblage which included island radiations in Madagascar, the Mascarene Islands, and the Seychelles. We sampled 134 wild spider tortoises across their geographic range in southern Madagascar and generated RAD-seq data for 120 individuals and whole-genome short-read data for an additional 14. Our genomic analyses indicate that P. a. brygooi represents a deeply divergent lineage that is consistent with species-level differentiation. These results have direct implications for conservation management and are informative for studying the evolutionary history of Malagasy tortoises, Pyxis and Astrochelys, and their relationships with the other surviving and extinct west Indian Ocean tortoises, Aldabrachelys and Cylindraspis. Michelle E. Thompson
853: In the city of San Diego, 81% of residents live within a 10-minute walk of greenspace. One of the factors contributing to San Diego’s high walkability to greenspaces is its unique topography of steep canyons and flat mesas, where flat mesas are developed, leaving a patchwork of fragmented canyon natural areas. These canyonto-coast landscapes are critical for climate resilience and providing wildlife habitat and community access to nature. Despite their being a common feature in the landscape and proximity to residents, there is a lack of information about these fragments, including how they contribute to conserving wildlife, the extent of ecological services they provide to residents, and how to better manage them to maximize benefits for nature and people. The objective of the Healthy Canyons Initiative is to conduct a multidisciplinary biological inventory of urban canyons in San Diego to assess the current state of these ecosystems. The initiative is grounded in three core pillars: generating actionable biodiversity data to inform conservation and management, building local capacity through training of students and community scientists, and cultivating meaningful connections between communities and urban ecosystems to support long-term environmental stewardship. To date, the initiative has generated tens of thousands of biodiversity records, has had active participation from over 230 community scientists, has supported 11 student researchers, and engaged over 95,000 community members through outreach. Here we present preliminary results from amphibian and reptile surveys highlighting patterns of diversity and distribution across canyon fragments, providing critical insights for urban conservation planning and management. Abigail Thomsen
854: Adaptation to low-light environments has evolved frequently across diverse clades of marine and freshwater fishes, making traits associated with these habitats particularly useful for studying diversification and convergent evolution across clades. In this study, we examine positive selection in the RH1 gene in rockfishes (genus Sebastes), a diverse clade of marine fishes in which closely related species occupy various depths and light environments. We compare signatures of positive selection in this candidate gene across representatives of 33 species, spanning the clade. Although RH1 is highly conserved, we found that deep-water species show significantly stronger signals of positive selection than shallow-water species, and cluster together at a gene-tree level despite large evolutionary distances. In addition, while RH1 haplotypes from deep-dwelling species are more consistently species-specific, shallow-water alleles are frequently shared among multiple, often distantly-related species, suggesting incomplete lineage sorting. Patterns at the gene and gene-tree level provide compelling evidence for the prevalence of convergent evolution toward low-light environments across independent clades. Benjamin Torres
855: The dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) is a large, widely distributed, coastal and offshore species found throughout the Western North Atlantic (WNA) Ocean. Characterized by relatively low reproductive output, the dusky is particularly vulnerable to overfishing. As a result, the WNA population has experienced significant declines and is currently subject to strict management measures, with ongoing research focused on understanding its movement patterns, habitat use, and recovery potential. In May 2025, OCEARCH researchers successfully sampled and tagged a 294 cm TL adult female specimen, nicknamed Mira. This shark was fitted with a fin-mounted SPOT258 tag but because dusky sharks are considered less surface-oriented than many other large shark species, the utility of this tag type was uncertain. Following her release, Mira’s SPOT locations indicated a pattern of coastal and shelf-associated habitat use, with periodic excursions into offshore waters ranging from Georges Bank to the Gulf of Mexico. However, there were large temporal gaps between locations received by the Argos satellite system (max. 103 days). Although nearly 8 times as many locations were received by the new CLS Argos-Kinéis system with its enhanced satellite coverage, gaps between locations were still relatively large (max. 24 days) indicating limited near-surface swimming. These preliminary results suggest that PSATs and/or a combination of PSAT and SPOT tags may be more suitable for this understudied species. By improving our understanding of dusky shark behavior and habitat use, more effective management strategies can be implemented as the population recovers from significant historical declines. V Tyson
856: Climate change, habitat loss, and fragmentation are forcing wildlife populations out of once suitable landscapes, causing local declines and extirpation events across taxa. The Mojave Desert Tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) is threatened by encroaching urban development and climate change throughout its range. Past efforts to predict the connectivity and viability of this species have failed to account for the impacts of a changing climate, the continued loss of developable lands, and the permeability of anthropogenic barriers. Our work uses agent-based modeling to forecast G. agassizii populations through 2100, incorporating the most current research to accurately parameterize the lives and mortality risks of desert tortoises. We simulate populations in Clark County, NV under four Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) and their associated Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) with varying barrier permeability. We evaluated metrics of viability including adult population size, mortality, and birth rate and found large population declines in high emissions scenarios, which were further exacerbated by impermeable barriers. Our results indicate that even moderate increases in emissions can increase birth rate variability and drive episodic declines. The movement of individuals in our model was heavily impacted by the prescribed barrier scenario. Climate change stressed the importance of key corridor locations, but connectivity was largely maintained except under the most extreme barrier scenarios. These results demonstrate the importance of reducing emissions for the continued survival of G. agassizii populations and highlight the need for climateinformed corridor designs that will preserve connectivity as habitat loss accelerates. Michael Yuan
857: Taxonomic nomenclature in ichthyology is continuously revised as new phylogenetic evidence accumulates, creating a persistent gap between current taxonomy and the names used in the literature. The eighth edition of Common and Scientific Names of Fishes from the United States, Canada, and Mexico introduced 850 name changes, but no existing tool validates fish names in unstructured manuscript text against this authority. I developed 'Fishfinder', a free, easy-to-use browser-based web application that classifies scientific and common fish names by comparing them against the 5,086 species in the eighth edition and 8,740 synonyms compiled from Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes. An analysis of synonym data revealed that species accumulate a mean of 1.72 synonyms (median 1.0, max 38), with 60.8% of species having at least one historical synonym that could appear in the literature. To quantify the prevalence of naming errors in recent literature, I applied the 'Fishfinder' classification engine to 95 papers on North American fish communities. Of these, 40.0% contained at least one outdated synonym or misspelled species name: 30.5% used outdated synonyms, and 23.2% contained misspellings. An additional 50.5% of papers referenced species whose names changed between the seventh and eighth editions. These findings demonstrate that nomenclatural errors are common and that automated validation tools can help authors, reviewers, and editors ensure taxonomic accuracy before publication. Evgenia (Jane) Zheltov
858: Anolis lizards have long served as a model taxon for studying evolutionary adaptation in response to natural disturbances and habitat alteration, and more recently for investigating the impacts of urbanization on morphology, physiology, and reproduction. The widespread establishment of A. sagrei as invasive populations across the United States and beyond has further positioned them as a valuable system for biological invasion research. Here, we present evidence of morphological change and behavioral plasticity drawn from a series of metaanalytical reviews and a pilot field study conducted across the heterogeneous urban landscape mosaic of New Orleans, Louisiana. Analysis of evolutionary morphological data spanning five decades reveals that both native (A. carolinensis) and invasive (A. sagrei) anoles are under selection for larger body size in urban environments; however, native individuals show a reduction in body size in areas of sympatry with the invasive species, with urban male A. carolinensis shrinking by approximately 10 mm per decade. Plasticity in energetic allocation appears to confer a competitive advantage to the invasive species, while reduced risk-taking behavior and decreased aggression enable its persistence in more environmentally stressful sections of the urban mosaic. Together, these findings highlight the utility of urban landscapes as natural experimental systems for disentangling the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of biological invasions. Taya de Blonk Taya de Blonk; Ricardo Betancur-R; Dahiana Arcila; Will White; John Pogonoski; Mark Westneat; Carole Baldwin;
859: Nest site selection critically influences offspring survival, particularly in species that rely on specific microhabitats for successful reproduction. When competition results in males monopolizing critical resources for reproduction, offspring survival depend on both the female's assessment of the resources at those sites and the traits of the defending male. Eastern Hellbender salamanders (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis alleganiensis) are experiencing a range-wide decline in recruitment, yet the conditions that lead to defending males receiving eggs remains largely unknown. The objective of our study was to identify the resources female Hellbenders prioritize during nest establishment. We analyzed attributes of 52 defending males, defended rocks and cavities, and the local mesohabitat in western North Carolina. Our AIC analysis strongly supported a multi-cue integration hypothesis, revealing that nest establishment is primarily driven by the proportion of benthic sand substrate inside the defended cavity, but female choice was also influenced by the amount of cobble substrate and water velocity in the local mesohabitat surrounding the defended rock as well as the size of the defending male. High amounts of cavity sand substrate may serve as a proxy for the unobstructed space necessary for parental care behaviors like tail-fanning, while vulnerable larvae may benefit from a high amount of cobble substrate and low water velocity immediately outside the nest rock. By balancing multiple decisions, it seems that female Hellbenders establish nests that prioritize the development and survival of their eggs and larvae. Identifying these fine-scale resources associated with successful reproduction expands our framework for future Hellbender conservation.
860: The rattlesnake rattle is a complex aposematic structure found in Sistrurus and Crotalus, enabling the production of an iconic buzzing sound that may have contributed to the diversification of more than 50 rattlesnake species. Despite its prominence, the deterrent effectiveness of rattling, compared with hissing from other snakes, and the selective pressures acting on early proto-rattles, remains poorly understood. Although rattling has long been hypothesized to deter predators or prevent trampling by large herbivores, empirical evidence is limited, and the effectiveness of small- versus large-rattle proxy sounds has never been tested. To evaluate these hypotheses, we conducted field experiments using automated behavioral response systems (ABRs) to assess how wild vertebrates respond to rattling, hissing, human, and bird sounds. We also tested whether deterrent effectiveness scales with rattle size, providing insight into whether small proto-rattles could have functioned during the incipient stages of this complex trait. Behavioral responses were quantified using a standardized ethogram across diverse taxa in South Carolina and West Texas, including ungulates, mesocarnivores, and birds. Preliminary analyses indicate that rattling and hissing elicit similar fear responses and are nearly as effective as human sounds at inducing avoidance behaviors across a wide range of species. These results challenge long-held assumptions about the unique deterrent function of the rattle and offer new insight into the early evolutionary pressures shaping this iconic trait. Ben Frable
861: Noise pollution transforms natural soundscapes and can disrupt auditory communication, which is crucial for mate selection. Túngara frogs (Engystomops pustulosus) rely heavily on acoustic signaling, and their inner ear organs are tuned to distinct call components. While noise is known to often mask signals, no studies have explicitly integrated an animal’s sensory biology to investigate how noise affects mate selection. Here, we explore how noise influences female choice and male calling behavior through controlled experiments targeting peak auditory sensitivities. An understanding of how targeted noise influences signal masking will inform more effective mitigation practices. Francesco Janzen
862: Urbanization introduces linear anthropogenic features effectively creating and isolating pockets of habitat within human altered landscapes. These features may function as barriers, corridors, and/or habitat, potentially in unexpected ways. Persistence of urban and suburban animal populations depends on their ability to navigate such fragmented landscapes. From 2018-2023, we used radio telemetry to document the movement and spatial ecology of eastern copperheads (Agkistrodon contortrix) in a suburban nature park near St. Louis, Missouri, USA to determine the extent that roads, paved foot trails, and powerline clear cuts influence movement and habitat selection. We tracked the movements of 14 adult snakes amassing 1,950 radiolocations and used random paths analysis, step selection functions, and context-dependent movement models to evaluate their avoidance of, or attraction to, anthropogenic linear features. Both sexes avoided crossing roads at all spatial scales, yet preferred roadside habitat. Both sexes also selected for foot trail crossings and occupancy of powerline clear cuts, potentially utilizing these features for improved foraging habitat, thermoregulatory opportunities, and refugia. Snakes were less likely to move when occupying roadside habitat and more likely to move when occupying powerline clear cuts, suggesting differing behavioral states within, and functions of, these habitats. Our findings show that linear anthropogenic features can simultaneously act as barriers, movement corridors, and preferred habitat, underscoring the need to determine whether such features provide genuine benefits or function as ecological traps for wildlife occupying urban landscapes. Tereza Jezkova
863: Eastern hellbenders (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis) are large, predatory salamanders that facultatively specialize in crayfish prey. As crayfish are considered ecosystem engineers and keystone species, the effects of a top predator on crayfish populations could have major implications to ecosystem functions such as primary production. However, very little is known about whether or how hellbenders are capable of influencing crayfish populations. In this study, we tracked crayfish and hellbenders using passive integrated transponder (PIT) telemetry to investigate whether crayfish alter their space use (i.e., location and home range size) in the presence of hellbenders. With the tracked locations, we used 3-D kernel density estimation to build utilization distributions for each crayfish and hellbender. We used linear regression in an information theoretics framework to determine whether our measured predictors (e.g., proximity to hellbenders, crayfish size, crayfish personality, etc.) affect crayfish home range size and the amount crayfish are willing to overlap with hellbenders. Our results suggest that crayfish home range size is reduced by the number of hellbenders locally present. Additionally, our results suggest that crayfish home ranges overlap considerably with hellbender home ranges, but overlap is reduced in regions with high hellbender activity. Overall, our study provides evidence that hellbenders exert top-down control over their crayfish prey. The identification of this predator-prey relationship is particularly important as hellbenders are facing widespread declines throughout their range. As such, hellbender population losses may release top-down control over crayfish, and potentially trigger cascading ecosystem effects. Ryan Knotek
864: The durability and affordability of plastics have resulted in a proliferation of uses and products since the 1950s. This has increased the welfare of many people on Earth. However, one of the downsides is that their durability results in the plastics breaking down into microplastics, which contaminate virtually every ecosystem on Earth. Even though microplastics are wide-spread, we still are lacking data on the effects of long-term exposure to ecologically relevant concentrations, especially in amphibians (an especially imperiled class of animals). This presentation compares results of multiple studies in Northern Leopard Frog tadpoles (Lithobates [Rana] pipiens) and African Clawed Frog tadpoles (Xenopus laevis) to determine if the effects of long-term, chronic exposure to low levels of microplastics during development have similar effects in different species of anurans. Interestingly, we found similar behavioral and anatomical changes caused by microplastics in these two very different species. This study provides insights into the potential ecological consequences of microplastics and provides a warning that their use may be having real consequences on wildlife. Heather McClendon
865: Environmentally induced stressors include threats from predators and competitors. In territorial species, individuals face ongoing competitive threats, and loss of contests might be more consequential to territory owners (losing a territory) than to intruders (continuing to be transient). When the threat of increased predation risk is added, residents might respond differently than intruders. We tested the impact of simulated predator attack, residency status, and sex on the territorial behavior of Southern Red-backed Salamanders, Plethodon serratus. Territorial behavior was assessed through staged contests with same-sized and same-sexed individuals, with either territory owners (residents) or intruders experiencing the simulated predator attack. The amount of time salamanders displayed an aggressive posture was affected by interactions among risk level, residency status, and sex. Overall, salamanders in the high-risk treatment (with simulated attack) showed fewer aggressive displays than salamanders in low-risk treatment (without simulated attack), but this difference was stronger for intruders, and particularly female intruders, than for residents. Marking behaviors (e.g., chin taps) were generally more common for salamanders in the low-risk treatment, with the most frequent expression by female intruders. The stronger response to predation risk by intruders compared to residents and the particularly strong effects among female intruders likely reflect a difference in the costs and benefits of territory ownership. For residents, the benefit of maintaining ownership of a territory might outweigh the cost of increased predation risk. We discuss our findings in the context of territoriality and trade-offs related to competitive contests. Renato Nali
866: A form of deceptive signaling, aggressive mimicry is when a predator sends a signal which indirectly manipulates subsequent behavior of their prey, with prey behavior ultimately benefiting the predator. In snakes, aggressive mimicry is most often expressed as caudal luring; individuals use vermiform (worm-like) tail movements to mimic invertebrates and attract lizards and frogs, which are predators of the “invertebrates”, but prey of the snakes. Despite caudal luring being a relatively common foraging tactic, particularly in viperids, previous studies have predominantly investigated this behavior in artificial laboratory settings. Here, we used field videography to study the foraging ecology of a robust central Florida population of Pygmy Rattlesnakes (Sistrurus miliarius), a small pitviper that caudal lures. From our captured video of over 700 snakes, we documented nearly 100 unique caudal luring events, representing the largest caudal luring dataset for any free-ranging viper. Caudal luring observations can be categorized into three distinct types: 1) prey-elicited luring, 2) spontaneous luring, and 3) luring-and-leaving. Across all observations, we found that both snake age and time of day had a significant impact on caudal luring occurrence in Pygmy Rattlesnakes. Our results better our understanding of the influence of stimuli and ontogeny on caudal luring in Pygmy Rattlesnakes, and importantly, provide insight into the factors that favor deceptive signaling tactics. Taegan JM Perez
867: Aerial respiration and the evolution of air-breathing organs are critical for fishes that frequently inhabit hypoxic environments. One such group is Anabantaria, which includes famous air-breathing fishes like bettas, gouramis, and snakeheads, as well as non-air breathing mud perches and spiny eels. Aerial respiration (and, ostensibly, air-breathing organs) is hypothesized to have evolved several times in this clade; however, the terminology applied to the air-breathing structures found across anabantarians has been inconsistent and leads to questions about the putative origin of aerial respiration and its associated structures. The air breathing organ (ABO) of bettas and gouramis is called the labyrinth organ, a novel extension of the first epibranchial consisting of a vascularized, highly folded, thin bone. The ABO of snakeheads is only sometimes referred to as a labyrinth organ, with conflicting reports as to the structure and developmental origin of the organ. Some swamp eels (e.g., Monopterus) are reported to have ABOs that are distinct from both labyrinth organs and channid ABOs. Here, we combine contrast-enhanced computed tomography (diceCT), nanoCT, and traditional histological methods to describe the micro and mesostructural anatomy of the ABOs found in various anabantarians and assess the similarity of these structures. We define the phenotype of ABOs using characters including ABO size, placement, and tissue composition. We couple these characters with a recent comprehensive molecular phylogeny and ancestral state estimation to reconstruct the history of ABOs across Anabantaria and determine which lineages’ ABOs are homologous, if any. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation awards DEB-2333683 and DEB2333684. Rose A. Arnold
868: Since at least 2022, the Japanese sardine, Sardinops melanosticta, has been present in the California Current ecosystem where it now coexists with its sister species, the Pacific sardine, Sardinops sagax. Revealed through the integration of ‘omics with ongoing biomass surveys, the co-occurrence of these two morphologically indistinguishable species was nearly overlooked. It is hypothesized that Japanese sardine took advantage of habitat corridors that were opened during periods of anomalously warm water in the north Pacific Ocean. Since the initial pulse of immigration to the northeastern Pacific, Japanese sardine have succeeded in cohabitating with Pacific sardine to such an extent that they occur in mixed schools, are capable of reproducing, and have a geographic footprint that extends from at least Washington state to the U.S./Mexico border. In addition to yielding an opportunity to study the dynamics of an immigrant species in a new area, the detection of this phenomenon highlights the importance of routine surveys with integrated sampling methodologies. This presentation will provide a review of ongoing work on the Japanese sardine in the northeastern Pacific Ocean. William G.R. Crampton
869: Holosteans (bowfin and gar) have a one-to-one correspondence of vertebral centra, epaxial, and hypaxial elements in the trunk and caudal regions. Teleost fishes lost the one-to-one correspondence of vertebral elements, so that the segmentation pattern in the caudal region is different than the trunk region. As a result, teleosts have one or two vertebrae in the caudal region and ancestral bony fishes have many. This change in segmentation makes comparison of vertebrae among fish groups problematic because phylogenetic analysis depends on an accurate homology assessment. Additionally, vertebral centra develop differently in early bony fishes and teleosts. Vertebrae may develop from a chordacentrum within the notochord sheath, or as a bony ring around the notochord called an autocentrum. The distribution of these characters among the bony fish phylogeny is interesting from an evolutionary perspective. In elopomorphs, basal teleosts, salmoniforms and stomiids centra form initially from chordacentra. With few exceptions, ctenosquamates studied lack chordacentra, and vertebrae formation is entirely from autocentra. One or two of these autocentra develop in the caudal region, but these do not seem to correspond to the segmentation pattern in more basal groups. Because of this apparent loss of segmentation, these caudal autocentra are not serially homologous with the caudal centra of more basal teleosts that are composed initially of chordacentra. A survey of the developmental anatomy of euteleosts and problems in homology assessment of caudal centra of bony fishes is discussed. Ziva Dowd
870: The lateral line is a mechanosensory system found in all fishes and many amphibians. It detects hydrodynamic stimuli via neuromast organs embedded superficially and within fluid-filled canals across the head and trunk. Because the lateral line informs key behaviors such as prey detection, predator avoidance, and schooling, its morphology may be coupled with feeding ecology and associated cranial anatomy. In this study, we test predictions of competing hypotheses on the relative influence of ecology and phylogeny on lateral line morphology. We examine whether cephalic lateral line canal morphology predicts feeding ecology across an ecologically diverse sample of sciaenid fishes. We quantified canal neuromasts within the mandibular, preopercular, infraorbital, and frontal canals to assess whether neuromast number is conserved within specific canal regions. Neuromast distributions were visualized using the vital stain DASPEI, and cleared-and-stained preparations were used to characterize gross cranial morphology across species. Landmark-based geometric morphometrics was applied to the lateral view of the preopercle and dentary + anguloarticular, as well as the ventral view of the mandibular canalbearing bones, to quantify shape variation in canal-bearing cranial elements. Together, these analyses evaluate the relationship between sensory and skeletal morphology and provide insight into the functional and evolutionary significance of mechanosensation in sciaenid fishes. Julian Gallego
871: The hyobranchium is an intermediary between the head and torso in tetrapods, playing a key role in a variety of behaviors including respiration, feeding, and vocalization. In some lizards, the hyobranchium has been coopted for another function: support of protrusible gular structures for visual display. One such display structure is the dewlap, which is present in groups such as anoles, fan throated lizards, and flying lizards. Although extensible dewlaps exist only in a single squamate clade, Iguania, they appear multiple times across the clade through repeated evolution. Therefore, iguanians with dewlaps may be taking advantage of shared ancestral modifications in the evolution of these structures. This study leverages broader hyobranchium diversity in squamates to determine if the modifications to this structure observed in the repeated evolution of dewlaps in iguanians suggest convergence or parallelism. The morphology of the hyobranchium was characterized from 3D models based on diffusible iodine- based contrast-enhanced computed tomography (diceCT). Hyobranchial morphology, specifically, lengths, shapes, and ratios of individual skeletal elements, was compared among three groups: squamates with dewlaps, iguanian squamates without dewlaps, and non-iguanian lepidosaurs. Results indicate that iguanian squamates have relatively elongate second ceratobranchials and narrowed hyobranchial bodies compared to non-iguanian lepidosaurs. These characteristics that have been previously implicated as important to dewlap function. Therefore, shared ancestry and deep parallelism, as opposed to simply convergence, may have played a strong role in the evolution of extensible dewlaps in iguanian squamates. Hope George
872: Genital spines are present in many groups of animals, including insects, squamates, fish and mammals, and their diverse functions have been established in some species. However, we have yet to characterize the morphology of genital spines in depth. Genital spines are known to influence mating success through several natural and sexual selection mechanisms and examining their morphology may help us to understand their function. Snakes have extraordinary genital spine diversity that has been used in taxonomy for decades. In this study, we characterize the morphological attributes of hemipenial spines in 14 snake species, based on μCT scan segmentations of 39 hemipenes with over 10,000 spines and describe continuous variation in spine morphology, including number, volume, sphericity (shape), and distribution that does not serve to categorize spines into types as has been done in some taxonomic studies, with the exception of the basal hook. We identify areas of the volume/sphericity morphospace that may impose a constraint in spine functional morphology, and find significant variation in ontogenetic changes of the spines that include spine size and number, mineralization rate during ontogeny, and relationship with hemipenis shape development. Our work is clearly only the first step to understanding the complex spine morphology in this group, and further work must consider puncture interactions with vaginal tissue as well as hemipenis eversion mechanics. This exploratory work gives us a baseline with which to compare the morphology of genital spines in other groups of animals and make better inferences about copulatory function. Keith Keel
873: Ray-finned fishes have skin that is covered in mineralized, overlapping plates known as scales. Scale diversity has been studied for hundreds of years and we generally know that species can have distinct scale morphology, and that differences among species largely reflect evolutionary relationships. The primary way of describing scales is by using categories that divide scales into spiny-edged and smooth-edged varieties, and these categories have created a useful language for morphological descriptions since before Darwin. However, to explore beyond these classic categories we have been using topographic imaging methods to quantify the morphology of embedded fish scales. In this study, we measured surface topography, as well as scale size, shape, and spiny-ness, from nearly 400 reef fishes to examine two questions: 1) what are the major morphological axes of scale diversity, and 2) how important are spiny-edged and smooth-edged categories for describing scale diversity. Our focus on reef fishes allowed us to examine these questions using a wide range of phylogenetic, ecological, and functional diversity, and we found that spiny vs smooth-edged scale categories represent just a small portion of overall scale diversity, indicating that scale forms extend well beyond these classic types. Our work highlights that new discoveries await in scale diversity and a broad comparative approach will help us understand the diversity of these structures. Brian Waldron Brian Waldron; Maggie Hantak; Emily Watts; Josef Uyeda; Alan Lemmon; Emily Lemmon; Robert Guralnick;
874: The neuromasts of the mechanosensory lateral line (LL) system of fishes detect unidirectional and oscillatory water flows and pressure fields and mediate critical behaviors such as prey detection, predator avoidance, navigation around obstacles, and communication. Functional correlates of certain aspects of variation in LL system morphology (e.g., canal vs. superficial neuromasts; narrow vs. widened canal morphology) have been examined in a small number of species. Scanning electron microscopy has revealed that neuromasts vary dramatically with respect to shape and size among species, but the functional consequences of thisimpressive feature of morphological variation have not been explored. A new fluid–structure interaction (FSI) model used variation in the shape and size of the base of the cupula (the gelatinous cap covering the entire apical surface of each neuromast) as a proxy for neuromast shape and size. Simulations showed that sensitivity of the cupula to unidirectional flows (displacement of cupula tip) varies with cupula shape (round, oval [robust, elongated], diamond [equilateral, robust, elongated], cross, bar; all documented among fishes), size (25-100 µm), flow velocity (1-11 mm/sec), and direction of water flow relative to the major axis (0-360o) of the neuromast. In addition, responses varied with height (= cupula “length” in the fish literature; 250-600 µm) and material properties (elastic modulus; 25-500 kPa) of the cupula. This new computational model has shed light on the adaptive significance of known variation in neuromast morphology found among fishes living in different hydrodynamic regimes and employing different locomotory strategies. Jacqueline Webb
875: Large adaptive radiations underpin our understanding of how species evolve and their interactions with the environment allowing for diversification. Loricariid catfishes represent one of the largest families of fishes while exclusive to Central and South American freshwaters they display a wide range of morphological disparity. This family of armored catfishes contrasts from other large adaptive radiations of fishes due to being largely riverine opposed to lentic. Previous research largely focused on the taxonomy and phylogenetics of this clade regardless of a diversity of ecological niches exploited particularly at the lower trophic levels. Understanding Loricariid ecomorphology can aid in understanding niche partitioning and diversification of herbivory in freshwaters. Loricariidae like many fishes contain two pairs of jaws, oral jaws for food capture and pharyngeal jaws for food processing. Unlike many other fishes Loricariids feed in a rasping motion, avoiding gape limitations but also pre-pharyngeal food processing. We were able to identify a range of morphological disparity in both pairs of jaws including new morphologies using Computerised Tomography (CT) scanning technology from over 65 species, representing the largest analysis of trophic morphology within Loricariidae. Jaw diversity was mapped across the clade to identify how jaw shape has diversified. We were able to link morphological traits associated with niche partitioning within broader ecological groupings and specialization such as into durophagy. Additionally, diet was shown to be more closely linked to jaw shape then to head shape.
876: One of the important tenets of evolutionary theory is that genic variation within populations arises through immigration. Variation that arises from in situ evolution is either swamped out through immigration or the number of individuals within populations is low enough that novel mutations will be lost through extinction. That is, metapopulation dynamics will eliminate novelties that arise within small demes. Riverscapes are a perfect ecosystem within which to test these ideas. While streams and rivers often appear homogeneous from a terrestrial perspective, there are a variety of habitats within which fishes partition their distributions, such as riffles, pools, channels, etc. Riverscapes also include physical barriers to gene flow among populations such as waterfalls and drainage divides. Thus, the flowing freshwater ecosystems present habitat heterogeneity within sections that lack physical barriers to gene flow as well as within sections that are separated by physical barriers. Expectation, therefore, is that habitats not separated by physical barriers should be inhabited by demes that are less genically variable than those separated by physical barriers. We will use genetic and genomic data principally from Eastern Blacknose Dace, Rhinichthys atratulus, to test these ideas. R. atratulus, is a common inhabitant of small to medium streams that prefer riffle habitats. Our selection of populations from previously glaciated areas have gone through genetic bottlenecks during recolonization, thus, reducing the genetic variation of the colonists. Geological dates for retreat of glaciers and exposure of lotic habitats allow us to calculate rates of evolution. Jackie Childers
877: Adaptive radiations can generate extraordinary morphological diversity, yet diversification rarely proceeds uniformly across traits, producing mosaic patterns of evolution where traits differ in their relative tempo and mode of evolution. Modularity (the semi-autonomous organization of traits) is thought to structure how selection and constraint interact with traits during these episodes, but its macroevolutionary consequences remain poorly understood. Here we examine the role of skull shape modularity during the post-Cretaceous adaptive radiation of carangarian fishes (ca. 1,100 species), a major marine clade that includes flatfishes and other seemingly disparate taxa such as marlins and archerfishes that diversified rapidly along the benthic-pelagic axis following the end-Cretaceous mass extinction. Using high-resolution three-dimensional morphometric data from 188 species, integrated with phylogenetic comparative analyses, we show that the carangarian skull is highly modular and exhibits pronounced mosaic evolution across anatomical systems with striking contrasts in evolutionary rate and disparity among modules. Oral jaw and “uro-cranium” modules show rapid evolutionary rates and elevated morphological disparity in benthic and pelagic lineages respectively, whereas hyoid arch–derived modules evolve more slowly and remain comparatively constrained. By linking ecological opportunity, developmental architecture, and trait integration, this study reveals how mosaic evolution emerges during a dynamic vertebrate radiation. Taylor Evans
878: Percopsiformes is a small, entirely North American order of fishes that spans an unusual ecological range, from cool northern lakes and rivers to lowland swamps and subterranean karst systems. This diversity makes the group a compelling model for testing whether mitochondrial genome evolution is associated with habitat linked metabolic adaptation. We assembled and compared complete mitogenomes across percopsiform lineages, focusing on genome structure, gene tree patterns, and variation in non-coding regions. Preliminary analyses revealed discordance in ND3 relative to other mitochondrial loci, suggesting region specific evolutionary histories within the mitogenome. We also detected significant differences in total mitogenome length and D-loop length, with cave associated amblyopsids showing especially pronounced control region variation. Because the D-loop contains key elements involved in mitochondrial replication and transcription, this pattern may reflect altered promoter architecture, replication motifs, or repeat instability associated with subterranean life. More broadly, these findings are consistent with the idea that cave environments, which impose distinctive energetic and physiological constraints, may shape the evolution of non-coding mitochondrial regions. Ongoing analyses will test for additional habitat associated patterns in nucleotide composition, start codon usage, synonymous and nonsynonymous substitution rates, and selective pressure across protein coding genes. Together, our results identify Percopsiformes as a promising system for investigating how mitogenome evolution relates to habitat specialization and metabolic divergence in fishes. Anna Faust
879: Vertebral morphology plays a key role in undulatory swimming in fishes, functioning in force transmission and flexibility during locomotion. However, the morphometrics and biomechanics of caudal vertebrae and the neural and hemal spines remain to be explored in most fishes. Sand diving, a burrowing behavior in which individuals burrow into the substrate, is exhibited by some wrasses (family Labridae) and has been associated with distinct morphological traits, including body shape and depth, head shape, vertebral prezygapophyses, and neural spine overlap. Here, we use geometric morphometrics to quantify variation in neural and hemal spine shape, including angle, length, and overlap, across 110 wrasse species to evaluate how spine morphology is structured by phylogeny and locomotor behavior. We introduce VertMorph, a Xcode-based 3D biomechanical modeling platform designed for the visualization, modification, and measurement of vertebral landmark data. Using multivariate approaches, we identify major axes of variation in caudal vertebral spine shape and evaluate whether these axes reflect functional trade-offs between stiffness and flexibility. We assess the extent to which phylogenetic relationships and locomotor behaviors structure vertebral morphospace, with a focus on sand diving taxa, which are found to be constrained to a restricted region due to the mechanical demands of burrowing. Finally, we test for evidence of morphological convergence in caudal vertebral traits among sand-diving wrasses. Morphometrics and biomechanical modeling provide new insight into back bone function in fishes and how functional demands shape vertebral morphology in the wrasses. Brithany Melissa Luna Guizar
880: The freshwater ichthyofauna of Sahul (Australia and New Guinea) is unique because the majority of its actinopterygian representatives are thought to be derived from marine ancestors. Similar to island radiations of terrestrial fauna, the repeated colonization of freshwater habitats in Sahul may have offered ecological opportunity for adaptive radiation. As a continent, Sahul is far older and geographically complex than traditionally studied systems of adaptive radiations, such islands and glacial lakes. Moreover the mixture of marine-derived fish lineages that vary in species richness and clade age creates a vastly different context for diversification than island-like scenarios. In this study we explore diversification patterns for signatures of adaptive radiation stemming from invasions of the continental freshwater ecosystems of Australia and New Guinea. We test the hypothesis that early arriving lineages experienced reduced competition and greater ecological opportunity for diversification. We assembled a morphometric dataset of linear traits associated with movement and feeding for over 1000 species of bony fishes from both marine and freshwaters of Sahul. The disparity in diversification rates and patterns in these co-existing marine-derived freshwater lineages suggests a mosaic of evolutionary trajectories due to changing ecological opportunity and competition. Our results suggest that diversification proceeds in both predictable and contingent modes based on arrival timing, and that freshwater invasions can accelerate rates of phenotypic evolution within marine-derived freshwater lineages. Claire Kim Claire Kim; Sierra Smith; Siddharth Gopalan; Samuel Kerwin; Kaas Ballard; Blair Perry; Cara Smith; Anthony
881: Air-breathing in fishes, and the evolution of organs facilitating air-breathing, have been linked to the pioneering ability of lineages to occupy new habitats across both deep- and shallow-time scales. One such example is the labyrinth fishes and their allies (Anabantaria), which include familiar species like bettas, gouramis, and snakeheads with relatives like leaf fishes, spiny and swamp eels. Air-breathing is thought to have evolved several times independently in this clade, making them an ideal model for exploring whether air-breathing organs and the ecological flexibility they confer impact patterns of phenotypic evolution. We used 2D radiographic images and geometric morphometrics to quantify body shape and tested for differences in morphological disparity and evolutionary rate between air-breathing and non-air-breathing lineages. We also assessed whether air-breathing organs function as key innovations, producing macroevolutionary patterns consistent with adaptive radiation, and whether air-breathing lineages ever revert to non air-breathing states. Specifically, we tested whether morphological disparity through time is greater within clades than between clades among air-breathing lineages, consistent with patterns of resource partitioning among close relatives. We found that air-breathing and non air-breathing lineages occupy partially overlapping but largely distinct regions of morphospace. We also confirm that air-breathing lineages exhibit faster evolutionary rates than non air-breathers. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation awards DEB-2333683 and DEB-2333684. Kathryn Koo Kathryn Koo; Shannon Buttimer; Renato Martins; Matheus Vergne; Rodrigo Valim; Nathan Alves; Ian da Cunha; L.
882: Comparative mitochondrial genomics was used to investigate phylogenetic relationships and diversification patterns among four major Polypterus lineages - the Retropinnis, Bichir, Weeksii, and Senegalus groups. All analyzed mitogenomes were highly conserved in size within 16,557–16,637 bp and structure, comprising 13 protein-coding genes, 22 tRNAs, and 2 rRNAs with no gene rearrangements, indicating genomic stability across lineages. Base composition showed a consistent AT bias (A = 31–32%, T = 27–29%) relative to GC (G = 14–15%, C = 25–27%), with Weeksii and Retropinnis groups exhibiting slightly elevated AT content compared to the Bichir group. Positive AT skew and negative GC skew were conserved across taxa. Phylogenetic analysis recovered supported clades, with the Senegalus group occupying a basal position, while the Bichir group formed tight cluster indicative of recent divergence. The Weeksii and Retropinnis groups displayed intermediate placement, supporting a diversification pattern. Codon usage conserved, however, biases in leucine, isoleucine, and serine codons distinguished Weeksii and Retropinnis from Bichir lineages, suggesting lineage-specific translational adaptations. Evolutionary rate analyses revealed selection across protein-coding genes with dN/dS < 1, with higher values observed in ATP8, ND2, and ND6 genes, particularly in Weeksii and Senegalus groups, indicating localized adaptive pressures. Sliding-window analysis identified heterogeneous nucleotide diversity, peaks exceeding Pi > 0.20 in several regions, marking divergence hotspots. Despite conserved mitochondrial architecture, compositional variation and differential evolutionary rates reflect lineage diversification within Polypterus. This lineage differentiation supports and widens understanding of evolutionary relationships among the Retropinnis, Bichir, Weeksii, and Senegalus groups. Kehinde Ologbonjaye
883: Sculpins of the family Cottidae represent a diverse radiation of benthic fishes distributed across the Northern Hemisphere, yet generic-level relationships within the family remain poorly resolved and existing taxonomy inadequately reflects evolutionary history. Here we present a comprehensive phylogenomic assessment of Cottidae using double-digest restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq), generating over 100,000 SNPs from representatives of all known genera and approximately 85% of described species diversity. Our results provide a well-supported hypothesis of intrafamilial relationships and reveal significant incongruence between molecular topology and current taxonomy, necessitating formal revision. Most notably, we demonstrate that the largest cottid genus, Cottus, is non-monophyletic as currently circumscribed. To rectify this, we propose a novel taxonomic arrangement supported by both phylogenetic evidence and morphological consideration. We resurrect the monotypic genus Uranidea for U. cognata, which our analyses place as sister to the remarkable adaptive radiation of sculpins endemic to Lake Baikal, a relationship with important implications for understanding the origins of that fauna. We further resurrect Potamocottus to circumscribe the majority of North American sculpin diversity previously subsumed within Cottus. Across the broader phylogeny, Trachidermus is recovered as sister to all remaining Cottidae, followed sequentially by Cephalocottus, Cottopsis, a monotypic lineage corresponding to Cottus aleuticus, Cottus sensu stricto + Mesocottus, and Potamocottus, with Uranidea and the Baikal sculpins forming a terminal sister pair. This revised classification provides a stable, monophyletic framework for ongoing ecological and evolutionary research in this ecologically important group. Diego Santana François Humbert; Jade Mercier; Rafaela Machado; Álvaro Aragão; Ryan Kridler; Sean Keuroghlian-Eaton; Priscila
884: It has been 23 years since the smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata, was listed as endangered under the U.S. Endangered Species Act and 8 years since the last status review was published. Post-listing research efforts have provided a wealth of updates, particularly as it relates to life history, population trends, and habitat use. We have also refined our understanding of ongoing threats to the population and identified previously undocumented threats. Prior to the spinning fish events in 2024 and 2025, information suggested that management efforts since listing had stabilized the population and provided optimism that the population may have begun slowly increasing in abundance. However, the mortality of the mature or nearly mature sawfish associated with the spinning event highlighted the precarious nature of this endangered population and how stochastic events could affect recovery progress. This large-scale mortality event obviously affects the immediate population size but the loss of these mature or nearly mature sawfish will also limit reproduction, parturition, and juvenile recruitment over the next several years. Now the question begs, “Where do we go from here?” in terms of addressing this new threat and managing this endangered species. Matthew R. Brander
885: An age-structured Leslie matrix model previously developed for the US population of smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata, was updated to determine their ability to recover under new scenarios of bycatch from the US southeast shrimp trawl fishery. Additionally, the model considered a large-scale mortality event in 2024, which killed many large juveniles and adults. From 2019, population projections under updated levels of shrimp trawl mortality indicated the population was relatively stable but when the mortality event was introduced in 2024, the population significantly declined. In all scenarios evaluated, there was at least a 25% probability of population extinction. In scenarios with lower initial population sizes, the median (50%) predicted outcome was population extinction. In a scenario with lower initial population sizes, higher than average bycatch mortality, and the assumption that all reported spinning fish perished in 2024, the model predicted a >75% likelihood of extinction. However, in scenarios with higher initial population sizes, the population slowly recovered from the mortality event, with faster recovery at lower bycatch levels. Model outcomes suggest the U.S. DPS of smalltooth sawfish is on the brink; the next few years will be critical to the viability of this endangered species. The moderately high rate of intrinsic increases suggests they have the capacity to recover, but only if bycatch remains low and another large mortality event does not occur Céline Carneiro
886: The Critically Endangered smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) stands out as one of the most imperiled marine vertebrates in US waters, demanding urgent and focused research to inform conservation action. While Critical Habitat was designated for small juvenile sawfish over a decade ago, it remains undesignated for large juveniles and adults, the size class primarily affected by recent mortality events in the Florida Keys. We assessed long-term movement behaviors of 183 large juvenile and adult (91 male, 92 female) sawfish tracked using passive acoustic telemetry between 2016 and 2025. Tagged individuals were detected across 1,867 unique receivers spanning over 2,000 km of coastline. Migrations were taken by 96% of assessed individuals, representing four unique migratory contingents. Residency analyses revealed strong regional fidelity across life stages, with persistent use of estuarine and coastal habitats. Network analyses revealed a highly connected system with ontogenetic expansion in movement, transitioning from localized juvenile networks to broader adult connectivity and habitat breadth. Habitat use and connectivity varied seasonally, with increased reef and offshore use in winter, a return to estuarine habitats in spring, and transitory periods in summer and fall. Together, these findings identify a densely connected network of important habitats and movement corridors essential for the conservation of US sawfish. Here, we use movement data from before and after the spinning event to estimate the proportion of adult population affected, in addition to investigating movements of affected individuals leading up to their mortalities. Understanding how movement dictates effect scope can guide responses to future events. Juan Daza
887: Shark depredation on target species in U.S. Atlantic recreational fisheries is a growing source of human-wildlife conflict. Efforts to mitigate this conflict require an understanding of how its three principal components – anglers, fisheries, and sharks – have evolved over time. Through a historical perspective, we offer a conceptual framework that characterizes the dynamics of these components in the context of complex management systems for the affected fisheries. Specifically, we integrated observations of shark depredation from the published literature, angler surveys, and social media content to provide a comprehensive overview of the breadth of shark depredation in recreational fisheries in U.S. Atlantic waters from Maine to Texas, and the U.S. Caribbean. This exercise revealed that shark depredation is widespread, with 207 unique target-depredator connections (at least 51 target species impacted by 22 shark depredators). The most prevalent shark depredators included both authorized species that may be harvested (e.g., bull sharks Carcharhinus leucas) and prohibited species that may not (e.g., sandbar sharks C. plumbeus). This broad characterization further clarifies the actors (anglers, fisheries, sharks, and managers) that should be considered in ongoing efforts to establish valid shark depredation solutions, evaluates mitigation options given U.S. regulatory constraints, and identifies priorities for future research. Guy DuBeck
888: Assessing recovery of the endangered smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata, requires demographic tools capable of integrating complex life history characteristics, fluctuating environmental stressors, and numerous threats. We developed a stochastic individual-based model population viability analysis (IBM-PVA) that introduces several critical refinements to previous matrix-based assessment frameworks. This IBM-PVA incorporates updated life history parameters and population trends revealed by kin-based genomic approaches. The IBM-PVA explicitly models distinct nursery areas with area-specific environmental stochasticity and implements dynamic reproductive traits, including stochastic pupping periodicity and uniform litter size distributions.
