To accurately capture the demographic momentum of a depleted population, we used model-specific transient initial age distributions assuming a 93–96% population decline rather than assuming stable age distributions. The IBM-PVA further incorporates a trophic feedback loop where juvenile survivorship is scaled by prey biomass indices. Projections evaluated 13 distinct candidate survivorship models and were empirically calibrated using a goodness-of-fit procedure that identified top-fitting scenarios by comparing simulated abundance against independent field-derived abundance indices. Preliminary results highlight the sensitivity of population trajectories to fisheries bycatch, trophic variability, and catastrophic mortality events (e.g., cold kill, spinning fish). This framework provides an empirically anchored tool for evaluating management strategies, and preliminary results will be presented for discussion regarding long-term population resilience. Emily Farrell
889: The Critically Endangered smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) faces severe range contraction, necessitating a deeper understanding of its unique biology to inform conservation. To gain this understanding we generated transcriptomic data from multiple tissues to investigate the genetic basis of species-specific and recently recognized potentially maladaptive traits. Findings reveal episodic positive selection in genes governing fundamental morphogenesis and biochemical pathways, such as MAPK signaling, which directly influence responses to heat, salinity, and marine pollutants. Samples were also sequenced from unexpected but commonly found ovarian follicle-like tissue found in male gonad. This tissue displays a distinct gene expression profile characterized by steroid precursor production and pituitary hormone activity, potentially influencing aggression and maturation. We also discovered a mutation in Dmrt1, a master regulator of male development, that may be widespread in P. pectinata populations with all animals surveyed being heterozygous for the allele. The presence of the mutation may impact population fitness by reducing effective population size by affecting male development. Together, these results highlight how species-specific genetic traits and mutations may impact sawfish fitness, resilience to environmental stressors, and prescribe additional genetic screening to benefit recovery efforts. Edita Folfas Edita Folfas; Luke Frishkoff
890: The alarming loss of smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) in the Florida Keys from recent bouts of “spinning sickness” increases overall risk to the already endangered U.S. population. Such mortality events are difficult to predict and prevent in the short-term, making it all the more vital to strengthen remedies for threats that can be more directly and immediately mitigated. The 2009 Smalltooth Sawfish Recovery Plan, developed under the U.S. Endangered Species Act (ESA), identified shrimp trawl bycatch mortality and destruction of key mangrove shoreline habitat as top impediments to the species’ survival. For decades, despite ESA obligations, federal authorities have resisted advice to increase observer coverage for Gulf of Mexico shrimpers to allow for reliable estimates of associated sawfish mortality. Extrapolation of inadequate observer data has led to egregiously high levels of allowable sawfish take; the federal “Biological Opinion” needed to lower this limit has been seriously delayed. Scientists’ 2021 recommendations to protect reproductive female sawfish by expanding the areas closed to pink shrimp trawling have also gone unheeded while construction plans for southwest Florida areas designated as sawfish “Critical Habitat” are progressing despite conservation commitments. Mitigating spinning sickness, preserving habitat, and minimizing bycatch to a degree sufficient to promote sawfish recovery will require a substantially increased demonstration of public concern. The latest state and federal sawfish policy landscape will be presented along with a range of opportunities for intervention with a view to motivating engagement from scientists. Caitlin Forsyth
891: The sawfishes (Family Pristidae) include five species of large coastal rays that are among the most imperiled groups of marine fishes. The smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) is endemic to the Atlantic Ocean but has been extirpated from much of its range due to overfishing and habitat loss with few viable populations remaining. The U.S. harbors the largest population of smalltooth sawfish, concentrated in Southwest Florida. The persistence of this population reflects conservation actions including sawfish protection in Florida since 1992 and federally under the US Endangered Species Act since 2003. Since 2011, we have used fishery-independent longline surveys (>1,200 sets, >60,000 hooks) to assess spatial and temporal trends in relative abundance of adult smalltooth sawfish in their core region. We also employed acoustic and satellite telemetry to study habitat use, migration, and bycatch risk of large sawfish and to collect samples for assessing reproductive and stress physiology, trophic ecology, and toxicology. A total of 161 large smalltooth sawfish were captured along with over 5,000 other elasmobranchs from 16 species. By 2023, following 30 years of protection in Florida and 20 years since the ESA listing, the US sawfish population appeared to be recovering, prior to the “spinning fish” phenomenon in the Florida Keys that led to mass mortality of large smalltooth sawfish. Our research is now focused on assessing what proportion of the sawfish population was affected by these mortality events and the magnitude of the associated setback to species recovery. Olivia Guerra
892: Accurate estimates of age, somatic growth, maturity, and natural mortality are essential for effective conservation of endangered species. Using samples collected in part during the 2024 fish spinning event in the Florida Keys, this study provides updated growth data and the first direct assessments of length and age at maturity for the endangered smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata). A Bayesian approach using the von Bertalanffy growth function was applied to combine vertebral band counts, mark-recapture data, and results from increment analysis to estimate somatic growth and to derive age at maturity and natural mortality rates. Smalltooth sawfish grow rapidly in their first 3 years, reaching 235 cm stretch total length (STL), 3.2 times their mean length at birth (73.7 cm STL), before growth slows. Asymptotic length was 446 cm STL for males and 484 cm STL for females, with Brody growth coefficients of 0.178 per year for males and 0.170 per year for females. Median age at maturity was 6.9 years for males and 7.9 years for females, and natural mortality was highest for young individuals (<2.5 years old). The oldest individual examined was a 30.1-year-old female, confirming that the species exceeds 30 years in the wild. Ongoing challenges, particularly elevated adult mortality in recent unusual mortality events, underscore the need for focused conservation efforts to mitigate these risks and support population stability. Improved understanding of life history parameters and shifting mortality dynamics will help refine management strategies to better protect smalltooth sawfish and ensure their long-term survival. Sage Kruleski
893: The Smalltooth Sawfish (Pristis pectinata) is an endangered species native to the southern United States. While the population distribution has been centrally located in Florida, as numbers declined, observations of sawfish in adjacent states along the Gulf and the eastern seaboard of the South Atlantic Bight have become rare. Recently, recreational anglers near Little St Simons Island, Georgia, reported two separate instances of carcharhiniform sharks, a Blacktip (Carcharhinus limbatus) in 2020 and an Atlantic Sharpnose (Rhizoprionodon terraenovae) in 2022, with a linear pattern of round puncture wounds. To determine if these wounds could have resulted from sawfish strikes, wound images were compared to archived specimens of Smalltooth Sawfish rostra. ImageJ was used to determine spacing between the puncture marks as well as strikes on a hammerhead shark cohoused with a sawfish in human care. Inter-tooth distance was measured on archived rostra with calipers to characterize tooth spacing across a range of sawfish lengths. Wound and tooth spacing from the aquarium sawfish strike was used as a reference to compare field wound pictures with archived rostral tooth distances. In the past decade, there have been several verified reports of sawfish presence in Georgia and South Carolina. As sawfish are not currently listed as a species of conservation concern in Georgia, future protections and public education may be warranted to conserve this imperiled species. Dylan Maag Dylan Maag; Ryan Hanscom; Craig Fischer; Vincent Marcantonio; Emma McAndrews; Kristin Kabat; Jessica Hill;
894: The smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) is an endangered ray historically found in tropical and subtropical Atlantic waters. It is one of only five sawfish species worldwide, and its range has been reduced to south Florida and the western Bahamas. In elasmobranchs, ovotestes are considered rare and anomalous. However, bilateral ovotestes were confirmed for all necropsies conducted on immature and mature males in Florida (n = 51), including those conducted during the 2024 and 2025 “spinning events” in the Florida Keys. This presentation will focus on the macroscopic and microscopic morphology of ovotestes and serves as an introduction for a subsequent talk on gene expression profiling of this unique aspect of smalltooth sawfish reproductive biology, made possible by samples taken during the 2024 spinning event. Kylie Powers
895: The Lower Florida Keys are an important habitat for several species of coastal sharks, including for individuals transiting between the Gulf and Atlantic coasts of the USA. From late 2023 through early 2025 fish communities inhabiting the shallow waters of this area were heavily impacted by the ‘anomalous fish spinning’ conditions. Most of the scientific and public attention was justifiably focused on the mass mortality events of the heavily impacted smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata), but the effects on other elasmobranch species was thought to have also been significant. Fisheries independent longline surveys conducted prior to, during, and following the peak spinning conditions indicated that the relative abundances of several coastal species declined during these conditions but have since rebounded. In addition, biochemical assays of blood were used to assess health of captured sharks. As the reports of spinning fish conditions and sawfish mortalities declined through 2025 and 2026, continued monitoring is being conducted to determine if relative abundances of sharks return to prespinning levels. Anthony Snead
896: The smalltooth sawfish (Pristis pectinata) population in the United States experienced a stark decline and range contraction during the 20th century, primarily due to overfishing and habitat loss. Understanding changes in abundance is critical to inform conservation actions that promote recovery and long-term viability. We assessed changes in multiple abundance metrics using genomic data from ~1,000 individuals sampled across Florida over 20 years. We estimated an effective population size of ~500 and a ~94% decline from a historical baseline of ~8,000, approximately 300–700 years in the past. Regional effective size estimates indicated that the Ten Thousand IslandsEverglades region contributes disproportionately (~65%) to the total effective population size relative to Charlotte Harbor (~35%). Using hundreds of inferred kin relationships, we examined life history traits and estimated census population size via close-kin mark-recapture. Mitochondrial genomes indicated that ~75% of half-siblings shared a mother and ~25% shared a father. More than 90% of maternally related half-sibling pairs were born in the same region two years apart, consistent with a biennial female reproductive cycle and strong site fidelity. This behavior generated nonrandom spatial and temporal patterns that complicate estimation of female census size. By contrast, paternal half-siblings are distributed randomly across space and time, facilitating estimation of male census size. By integrating male census size estimates with sex ratio, we inferred adult census size for both sexes. The applied genomics framework will enable assessment of how fisheries mortality and unusual mortality events affect smalltooth sawfish recovery and long-term viability. Nathan Swinburne Nathan Swinburne; Jessica Yates; Hannah DeGraw; Emma Palmer; Juliette Rodrigue; Abigail Clark; Abbey Shields; Jack Budd; Renato Guzman; Ethan Holladay; William Fausnaugh; Amanda DeSante; Giavanna Harrington;
897: Situated in the northwest region of the Sargasso Sea, Bermuda comprises a group of oceanic islands and surrounding reefs that approximate an atoll formation. While unique in its relatively high-latitude position and low elasmobranch diversity, the Bermuda islands do support multiple shark and batoid species, including the resident whitespotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari). This species was regularly encountered in Harrington Sound, which is the largest of Bermuda’s semi-enclosed lagoons and home to previously exploitable molluscan shellfish prey such as the calico clam (Macrocallista maculata). Here, we present data documenting major changes in both the benthic community of Harrington Sound as well as the abundance and size composition of eagle rays, which have both transitioned between historical (2007-2010) and recent (2022-2024) sampling periods. Briefly, despite extensive survey efforts over multiple years, larger adult eagle rays (>120 cm Disc Width) were not encountered in Harrington Sound recently, although they are still being reported in other areas of Bermuda. Additionally, although the calico clam historically served as primary prey for the whitespotted eagle ray, this bivalve species has not been documented in Harrington Sound for over a decade, coincident with the arrival of another elasmobranch molluscivore, the cownose ray (Rhinoptera bonasus). Such dynamics question whether apparent extirpation of this bivalve is due to top-down or bottom-up controls, which are discussed in the context of other ecological changes in Bermuda. Molly Albecker
898: Sexual segregation is caused by sex-specific differences in reproductive strategies and is common in elasmobranchs. Sexes may differ in habitat, diet, activity budgets, temperature preferences, and predation risk. Although specific evidence of sexual segregation is lacking for the blacktip shark off the US East Coast, previous findings suggest that sexual segregation occurs in this population. Sexual segregation can lead to biased commercial and recreational landings of a particular sex and, if landings are high, may lead to an unbalanced population, hindering management. Thus, it may be necessary to consider sex-specific differences in distribution and environmental drivers of movements to understand how landings may be affected by sexual segregation. We used movement models to reconstruct tracks from acoustic telemetry data and a skew cluster analysis to examine sexspecific seasonal distribution and set reference categories in a generalized least squares model to determine reliable environmental drivers of blacktip shark movements over multiple years. Our methods demonstrate that the blacktip shark exhibits sexual segregation, where females exhibit greater fidelity to the mating and nursery grounds in Georgia and South Carolina (spring, summer, and autumn) and males inhabit more extreme latitudes along the migratory route, off southeastern Florida (spring) and from North Carolina to New Jersey (summer and autumn). Photoperiod reliably predicts the latitudinal movement of sexes overall as well as seasonally (summer, autumn, and winter). However, during spring chlorophyll-a is the most reliable predictor of movement for sexes combined. Sexual segregation may need to be considered when assessing this stock in the future. Susan Boyd Susan Boyd; Nicole Bass; Evan McVey; Bethany Milles; Paulina Guiterrez-Trejo; Natalie Claunch; Eric Tillman;
899: Variation in the shape of the tetrapod inner ear has been well-documented in relation to ecology and phylogenetic history; but few studies have focused on ear shape variation in fishes. We are using a combination of computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to capture, describe, and compare variation in the skeletal labyrinth across sharks, skates, rays, and chimaeras, assessing representatives of nearly every family of living chondrichthyan. Our data show astonishing variety. Differences abound in the curvature of semicircular canals, in their diameter and cross-sectional shape, and in the degree of their separation from the vestibule and from one another. Sizes of ampullae vary considerably, as do the sizes of the utricular recess and of the ascending ramus of the posterior canal. Some species have distinct passageways for the Glossopharyngeal and Vagus nerves, while others are indistinguishable. The shape of the vestibule ranges from bulbous to slender, from pear-shaped to hourglass-shaped. Skeletal labyrinths vary in size relative to the cranium, and in their degree of morphological fidelity to the membranous labyrinth within. This morphological smorgasbord provides numerous opportunities (and challenges) for comparison through geometric morphometrics. We discuss the methods used in this project to date, including comparisons of membranous versus skeletal labyrinth shape and change in labyrinth morphology with ontogeny, with the ultimate goal of assessing the relationship between form and function in the chondrichthyan inner ear. This work supported by the National Science Foundation, awards IOS 2402409, 2402410, and 2402411 George C. Brooks
AES Ecology 4 / Biomechanics & Morphology / Physiology / Pathology
900: Myliobatid stingrays—including manta, eagle, and cownose rays—differ from most other batoids in their ability to actively swim in the water column, undertake long-distance migrations, maneuver through complex environments, and form large schools. This pelagic lifestyle is reflected in their distinctive morphology, characterized by enlarged pectoral fins and an exceptionally long, slender whip-like tail that can exceed four times the body length. Despite its prominence, the biological significance of this tail has remained largely unexplored. In this project, we present the first comprehensive functional characterization of the myliobatid whip-tail through a multidisciplinary approach integrating morphology, kinematics, and hydrodynamics. We show that the tail contains a lateral line system on both sides, which, unlike in other fishes, is highly ramified into numerous subcanals and pores. Comparative 3D morphological analyses reveal that the complexity of the lateral line varies across myliobatid species, being more elaborate in fully pelagic rays (e.g., mantas) than in more benthic taxa (e.g., dasyatids), suggesting a relationship between morphology and signal filtering capacity. Using 3D-printed models tested in a flow tank, we further demonstrate that, beyond its sensory role, the tail contributes significantly to body stability, functioning analogously to the long tails of kites. Together, these findings indicate that the myliobatid whip-tail is a multifunctional organ with both mechanosensory and hydrodynamic roles, representing a key structure underpinning the lifestyle of these rays Luis M. P. Ceríaco
AES Ecology 4 / Biomechanics & Morphology / Physiology / Pathology
901: The mortality of discarded elasmobranchs in non-target fisheries is an ongoing conservation and management challenge. Soak time is well documented as an important contributor to shark at-vessel and post-release mortality rates in commercial longline fisheries. Limits on gear soak time have, therefore, been proposed as a mechanism to reduce bycatch mortality, with shorter soak times generally resulting in lower mortality. However, the means to effectively monitor and enforce soak time limits at sea remain elusive. We tested a novel Electronic Monitoring (EM) sensor system on bottom longline vessels in the U.S. Atlantic Shark Research Fishery, and compared EM sensor estimates of soak time to those recorded by fishery observers on the same hauls (N=77). A subsample of released sharks were fitted with pop-up satellite archival tags (N=36) to characterize how post-release mortality rates and recovery times correlate with soak time. Preliminary results indicate good agreement (less than 5 min difference) between the EM sensor data and observer recorded soak times, providing proof of concept for remotely monitoring soak time under certain conditions. Preliminary post-release mortality rates for tagged dusky (Carcharhinus obscurus), bull (C. leucas), and spinner (C. brevipinna) sharks ranged from 0% for bull shark to 25% for spinner shark. Recovery periods for surviving sharks were positively correlated with soak time. The combination of technological advances and cooperative research with fishing industry partners has introduced the potential for new management tools to help better quantify and reduce shark bycatch mortality. Lei Curtis
902: From over 30,000 elasmobranch papers indexed by Shark-References.com, we extracted data using various novel search strategies across 8 schema groups: ocean basin, ecosystem, species, anthropogenic pressure, fishing gear, impact on elasmos, scientific discipline, and analytical method. Genetics, data science, and movement disciplines publish most, with conservation/policy and movement growing fastest. USA, Australia, UK, and Canada publish most by nation, with others increasing, as is open access publishing. Female first authorship has risen towards parity, with differences across disciplines (more conservation & genetics, less trophic & movement) and regions. We’re publishing in higher quality journals, and generally have poor social media metrics, though they’re improving. Popular study areas are the Med and North Atlantic, with few studies in polar seas. Coastal, pelagic, and demersal habitats are common, kelp, deeps, and rivers rare. Carcharhinids are more than twice as studied as catsharks; rays follow. Eagle rays, torpedo rays, then rays are the most understudied families. Status dashboards highlight trends and disparities in research by technique, species, nation, and discipline, with co-occurrence heatmaps linking parameters. This resource can unlock rapid elasmo-specific literature reviews and aid conservation prioritisation by identifying geographic and taxonomic research gaps. The pipeline auto-updates from SharkReferences, maintaining a living resource enabling research queries. Integration is planned with Sharkipedia, community curation will be invited for expert-validated reviews, and an LLM interface will allow for conversational queries across the full corpus. Papers are planned for each of the major findings categories; collaboration is welcomed. Hannah DeGraw

903: Sharks can detect electric fields within their environment, mainly for prey capture, via their Ampullae of Lorenzini, which are comprised of sensory receptors at the base of conductive gel-filled canals. These canals terminate in visible pores primarily across a shark’s head, whose number and distribution can vary with phylogeny, biology, and life history stage, providing insights into specific behaviors and movements. Traditionally, the ampullary pore distribution is mapped on a flat plane by removing and illuminating the skin of a shark, then marking the pore locations. While effective, the process is time-intensive and destructive, making it unsuitable for museum specimens and live individuals. Therefore, we developed an efficient, non-destructive, and entirely digitized method as an alternative. We created a 3D model using photogrammetry to generate a “digital skin” (a 2D, 360-degree view of the head) and assessed efficiency and accuracy of the resulting digital skin maps compared to standard pore maps. We then applied the method to select shark species, analyzed differences across and within species, and recorded the ampullary pore maps of some species for the first time. These analyses provide further insight into shark electrosensory systems and demonstrate the effectiveness of a novel non-destructive method to map ampullary pores. Sarah Donelson

904: Juvenile white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) aggregate along Southern California beaches, where they primarily feed on benthic elasmobranchs, especially the round stingray (Urobatis halleri). Both direct and indirect predation may influence the abundance, behavior and distribution of benthic prey species such as stingrays. In these nearshore environments, stingray injuries to beachgoers are a common human-wildlife interaction, particularly in shallow surf zones where round stingrays forage and bury in sediment. This study examined whether juvenile white shark (JWS) aggregations are associated with changes in round stingray abundance or behavior and thereby influence injury frequency to humans. We hypothesized that areas and periods with higher JWS activity would correspond with reduced stingray injury rates due to predator-driven changes in stingray abundance. Stingray injuries, environmental conditions and daily human attendance at Del Mar Beach, CA, were compiled from lifeguard records. These data were compared with JWS acoustic telemetry data and drone survey data, which further quantified shark and human presence. Temporal trends in injury rates were analyzed relative to periods of documented shark aggregation to evaluate potential predator-prey or risk-mediated effects. Preliminary analyses suggest that stingray injury rate increased prior to the aggregation and decreased substantially after prolonged residency. Additionally, injury risk increased after the JWS aggregation dissipated. These findings suggest that predator presence may indirectly influence human–stingray interactions through ecological or behavioral mechanisms. Future research should investigate how JWS aggregations alter prey populations over the course of their residency and further explore how the abundance of round stingrays influences stingray injury risk. Vinicius Correa Espindola

905: The Pacific sharpnose shark, Rhizoprionodon longurio, is a coastal species of significant ecological and economic importance in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, distributed from southern California to Peru. While existing literature focuses on its general biology and trophic ecology, the histological characterization of its reproductive system remains understudied. In particular, comprehensive analyses integrating the primary components of both female and male reproductive tracts, and their relationship to different maturity stages, are still lacking. In this context, the present study adopts an integrative approach to examine the reproductive biology of R. longurio. The methodology combines macroscopic assessments with a detailed histological characterization of the ovary, oviduct, oviducal gland, uterus, testis, and epigonal organ, as well as embryonic development. This framework allows for the exploration of cellular and tissue dynamics associated with sexual maturation, allowing evaluation of the correlation between external morphological indicators and physiological reproductive status. Macroscopic and morphometric evaluations were conducted on 198 specimens collected in Santa Rosalía, Baja California Sur, Mexico, between 2018 and 2021. Monthly variations in oocyte diameter and embryonic development suggest the presence of an annual reproductive cycle. Logistic models estimated the size at maturity (L50) at 91 cm total length (TL) for females and 89 cm TL for males, as well as a size at maternity (Lm50) of 103 cm TL. These findings provide a baseline reference that can be contrasted with histological results, allowing for accurate documentation of the microscopic progression of gametogenesis throughout the reproductive cycle of the species in this region. Dan Gonzalez-Kosasky

906: Recent advances in animal-borne biologging tag technology have revolutionized our ability to study the movements of free-swimming elasmobranchs within the context of their environment. The RemO2ra is a multisensor, animal-borne tag capable of directly collecting oxygen consumption data in the wild. It uses accelerometer-based metrics of activity and behavior coupled with point oxygen utilization measurements at the gills to estimate metabolic requirements from free-swimming sharks. Taken together, this tag allows for more direct observation of how behavior and environmental conditions contribute to metabolic rate in the field for gill-breathing aquatic species. Here we present the results of an initial deployment in Indian River Lagoon on a Bull Shark (Carcharhinus leucas) in the spring of 2024, and further deployments on free swimming Sandbar Sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus) in Delaware Bay during the summer of 2026. Yuanxing Liao

907: Studies in numerous tetrapod groups indicate a form:function relationship between inner ear morphology and habitat, locomotion, and life history traits, as well as (in some cases) a strong influence of phylogenetic history. However, few studies have assessed the relationship between ear shape and habitat in fishes. Since the Early Jurassic, batoids have succeeded in occupying various ecological niches in marine and freshwater habitats, ranging from benthic to pelagic and some found in deep water or associated with reefs. The increasing availability of Computed Tomography (CT) data enables quantitative and qualitative comparison of the inner ear across a wide range of taxa. This study used CT scanning to visualize the inner ear morphology of sixteen species of batoids. We then used Principal Components Analysis (PCA) to identify main axes of shape variation and grouped species by habitat and diet to assess whether these factors might contribute to differences in ear morphology. Results showed that phylogeny may be a stronger predictor of ear shape, rather than habitat type. Visualizing ear shape in a phylogenetic context lends support to the idea that evolutionary history is a strong predictor of ear geometry, though this work is part of a broader project which will incorporate greater taxonomic coverage in a similar methodological framework. Further investigation into the functional significance of ear shape can potentially provide ecological context for some of the most unique ear morphologies, and ear traits associated with evolutionary history may be useful for developing characters for phylogenetic analysis. Maria Camila López-Posada

908: Rays populations are declining worldwide, but limited data on their diversity, distribution, and abundance hinder their effective management and conservation. Non-invasive tools like Baited Remote Underwater Video Systems (BRUVS) provide a robust platform to improve the monitoring and collection of biological and ecological data for rays. However, manual identification at the species level can be slow, costly and labordemanding, especially when a large amount of data has been gathered.  To address this, we developed an automated progressive deep-learning pipeline for the robust detection and identification of batoids in underwater videos from BRUVS. Videos were collected in a Marine Protected Area in the Gulf of California, Mexico, which was recognized as an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA). In this area, 14 ray species regularly occur. We built a labeled dataset with manual annotations of rays. Then, we implemented a general batoid (ray) detection model, which served both as a performance baseline and as a semi-automated labeling tool. In a second stage, the annotated data are used to train multiclass classifiers to discriminate at the genus or species level. This workflow allows the system's taxonomic resolution to be scaled as the dataset grows. Model performance was evaluated in terms of F1score and efficiency (inference time). A qualitative comparison of the time required for manual versus automatic labeling is also presented. The approach is introduced as a scalable alternative for ecological monitoring of batoids. Brynne Loudenslager

909: Societal response to shark-human interactions (shark bites) has varied widely around the world, historically driving an array of shark-bite mitigation measures and have often employed culling as a mode of shark control. Population recovery of white sharks off California and increased human ocean recreation activity have raised concerns over human safety, driving development of the CA Shark Beach Safety Program funded by the State of CA in 2018. The primary goal of this program included research and population monitoring to inform a large education and outreach initiative for improving beach safety, mitigate risk water user risk and preserve shark conservation measures. Shark activity monitoring uses UAVs, eDNA, acoustic and satellite telemetry and datalogging to provide movement resolution across differing spatial and temporal scales and behavioral characterizations that might indicate bite risk. Socioeconomic research has focused on characterizing public perception of ocean wildlife risk, financial costs associated with incidents, and how to change those perceptions via education. Monitoring data are included in ocean lifeguard training, as well as in our K-12 education program curricula designed to get students interested in STEM and reinforce beach safety tenets. Information gained from ongoing research is incorporated into a public-friendly outreach curriculum focused on ocean wildlife interactions (e.g., stingrays, sharks) to modify beach user behavior to mitigate risk. California has the lowest white shark related fatality rate relative to global comparisons with other government managed shark mitigation programs, which are likely attributed to better EMS and trauma services in California. Carl A. Luer
910: There is considerable interspecific variation in the brain of cartilaginous fishes that correlates with ecological parameters, suggesting that brain size and organization may be informative about sensory specialization and behavior. However, far less is known about shifts in brain organization as species occupy new ecological niches throughout ontogeny. This study examined brain morphology of the closely related Carolina (Sphyrna gilberti) and scalloped (S. lewini) hammerheads. These species are sympatric as juveniles, overlapping in habitat and resource use. However, they exhibit different ecological characteristics as adults including primary habitat and hunting strategies, where S. gilberti occupy deeper habitats and feed at a higher trophic level than S. lewini. To explore whether this ecological divergence is reflected in the brain, this study compared brain growth and the relative size of six major brain regions (olfactory bulbs, telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, cerebellum, and medulla oblongata) throughout ontogeny in each species. In both S. gilberti and S. lewini, brain size significantly increases with body mass throughout life, although growth is not homogeneous across brain regions. In both species, the olfactory bulbs and cerebellum scale with positive allometry compared to the rest of the brain, whereby the brain becomes disproportionately composed of these two regions. Additionally, adult S. gilberti have significantly larger olfactory bulbs than adult S. lewini. These results suggest shifts in sensory specialization as these animals mature and diverge ecologically. Exploring patterns of brain organization in these species may help predict whether ecological differences at key life stages can drive variation in the brain. Alexis Lundquist

911: Morphological differences in the peripheral (sensory) and central (brain) nervous system have been predicted to confer functional variation in elasmobranchs across taxa and throughout ontogeny. Additionally, the nervous system of fishes grows continually throughout life and may be highly plastic in relation to environmental change. Over the last century, sea surface temperatures have increased over 0.5°C and are predicted to rise 1–4° by 2100, potentially affecting species’ physiological performance. Therefore, assessing effects of temperature on changes in size and organization of the nervous system may have implications for brain function in future ocean conditions. Effects of increased rearing temperature on nervous system development were studied in the little skate (Leucoraja erinacea), epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum), and Port Jackson shark (Heterodontus portusjacksoni). Egg cases from each species were collected and placed into either ambient or 3–5° above ambient seawater conditions through hatching, for up to five months. Using histological analyses, relative volume of the olfactory rosette, total brain, and major brain regions were compared between treatment groups. Results indicate significant, species-specific differences in both total brain volume and size of major brain regions, possibly indicating sensory or motor impairment at elevated temperatures. While studies on acute responses to environmental conditions cannot inform true adaptation across broad timescales, understanding effects of increased temperature on neural phenotype can aid in predicting consequences of environmental perturbations in elasmobranchs. Nicolas Pennacchio

912: Most primary literature surrounding white sharks, Carcharodon carcharias, focuses on negative human-shark conflicts, movement ecology, or predator-prey interactions. Little research has been conducted on the potential role of white sharks as a host species, despite evidence that other large shark species provide mobile shelter, facilitate transportation, or generate feeding opportunities in symbiotic relationships with other fishes. The recovery of the Northwestern Atlantic white shark population and subsequent emergence of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, USA, as a seasonal aggregation site, has created a unique opportunity to study symbiotic relationships in the largest predatory shark species. We used an extensive photographic-identification database of over 750 individuals collected from 2014 to 2024 to screen for instances of fish symbiosis. For each occurrence, we identified the associated fish to the lowest taxonomic level possible, recorded shark-host estimated length, and the occurrence date. Lastly, we classified the location of the fish on the shark’s body, as body region selection may provide insight into the nature of these species-specific relationships. To date, we have observed symbiosis involving eight fish species. These observations were dominated by three species (banded rudderfish, Seriola zonata, crevalle jack, Caranx hippos, and sea lamprey, Petromyzon marinus), which varied by month of occurrence and white shark body region. Using these data, we infer that white sharks provide mobile refuge for fishes and a direct food source for hematophagous lampreys. This study adds evidence to limited existing literature that white sharks are an important host species for fishes and influence ecosystems outside of predation. Gabriela Ribau

913: Despite the wide distribution, abundance, and accessibility of the stingrays Hypanus sabinus and H. say, their parasite communities remain poorly described across much of their ranges, including the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) estuary. Stingrays from the IRL were examined externally and internally for parasites using standard procedures and recovered parasites were identified to the lowest possible taxonomic level. Multivariate techniques were used to explore similarities with published data on parasite communities from congeneric species. Parasite communities of both stingray species were dominated by Cestodes, primarily from the orders Trypanorhyncha and Rhinebothriidea, and include a diverse community of Monogeneans and Digeneans. Parasite communities of IRL stingrays were broadly consistent with those reported from conspecifics in other study areas; coupled with diet analyses, they reveal that the IRL supports a diverse host assemblage, implying that this heavily urbanized system remains functionally ecologically robust. Further study of these communities also provides information on natural enemies. As elasmobranchs typically fill the trophic role of mesopredators, parasites are the primary agents regulating host populations. 914: Studying the human dimensions of shark conservation challenges has been encouraged as an important path towards protecting these ecologically important and threatened animals. However, despite decades of calls for research into this aspect of shark conservation and management, progress has been slow compared to other research methodologies. To facilitate the growth and development of this important research discipline, we distributed a voluntary online survey to human dimensions scholars, inviting them to suggest priority research questions. 176 human dimensions of shark conservation and management scholars responded to our survey, submitting a total of 281 proposed priority research questions. These proposed questions were reorganized and synthesized into 53 questions across 16 categories of human dimensions of shark conservation and management research, including local ecological knowledge, human-wildlife conflict, socioeconomics of fisheries exploitation, alternative livelihoods, and public education. This expert-solicited list of research priorities can help shape the future of this important field by guiding scholars towards questions for their research to address.
915: In recent decades, many shark and ray populations have declined dramatically. In the wider Caribbean, this trend became apparent in the 2000s, when researchers used REEF survey data to conduct a regional assessment of reef-associated shark sightings. Now, more than 15 years later, we revisit the same dataset to evaluate sightings of sharks and rays from 1993 to 2025. Using models that account for variable survey effort across space and time, we generate decades-long time series of sightings probabilities for the most common species across multiple countries. We also assess changes in sightings following the establishment of national Shark Sanctuaries, which prohibit shark and/or ray fishing. For many of these nations, the resulting time series provide the first longterm insights into reef-associated shark and ray population trajectories, offering critical information for conservation and management decisions. These findings arrive at a pivotal moment as many wider Caribbean countries work to balance fisheries, dive tourism, and conservation, often in the absence of reliable data. Milton Tan
916: Stingrays use their spines for defense, with envenomation causing intense pain and inflammation, often followed by tissue necrosis in humans. Although the toxins and bioactive components mediating these biological responses are not well understood, venoms from many organisms possess the potential for development into therapeutic applications for humans. We report a bottom-up proteomic analysis comparing proteomes of tissue extracts from Atlantic stingray (Hypanus sabinus) spines and non-venomous epidermal mucus collected from the surface of Atlantic stingray pectoral fins. Using a comparative approach with H. sabinus reference genome, proteins belonging to a novel cephalotoxin (CTX)-like gene family were the most abundant putative toxins present in the venomous spine proteome. From phylogenic analysis, the CTX-like proteins represent a novel gene family found in cartilaginous fishes closely related to the Rapunzel (rpz) gene family exclusive to bony fishes and known to have activity such as prey paralysis, antimicrobial effects, and anti-tumor activity. Other putative venom toxins enriched in spine tissue extracts include hyaluronidase 6, galectin-12, kininogen-1 (chondrichthyan-kinin precursor), and a pore-forming actinoporin-like toxin. Spine tissue extracts also demonstrate growth inhibition and induction of apoptosis against an acute T-cell leukemia cell line (Jurkat E6-1). This bioactivity was present in venom gland extracts but not in extracts of epidermal mucus. Putative venom toxins abundant in Atlantic stingray spines may collectively produce the observed biological responses and may possess the potential to be developed into therapeutic compounds for human health. 917: Fast swimming sharks exhibit a dorsoventrally compressed and mediolaterally expanded pre-caudal body region, or keel, which is hypothesized to increase mediolateral bending resistance. The vertebral column is the central axis of bending, which operates like a spring or a brake, depending on the loading regime, to modulate body stiffness. Previous research on this body region found that vertebrae are wedge-shaped and shorter compared to other regions, and intervertebral joint (IVJ) number increases posteriorly; but the mechanical consequences of this morphology have not been explored. We quantified second moment of area ratios (I, an object’s ability to resist bending based on its shape) of the pre-caudal body, vertebral centra and IVJs to examine mediolateral bending resistance along the posterior region. For example, when I is greater than one, the structure is dorsoventrally compressed and mediolaterally expanded. Using µCT imaging and 3D reconstructions, we examined eight keels from three lamnids [Isurus oxyrinchus (n = 6), Carcharodon carcharias (n = 1), Lamna nasus, (n = 1)], and compared them to one sphyrnid (Sphyrna mokarran). Axes exhibiting maximum and minimum bending resistance were determined as ratios for pre-caudal body shapes (IBmax:IBmin), centra (ICmax:ICmin), and IVJs (IJmax:IJmin), providing estimates for stiffness. All pre-caudal body and centrum ratios were greater than one, suggesting their shapes resist mediolateral bending; but IVJ ratios were less than one, indicating they are more compliant with mediolateral bending. This study introduces an approach for quantifying the impact pre-caudal body shapes and their vertebral morphologies have on shark swimming. Jake J Wood

918: Stable isotope analysis (SIA) is a widely used chemical tracer tool for studying short-term ecology and movement of elasmobranchs. However, to robustly use SIA from plasma and red blood cells in the field, laboratory studies quantifying the trophic discrimination factor (TDF) and turnover rate of elasmobranch blood are critical. Collaborating with public aquariums that commonly hold large elasmobranchs for the extended periods of time needed to estimate TDF and tissue turnover provides the opportunity to characterize these dynamics on mature individuals, as previous studies have only focused on small, fast-growing sharks. We collaborated with Ripley’s Aquarium of Myrtle Beach to estimate turnover rate and TDF for three stable isotopes (δ13C, δ15N, and δ34S) in plasma and red blood cells of resident Sand Tiger Sharks (Carcharias taurus). Red blood cells showed a larger TDF (the difference between the isotopic composition of diet and the tissue) compared to plasma proteins across all three stable isotopes, with mean values between 0‰ and 2.5‰. Consistent with previous studies, we found slower turnover rates in red blood cells (half-life of 3-6 months) compared to plasma proteins (half-life of 1-3 months). Using detailed information collected by aquariums, we were able to identify how TDF and turnover are affected by differences in diet over time, mimicking how these dynamics function in wild elasmobranchs. This collaboration allowed us to estimate critical stable isotope dynamics with the goal of their application to wild ecology studies in elasmobranchs. John Carlson
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 3
919: Assessing the success of reintroduction programs for small-bodied animals, such as reptiles and amphibians, has been challenging. Conventional telemetry studies can provide information about space use, activity and survival, but are limited by battery life and labor logistics. We have been releasing captive-reared blunt-nosed leopard lizards (Gambelia sila; BNLL) to restore a nearly extirpated population on Panoche Plateau in western Fresno County, CA, USA since 2023. To better monitor reintroduction success and remnant wild animals, we established an automated radio telemetry system (ARTS) comprised of over 300 listening nodes that detect signals from solar-hybrid powered, ultra-high frequency (UHF) tags. We released captive-reared BNLL in 2024 (n = 20) and 2025 (n=35), half of which were given UHF tags and we tagged four wild BNLL. By relating signal strength to distance, BNLL locations were estimated at a high temporal scale with a mean error (distance between hand-tracked and ARTS locations) of 32.6 meters. Home ranges (autocorrelated kernel density estimates) generated from ARTS data suggest that released lizards used more space (mean: 15.5x larger) than hand-tracking data indicate. ARTS data also provides evidence of BNLL selecting habitat experimentally grazed to reduce invasive grass cover. Finally, the ARTS provides information about seasonal and daily activity, allowing inference on potential predation events and dormancy timing including a female that skipped surface activity in 2025. Our results suggest that the ARTS increases our power to monitor small-bodied vertebrates and is especially useful for assessing the success of reintroductions. Tianqi Huang
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 3
920: Zoos and aquariums have been playing an increasingly valuable role in animal research and conservation. By providing researchers with access to a wide range of species in controlled environmental conditions, zoos and aquariums enable ex situ research when field-based studies are challenging or impossible. Concurrently, zoos and aquariums play an important role in animal conservation through public education and sustainability efforts including breeding and reintroduction programs. Sand tiger sharks (Carcharias taurus) are a popular aquarium species that rarely reproduce in aquariums. Here, we deployed acceleration biologgers to monitor the fine-scale activity patterns of four male sand tiger sharks, two control sharks and two implanted with Deslorelin, a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist, before and throughout the reproductive season. Deslorelin causes a flare in reproductive behavior followed by suppression through its influence on GnRH receptors in the pituitary. These long-term deployments revealed that sand tigers generally displayed lower levels of activity at night compared to day and overall higher activity periods during the reproductive season. Preliminary analyses did not indicate differences in activity between the control and treatment groups over the six months following the insertion of the implant suggesting there is no flare in reproductive behavior for this taxon. Biologging allowed behavior to be quantitatively measured long-term and continuously to better characterize the mating season and novel methods to influence reproductive behavior of this iconic species.

921: According to the Zoological Information Management System (ZIMS) - a global database of zoo and aquarium holdings, there are more than 3,300 species of reptiles and amphibians presently held in zoological parks worldwide. Such diversity maintained under controlled and semi-controlled conditions presents near-limitless opportunities for integrative biological research, especially on rare, enigmatic and protected species that may be physically or logistically difficult to study in the field. Many institutions have capitalized on these opportunities and gone on to produce rich traditions of scientific contributions to the study of reptiles and amphibians through a wide range of investigations; however, zoos and aquariums as a whole may not be realizing their true potential for herpetological research, and some facilities may not know how or where to begin. Here, opportunistic observational studies on captive zoo specimens have the potential to yield important biological information and may be more accessible to a broader range of institutions than formal hypothesis-driven experimental studies. In this presentation, some examples of opportunistic studies at Audubon Zoo are highlighted to help illustrate the value and capacity that all zoos and aquariums have in contributing new information to the study of reptiles and amphibians as well as raising new questions and hypotheses that then can be pursued through more formal experimental investigations. Mark Merchant
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 3
922: Amphibians are one of the most imperiled groups of vertebrates, making conservation action more important than ever for this group. One major intervention is the release of captive-bred animals back to the wild to create new populations or supplement existing populations. However, we do not fully understand the impact of release on the behavior of the released animals. Therefore, we conducted a soft-release study with the dusky gopher frog (Lithobates sevosus), a critically endangered amphibian. The Memphis Zoo has bred and released dusky gopher frogs since 2017, making it an ideal species to better understand the effects of releases. To simulate a reintroduction, half of a group of dusky gopher frog yearlings were released into outdoor man-made ponds, while half remained in glass tanks that are typical of zoo housing for a 6-month period. We then examined behavioral responses at the end of the 6-month period, as well as 3 months and 6 months later. For these trials we measured latency to emerge from a hide and distance traveled in the experimental arena. Overall, we did not find significant differences in latency to emergence or distance traveled between treatment groups or between each set of sampling. Therefore, release conditions and environment did not strongly affect the behavior of these frogs compared to traditional captive housing. Further study should explore if different behaviors promote differential success for individuals post-release. 923: Blunt-nosed Leopard Lizards (Gambelia sila) are endemic to central California and despite nearly 60 years on the endangered species list, their populations continue to decline. In 2020, we received emergency permission to found a captive breeding colony and release captive-reared animals in an effort to restore a unique, remnant population that had declined to fewer than 10 individuals. To date, we have produced 234 hatchlings and released 110. To assess survival, habitat selection, and reproductive success, all released animals and remnant wild animals (N =4) were outfitted with radio telemetry transmitters and manually relocated weekly during the active season. We also constructed an Automated Radio Telemetry System (ARTS) composed of >300 remote nodes to monitor animals year-round at high temporal resolution beginning in 2024. Our monitoring revealed that thick thatch from invasive annual grasses greatly limits G. sila, with the most successful animals selecting areas dominated by bare ground, such as a gravel roadway. Following this result, we initiated an experiment testing the efficacy of targeted sheep grazing to facilitate G. sila recolonization. Four 100×200m patches were heavily grazed for 3-10d in spring immediately prior to G. sila release. Both released and remnant G. sila selected grazed areas and had greater survival when occupying the grazed areas, with 29 of 35 animals released in 2025 surviving. Our work illustrates the utility of captive propagation and release programs for testing the efficacy of habitat management strategies while simultaneously increasing the population sizes of at-risk species. Emma Teng
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 3
924: Public aquaria showcase aquatic life while raising awareness and educating the public on biodiversity and the need for conservation. Increasingly, aquaria include a dedicated research and conservation program as part of their institutional commitment to the wellbeing of the animals in their care. Research programs at aquaria can include animals in their natural environment and ex situ studies that allow for long-term monitoring. Thanks to husbandry and veterinary expertise, aquaria can house animals that are often not feasible to care for in traditional academic settings, and for long durations, often throughout entire life cycles, allowing important life history information to be investigated. Ripley’s Aquariums has an active and growing research program that includes independent and collaborative efforts. Projects include invertebrate, fish, reptile and bird species with studies that focus on various aspects of reproduction, aging, and general health. Lila Xenakis
ASIH, HL and SSAR Zoo & Aquarium Conservation and Research Symposium 3
925: Molecular datasets have expanded in length and quality over the last several decades. In the field of systematics, larger datasets are often desired, with an expectation one will find the 'true' evolutionary history of a study group with ease, with whole genomes being the holy grail. In this study, I use the rattlesnakes of the Western USA (Crotalus) as a system to show how whole genomes yield multiple, strongly supported species tree that each correspond to different evolutionary phenomena. I find that processed like introgression and co-evolution of nuclear and mitochondrial genes yield different tree topologies in Crotalus. This study highlights that rather than viewing genomic datasets as a way to find a single evolutionary tree, the genome is a mosaic of evolutionary phenomena that each can manifest as an alternative topology. Rather than viewing alternative topologies as erroneous or artefacts, these have the potential to enhance our understanding of the evolutionary process.
926: The process of speciation is often accompanied with gene flow. Numerous examples across snake phylogeny show evidence of past reticulation. Where terminal species formed even in the middle Pleistocene, taxa often still retain some gene flow through hybrid zones. In North American snakes, these hybrid zones between parental species often occur in ecotonal regions situated between major biomes. Despite continued hybridization through time, the parental lineages/species fail to collapse. Using annotated whole genomes, we examine major hybrid zones in North American snakes to understand how genome architecture plays a major role in isolating parts of the genome, thus providing adaptive boundaries for parental lineages where alleles fail to cross through the hybrid zone. Alternatively, we show how genome architecture also facilitates adaptive introgression through the hybrid zone. This view of the hybrid zone as a filtration zone provides a clearer understanding of taxonomy, how species boundaries are maintained, and how gene flow permits adaptive alleles to pass between taxa. Breanna Burke
927: Deep time reticulation, resulting from introgression between different species due to hybridization and backcrossing, is a widespread phenomenon observed across diverse taxa. This process increases genetic variation within species, allowing evolution and adaptation to act more rapidly on pre-existing variation that has already been shaped by selection. Furthermore, assessing introgression across clades inhabiting different environments can improve our understanding of how ecological factors shape diversification patterns. Within snakes, introgression and ancient reticulation events have been documented in terrestrial and arboreal snakes. Freshwater snakes within the Hydropsini tribe provide an excellent system to test whether their evolutionary history has been influenced by introgression, given their restricted aquatic habitats and sympatric distribution of many species throughout the Amazon Basin. Here, we examine relationships within Hydropsini using whole genomes and evaluate whether the phylogenetic history of the group reflects both bifurcating and reticulating evolutionary histories influenced by the dynamic nature of Amazonian River systems. This work provides a foundation for identifying lineages that have undergone introgression for further investigating the role of adaptive introgressed traits in aquatic snakes. Eric Coburn
928: Joseph B. Slowinski, at 38 years old, died from a krait bite in Myanmar on 12 September, 2001. I will introduce the Frontiers in Snake Evolution: Honoring the Legacy of Jospeh B Slowinski Symposium by introducing Joe to those who did not know him. This introduction will briefly answer the questions: who was Joe as a person and as a scientist? Hayley Crowell Hayley Crowell; Anthony DiMeglio; Alison Davis Rabosky; Hannah Owens; Jenna Crowe-Riddell; Samuel
929: The Madagascar gemsnakes (Pseudoxyrhophiidae) are a 22 million-year-old family comprising 119 endemic species. Their history has been characterized by rampant gene flow and rapid speciation, resulting in highly mosaic genomes of evolutionary histories. A central challenge in the field is disentangling these discordant genomic signals to accurately infer both the species tree and patterns of reticulate evolution. Here, we take a genomic architecture–aware approach to identify regions of the genome that are most likely to retain signal of the species tree and introgression history in this group. We sequenced and assembled whole genomes for the majority of the species in this family, including 2 reference-level sequences, and inferred recombination maps for representatives from the two major clades of arboreal and terrestrial taxa. Our work highlights how targeted, recombination-aware phylogenetic analysis, not just more data, are necessary for improved inference. Simon Dedman
930: The infrared-sensing pits of snakes are a key innovation that enables the exploitation of novel ecological niches. These specialized pit organs have evolved multiple times independently across different snake lineages. Previous studies have identified molecular signatures of convergent evolution among pit-bearing snakes, particularly in transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1), a heat-sensitive calcium ion channel. Although most boas lack infrared-sensing pits, these structures occur in four boid lineages. Within the Madagascar-endemic boa subfamily Sanziniinae, both pit-bearing and non–pit-bearing species are present, providing a valuable system for investigating the evolution of infrared sensing. We assembled whole genomes of two Malagasy boa species, pitbearing Sanzinia madagascariensis and non-pit-bearing Acrantophis madagascariensis. Combining these new genomes with all currently available snake genomes, we conducted a genome-wide comparative analysis to identify candidate genes associated with pit-bearing lineages and positively selected sites within those genes that are potentially involved in infrared sensing. This study provides new insights into the genomic mechanisms underlying the evolution of heat sensing and evaluates whether this key innovation has contributed to diversification in boas. Danny Hughes
931: Introgression and incomplete lineage sorting can generate phylogenomic conflict during rapid radiations, yet their relative contributions and functional consequences remain poorly understood. However, it has been shown in several systems that introgression can result in trait evolution and adaptation. We investigated these processes in western North American rattlesnakes (Crotalus cerberus–viridis–oreganus–scutulatus) using data derived from venom gland transcriptomes. This group has been extensively studied due to contrasting venom phenotypes, in which some species have a hemotoxic venom (type B) while other species or populations exhibit a neurotoxic venom (type A). We confirm the geographical structure of venom phenotypes does not track neutral ancestry; instead, type B venom was widespread whereas type A and mixed AB phenotypes were concentrated mainly within C. scutulatus and nearby regions. Concatenated and coalescent phylogenetic analyses revealed substantial genealogical discordance. We identified multiple introgression events, with recurrent ancestral exchanges predominating over more recent gene flow among extant lineages. Genomic window scans showed that introgression is highly heterogeneous across chromosomes, with significant chromosome-level differences in permeability. Notably, introgressed windows were also detected on the Z chromosome, indicating that it does not act as a uniformly stronger barrier to gene flow. Genes within introgressed windows were enriched for functions related to membrane trafficking, endocytosis, and intracellular transport, raising the possibility that introgression may affect cellular pathways including those underlying venom production. These results support a reticulate model of rattlesnake diversification in which repeated introgression, heterogeneous genomic permeability, and ecological selection shape evolutionary history and phenotypic diversity. Abigail Nagl
932: Snake venom has emerged as a powerful model for examining how genomic diversity arises through gene duplication, as it comprises multiple toxin gene families that originated and expanded from non-toxin genes. Many venom gene families occur in tandem duplication arrays, often shaped by repeated gene duplication events. Transposable elements (TEs) have long been known to associate with these tandem repeat regions, although their direct contribution to venom gene evolution remains poorly understood. The Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) gene family is one of the most important components of many snake venoms and underlies a well-known venom polymorphism in pitvipers. A venom phenotype produced by the Crotoxin-like heterodimeric neurotoxin formed by two PLA2 subunits, which generates both intra- and interspecific venom variation in pitvipers. Crotoxin-like neurotoxins occur across New World pitvipers and in the Asian genus Gloydius. However, previous genomic studies of the PLA2 genomic architecture in rattlesnakes have produced conflicting hypotheses regarding whether these subunits originated once or multiple times. We analyzed the most comprehensive genomic dataset of New World pitvipers to investigate the origin of Crotoxin-like genes. Using a phylogenomic reconstruction reconciled with a species tree, we found support for a single origin of both subunits in the MRCA of Gloydius and New World pitvipers, along with a second independent origin of the acidic subunit in Ophryacus. We proposed a novel hypothesis in which current rattlesnake PLA2 haplotypes arose through consecutive duplications and lineage-specific gene losses, supported by phylogenomic patterns and conserved TE–gene associations. Luke Rose
933: Natural history collections contain a majority of the described snake diversity, yet many taxa, particularly those known only from holotypes or historical material, remain excluded from modern phylogenomic analyses. Recent advances in sequencing degraded DNA provide an opportunity to integrate these critical specimens into evolutionary studies. Here, I discuss how modern studies can leverage phylogenomic datasets with respect to including historically inaccessible material. As one example, I discuss a recent study (Bernstein et al. 2026) focused on a taxonomically confusing group of Old World colubrids (Lycodon, Stegonotus, and allies) that combines target capture of ~5000 nuclear loci from fresh tissues with mitochondrial data derived from formalin-fixed museum specimens to allow us to better understand the best taxonomic practices for the group combined with its historical biogeography. This work includes the first well-resolved phylogeny for this clade and reveals an origin in Southeast Asia, followed by dispersal across Sundaland and adjacent regions. Incorporating degraded museum DNA substantially improves taxon sampling, enabling inclusion of lineages otherwise absent, an issue that has historically limited snake systematic studies. This work demonstrates that modern sequencing approaches allow for both advancements in snake systematics and broader evolution-based questions. By unlocking genomic data from historical specimens, we can directly link names to evolutionary lineages, test longstanding biogeographic hypotheses, and refine species boundaries. I also discuss more broadly in how this approach reframes snakes as a powerful system for investigating macroevolutionary patterns, showing how integrating legacy collections with genomic data enables more accurate inferences of biodiversity through time. Dan Rubenstein
934: Heat-sensing pits have evolved multiple times in boas (Boidae), and evidence suggests that many boas without external pits are still capable of detecting infrared radiation via specialized nerve structures in their labial scales. However, little research has been done on the morphology of these heat-sensing structures in boas, despite being such a phenotypically diverse and ecologically important feature across many members of the family. Advances in imaging technology (e.g., SEM, XCT) provide new ways of studying anatomy, both external and internal, allowing deeper understanding of morphological evolution than has been previously possible. Here, we explore the morphology of heat-sensing structures among boas with and without pits in the Neotropics and Madagascar at multiple anatomical scales. Using scanning electron microscopy on samples taken primarily from preserved museum specimens, we examine the distinctive ultrastructure of labial scales. We also use XCT scanning to compare the skeletal anatomy associated with the innervation of heat-sensing structures. These methods allow us to not only describe and quantify the morphology of these snakes with respect to heat-sensing organs, in some species for the first time, but to compare across convergent lineages in order to understand how these complex, multivariate structures have evolved across boas. Amber L. Singh
935: The evolution of novel phenotypes requires the evolution of new gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and may involve the evolution of new gene regulatory elements. These GRNs are comprised of several components including cis-regulatory (e.g., enhancers and promoters) and trans-regulatory elements (e.g., transcription factors). Together, these elements coordinate the expression of genes, and variation in the function of these GRNs manifests in phenotypic variation. Here, we focus on snake venom gene regulatory evolution as a model for exploring the evolution of novel GRNs. Over 60MY of snake venom evolution, distinct lineages of snakes have differentially recruited and expanded over 20 distinct gene families into venom systems, making them ideal models for studying GRN evolution. Indeed, members of the front-fanged venomous snakes: elapids and viperids exhibit substantial variation in venom gene expression patterns which manifest in drastic differences in the composition and physiological effects of their venoms. Recent work has advanced our understanding of the gene regulatory mechanisms that control the expression of snake venom genes within vipers; however, most studies that have investigated the gene regulatory mechanisms that control the expression of elapid venom genes are limited to select venom gene families and rely on gene expression data alone. Therefore, we integrate comparative analyses of diverse functional genomic data to trace the origins of elapid venom GRNs. Through this integrative approach, we explore the evolutionary origins of (I) cis-regulatory elements underlying venom gene expression, (II) identify suites of TFs that were differentially recruited by these cis-regulatory elements, and (III) identify shared and distinct signaling pathways that were recruited by viperid and elapid lineages to regulate venom gene expression. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding how novel GRNs evolve through a combination of diverse genomic mechanisms and how cis-regulatory sequences transition from early-stage to more well-developed and highly regulated cis-regulatory sequences. Matt Smukall Matthew Smukall; Alexandra Draime; Wyatt Albert; Alina Hussey; Jennifer Wyffels; Christopher Malinowski;
936: This study documents the first recorded case of lordosis in Colorado snapper (Lutjanus colorado) collected in Puerto Chale, Baja California Sur, México, representing the first record of this skeletal anomaly for the species in Mexican waters. Records of skeletal deformities in wild fish populations are scarce, despite the occurrence of abnormalities such as lordosis, kyphosis, and kypholordosis, which may severely affect swimming performance and reduce survival. Skeletal deformities are usually linked with both genetic and environmental stress factors, including poor water quality, contaminant exposure, and suboptimal management conditions. Biometric measurements and radiographic analyses were taken on the malformed specimen and on a morphologically normal individual of the same species to confirm the presence and characteristics of lordosis.Este estudio documenta el primer caso registrado de lordosis en el pargo colorado (Lutjanus colorado) colectado en Puerto Chale, Baja California Sur, México, representando el primer registro de esta anomalía esquelética para la especie en aguas mexicanas. Los registros de deformidades esqueléticas en poblaciones de peces silvestres son escasos, a pesar de la ocurrencia de anormalidades como lordosis, cifosis y cifolordosis, las cuales pueden afectar severamente el desempeño natatorio y reducir la supervivencia. Las deformidades esqueléticas usualmente están relacionadas con factores de estrés genéticos y ambientales, incluyendo mala calidad del agua, exposición a contaminantes y condiciones de manejo subóptimas. Se tomaron mediciones biométricas y análisis radiográficos en el espécimen malformado y en un individuo morfológicamente normal de la misma especie para confirmar la presencia y características de la lordosis. Jonas Andrade-Santos
937: Ostariophysan fishes are comprised of two major groups, the remarkably speciose Otophysi (>12,000 sp.) and the relatively depauperate Anotophysi (41 sp.). Members of the Otophysi are characterized by many unique and highly complex synapomorphies, including several skeletal modifications related to the otophysan key innovation: the Weberian apparatus, an elaborate sound reception system. Unsurprisingly, there have been numerous anatomical investigations of the skeleton in Otophysans, including its development. However, comparable studies of the skeleton in Anotophysi are notably scarce despite potentially contributing to our understanding of the evolution of the Weberian apparatus. To further our understanding of the skeletal system of ostariophysan fishes and to determine the role heterochrony may have played in the evolution of the Weberian apparatus, we document the development of the entire skeleton in a species of Kneria, a representative anotophysan. Our investigation is based on 128 cleared and double stained individuals ranging in size from 4.4 mm notochord length to 26.8 mm standard length. We examined and scored each individual for the presence/absence of 158 skeletal elements and generated an ossification sequence for the entire skeleton. This sequence, along with those available for otophysan fishes, was used to check for sequence heterochrony. Our results demonstrate a heterochronic shift in the sequence of ossification for the elements of the Weberian apparatus in Otophysi compared to their homologous counterparts in Kneria. This indicates a potential evolutionary link between heterochrony and the most important morphological and functional novelty of the largest group of freshwater fishes on the planet. Kole M. Kubicek
938: Pacific newts (Taricha spp.) are poisonous salamanders common to the west coast of North America. Taricha are chemically defended against predation by tetrodotoxin (TTX), a paralytic neurotoxin that is synthesized by bacteria living on their skin and is most concentrated in cutaneous granular glands. The existing literature shows a predictable pattern in toxicity across rough-skinned newt (Taricha granulosa) development, wherein TTX is present in eggs, declines after hatching and during larval development, reaches its lowest point in newly metamorphosed newts, and then dramatically increases in the first three years of adulthood. Granular glands develop during metamorphosis, and amphibian skin microbiomes typically change dramatically at this time as well, suggesting a relationship between morphological and microbial developmental changes and TTX acquisition. We seek to investigate the role and timing of microbial symbiosis and granular gland development in Taricha toxicity. We collected skin biopsies and whole animals of larval, metamorphic, and adult T. granulosa and T. torosa (California newts) found together in a breeding pond in Santa Cruz County, California over the course of three years. Our results narrow the developmental window in which TTX accumulation is known to start in T. torosa and T. granulosa. Additionally, we demonstrate that metamorphosing Taricha have unique distributions of TTX in their tissues and may encounter TTX in their diets. We subsequently investigate changes in microbiome composition, host and microbiome gene expression, and skin morphology across sampled age stages. Emily Peele
939: The Polypteriformes, comprising the genera Polypterus (Bichirs) and Erpeotichthys (reedfish or rope eels) are morphologically primitive African freshwater fishes that represent the basal-most lineage of the Actinopterygii. Because of a combination of retained ancestral and derived characters, polypterids have been of special interest to comparative anatomists ever since their scientific description in the early 19th century. Despite this wealth of research, questions remain regarding the homology of certain elements (e.g., pre-opercle, rostrals) as well as the developmental association of the lateral line canals with underlying bones. Because of the phylogenetic position of Polypteriformes, answering these questions has important implications for our understanding of early actinopterygian evolution. Studies of ontogeny can be useful to address such questions, however, to date most of these have concerned the more species-rich genus in the order, Polypterus, primarily due to the rarity of developmental material for the monotypic genus Erpetoichthys. To further our understanding of the cranial osteology in polypterids and early actinopterygians in general, we generated high-resolution computed tomographic scans of a subset of a unique developmental series of Erpeotichthys comprising 15 stages ranging from 7.2 mm NL to 39.4 mm TL. We document the development of the cranium of Erpetoichthys with an emphasis on those elements for which the homology remains uncertain. Amanda Pinion
940: Telomeres, the ends of chromosomes which shorten with each cell replication cycle, represent a biomarker of cell differentiation in many organisms.
