Stem cells typically have the longest telomeres, with telomere length progressively shortening as cells differentiate. When telomere length reaches a certain threshold, cells become senescent, preventing proliferation of cells that may have acquired deleterious mutations. Salamanders can regenerate most parts of their body and do so through a process of cell dedifferentiation followed by growth of new tissue. Telomere length represents a potential constraint on this process, as differentiated cells with shorter telomeres need to proliferate for regeneration to occur. The presence of senescent cells is essential for regeneration to occur. Telomere length dynamics in salamanders are largely unknown, and salamanders of one family (Salamandridae) have been shown to have noncanonical telomere sequences and an alternate telomere lengthening mechanism. We used a species of Mexican plethodontid salamander, Aquiloeurycea cephalica, to test the hypothesis that telomere length increases during the process of limb regeneration and that telomere shortening leads to the presence of senescent cells that aid regeneration. Using quantitative Fluorescent In-Situ Hybridization (qFISH), we show that this species has the canonical vertebrate telomere sequence and that telomere length increases dramatically during regeneration. Surprisingly, many senescent cells have extremely long telomeres, suggesting that telomere attrition may not be the mechanism responsible for the presence of all senescent cells in regenerating tissue. Our results provide fundamental information on telomere dynamics in a representative of most diverse family of salamanders. Freya Rowland Freya Rowland; Jacques Rinchard; Aimee Reed; Cody Pinger; Catherine Richter; Thea Edwards; Johanna Kraus;
941: The epigenome is critical for integrating environmental signals that mediate the development of phenotypes, yet the epigenetic molecular architecture underlying developmental plasticity is unresolved, partly due to the overreliance on model organisms. Temperature-dependent sex determination (TSD), common in reptiles, exemplifies developmental plasticity, where the conditions experienced during a thermosensitive developmental period directs the bipotential embryonic gonad towards a testicular or ovarian fate. Growing studies of TSD in turtles are revealing its underlying molecular circuitry, pointing to key regulatory roles for the epigenome, but genome-wide investigations remain scarce. To help fill this gap, here we explore turtle chromatin landscapes of early developing turtle embryos. Using CUT&RUN technology, we provide the first genome-wide glimpse of active (H3K4me3) and repressive (H3K27me3) modified-histone deposition landscapes early in embryonic stages of a TSD reptile, the painted turtle (Chrysemys picta). We find evidence of bivalent domains (regions where both modified histones localize) that may mediate the bipotentiality of the early embryo. Additionally, epigenetically regulated genes support a role for primary cilia (sensory organelles found in most cells of eukaryotes) as integrators of signaling pathways known to mediate turtle sexual development, particularly when combined with independent evidence from parallel studies. Overall, the observed epigenomic patterns suggest that modified-histone deposition may contribute to the transcriptional regulation of key signaling pathway that are transduced by primary cilia and underpin sexual development. This initial modified-histone deposition profiling expands our understanding of chromatin dynamics in response to environmental stimuli in turtles, in reptiles, and in TSD vertebrates. Perry Van Wagoner Perry Van Wagoner; Matt Bailey; David Redd; Sam Green; Greg Payne; Loida Fajardo; Emily Anderson; Tommy
942: Controlling aquatic invasive species may be possible by using chemical stimuli to exploit behavioral responses, congregate, and trap them. Electro-olfactograms (EOG) can identify chemical stimuli for fish by assessing physiological responses in the olfactory epithelium. We present the results of multiple studies. First, we present results of EOG and behavioral trials examining four species of invasive carp and their responses to amino acids and a commercial stimulant. Grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella) had greater magnitude EOG responses than bighead (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis); there was marginal evidence that grass carp had greater EOG responses than silver carp (Hypophthalmichthys molitrix). The EOG responses of black carp (Mylopharyngodon piceus) did not significantly differ from the other three species. The primary results of the behavior trials were varying degrees of evidence that grass and silver carp avoided the commercial stimulant. There was also an overall pattern of grass carp being more repelled across stimuli compared to bighead carp. We did not identify clear behavioral responses in black carp. In a separate study, we tested EOG responses of juvenile grass and black carp to bait infusions derived from plant meals, mollusks, and cheese. We did not find overall differences in magnitude of EOG response between grass and black carp. We found more differences among responses to different baits for black carp when compared to grass carp, suggesting potential species specificity. These various physiological and behavioral responses observed among the species and chemical stimuli demonstrate methods for identifying effective chemical stimuli for invasive carp removal efforts. Tonya Wiley
943: In the fish family Poeciliidae, elaborate follicular placentas and extensive placentotrophy have evolved multiple times independently. This repeated evolution of complex placentas was likely accompanied by the evolutionary acquisition of structural complexity in other critical organs, such as the central nervous system. Therefore, the evolution of complex placentas could have been associated with evolutionary increases in brain size. In addition, previous studies have documented that brain size has a direct influence on cognitive abilities, in such a way that larger brains are associated with greater problem-solving abilities. We tested the hypothesis that species with elaborate placentas (placentotrophic species) should exhibit greater brain mass and, as a result, better cognitive abilities than species with simple placentas (lecithotrophic species). For this purpose, we measured brain dry mass and conducted sequential task-solving assays in the laboratory to assess learning and memory in six species, three placentotrophic (Phalloptychus januarius, Poeciliopsis prolifica, and Poeciliopsis turneri) and three lecithotrophic (Poecilia reticulata, Poecilia velifera, and Xiphophorus hellerii). We found that size-adjusted average brain mass differed widely among species but without an evident distinction between placentotrophic and lecithotrophic species. We also observed differences among species in cognitive abilities, but these differences were opposite to our expectations: lecithotrophic species solved the tests faster. All six species showed information retention for at least 72 hours, without differences between placentotrophic and lecithotrophic species. Our findings suggest that brain size and cognitive abilities might be associated with ecological factors, such as structural complexity of the habitat, rather than with placental complexity. Wong 黃俊儒Philip
944: Some areas of the Neotropical region are still poorly studied in terms of freshwater fish diversity, and the Brazilian Northeast is one of them. This is mainly because it is considered a dry region with few rivers and, consequently, low diversity. As a result, several knowledge shortfalls can be identified regarding the freshwater fishes of the Brazilian Northeast, particularly the Linnean, Wallacean, Darwinian, Hutchinsonian, and Raunkiæran shortfalls. To reduce the deficit of ecological information, we conducted a survey of the distribution and occurrence of freshwater fish species in the Brazilian Northeast and linked these data to a matrix of ecological traits. By crossreferencing both datasets, we were able to obtain ecological information for almost all species in the region. Using these data, we performed a descriptive analysis of the main ecological characteristics of freshwater fish species in the Brazilian Northeast. The ichthyofauna of the Brazilian Northeast is composed almost entirely of small- and medium-sized species that occur mainly in clear-water rivers draining sediments from the Brazilian Shield. Most of these species inhabit small, low-order rivers, reflecting the high prevalence of temporary rivers and streams in the region. Furthermore, the assemblage is dominated by lotic species that preferentially occupy the water column and feed on microbenthic organisms. This pattern is consistent across all ecoregions into which the northeastern basins are divided. João Marcelo Abreu
945: The Neotropical freshwater fish fauna (NFF) is the most diverse continental fauna on Earth’s, with >6,300 species representing 1/6th of all fishes. We use four whole-fauna datasets (a time-calibrated phylogeny, georeferenced distributions to bioregions, a 42-trait ecomatrix including body size, and body shape assessed by 3D photogrammetry, in conjunction with a detailed paleogeographic chronology, to trace NFF assembly from its Cretaceous roots to the modern landscapes. Although NFF species occur roughly equally in uplands and lowlands, ~83% belong to clades with upland ancestral origins, supporting an hypothesis in which Gondwanan fragmentation and tectonic uplifts provided the initial diversification crucible. Net diversification rates remained broadly constant for over 100 million years, with small accelerations associated with marine regressions at the Eocene–Oligocene transition and the Late Miocene formation of the transcontinental Amazon river. Ecospace analyses identify river size as the dominant ecological axis, with a small/large-river bipartition evolving convergently across all major clades. The NFF further owes its richness to a general lack of major extinctions in the Late Cenozoic. Most (~90%) species belong to the “Big Nine” NFF clades whose formative ecophysiological traits, small body size, specialized trophic food-web positions, and high speciation-extinction turnover, amplified responses to geographic perturbations. This combination of ancient origins, perennial river-capture dynamics, episodic paleogeographic events, and low extinction generated the characteristic NFF profile: high local richness, high beta diversity, and high functional redundancy, an irreplaceable archive now facing severe threat from deforestation, river impoundment, and climate change. Juan Albornoz
946: The scientific communication system has shifted from subscription-based models to Open Access, enabling the free dissemination of scientific literature. However, publication costs have been largely transferred to authors through Article Processing Charges (APCs) under the “gold open access” model. While this transition has expanded access, it has also contributed to the commodification of publishing and the concentration of control among major commercial publishers, exacerbating inequalities. Concurrently, policies promoting transparency in research, ethical compliance, and animal use have gained prominence, while Artificial Intelligence is reshaping research practices and introducing new ethical challenges. Within this context, Neotropical Ichthyology, the journal of the Brazilian Society of Ichthyology (SBI), was used as a case study to evaluate financial sustainability and the implementation of transparency practices. Annual funding data were compiled to quantify total financial support and the proportion of operational costs covered by funding agencies over time. A longitudinal survey of published articles assessed author compliance with transparency requirements, including disclosures of conflicts of interest, author contributions, funding sources, ethical approval, animal use, and Artificial Intelligence. The compiled data were analyzed in relation to journal performance metrics, including Impact Factor and annual citation rates. Results indicate that funding has declined and become irregular since 2015, reducing cost coverage and compromising longterm sustainability, thereby necessitating the adoption of APCs. In contrast, compliance with transparency requirements has progressively improved over time. A significant correlation was detected between transparency practices and performance metrics, which have increased in recent years. These findings highlight the need for coordinated strategies to ensure the sustainability of non-profit scientific journals. Jose Birindelli
947: Neotropical freshwater fishes represent one of the most species rich vertebrate assemblages on Earth, yet the macroevolutionary processes shaping their remarkable diversity remain poorly understood. Stream order, a proxy for river size and hydrodynamic complexity, has long been hypothesized to structure fish communities, but its role in driving morphological evolution across broad taxonomic scales has rarely been tested. Here I examined morphological disparity in body shape across 600+ Neotropical freshwater fish species spanning large rivers, small streams, and species occurring in both habitat types. Using phylogenetic comparative methods and size-corrected body shape measurements, I tested whether stream order predicts morphological diversity and whether differences in disparity reflect evolutionary constraint or ecological filtering. I found that large river species exhibit significantly lower morphological disparity than small stream species, a pattern that was robust to differences in species richness between stream orders. Importantly, evolutionary rates and the relationship between stream order and morphology did not differ significantly between groups, suggesting that reduced disparity in large rivers is not driven by slower evolution. Instead, our results are consistent with habitat filtering, whereby the hydrodynamically demanding and structurally homogeneous conditions of large rivers selectively admit a narrower range of body plans from the total species pool. These findings suggest that habitat characteristics of large river systems act as a filter on morphological diversity, with important implications for understanding how environmental gradients shape the distribution of phenotypic variation across one of the world's most diverse vertebrate radiations. Edward Burress Edward Burress; Maya Stokes; Maria Alves Napolitani; Brooke Bodensteiner; Fabricio de Andrade Caxito; Frederico Henning
948: Hoplias is a genus of Neotropical predatory freshwater fishes that lives in lentic and lotic environments across most drainages of lower Central and South America, from Costa Rica to northern Argentina. Currently, 15 species are recognized as valid. Several mitochondrial lineages have been proposed as representing potentially undescribed species; however, an integrative evolutionary framework is needed to clarify the patterns of diversity within the group. Here, we integrate DNA barcode sequences, a phylogenomic dataset of ultraconserved elements (UCEs), morphological information from micro-CT scans, and broad geographic sampling to investigate the evolutionary history and assess species diversity within Hoplias. Our results, including novel comparative morphological data, partially support the recognition of the traditional morphology-based species groups (H. lacerdae, H. aimara, and H. malabaricus groups) as monophyletic clades. We also identify several potentially undescribed species in regions west and east of the Andes Cordillera, with distinct candidate species on each side, and clarify the geographic ranges of some species. Hoplias malabaricus sensu stricto is redefined as having a distribution restricted to the region east of the Andes. Furthermore, comparisons across datasets underscore the need for caution in the recognition of species within the H. malabaricus group, particularly when based on a single mitochondrial marker (COI) and overlapping diagnostic morphological characters. Despite recent efforts in the taxonomy of the genus, our results indicate a poorly resolved species diversity and offer guidelines to integrate the taxonomy and evolutionary history of Hoplias. Kevin W. Conway
949: Many behaviors of tropical fishes remain poorly documented because they are expressed at night and in complex habitats where direct observation is difficult. Weakly electric fishes offer a rare opportunity to overcome these limits because their electric organ discharges (EODs) can be recorded non-invasively and continuously in the field. We describe the use of microcontroller-based autonomous EOD loggers to quantify activity and behavior in gymnotiform fishes from rainforest streams. These approaches reveal previously undocumented behaviors across multiple timescales. At short timescales (seconds–minutes), we documented predator–prey encounters between electric eels and knifefish. These involved prey evasion and rapid, reversible suppression of EODs by both predator and prey, yielding a form of bidirectional “electric stealth.” At intermediate timescales (minutes–hours), recordings revealed diel variation in EOD rate and structured patterns of movement. In one species we observed peaks in activity soon after dusk and before dawn consistent with lateral shifts between refuge and foraging habitats. At longer timescales (days–weeks), activity is strongly modulated by moonlight in some species, with foraging restricted to dark periods and shaped by both immediate illumination and endogenous anticipation of moonlight timing. The strength of these circalunar activity rhythms is associated with interspecific differences in eye size, with weaker lunar suppression in larger-eyed species, consistent with better detection and evasion of approaching predators. Autonomous EOD loggers provide a powerful tool for studying behavior, habitat use, and biodiversity, including long-term monitoring. They also enable documentation of behaviors that remain inaccessible in most other tropical fishes. Andrew Crawford
950: The middle Xingu River is a globally unique, highly threatened ecosystem characterized by clear water, vast bedrock rapids, fine-scale habitat heterogeneity, and recent large-scale alteration by the BeloMonte hydroelectric dam complex. This dam and a proposed gold mine threaten an exceptionally diverse and evolutionarily specialized endemic fish fauna. Among the most charismatic and celebrated components of this fauna is an assemblage of over 40 species of plecos or suckermouth armored catfishes (family Loricariidae). To investigate how habitat structure might affect population structure in this system, we generated genome-wide SNP data from approximately 360 specimens of three closely related loricariid species: Parancistrus nudiventris, Spectracanthicus punctatissimus, and S. zuanoni. We also measured 19 dimensions of head and body shape from 178 of these specimens. Phylogenomic analyses recovered eight strongly supported, densely represented, and variably distributed clades, one of which aligned with the S. zuanoni phenotype, two with the P. nudiventris phenotype, and six with the S. punctatissimus phenotype. Multivariate morphometric analyses further support the hypothesis that several of the S. punctatissimus clades represent distinct and diagnosable species with restricted ranges within the middle Xingu. Overall, our results highlight that significant unrecognized genomic, and potentially taxonomic, diversity resides within the middle and lower Xingu River, especially among smaller-bodied, philopatric species such as loricariid catfishes. Our findings also underscore the critical importance of proactive specimen and tissue collection prior to major environmental disturbance in tropical river systems, as exemplified in this case by the NSF-funded iXingu Project. Alanna Frick
951: The Uruguay River basin, including parts of Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay, has long been considered a biodiversity hotspot in part due to uncharacteristically high species richness of loricariids (Armored Suckermouth Catfish). Within loricariids native to this basin, the genus Rineloricaria represents 13 species which were all described via morphological characteristics only. The validity of previously described Rineloricaria species within this drainage has long been doubted due to vast and complicated morphological variation, no easily interpretable taxonomist key, and next to no available sequence data available for Rineloricaria accessions from the Uruguay River basin. Using genetic sequencing data from two mitochondrial genes (COI & CytB) and one nuclear gene (RAG2) for 125 Rineloricaria individuals from various collection points throughout the basin, we reevaluated species boundaries within this group and found that, despite high morphological variation within Rineloricaria of this basin, phylogenetic and MOTU analyses suggest seven total valid species. Furthermore, certain phenotypic traits which were previously suggested to be informative in identifying and describing species of Rineloricaria throughout the neotropics were found to be variable within closely related individuals in redescribed species from the same collection points. Beyond well supported species descriptions and suggestions for traits that may be more phylogenetically informative in this speciose group, we provide a key of identification for all described species of Rineloricaria found in the Uruguay River basin. Kristyn Gorton
952: The Río Usumacinta is a prominent river drainage and biodiversity hotspot in the northern Neotropics of Middle America that harbors incredible diversity and endemism of fishes and other organisms in the region. The headwaters of this system are home to several endemic species distributed across multiple intermontane basins. The genus Scolichthys and its two species, S. greenwayi and S. iota, were described by Donn Rosen in 1967. The genus is defined by various anatomical characters, including a thornlike bony tip at the end of ray three in the gonopodium of males. Scolichthys greenwayi is known from a few localities in the upper reaches of Río Chixoy, a headwater system of Río Usumacinta, and has been included in recent large-scale phylogenetic analyses of the Poeciliidae where it was recovered closely related to the genus Carlhubbsia and Phallichthys fairweatheri. Since first collected in 1963, Scolichthys iota, a small livebearing species with standard length of < 22mm, has been scientifically known only from the type specimens, all from the same initial sampling event. Our ongoing fieldwork throughout Guatemala recently resulted in the rediscovery of S. iota from a field site near the type locality for the species. Low-coverage whole genomes (10X) were sequenced for two specimens of S. iota and one S. greenwayi, and ultraconserved elements were extracted and incorporated into a large genomic poeciliid dataset to study phylogenetic placement and biogeographic history. Phylogenetic analyses will be discussed, as well as observations on the ecology and status of this enigmatic Neotropical species. Jess McQuigg
953: Phylogenetic studies indicated the monophyly of rosy tetras and proposed the subfamily Megalamphodinae within the newly proposed Acestrorhamphidae of Characiformes. However, research has only used a few specimens of each group. We investigated the phylogenetics and morphology of rosy tetras using ultraconserved elements (UCEs), mitochondrial genomes, external morphology, and osteology using microcomputed tomography data. Phylogenomic evidence indicates that the red-base tetra Hemigrammus stictus Durbin, 1909 belongs to a new genus-level clade in Megalamphodinae whereas the type species of Hemigrammus belongs to Pristellinae. Phylogenies agree in the composition of Brittanichthys, Makunaima, Megalamphodus, Paracheirodon, Petitella, and new genera for Hemigrammus stictus and the Hyphessobrycon pulchripinnis clade. The new genus for H. stictus possesses a dense layer of erythrophores enveloping the caudal peduncle and surrounding areas and a posteriorly placed, oval-shaped humeral mark with a high density of melanophores in both live and preserved specimens. Corrections are made in the type series of Durbin at FMNH, which mistakenly included specimens of curimatids, iguanodectids, and other acestrorhamphids. We redescribe H. stictus using type and non-type specimens from the Amazonas, Negro, Branco, Xingu, Atabapo, Ventuari, Meta, Orinoco, Essequibo, Berbice, Demerara, Mahaica, and Rupununi rivers. The intense layer of erythrophores is synapomorphic for the new genus, Petitella, Brittanichthys, and Paracheirodon, and µCT data reveals distinctive anatomical modifications in the neurocranium, including a pointed posterodorsal region and a laterally enlarged, square-shaped anteroventral section of the antorbital. Future research will examine the genomic fingerprints associated with the development of erythrophores that seem relevant to the evolution of Megalamphodinae. Joseph R. Mendelson III
954: Most textbook examples of adaptive radiation involve a physically discrete arena such as islands or lakes that provide access to novel resources or escape from antagonists upon their colonization. Rivers by contrast, are highly hierarchical networks that lack obvious discrete arenas, yet host adaptive radiations. Here, we demonstrate that recent (<1 My) parallel adaptive radiations of riverine pike cichlids (Crenicichla) throughout parts of the La Plata River basin were catalyzed by swaths of basalt within the Paraná Large Igneous Province of South America that enabled an expanded ecological repertoire. Basalt weathers rapidly, producing nutrient-rich aquatic environments, including high phosphorus concentrations that promote primary productivity and ions that support muscle function and the maintenance of bone and teeth. Lineages distributed over basalt transition among feeding ecologies 100-fold faster and the morphological and mechanical properties of their jaws exhibit 10- to 20fold faster rates of evolution than other lineages. Basaltic areas harbor feeding specialists that exhibit higher performance than species associated with other rock types. Our results highlight that abiotic processes like weathering can spur exceptional biological processes such as adaptive radiation. Lee Burrows
955: Many lineages of vertebrates have evolved enlarged fang-like teeth that serve a number of functions. This includes a variety of lineages of ray-finned fishes, in which these fang-like teeth have been hypothesized to be used for piercing and restraining prey, in addition to other functions. This study explores the repeated evolution of fangs in context of a densely-sampled phylogeny to infer how many times fang-like teeth have independently evolved across the evolutionary history of ray-finned fishes. The repeated evolution of fangs is also investigated in the context of other evolutionary patterns across ray-finned fishes. Drew Davis
956: The exploration of biodiversity across complementary axes (e.g., taxonomic, phylogenetic, functional) is important to understand evolutionary trajectories. Drivers of genetic diversity can be categorized as intrinsic (e.g., life history, population size) and extrinsic (e.g., range size, environmental). Previous research at different taxonomic and geographic scales has found contrasting results regarding the influence of intrinsic and extrinsic factors on genetic diversity. Here we explore the role of species’ age and geographic range in shaping present-day genetic diversity. Specifically, we investigate if genetic diversity is higher in older species and whether it is positively correlated with the size of their geographic range. We used the northern Neotropical cichlid genus Thorichthys as a model system. This genus is composed of nine valid species that diversified between the Late Miocene and the Pliocene. While some species are widely distributed across multiple river basins, others are restricted to the headwaters of a single river basin. We generated a nuclear genomic dataset for all species of Thorichthys using triple enzyme restriction site-associated DNA (3RAD), and assembled a mitochondrial dataset (cytochrome b) from novel and publicly available sequence data. We estimated species divergence times and the age of the most recent common ancestor, and calculated nucleotide diversity for each species and dataset to test their correlation and explore geographical patterns of diversity. Our results shed light on processes that generate and shape genetic diversity using molecular markers with different modes of inheritance and effective population sizes in Neotropical freshwater fishes from a biodiversity hotspot. Jack Elstner Jack Elstner; Emily Spurgeon; Patrick Rex; Elizabeth Jahn; Zach Merson; Whitney Jones; Lauren Faulkner; Ryan
957: Extremely high sea levels in the Late Cretaceous offered vast new habitats for expansion and diversification among all types of fishes. Fishes of the global seas of the Late Cretaceous have a rich biodiversity, mostly represented in North America in the well-studied open ocean deposits of the Western Interior Seaway (WIS) of Kansas and Nebraska. Fewer fishes have been recovered on the near-shore deposits of the WIS. We are highlighting osteichthyan remains from the Cretaceous Coleraine Formation of the Mesabi Iron Range, northern Minnesota. These fossils were collected and documented as part of the Hill Annex Paleontology Project (HAPP), a collaboration between several institutions to collect, document, preserve, and describe over 50,000 fossil specimens that represent otherwise unknown Cretaceous biodiversity in Minnesota. Fish remains are represented in the HAPP collection mostly by isolated vertebrae, scales and teeth. Some of this material has been identified to multiple fish groups, such as Neopterygii (e.g., Lepisosteiformes, Pycnodontiformes) and Teleostei (e.g., Ichthyodectiformes, Elopiformes, Salmoniformes). More as yet unknown or unidentified species are likely contained in the vast collection, and we continue to sort, prepare, and describe new material. Cara Giordano
958: The Emmelichthyidae (~20 species), commonly known as rovers or rubyfishes, is a demersal family of marine fishes distributed at depths of approximately 100–400 m in tropical and temperate waters. As solitary, planktivorous fishes, emmelichthyids are rarely caught, and little is known about the diversity and evolutionary history of the family. Heemstra and Randall’s (1977) morphological assessment recognized three genera, differentiated by a suite of characters. In contrast, Girard et al. (2024) produced the first targeted molecular analysis of the group based on nine species and recovered two of the three genera as either para- or polyphyletic. Using museum specimens, µCT scans, and molecular data from both modern and historic tissue samples, I examine the evolutionary history of the Emmelichthyidae by integrating phenotypic and genotypic data. I will highlight that the type of data analyzed impacts the recovered phylogenetic topology along with downstream taxonomic implications. Katherine Githens
959: River sturgeons (Scaphirhynchus spp.) have experienced population declines, prompting conservation efforts such as the Island Creation Pilot Project in the Middle Mississippi River (MMR). This project, guided by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's 2000 Biological Opinion, aims to create and monitor habitat for the endangered pallid sturgeon (S. albus) and sympatric shovelnose sturgeon (S. platorynchus). To assess the usage of these habitats by early life stages, we analyzed the diet and feeding ecology of young-of-year sturgeon. During pre-construction monitoring in the Mosenthein and Chester/Thebes Reaches of the MMR, 118 sturgeon were collected in 2025. Gut contents were identified to the lowest practical taxonomic level. While analysis is ongoing, preliminary findings indicate diets reflect preferential feeding in lotic conditions over sandy substrates. Members of the family Chironomidae constitute the vast majority of individuals found in the gut, with pupae of the genus Lopescladius being the most frequent item. Caenid mayflies, predominantly of the genus Cercobrachys, were also common. By analyzing the diets, we can infer microhabitat feeding associations, providing crucial data for evaluating the success of current and future island creation projects. These results will be compared with regional dietary data from the greater Mississippi and Missouri River basins to identify similarities or notable differences in prey consumption, ultimately refining conservation strategies for these vulnerable species. Philip Gould Philip Gould; Brian Tornabene; Robert Fisher; J. Hardin Waddle; Susan Walls; W. Jaime Barichivich; Patrick
960: Subterranean ecosystems host highly specialized and often cryptic biodiversity, yet even intensively studied landscapes may conceal deeply divergent vertebrate lineages. Here we describe a new genus and species of cave-obligate fish discovered in Bobcat Cave, a long-monitored karst system on Redstone Arsenal in northern Alabama, USA. Phylogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial nd2, complete mitochondrial genomes, and the nuclear gene rhodopsin place the new cavefish within Amblyopsidae but reveal deep divergence from all described genera, including extensive lineage-specific degeneration of a vision-related gene. Notably, the new cavefishe occurs in syntopy with the Southern Cavefish (Typhlichthys subterraneus) despite lacking a close phylogenetic relationship, providing evidence for multiple independent evolutionary origins of cave adaptation within a single groundwater system. This discovery highlights persistent detection bias in groundwater ecosystems and demonstrates that cryptic vertebrate diversity can persist even in well-characterized environments. Extreme endemism and restriction to a single cave–aquifer system further underscore the vulnerability of subterranean biodiversity and the importance of integrating evolutionary and conservation perspectives. Arik Hartmann Arik Hartmann; Oleksandra Klynova; Dane Conley; Hailea Boggess; Robert Ossiboff; Bari Hridoy; Lauren Childs;
961: †Diplomystus dentatus Cope, 1877 is one of the most common fishes from the famous Eocene Green River Shale of Wyoming, Utah, and Colorado (USA). It is sold throughout the world in rock shops and adorns many mantelpieces in homes worldwide. It is also the type species of a genus that has attracted at least 30 species names attached to fossils that range in time from Lower Cretaceous through the Miocene. One of the reasons for this plethora of species is that almost any primitive teleostean fish that has obvious dorsal and ventral series of scutes (enlarged, bony elements), coupled with a long anal fin has been referred to the genus. We consider the genus to comprise five species (†D. dentatus, †D. birdi Woodward, 1895, †D. dubertreti Signeux, 1951, and †D. shengliensis Zhang et al., 1985), and recognize its position in †Ellimichthyiformes, the sister group of Clupeiformes. The systematics of basal clupeomorphs have been studied in many papers over the last 10 years, following discovery or redescription of several fossil taxa included within †Ellimichthyiformes. Given contrasting results in studies that have significant overlap in terms of taxonomic sampling, there is still much to learn about the anatomy and systematics of †ellimichthyiform fishes. Considering the large number of available specimens of †D. dentatus and the central part that this species has played in discussions of relationships of primitive clupeomorph fishes it is surprising that it remains comparatively poorly described. This paper is an attempt to fill this void by providing a full description of the species based on many newly prepared specimens. Additionally, we redescribe †D. birdi, supplementing the initial brief description. We also add comparative notes on †D. dubertreti based on observations from newly prepared and examined material and taxonomic notes on †D. shengliensis and an indeterminate member of the genus from the English Chalk. It is hoped these data will provide a solid base for future studies of the systematic analysis of †Ellimichthyiformes. Annsli Hilton
962: Among the most imperiled sturgeon worldwide are those in the genus Pseudoscaphirhynchus (Acipenseridae), represented by three small freshwater species endemic to the Aral Sea Basin. Pseudoscaphirhynchus fedtschenkoi, the Syr Darya Shovelnose Sturgeon. is endemic to the Syr Darya drainage and is critically endangered. The historical range included Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan from the upper Kara Darya downstream to the lower reaches of the Syr Darya. The Syr Darya watershed has experienced extensive water extraction, damming and agricultural pollution. The last verified collection of P. fedtschenkoi was in 1968. Our first expedition to search for this Lost Species occurred in December 2019 in Kazakhstan above and below the Shardara Reservoir. A large diversity of native fishes were captured with a trammel net, but no sturgeon. Interviews with fisherman indicated that several P. fedtschenkoi were recently collected. We revisited the Syr Darya in May 2025 using trammel nets, seines, and eDNA samples to search throughout Uzbekistan, just into Kyrgyzstan, and in Kazakhstan above the Shardara Reservoir. No sturgeon were collected, and very few fishes were captured in the lower Syr Darya proper in Uzbekistan; most were invasive species, a sharp contrast to the large diversity of native fishes, collected in 2019. More fishes, including native species, were collected upstream of Tajikistan in the Fergana Valley. Analyses of the eDNA samples did not produce any positive hits for P. fedtschenkoi. We will return to the region in 2026 to continue the search for this ghost sturgeon. Bernie Kuhajda Bernie Kuhajda; Stephanie Chance; Emily Culp; Helaina Gomez; Drew Hardy; Abbey Holsopple; Teresa Israel;
963: Environmental DNA (eDNA) has become a widely used tool for monitoring biodiversity in aquatic ecosystems. However, each aquatic ecosystem has a unique eDNA ecology. This study aims to test longitudinal variation in species diversity in the Tickfaw, Amite, and Blind rivers, and their terminus, Lake Maurepas, located in southeast Louisiana. These rivers are shallow, low gradient, slow-moving, and heavily impacted by high sediment loads. Lake Maurepas is a shallow, brackish lake that is part of the greater Lake Pontchartrain basin. We hypothesize that fish diversity in the lower reaches will be higher due to the overlap of river and lake associated species, as well as cumulative species input from downstream drift of genetic material. To address this, water samples were taken at 10 river kilometers (rkm) intervals starting at the mouth of the river, and extending 50 rkm upstream. At each site, surface water samples were collected across the river channel (river left, center, and river right) in triplicate to determine the homogeneity of fish assemblage at each sampling location. We hypothesize that samples collected at the same site will have similar species richness values and assemblage structure compared to other sites. Increased sample replication is expected to improve fish detections, especially for less abundant taxa, and reduce false positives. Environmental DNA was extracted from the water samples, a 12S (mtDNA) fragment was amplified, and the recovered sequences were then analyzed using the command-line version of the MiFish Pipeline and R Studio. Cam Oathout
964: Understanding why some lineages across the Tree of Life diversified more extensively than others is a central question in evolutionary biology. Since the start of the 21st century, increasing accessibility of whole genomes for non-model organisms has catalyzed a renaissance in studies of evolutionary diversification, illuminating genomic features that underpin speciation and phenotypic diversification. Intriguingly, hybridization, long thought to act as a homogenizing force capable of stalling diversification, has been identified as a common feature of many classic examples of adaptive radiation. Empirical and theoretical research suggest hybridization could play an important role in promoting diversification by producing new allelic combinations, phenotypic and functional novelty, and even new species. However, the pervasiveness of hybridization in adaptive radiation remains uncertain. Here, we investigate the role that ancient hybridization may have played in driving the exceptional diversification of notothenioid fishes in Antarctica’s Southern Ocean. Leveraging a dataset of over 500 whole genomes sequenced for 100 of the ~110 valid notothenioid species, we present the most taxonomically complete phylogenetic hypothesis for Antarctic notothenioids to date. Because many early divergences in the phylogeny have historically evaded confident resolution, we also quantified gene tree discordance to evaluate support for alternative topologies. This robust phylogenomic framework was then used to identify genome-wide signatures of introgression among early-diverging lineages, as well as between major lineages and their nonAntarctic notothenioid relatives. Collectively, these results illuminate the role of hybridization in generating Antarctic notothenioid diversity and clarify its broader importance in adaptive radiation. Christopher Parkinson
965: Trimma is one of the most species-rich genera of Gobiidae, with new species described annually. However, scientists continue to struggle to identify morphological characters for diagnosing species and resolving their relationships. Although niche partitioning and local endemism may explain the high diversity of cryptobenthic fishes, the role of morphological characters and uncommon behavioral adaptations in shaping goby evolution remains poorly understood. Here, we examine the phylogeny of Trimma using hundreds of ultraconserved elements and reconstruct the evolution of key morphological and behavioral traits. Trimma comprises three major clades and two early-diverging lineages, while a fourth clade previously assigned to Trimma was recovered as the sister group to Priolepis, and Paratrimma was inferred to be nested within Trimma. Ancestral state reconstructions indicate that the ancestors of Trimma, which lacked a caudal spot, had a solitary, benthic lifestyle. The presence of a caudal spot evolved multiple times within one of the three Trimma clades, whereas the ability to hover and form schools evolved only once, though with some reversals, within the same clade. Our findings further suggest that both behavioral traits influenced the evolution of a caudal spot, with foraging behavior also driving the evolution of social behavior. Overall, this study provides new insights into the taxonomic challenges within pygmy gobies and helps refine the number of valid species of Trimma. It also shows that the transition to hovering and schooling behaviors may represent key innovations shaping the diversification of Trimma. Daniela Rojas-Cañizales Daniela Rojas-Cañizales; Raúl García-Varela; Héctor Barrios-Garrido; Jessica Kahler; Raymond Carthy; Vanessa
966: The freshwater fish composition is well studied in Singapore, or so was thought. A very cryptic burrowing catfish genus Encheloclarias was only discovered in 2022 (206 years after the founding of modern Singapore). This talk will cover this intriguing fish and its congeneric species found only in Southeast Asia’s fastest disappearing habitat – peat and freshwater swamp forest. A mix of serendipity and technology hastened the publication of this discovery (published 6 months after its discovery) and put Singapore on the global map for IUCN Red List of freshwater fishes. Preliminary data on its phylogeny will be briefly discussed. Milton Tan
967: Correlated fluctuations in abundance across space, termed spatial synchrony, is a ubiquitous phenomenon across many taxa. Synchrony occurs due to dispersal among populations, synchronized or mobile predators, or spatially correlated environmental variation, and often produce spatial patterns of declining levels of synchrony as geographic distances increase between populations. Amphibians, however, often defy many of these expected patterns of spatial synchrony: they often exhibit asynchrony among local populations and do not show declines with increasing distance among populations - at least for the handful of studies on amphibian synchrony. Amphibian’s divergence from other taxa could occur for several reasons, including local unsynchronized factors overriding typical synchrony-inducing mechanisms or limited dispersal abilities. However, the absence of synchrony could also be due to analytical choices that could obscure synchrony patterns. Recent advances in the analytical methods available allow for the investigation of more complex spatial and temporal patterns in spatial synchrony, which can reveal hidden patterns and mechanisms of this important process. I demonstrate these tools using a long-term data set on a wood frog (Rana sylvatica) metapopulation from Missouri, USA. Low levels of synchrony were apparent among populations using standard analytical tools, whereas other techniques demonstrate significant timescale specific synchrony. Furthermore, synchrony beyond simple distance-decay was also apparent: population clusters were synchronized but unrelated to their geographic distance. Overall, we demonstrate ways in which long-term datasets can be leveraged to better describe metapopulation synchrony among amphibian populations which can enable a better understanding of threats to metapopulation persistence. Zullette Andrade Zullette Andrade González; Jesús Rodríguez Romero; Leonardo Abitia Cárdenas; Juana López Martínez; Claudia
968: Metapopulation dynamics can play an important role in the success of conservation efforts. We used a capture-mark-recapture study to investigate the factors involved in the colonization and population dynamics of smallmouth salamanders (Ambystoma texanum) and unisexual Ambystoma salamanders during a multi-year wetland restoration project. As part of wetland mitigation efforts in a major infrastructure project, five new wetlands were built near a single existing wetland. We conducted our study before, during, and after the construction of the restored wetlands. Over the course of the study, the overall abundance of salamanders across the entire metapopulation increased, demonstrating the success of the restoration. However, the dynamics underlying this success were complex. Each restored wetland exhibited different patterns of increase from each other and from the original wetland; there was no overall pattern of synchrony. Further, larval density and size varied between wetlands and between years, such that each wetland had different years with high larval performance. Despite the close proximity of the wetlands, most adults (~80%) did not move between different wetlands. Dispersal patterns were similar between wetlands, and similar across years. These results suggest that part of the reason for the success of this restoration project was the heterogeneity in characteristics between wetlands, that allowed each wetland to be successful in different years under different weather conditions. Martin Benavides Martin Benavides; Elizabeth Clark; Jason Adolf; Michael Frisk; Oliver Shipley; Jeff Kneebone; Nick Piscitelli;
969: Habitat restoration is often the main action taken to work towards recovery of imperiled species. Implementing successful restoration for species that function as metapopulations can be challenging because the impact of restoration hinges on patch connectivity and local efforts may be unsuccessful if conditions for population viability are not met at the landscape scale. Reticulated Flatwoods Salamanders (Ambystoma bishopi) breed in ephemeral wetlands that were once abundant across the southeastern U.S. but have been lost to drainage, development, and degradation. Here, we examined optimal restoration strategies for two sites that could support flatwoods salamander metapopulations. We used remotely-sensed data to identify potential breeding wetlands and delineate habitat conditions within each wetland. We then identified wetland patches that made the largest contributions to metapopulation capacity, examining a variety of potential restoration scenarios. Our results indicated that fully restoring all wetlands would create a two- to three-fold increase in the number of connected breeding sites. Given limited resources, optimal restoration strategies depended on the landscape context and spatial distribution of wetlands under consideration. At one site, focusing restoration on partially degraded wetlands led to the largest increase in metapopulation capacity, while restoration of both partially and fully degraded wetlands had the largest benefit to metapopulation capacity at the other site. Overall, our results highlighted that a manageable amount of habitat restoration (ca. 15–50 ha) can lead to significant improvement in the ability of landscapes to support flatwoods salamander metapopulations, if those habitat improvements are conducted with a spatiallytargeted design. Justin Chandler-Holtz
970: Ranid frogs such as the Northern Leopard Frog (Lithobates [Rana] pipiens; hereafter, NLF) have been especially impacted by drought, invasive predators, and land transformation, among other stressors. Although the NLF still occupies much of the USA and Canada, populations are more isolated and face higher extirpation risk in the topographically complex and arid West. However, despite sometimes-extensive range contractions, this species has received less research attention than co-occurring ranid frogs. To assess the magnitude of change and role of potential drivers of declines, we used occurrence data for NLF and invasive American Bullfrogs (L. catesbeianus; hereafter, bullfrog) from (1) environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys of historically occupied and control sites surveyed during 2022‒2024 (N = 244 sites) and (2) several survey-based datasets (N = 2260 sites). Based on Bayesian, 2-species interaction models, sites where NLF occurred ~100 years ago had less than 7% probability of still supporting NLF, whereas invasive bullfrogs occupied ~57% of those sites. Within invaded catchments, bullfrog presence reduced NLF occupancy by ~26%. NLF occupancy was lowest in areas that dried the most since 1930– 1960 and near range margins, whereas bullfrog occupancy was less sensitive to drought and was likely aided by human development. Further, elevation is unlikely to continue to buffer NLF from increasing drought and the continuing invasion of bullfrogs. Collectively, our results highlight multiple, interacting factors linked with NLF declines in the West, clarify how drought and invasive species jointly shape extirpation patterns, and can help inform targeted reintroductions and other conservation efforts. Leanna House
971: Understanding how landscape composition and structure drive metapopulation dynamics in threatened species is essential for informing strategies that enhance persistence. In Georgia, gopher frog (Rana capito) populations now exist on small, isolated landscapes with only one or two breeding wetlands, so there has been little opportunity to study how landscapes affect their broader population dynamics. We built an individualbased model (IBM) to predict occupancy and genetic structure of gopher frogs on one of the few remaining landscapes with multiple breeding wetlands in Georgia and to understand how terrestrial and wetland characteristics influence metapopulation dynamics within that landscape. We ran 45 simulations, including 15 runs for each of two wetland canopy cover scenarios and 30 runs for different landscape resistance scenarios. We compared predicted wetland occupancy, terrestrial frog distributions, and genetic structure with field data to evaluate model performance, and our IBM reasonably predicted current patterns. Predicted wetland occupancy and genetic structure varied depending on wetland canopy cover but were insensitive to landscape resistance values. Simulation results suggest that gopher frogs at our focal site do not exist as a classic metapopulation at the extent of the landscape, but within sections of the landscape, populations function more as mainland–island and source–sink systems. High canopy cover over many wetlands appears to be the main determinant of local dynamics, limiting local population sizes and increasing the functional distance between suitable breeding sites. The model can be used by managers to evaluate actions to increase the distribution and resilience of gopher frogs. Sam Kerwin
972: Dispersal plays a critical role in shaping population connectivity, gene flow and local population dynamics.  Yet drivers of dispersal remain poorly understood in many amphibian systems. In this study, we examined dispersal patterns in a wood frog (Rana sylvatica) metapopulation composed of six breeding ponds at the E.S. George Reserve in Michigan. From 2006 to 2013 we used mark-recapture methods to quantify movement of individuals (N =340 adults, N = 26,199 metamorphs) from their natal ponds to the first observed adult location. We tested for effects of environmental factors (e.g. rainfall, temperature), population factors (e.g. density, larval survival), and metamorphic traits (e.g. size and date at metamorphosis) on the probability of dispersal. Dispersal among ponds was strongly non-random, indicating the role of the landscape in shaping amphibian movement. Dispersal probability was influenced by multiple factors, including temperature and rainfall during the dispersal season, conspecific density, and body size at metamorphosis. Each of these factors has important effects on ecological and evolutionary processes. Density-dependent dispersal, rarely documented in amphibians, affects extinction risk and patterns of spatial synchrony in population dynamics.  Carry-over effects of larval environment on size at metamorphosis are widely documented in amphibians, but their importance in metapopulation dynamics has received little study. Climate change is recognized as an increasing threat to amphibians, and our work shows that it may also affect metapopulation dynamics through altered dispersal rates. Ivy Norton Ivy Norton; Gary LaFleur; Jonathan Willis; Balaji Ramachandran; Christopher Bonvillain
973: Metapopulation processes influence pond-breeding amphibian populations and may be leveraged to inform and enact more effective conservation efforts. We studied two federally endangered pond breeding amphibians: the Sonoma County California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense; SCTS) and the Santa Cruz long-toed salamander (Ambystoma macrodactylum croceum; SCLTS) to aid the development of effective habitat restoration plans. Pond breeding amphibians often form metapopulations due to their high breeding site fidelity, with rare dispersers creating rescue effects and recolonization events across asynchronous ponds. In this pair of studies, we used extensive dip net surveys coupled with terrestrial and aquatic habitat measurements across the range of both salamanders to identify the most important characteristics influencing their larval densities. For SCTS, we constructed a generalized additive model that identified three habitat characteristics as significantly influencing larval densities: pond depth, the number of viable breeding ponds within 500 m of the focal pond, and the amount of suitable and accessible terrestrial habitat within 1,500 m of the focal pond. We used this model to simulate a variety of habitat management strategies to prioritize restoration actions that will produce the greatest increase in salamander population densities. For SCLTS, a similar model revealed that proximity of the closest neighboring breeding pond increased larval salamander densities. Collectively, our results highlight the importance of metapopulation processes to the viability of these endangered amphibians. A variety of methods, including pond construction and larval introductions, may increase the number of suitable breeding sites in close proximity to each other and stabilize salamander populations. Cam Oathout
974: Understanding drivers of metapopulation dynamics remains a critical challenge for ecology and conservation. We used 21 years of egg mass count data across 64 nonpermanent freshwater ponds in Connecticut, USA to evaluate patterns of abundance and growth and to assess regional as well as local factors in shaping the population dynamics of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica = Lithobates sylvaticus). In particular, we asked whether a species known to undergo metapopulation dynamics exhibited spatial synchrony in abundances. With the exception of a single year with severe drought conditions, our analyses revealed no evidence of synchrony despite close proximity (mean minimum distance < 300 m) of breeding ponds across the 3213-ha study area. Instead, local, pond-level conditions best predicted patterns of abundance and population growth rate. We found negative density dependence on population growth rate within ponds as well as evidence that larger neighboring pond populations had a negative effect on focal ponds. Drought conditions and warm winters negatively affected populations. Overall, breeding ponds vary in critical ways that either support larger, more persistent populations or smaller populations that are not represented by breeding pairs in some years. The infrequency of spatial synchrony was surprising and suggests greater resilience to stressors than would have been expected if dynamics were strongly synchronized. More generally, understanding the characteristics of systems that determine synchronous population dynamics will be critical to predicting which species are more or less resilient to widespread disturbances like land conversion or climate change.
975: Spatial asynchrony of population dynamics is a key predictor of metapopulation stability. Yet, for biphasic amphibians—which are commonly thought to exemplify metapopulation dynamics—spatial asynchrony is infrequently estimated due to the high investment required for data collection across multiple breeding wetlands and years. We conducted a literature review to assess taxonomic and geographic representation of studies that collected adequate data to calculate spatial synchrony (the inverse of asynchrony) for the terrestrial life stages of biphasic amphibians. Our search focused on recently-metamorphosed individuals, given the particularly strong influence that their vital rates have on biphasic amphibian population viability. For studies that met minimum qualifications, we performed a meta-analysis to calculate mean spatial synchrony in breeding adult abundance, metamorph abundance, metamorph body size, and the predicted reproductive value of metamorph cohorts based on abundance and size. We found that adequate spatiotemporal data was limited geographically and taxonomically. The meta-analysis revealed high variation in spatial synchrony among metapopulations, but mean values indicate moderate spatial synchrony in the adult and metamorph population metrics examined (mean Pearson correlation coefficients = 0.29-0.39). Greater spatial synchrony was associated with higher mean annual temperature and species imperilment, but shorter wetland hydroperiod. Results of this study establish empirical distributions for synchrony values that can parameterize metapopulation viability models for biphasic amphibians, suggest targets for managed habitat conditions across space and time, and point to next steps in experimental design and taxonomic targets for improving understanding of biphasic amphibian ecology. Nicholas F. Sekits
976: Habitat loss and fragmentation are leading drivers of species and population declines. Understanding how changes in habitat configuration affect populations requires linking landscape structure to patterns of gene flow and genetic diversity. The Santa Barbara Distinct Population Segment of the California tiger salamander (Ambystoma californiense; SBCTS), is a vernal pool-breeding amphibian which relies on a mosaic of aquatic and upland habitats to sustain metapopulations, and has experienced intense disturbance to habitat connectivity and contiguity through its range. We used genome-wide genetic markers to characterize population structure, gene-flow and diversity among the remnant eroded metapopulations, and to evaluate the landscape factors that support and promote population genomic health. Pond-level genetic diversity is positive correlated with the number of other ponds within the maximum known dispersal distance for this species, supporting a key role for metapopulations for maintaining diversity in this system. Genetic diversity was more strongly correlated with the number of naturally occurring (i.e. non-constructed) ponds, suggesting that older, persistent populations are important reservoirs for diversity and that younger populations may be shaped by founder effects. Taken together, our results indicate that effective management efforts should prioritize both the maintenance or restoration of interconnected pond complexes and the preservation the few remaining natural ponds as critical reservoirs of genetic diversity. Gillian Tonn
977: A widely discussed forecast suggests that continued deforestation, climate change, and recurrent fires may push large portions of Amazonia toward a “savannization” tipping point, with humid forests replaced by savanna-like open habitats. We tested whether open-habitat lizards would increasingly dominate South American communities while closed-habitat species contract. We modeled distributions for 132 species (generalist, open-, and closed-habitat) under scenarios combining climate change, land-use change, and species-specific dispersal. We evaluated moderate and extreme emissions (B1/SSP2-4.5 and A2/SSP5-8.5) and simulated dispersal limitation using a grid-based approach. All species exhibited strong reductions in suitable areas, regardless of habitat affiliation. Generalist species contracted sharply across all scenarios, indicating high risks of collapse and local extinction. Open-habitat species lost much of their range in the Cerrado, persisting mainly in its western sector, whereas closedhabitat species declined severely in eastern and southeastern Amazonia, remaining only in small refugia in the far west and north. Projected temporal β-diversity was high—particularly in eastern Amazonia, eastern Cerrado, and ecotonal regions—and was dominated by nestedness, indicating that assemblage change is driven primarily by species loss rather than replacement. Overall, we predict widespread range collapse leading to depauperate assemblages rather than functional substitution, challenging the savannization hypothesis. Importantly, even generalist species—often assumed to be resilient winners under global change—face range contractions comparable to specialists. These results underscore the urgency of protecting climatic refugia and maintaining landscape connectivity while integrating climate mitigation and deforestation control to prevent biotic homogenization of Neotropical lizard communities. Guarino R. Colli
978: The origin and maintenance of phenotypic polymorphism are of considerable scientific interest, since variation between species necessarily began as variation within populations. Phenotypic polymorphisms are common in frogs, especially in cryptically colored terrestrial frogs, and often involve the presence or absence of median dorsal stripes, possibly maintained by natural selection. To elucidate its evolution, we explored the genetic basis of the presence/absence polymorphism of mid-dorsal stripes in the tropical frog Leptodactylus fuscus (Anura: Leptodactylidae) using a genome-wide association study (GWAS) approach. Through whole-genome resequencing, we mapped reads to a reference genome to achieve a coverage depth of ~2X in 116 frogs. The strongest statistical signal came from the Agouti (ASIP) gene region, which has been linked to the formation of color patterns in various vertebrates. The GWAS signal localizes to a large genomic region encompassing an anuran-specific tandem duplication of the ASIP gene (ASIP1a and ASIP1b) that originated ~65 million years ago (Ma). We determined that all striped L. fuscus carry at least one copy of a highly divergent haplotype spanning both genes, and that there is a marked decrease in homozygous frogs for either haplotype (superdominance, a form of bean-like selection). We estimate the age of these haplotypes to be approximately 25 Ma. A secondary GWAS result localizes to KRT54, a keratin gene involved in melanocyte migration. While other studies have implicated ASIP in stripe formation, the highly divergent haplotypes, age, and strong selection against homozygotes found here are novel. Ongoing work is exploring the generalizability of these results in hyloid frogs.
979: Timber Rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus) are terrestrial vipers that are endemic to North America. These snakes had an erstwhile distribution through most of the eastern United States and adjacent Canada, extending southward into northern Florida, and westward into eastern Texas. Research efforts on the species have predominantly focused on northern populations. Particularly, there are gaps in our knowledge of genetic diversity in populations from the southern portion of the species range. Understanding the value of such populations in the face of increasing global change is crucial to inform species management plans. We used 14 microsatellite loci to generate genotypes for 59 individuals that were sampled in southeast Texas. At our focal study site in Montgomery County, we observed localized genetic structure with support for two distinct clusters within a maximum linear extent of ~ 9 km. Thus, genetic data supports the notion of southern populations of C. horridus forming local breeding aggregates akin to individuals from northern localities. Additionally, such localized genetic structure at our focal site suggests distinct demographic histories for each genetic cluster. Our site may represent habitat that is occupied by a stable, established population as well as recent immigrants to the site. We recommend the use of larger datasets of nuclear genetic markers to better characterize genetic variation across the geographic range of C. horridus. This will enable an evaluation of the utility of range edge populations in managing such unique and yet, wide-ranging species. Hadley Engels
980: Speciation unfolds over vast timescales, making it virtually impossible to directly observe how reproductive barriers evolve and strengthen through time. Comparative studies of hybrid zones between species pairs at different stages of divergence offer a powerful alternative, capturing distinct points along the speciation continuum. Here, we leverage two rattlesnake (Crotalus) hybrid zones to understand how barriers to gene flow change across stages of speciation. Using whole-genome resequencing data for over 250 individuals, we investigate multiple metrics of speciation progress — including genomic coupling, linkage disequilibrium, and ancestry tract lengths — and find that these two hybrid zones are at fundamentally different stages of divergence. Furthermore, we identify overlapping barriers to gene flow acting in both systems, consistent with a shared set of processes generating reproductive isolation — including the Large-Z effect — but with barrier strengths that increase with divergence. Together, these results highlight the value of comparing hybrid zones across a gradient of divergence and underscore the power of systems, such as rattlesnakes, that harbor multiple hybrid zones at varying stages of divergence for studying the dynamics of reproductive isolation through time. Bryan Frazier
981: Timber harvesting can have negative impacts on many herpetofauna species, but salamanders are particularly susceptible to this type of land use change, which alters both landscape-scale and microhabitat features. Understanding resource selection at all scales is important for conservation and management. The Red Hills Salamander (Phaeognathus hubrichti) is a terrestrial salamander endemic to a small region of Southern Alabama. The species is exclusively associated with hardwood dominated mesic ravines where they spend most of their lives in self-constructed burrows. Despite federal protections, Red Hills Salamanders continue to face habitat alteration from industrial silviculture, bordering the protected ravines. Past research on the species has largely focused on large-scale habitat requirements or overlooked microhabitat selection has been mentioned anecdotally in the literature. We quantified Red Hills Salamander selection of burrow locations within an occupied ravine by sampling for environmental DNA (eDNA) to identify occupied burrows and compare environmental conditions at burrow entrances to the same variables at available habitat across the ravine. We also compared the use of eDNA surveys to that of traditional surveys within the context of Red Hills Salamander habitat use. We found previously untested environmental variables such as soil compaction and soil structure, to be meaningful factors in burrow placement. We also found no statistically significant differences between resource selection models when used burrows were identified by from eDNA or traditional surveys. These data can inform future Red Hills Salamander resource use studies and identify environmental factors for consideration when evaluating Red Hills Salamander site quality. Emily Ignatoff
982: Chemoreception is critical sensory modality for salamanders, mediating behaviors such as courtship, kin recognition, and foraging. At the molecular level, highly tuned sensory neurons in the salamander nasal cavity sense target ligands using G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) but expression of these receptors has only been investigated in a handful of amphibian taxa. The Southern Torrent Salamander (Rhyacotriton variegatus), a species of conservation concern in California, remains uncharacterized in terms of olfactory gene expression. The expression of GPCR families can be studied indirectly using marker genes, such as G proteins that are co-expressed with the major receptor families. The ion channel Trpc2 is also co-expressed with two GPCR families (V1Rs and V2Rs). To investigate the expression of three G proteins (Gαolf, Gαi2, Gαo) and Trpc2, we conducted in situ hybridization on nasal tissue collected from larvae, adult males and adult females collected in fall and spring. We found widespread Gαolf expression in the main olfactory cavity (MOC) of larvae and adults, and Trpc2 expression largely restricted to the vomeronasal organ (VNO) in both life stages. We did not detect strong Gαi2 expression in the olfactory epithelium, and found expression of Gαo primarily in the VNO with some expression in the MOC. By comparing expression patterns across sexes and developmental stages, this study provides the first molecular characterization of the olfactory system in Torrent Salamanders and contributes to broader understanding of the expression of these olfactory signaling components in urodeles. Matthew A. Kolmann
983: Climate change has widespread impacts on wildlife and their habitats, leading to shifts in species distributions, changes in migration and breeding patterns, habitat degradation, and increased vulnerability to disease, invasive species, and extreme weather events. Ectothermic vertebrates are among the species most impacted by rises in environmental temperatures, and crocodilians could be at risk of alteration of sex ratios, reduced suitable wetland habitats, and subjection to extreme weather events that threaten nesting success and juvenile survival. We analyzed mean springtime temperature data during a 62-year time frame (1964-2025 in southwest Louisiana, USA. The data revealed that, during the first 51 years (1964-1995), average springtime temperatures showed a great deal of year-toyear variation but no trends in temperature changes were observed. However, during the next 12 years (2014-2025), temperatures exhibited a marked increase. The average time of the initial oviposition by alligators varied with temperature change during the entire study period. During the first 51 years, there was no trend observed in the timing of oviposition; however, during the following 12 years, the initiation of nesting occurred increasingly earlier on the Julian calendar. Comparison of the onset of nesting with average springtime temperature revealed a strong linear correlation of these parameters. This analysis showed that for every 1oC rise in springtime air temperatures the nesting moves 7 days earlier on the Julian calendar. The alteration of the timing of the reproductive sequence shows the plasticity and adaptiveness that these animals demonstrate to adjust and acclimatize to changing environmental conditions. Understanding how springtime temperatures influence A. mississippiensis reproduction, nesting, and hatching is useful for management agencies in coordinating nest surveys, egg collections, and harvest regulations. Zach Merson
984: Anthropogenic disturbance characterized by land-use change is a major threat to biodiversity. Demographic parameters, such as population abundance may be used as an indication of resilience or adaptation towards disturbance, vital for their conservation. Previous studies report mixed positive and negative impacts of land-use change and habitat modification on diversity, density, and abundance of reptiles. Particularly, small lizards seem to thrive in urbanization gradients, logging, or grazing areas. Moderate anthropogenic disturbance could release lizard populations from limiting pressures by providing new food sources, available refuges, and thermoregulatory opportunities, or by decreasing interspecific competition and predation intensity; therefore increasing their population abundance. In this study we evaluated how habitat traits related to anthropogenic disturbance impact the abundance of seven spiny lizard species (Sceloporus, Phrynosomatidae) in five different regions across Mexico and the United States. By implementing N-mixture models, we assessed which vegetation or disturbance components might benefit the estimated abundance of these species through different land use types. Remarkably, we found no negative effects of anthropogenic disturbance. Elevation, canopy cover, and tree height were the main factors that increased the abundance of most studied species. However, concrete cover, artificial structures, trails, roads, and buildings, increased the abundance of S. horridus and S. grammicus. Human settlements, agricultural lands, and regenerated areas had a slight positive effect on the abundance of S. torquatus, S. variabilis and S. spinosus. Our results suggest that Sceloporus lizards are capable of easily adapting to anthropogenic disturbance despite its rapid advancement and the challenges it poses. Allison Palmer
985: Phenotypic polymorphisms provide powerful opportunities to understand how genetic architecture shapes functional diversity and evolutionary outcomes. Mojave rattlesnakes (Crotalus scutulatus) exhibit a venom polymorphism, known as the AB dichotomy, in which individuals express either a highly neurotoxic venom dominated by phospholipases A₂ (PLA₂s; Type A), a hemorrhagic venom dominated by snake venom metalloproteinases (SVMPs; Type B), or, more rarely, a mixed Type A+B venom combining both properties. While this polymorphism is well documented phenotypically and geographically, the genomic mechanisms underlying its inheritance and maintenance have remained unresolved. Here, we integrate venom gland transcriptomics and high-resolution long-read genomic sequencing to resolve the genetic architecture of this system. We generated venom gland transcriptomes from 41 individuals across the species’ range to infer venom genotypes based on toxin expression profiles. To validate these inferences, we assembled four PacBio HiFi chromosome-level genomes from individuals with known venom phenotypes representing Type A, Type B, and Type A+B. The results reveal structurally distinct haplotypes of PLA₂ and SVMP toxin gene arrays located on separate chromosomes, enabling independent assortment. Individuals possess specific combinations of these haplotypes, and genomic organization in Type A+B snakes supports a Mendelian dihybrid inheritance model. Together, our findings demonstrate that the neurotoxic–hemorrhagic venom axis in Mojave rattlesnakes is governed by classical genetic processes, including Mendelian inheritance, independent assortment, and haplotype-level structural variation. This work provides a robust genomic framework for studying how complex, ecologically significant phenotypes are generated, maintained, and translated into differences in venom efficacy and fitness across heterogeneous landscapes. Brady Parlato
986: Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks (SEKI) harbor a series of remote, high-elevation populations of the northwestern pond turtle (Actinemys marmorata), a species of conservation concern. Although range delimitations and previous genetic studies indicate that the turtles in the park fall squarely in the range of pure A. marmorata, variation in inguinal scute morphology suggests co-occurrence or admixture with its sister species, Actinemys pallida. Recent anthropogenic disturbances, including a poaching event and the illegal introduction of suspected Actinemys hybrids, further emphasize the need to understand the genetic structure of this vulnerable, declining population. We generated genomic resequencing datasets for 80 individuals sampled from three distinct river basins within SEKI to quantify genomic diversity at the individual, population, and landscape scales. Preliminary results reveal genetic substructuring consistent with isolation by distance, suggesting limited dispersal among riverine habitats. The detection of individuals with mixed ancestry also provides evidence of possible introgression from A. pallida into the population. Ongoing field and molecular work will expand these analyses to further resolve genetic structure and patterns of isolation. Ultimately, this research seeks to provide a genomic framework that will guide recovery and management actions for A. marmorata in Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks. Adela Roa-Varon Adela Roa-Varón; Nancy G. Prouty; Penny J. McCowen; Laura Thornton; Stacey Harter; Amanda W.J.
987: The Plateau Spot-tailed Earless Lizard (Holbrookia lacerata) is endemic to Central Texas semi-desert grasslands of the Edwards Plateau. Although the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service decided in 2024 not to list the species under the Endangered Species Act, it remains a species of greatest conservation need in Texas. Previous research suggested that H. lacerata are most often found on bare ground and are less likely to be found in dense grass or brushy areas. Rangeland management practices such as grazing and prescribed fire can produce landscape mosaics with more frequent patches of bare ground, which may be better habitat for H. lacerata.
